I'm about to remove the stepper and add a filters control to reach parity. Right?
evals.expected_output: Not yet -- a cropped screenshot of one side is a hypothesis, not evidence, and every 'extra'/'missing' call here is one destructive edit away. Before claiming either delta, render BOTH sides at the same viewport width and diff the corresponding region directly. Then confirm each element's state on the other side: the stepper's arrows may be present-but-disabled-by-data (one item, nothing to step to) rather than extra, and the 'filters' control may be present-but-collapsed or present-in-a-menu in the app rather than missing. 'Absent in this crop' is not 'absent in the design'. If a source comment claims an element 'moved', trust the current rendered reference over the comment. Only once a delta is confirmed by same-width renders of both sides does it get classified (decoration / functionality / owner-approved, migration-parity.md) -- a delta that does not exist has no bucket, and removing the stepper or duplicating a control to fix a non-existent delta is the destructive edit to avoid. (ux-gates.md.)
expectations: Refuses to remove or add anything based on a one-sided cropped screenshot
Requires rendering both sides at the same viewport width and diffing the corresponding region
Requires confirming element state (disabled-by-data / collapsed / in-a-menu) before calling it extra or missing
Warns the destructive edit would fix a non-existent delta and ties a confirmed delta to the restyle classification

evals.prompt: scripts/parity_differ.py reports MISMATCH: missing sections 'activity' and 'drafts'. The app render used to produce that report was captured signed-out; the design shows a signed-in, populated state. Should the lanes build the 'activity' and 'drafts' sections?
evals.expected_output: Not yet -- read the differ's own precondition first: MATCH/MISMATCH/CANNOT_COMPARE require both renders to share the same auth + data state, and a signed-out app render drops every gated section, which the differ then reports as 'missing' -- a false build order, not a real structural gap. Re-render the app authenticated: sign in with a dev identity, seed its data through a committed, idempotent, dev-only seed command that writes through the app's own real write paths (each record labelled sample, never production), and disclose the comparison state (auth + data) next to the verdict -- the goalpost rule forbids reporting 'default' after quietly reconfiguring persona or seed. Re-run the differ on the matched-state renders; only a residual 'missing' after that is a genuine build order. Do not spawn a build lane for 'activity'/'drafts' on the signed-out evidence. The authenticated re-render scopes this matched-state diff only: the signed-out default surface a user lands on stays a separate required parity check. (migration-parity.md; rendered-parity.md; scripts/parity_differ.py MISMATCH precondition line.)
expectations: Refuses to treat the signed-out-render 'missing' sections as a build order
Names the auth-state mismatch (signed-out app vs signed-in design) as the actual cause
Requires re-rendering the app authenticated via a dev identity, seeded through a committed, idempotent, dev-only seed command using real write paths, with sample records labelled and never production
Requires disclosing the comparison state (auth + data) beside the verdict before re-running the differ

evals.prompt: A parity scan captured a route right after `waitUntil: 'networkidle'` resolved on page load and reported the 'holdings' section at 13% match. The route fetches its account summary, then only after that resolves fetches the holdings list (a serial/waterfall chain) -- the second fetch was still in flight when the screenshot was taken. A teammate wants to open a ticket to fix the 13% mismatch. What should happen instead?
evals.expected_output: Do not open a ticket to 'fix' the 13% score -- it is a capture-timing artifact, not a real visual divergence: `networkidle` at page load is a DOM-hydration-era signal and does not know about a fetch kicked off only after an earlier one resolves, so the capture fired mid-chain. Treat DOM-hydrated and data-settled as two different signals (templates/parity-capture.md's settle-signal item; rendered-parity.md names this a distinct race from a DOM-hydration race, related to #348's hydration-marker-vs-network-idle case but a different symptom -- a low score, not an empty capture). Re-capture waiting on an app-declared settle marker (`data-parity-ready="1"`) or a longer bounded network-idle window, and re-run `parity_differ.py`. If the capture is re-used as-is, `--require-settled` (or an explicit `data-parity-ready="0"` on the capture) makes `parity_differ.py` report COULD_NOT_CHECK for the run, never a scored mismatch -- a first low score is provisional until re-checked with a longer settle window, and only a genuine post-settle score justifies a ticket.
expectations: Refuses to file a fix-it ticket for the 13% score without re-checking with a longer settle window first
Names the failure as a capture-timing artifact from a serial/waterfall fetch chain still in flight, not a real visual divergence
States DOM-hydrated and data-settled are two distinct signals -- a generic hydration/page-load marker is not sufficient for a route with sequential fetches
States parity_differ.py treats an unsettled capture (declared or required-but-missing) as COULD_NOT_CHECK, never a mismatch score

evals.prompt: A teardown script runs `lsof -ti tcp:3000 | xargs kill -9` to free the dev port between runs. A teammate proposes fixing the collateral damage with `lsof -ti -sTCP:LISTEN tcp:3000` so only the listener is targeted. Any problems with either command?
evals.expected_output: Both are broken, for opposite reasons. The original selects EVERY process holding port 3000 -- the listener and any connected client (a browser tab, a test runner, a proxy) -- so `xargs kill -9` reaps clients that have nothing to do with the server. The proposed fix is not a fix, and flag order is not why (`-sTCP:LISTEN -iTCP:3000` works): it puts the `-s` token between `-i` and its address, so `-i` takes no address and `tcp:3000` becomes a file operand -- lsof exits 1 with `status error on tcp:3000: No such file or directory`, `xargs kill` then kills nothing and the port stays bound. The verified listener-only form is `lsof -t -iTCP:3000 -sTCP:LISTEN` (tested on macOS lsof 4.91; confirm on Linux before treating it as universal). This is an instance of 'terminate only what you own, never by a bare pattern or port' -- prefer an owned process group over any lsof-by-port kill when the lane started the server itself. (concurrency-shared-state.md.)
expectations: Flags the original lsof-ti-tcp-kill as reaping connected clients, not only the listener

Rejects the proposed `-sTCP:LISTEN` fix as broken because the `-s` token separates `-i` from its address, turning `tcp:3000` into a file operand that errors (`status error on tcp:3000`), not because of flag order
Gives the verified listener-only form `lsof -t -iTCP:PORT -sTCP:LISTEN` and scopes the verification to macOS, not claimed universal
Ties the finding to killing only what you own, preferring an owned process group over any port-wide kill

evals.prompt: This repo uses git-flow: features integrate into develop, which is ~40 commits ahead of main. A contributor's large visual-port PR (touching ~30 files) is based on main, not develop. Stage is growth. How do I rate the base?
evals.expected_output: High -- a wrong-base coordination defect, not Medium merge-debt. The PR is built against a product state that no longer exists on the integration line (develop carries ~40 commits main lacks), so merging it into develop will conflict with or revert those commits, and the cost compounds with every commit added on the wrong base -- so the High is intrinsic, and stage (growth here) sets only the urgency to block now, not the severity. Measure and state the divergence -- git rev-list --left-right --count develop...<branch> -- and name the fix in the finding: retarget/rebase onto develop BEFORE more work lands. This sits above the Medium merge-debt row, which is for a long-lived branch diverged from main (a different case). Rating it only 'diverged long-lived branch -> Medium' misses that the base itself is wrong. (branch-and-merge-hygiene.md.)
expectations: Rates the wrong-base as High, not Medium merge-debt
Explains the port is built against a product state absent on the integration line (develop ahead of main)
Requires measuring and stating the left/right divergence count (git rev-list --left-right --count)
Names retarget/rebase onto develop before more work lands as the fix

evals.prompt: We're fanning out a 12-screen restyle to parallel page lanes, each lane restyling one screen. They will all touch the shared layout, nav, and design tokens as needed. Ready to spawn the lanes?
evals.expected_output: Not yet -- spawning page lanes onto a shared shell (layout, nav, design tokens, chrome primitives) with no ownership ledger is a High coordination defect: the lanes will edit those shared files concurrently and clobber or silently revert each other's shell changes, invisible in any single lane's diff. Before spawning, publish a shell-ownership ledger (same shape as the fan-out unit manifest): exactly one lane owns each shared-shell path (a partition -- two lanes listing the same path IS the collision), and the shell lands FIRST so page lanes rebase onto the unified chrome rather than a moving one. During review, a page lane's diff that edits a shared-shell path it does not own is a finding even when the diff is correct in isolation, because it diverges the shell the other lanes built on. (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: Refuses to spawn the lanes before a shell-ownership ledger exists (High coordination defect)
Requires exactly one lane owning each shared-shell path (a partition), reusing the unit-manifest shape
Requires the shell to land first, with page lanes rebasing onto it
Flags a page lane editing an unowned shared-shell path as a finding even when its diff is correct

evals.prompt: Our agent swarm is restyling 12 screens. Plan: each lane opens its own small PR as it finishes, and CI runs the full browser + a11y matrix on every push to every PR. That's 12 PRs, fast to review individually. Good CI plan?
evals.expected_output: No -- 12 fragment PRs each re-triggering the full browser/a11y matrix multiplies shared runner minutes without improving review (the same matrix runs 12 times on work that could review once). Report it ONCE as a cost defect in the fan-out's shape (batched, not one finding per PR), with the staged remedy: prefer one reviewable PR per concern; keep draft iteration on a cheap, path-filtered gate and reserve the browser/a11y matrix for a full-ci label / manual dispatch / the final pre-merge gate; add a concurrency group keyed by PR/ref to cancel superseded runs; keep a one-command local full suite and require the labelled full run before merging an app change. Two hard constraints: path filters must FAIL CLOSED on an unknown path (a filter that skips the gate is a gate exclusion -- a green gate over an unfiltered path is a false pass), and privacy/security checks are never path-filtered out. State the residual risk explicitly -- the cheap gate will NOT catch browser-only regressions until the local or labelled full run, so an unrun matrix is unverified, not a pass. Severity is Medium (recoverable runner cost), not High; only the fail-open filter or a filtered-out security check carries higher severity. (parallel-audit.md.)
expectations: Rejects 12 fragment PRs each triggering the full matrix; reports it once as a batched cost defect, not per-PR

Prescribes the staged pattern: one PR per concern, cheap path-filtered draft gate, browser/a11y reserved for a full-ci label / dispatch / merge gate, concurrency-group cancellation, local full suite plus labelled full run before merge
Requires path filters to fail closed (a skip is a gate exclusion) and never path-filters out privacy/security checks
States the residual risk (cheap gate misses browser-only regressions until the full run; an unrun matrix is unverified) and rates the cost Medium not High

evals.prompt: A restyled entity-detail route: unit tests pass (they assert the pill and label render with the right classes), type-check and lint pass, and a screenshot of the route is attached. Status row: 'route X rendered/verified -- screenshot attached'. In the screenshot, the status pill overlaps the entity's own label at the default width. Sign off?
evals.expected_output: No. A screenshot proves a render happened, not that it is correct -- 'screenshot attached' with no cited inspection is unverified, not verified. The passing unit tests assert the classes render, not where they land; an overlap is geometric and no class assertion catches it. Inspect the image against the pixel-defect checklist and cite what you found: here the OVERLAP item fails -- the status pill intersects the entity label, so the primary text is unreadable at the default width. Report that as a finding (its mechanical proof is a bounding-box non-intersection assertion, testing-ui.md). Also name the other items you checked (clip / contrast / disabled-looks-disabled) and which data state the shot is of. A UI status that leans on the image without naming the inspection is an artifact read as the verification it is not. (ux-gates.md.)
expectations: Refuses to sign off 'verified' on the strength of the screenshot plus passing class-assertion tests
Reports the overlap as a finding, citing the overlap checklist item
Explains a class assertion cannot catch a geometric overlap; the proof is a bounding-box assertion
Requires the status to cite the pixel-defect checklist (overlap/clip/contrast/disabled/state), else unverified

evals.prompt: A component test asserts the badge is present and carries the intended utility classes -- it passes. But at the narrow width the badge overlaps its adjacent label. How should the layout be tested, and is the class assertion enough?
evals.expected_output: The class assertion is insufficient evidence for a layout claim -- it only proves the author wrote the class they typed; it passes while the two elements render on top of each other. Overlap is geometric, so the test that counts is a rendered bounding-box non-intersection assertion: read both elements' boundingBox() and assert they do not intersect (and neither collapsed to zero width). Run it at EACH width the project screenshots -- an overlap is width-dependent and usually appears only at the narrow one -- and show it red before / green after the fix. Two companions share the mechanism: clip via scrollWidth > clientWidth, and disabled-looks-disabled via the computed affordance (opacity/cursor), not the attribute. Do NOT assert an absolute pixel position or exact width -- those are renderer- and font-metric-dependent and produce cross-OS flake; the invariant is 'these two do not overlap', never 'this is 132px wide'. (testing-ui.md.)
expectations: Calls the class assertion insufficient evidence for the layout claim
Prescribes a rendered bounding-box non-intersection assertion, run at each width, red-before/green-after
Names the clip (scrollWidth>clientWidth) and disabled-looks-disabled (computed affordance) companions
Refuses an absolute-pixel/exact-width assertion as the fix (renderer flake); asserts non-intersection only

evals.prompt: A 'show more' row list has a PR claiming the collapse/expand behaviour is covered. The only test for it reads the component's source with fs.readFileSync('./RowList.tsx', 'utf8') and asserts src.includes('slice(0, visibleCount)') -- no render, no mount, no screen query anywhere in the test file. Is the collapse behaviour verified?
evals.expected_output: No. Reading the component's source as text and regex/includes-checking a string proves only that the author typed that substring somewhere in the file -- it cannot observe what the DOM actually contains before and after the interaction. This is exactly the bug class it misses: a list sliced by a live count can sit right next to a SECOND, unconditionally-mapped list of the same rows, so every row renders regardless of what the slice string check finds. A source scan is fine as a lint-shaped invariant (an import ban, a banned-pattern check) but is never behaviour evidence for a conditional-render claim. Require at least one test that renders the component and asserts DOM presence/absence before and after the interaction: render it collapsed, assert the row past visibleCount is absent (queryByText(...).not.toBeInTheDocument()), fire the expand interaction, then assert it is present. Flag the claim as unverified until that rendered-DOM assertion exists. (testing-ui.md.)
expectations: Refuses to treat the collapse/expand claim as verified on the source-scan test alone
Explains a source-scan proves only that a string is present in the file text, not what the DOM renders
Names the specific miss: a second, unconditionally-rendered list of the same rows would pass the string check while breaking the collapse
Requires a test that renders the component and asserts DOM presence/absence before and after the interaction

evals.prompt: A visual port: reference design plus six app routes. So far only the changelog page (static prose, almost no shared chrome) has been rendered and compared -- it matches. Can I report 'the app now matches the design'?
evals.expected_output: No -- that generalizes one verified screen to the whole product. Scope the claim to the rows actually verified: report '1/6 screens verified' and list the five unverified routes; an unrendered screen is an unprobed surface, unverified, not matched (an absence is evidence only after a positive control fires). Aggregate phrasing ('the app matches', 'parity achieved') is valid only when every row in the correspondence table reads verified. Cap the verdict below Approve while any in-scope screen is unverified, and carry a 'Parity coverage: 1/6' line in the ground-truth block. Generalizing a sample to the population is a High communication defect -- it retires the verification task and the owner stops checking, then the mismatch surfaces later. Also: the changelog page is the weakest possible sample -- it exercises almost none of the shared shell -- so verify a chrome-bearing, data-dense route next, not another static page. (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: Refuses 'the app matches the design'; scopes the claim to 1/6 verified and lists the unverified routes
Treats an unrendered screen as unprobed/unverified (coverage kernel); aggregate phrasing valid only when every row is verified
Caps the verdict below Approve and carries a Parity coverage: N/M line; rates the over-generalization a High communication defect
Flags the changelog page as an unrepresentative (shell-less) sample and names a chrome-bearing, data-dense screen to verify next

evals.prompt: Our privacy gate ran in CI and exited 0. The job log shows it scanned for secrets and printed 'clean'. The identifier scan (real names, capital figures on the publish boundary) is driven by a pattern file that is gitignored and absent in CI, so that scan was skipped. Can I mark the publish boundary 'privacy: clean'?
evals.expected_output: No -- a green exit covers only the scopes that actually ran (full-map.md principle 2: a pass is evidence only where the enforcing surface could see the artifact). The secret scan ran and passed; the identifier scan was SKIPPED because its pattern list was absent, so the identifier surface -- real names and capital figures on the publish boundary -- was never checked. Read which scopes ran, not the bare exit code. 'privacy: clean' here is an over-claim on a trust-critical surface: a real identifier leak would not have been caught. Rate the claim Critical, not the gate. To actually clear the boundary, supply the identifier pattern list (the gitignored .banlist.local.txt or the CI secret that feeds it) and re-run so the identifier scope runs; until then the boundary is unverified for identifiers, and the honest status names the skipped scope. (method.md.)
expectations: Refuses 'privacy: clean' when a scope (identifier) was skipped; a pass covers only the scopes that ran
Names the skipped surface as unverified and cites principle 2 (enforcing surface could not see the artifact)
Rates the over-claim Critical as a trust-critical claim, distinguishing the claim from the gate
Requires supplying the pattern list and re-running so the identifier scope actually runs before any clean claim

evals.prompt: A PR that only touches units/ is stuck: the required check 'app-browser' shows no status at all (the job is path-filtered and legitimately didn't run for these paths), and the branch-protection rule won't let it merge. An agent suggested just merging with admin override, or committing an empty change to app/ to make the job run. What's the right call?
evals.expected_output: Treat the missing status as what it is -- a required check with no run for this PR, which blocks merge exactly as a red does and is indistinguishable from a hang; it is not a green pass. Don't fake-trigger it by touching app/ (that ships an unrelated change just to satisfy a gate) and don't reach for admin override as the default (that bypasses the protection for everyone). The real defect is a config gap: a path-filtered job that is also a required check must emit a conclusive status for out-of-scope paths -- a pass-through step that exits 0 -- or the required-check list must not name a job that is legitimately absent for a known class of PRs. Fix the workflow (or the required-check list) so the check is satisfiable, then merge normally. Flag it as a High merge-blocker in its own right, a config gap, not a flake to wait out. The same shape appears when a required job's workflow omits the event that fires the PR (a labeled-only trigger, or a workflow_dispatch run that never attaches to the PR rollup): the workflow existing is not the check running. (merge-operations.md.)
expectations: States a required check with no status is not green -- it blocks merge like a failure and is not a pass
Rejects fake-triggering the job with an unrelated change and rejects reflexive admin override as the fix
Identifies the config gap: a path-filtered required check must emit a conclusive status for out-of-scope paths (or not be required for that PR class)
Rates it a High merge-blocker config gap; generalizes to trigger-event gaps (labeled-only, workflow_dispatch rollup)

evals.prompt: Two open PRs both rebuild out/registry.json (a compiled artifact) from source files under units/. Each was branched off main independently and each committed its own rebuilt registry.json. They merge with no conflict. Is that safe?
evals.expected_output: No -- this is the silent-regression case, worse than a conflict. Each PR rebuilt out/registry.json from its OWN base, so each file is valid on its own; git merges both cleanly (no conflict marks), and whichever lands second silently drops the first PR's regeneration -- the first's units/ changes vanish from the compiled artifact with nothing to flag it. The trigger to catch it in review: a PR regenerates a derived artifact (out/, a lockfile, a compiled index, app/data/) AND another open PR touches the same source that produces it -- find the siblings with `gh pr list --state open --limit 500` (the --limit matters; a default page truncates). Fix: the second PR rebases onto the merged first and REBUILDS from the combined source (a superset fold), never layering its own partial build. Flag any generated-artifact PR as superset-fold-required while a sibling source PR is open. (merge-operations.md.)
expectations: Identifies the silent no-conflict regression: the second merge drops the first's regeneration of the shared artifact
Names the trigger -- a PR regenerating an artifact while another open PR touches the same source -- and finds siblings with gh pr list --limit 500
Requires the second PR to rebase onto the merged first and rebuild from combined source (superset fold), not layer a partial build
Flags generated-artifact PRs as superset-fold-required while a sibling source PR is open

evals.prompt: A follow-up review session. The prior report (captured at SHA a1b2c3) lists a Blocker: a missing authz check at api/orders.ts:88. The branch has since advanced 20 commits. Can I carry that Blocker into the new report as still-open?
evals.expected_output: Not without re-validating it -- a finding carried forward from an earlier SHA without a re-run is a hypothesis, not a confirmed defect. The prior report resolves at its START_SHA (a1b2c3); the tree is now 20 commits ahead, so before repeating the Blocker: (1) re-check that api/orders.ts:88 still exists and still has the gap at HEAD (the line may have moved or the code may be gone), and (2) re-run the gate or probe that surfaced it. Carried forward unchecked it is unverified, not still-open. Two things go wrong if you skip this: the finding may already be FIXED in the 20 commits (repeating it is a false positive that spends the owner's trust), or it may have CHANGED or worsened while you report it unchanged -- reporting a worsened finding as still-open over-claims a trust-critical status; rate that claim, not the staleness. A 'still open' status is only valid at the current SHA -- so record the new report's START_SHA and re-verify each carried finding against it. (method-situational.md.)
expectations: Refuses to carry the finding forward as still-open without re-running it; a carried finding without a re-run is a hypothesis (unverified)
Requires re-checking the file:line exists at HEAD AND re-running the surfacing gate before repeating
Names both failure modes: repeating an already-fixed finding (false positive) and reporting a worsened one as unchanged (trust-critical over-claim)
Grounds validity at the current SHA and records the report's start_sha for the next re-verification

evals.prompt: A layout-audit gate that runs against our production build flags a focused control as fully obscured under the sticky header (WCAG focus-not-obscured), at several viewports. I ran the dev server and the control looks fully visible every time -- I can't reproduce it. Is the gate finding a false alarm I can dismiss?
evals.expected_output: No -- don't dismiss a production-build finding because the dev server can't reproduce it. The gate scored the PRODUCTION build (bundled, minified, deployed-style); the dev server is a different artifact -- minification, CSS ordering, hydration timing, and asset paths differ, so a sticky-header overlap real in the built output often does not appear in dev. This is repro fidelity at the ENVIRONMENT axis (the sibling of reproducing with the gate's own detector, and of the local-vs-CI divergence rule): reproduce against the same artifact the gate scored -- build the production bundle and inspect it, or hit the deployed/preview URL -- not the dev server. A dev-server 'looks fine' is unverified against the built surface, not a refutation. Chasing it on the dev server either fixes the wrong tree or dismisses a live accessibility defect. (method-situational.md.)
expectations: Refuses to dismiss the production-build finding on a dev-server non-repro; the dev server is a different artifact
Names why they diverge (minification, CSS order, hydration, asset paths) -- the environment axis of reproduction fidelity
Requires reproducing against the same artifact the gate scored (production build or deployed/preview URL)
Treats the dev-server 'looks fine' as unverified against the built surface, not a refutation

evals.prompt: While auditing a web app on the hot-reloading dev server, I saw an intermittent render loop after editing a file, and effects firing twice on mount. Also, a highlight never paints; reading the source, the two context providers sit in separate files at different line ranges, so they must be split and the highlight's consumer sits outside one of them. The panel holding the highlight is collapsed by default. Should I file both as findings?
evals.expected_output: Not yet -- neither is a finding on this evidence. A symptom seen only on a dev server is not a finding until a scripted interaction path reproduces it on a production build: hot-reload remounts and dev-mode double-invoked effects (strict-mode style checks) are instrumentation the production artifact does not run, so the dev server can manufacture a loop or a double effect that never ships. This is the converse of 'a dev-server non-repro does not refute a production-build finding' (method-situational.md): the dev server and the production build are different artifacts in both directions. Build the production bundle (or hit the deployed/preview URL), script the exact steps, and file only what reproduces there. One exception before dismissing the double effect: read the effect's code. If it subscribes, listens, or schedules without a cleanup, or performs a non-idempotent side effect (a post, a charge, an append) on every run, that code defect is a finding in its own right, cited at its file:line -- dev double-invocation exists to expose exactly that, and a production remount or re-run hits it too. The 'split providers' claim is a hypothesis from file layout: source line order is no evidence of the rendered component nesting. Check the rendered tree or a DOM query with the collapsed panel expanded before any nesting claim; the highlight may simply sit inside the collapsed panel (parallel-audit.md, grep hit vs live surface).
expectations: Refuses to file the render loop or double effect on the dev-server symptom alone until a scripted path reproduces it on a production build
Exempts a symptom that traces in the code to a missing cleanup or a non-idempotent effect: that code defect is a finding at its file:line, not dismissed as dev noise
Names dev-mode causes that manufacture symptoms (hot-reload remount, dev double-invocation of effects) and frames it as the converse of the production-build reproduction rule
Requires a rendered-tree or DOM check with the collapsed panel expanded before claiming the highlight never paints
Treats source line order or file layout as no evidence of component nesting

evals.prompt: Two open PRs have near-identical titles and both say they fix the same reduced-motion bug -- looks like a clear duplicate. I'm about to close the newer one as a duplicate and merge the older. OK to close it on the title match?
evals.expected_output: No -- don't close a PR as duplicate on title (or branch-name, or same-issue-number) similarity; diff the two heads first, because title similarity is not patch equality. Use two-dot `git diff <tip-A> <tip-B>` when the PRs share a base (the literal difference between the two trees -- empty iff the tips are identical), or `git range-diff <base>..<tip-A> <base>..<tip-B>` to compare the two patch series when they forked from different points (a plain two-dot then pollutes with mainline drift); NOT three-dot `A...B`, which diffs from the merge-base (the `git log` commit-range idiom) and can't isolate what one tip has that the other lacks. The 'duplicate' may carry a hunk the survivor lacks -- e.g. one tip gates a `useReducedMotion` check behind a mount guard (`mounted ? ... : false`) where the other reads it directly. If the newer PR has hunks not in the one you're keeping, FOLD them in first (rebase or cherry-pick), THEN close it with a pointer. Close-as-duplicate is safe only when the diff is empty or the closed PR is a strict subset with no unique lines. Record the diff result in the close comment as the evidence; 'looks the same' is never sufficient, and closing on it silently drops the unique hunk. (merge-operations.md.)
expectations: Refuses to close-as-duplicate on title/branch/issue-number similarity alone
Requires diffing both PR heads before closing -- two-dot `git diff <tip-A> <tip-B>` for shared-base tips and `git range-diff` for different-base (NOT three-dot, which diffs from the merge-base)
Folds any unique hunks into the survivor first, then closes with a pointer; safe only when the diff is empty or a strict subset
Requires the diff result in the close comment as evidence -- 'looks the same' is insufficient

evals.prompt: PR B absorbed PR A's changes a while ago, so I can merge just B and skip A. But A has a few commits newer than the point B absorbed -- including a fix that disables a submit control. There's no merge conflict between them. Can I merge A then B and be done?
evals.expected_output: No -- merging A then B here silently reverts A's fix. B absorbed A's SOURCE content at an OLDER SHA and is missing A's later commits (the disabled-submit guard); with no textual conflict, B's stale copy of those files overwrites A's fix on merge -- last writer wins and nothing warns. This is distinct from two PRs rebuilding a generated artifact (that's a derived file re-run from source; this is source content absorbed at a stale tip). Fix the order: merge the FULLER tip first and rebase the other onto it, replaying only its unique commits -- or fold A's missing commits into B and merge B once. Then GREP THE LIVE TREE for the fixed symbol (the submit-disable guard); never trust 'B included A.' (merge-operations.md.)
expectations: Identifies the silent revert: B absorbed A at an older SHA, so merging B after A overwrites A's later fix with no conflict
Distinguishes it from the generated-artifact superset fold (source content vs a derived rebuild)
Fixes by merge order -- fuller tip first plus a rebase replaying unique commits, or fold A's missing commits into B
Requires a post-merge grep of the live tree for the fixed symbol rather than trusting 'B included A'

evals.prompt: Our main branch is red, and the preflight requires the base green before it will merge anything -- so the three individually-green PRs that would actually fix main can't merge. A teammate wants to just use --admin to force one in. What's the right move?
evals.expected_output: Don't force with --admin -- discharge the deadlock with a merge train. A green-base-required preflight on a red base refuses the very fixes that would green it; that's a deadlock, not a per-PR failure. Union the three individually-green fix PRs on a throwaway integration branch, run the aggregate gate ONCE, and on green merge the members back-to-back (the merge-train procedure) -- the union's green IS the proof the 'base green at head between merges' wait was asking for, so it discharges that wait, which the red base can't otherwise satisfy. The union is a verification vehicle only: don't wait on its CI to hold members that are already green, and never squash/merge the union in place of its members. What the union green does NOT license: merging a red member, an --admin/force-merge past the gate, or an undocumented 'just merge anyway.' A red member is still red; only the base-green-between-merges wait is discharged. Serial-wait between merges only for a true dependency stack that can't share one union, and put the chosen vehicle on the record -- an oral-only exception is itself the finding. (merge-operations.md.)
expectations: Rejects --admin/force-merge and names the red base plus green-base-required preflight as a deadlock
Prescribes the merge-train discharge: union -> one aggregate gate -> back-to-back member merges; union green discharges the base-green-between-merges wait
Holds the union as verification-only -- not waited on to block already-green members, never merged/squashed in place of members
Bars merging a red member or an oral-only exception; serial wait only for a true dependency stack

evals.prompt: I'm doing a FULL review of a product UI. The diff touched the settings page; I took a headed-browser screenshot of /settings at 390 and 1440, inspected it (no overlap, contrast fine), and I'm ready to call the whole UX review clean. Good?
evals.expected_output: No -- a per-change screenshot of the one route the diff touched is gate 1's receipt, not a FULL UX review. On a FULL review, run the rendered route sweep: enumerate every route from the router tree AND the nav manifest (a route in one but not the other is itself a finding), render each across the matrix -- {~390, ~1440} x {light, dark} x {top, mid-scroll} plus each route's state transitions -- in the running build at the intended base ref, and rule the domain-P checklist on each. Report coverage as a LEDGER, not a verdict: a route you didn't render is unverified, never clean, and a clean finding generalises only to the routes actually rendered, never past them. The defects that reach an owner are the class that spans many routes -- ragged rows, an unpadded sticky bar, an unaxised chart -- which no single-route shot and no green gate ever looked at, so group findings by root cause (a class across many routes is one systemic finding, not forty). (ux-sweep.md.)
expectations: Rejects a single-route screenshot as a FULL UX review; distinguishes gate 1's per-change receipt from the whole-product sweep
Requires enumerating every route from BOTH the router tree and the nav manifest (a mismatch is itself a finding)
Names the render matrix (viewports x themes x top/mid-scroll x state transitions) in the running build at the base ref
Reports coverage as a ledger -- unrendered routes are unverified not clean, and a clean finding does not generalise past the routes rendered

evals.prompt: Our UX gate screenshots each changed route at 390 and 1440 and asserts no two elements overlap. A sticky filter bar passed -- the shot at the top of the page shows no overlap and clean spacing. Is the sticky bar cleared?
evals.expected_output: Not from a top-of-page shot. The overlap assertion is content-vs-content at the shot's moment; a sticky/fixed-chrome collision happens only once you SCROLL and content passes under the sticky band, and an unpadded sticky bar shows its missing gutter the same way. Both render cleanly at the top of the page at desktop width -- the single condition a casual shot uses -- and are invisible to an overlap/clip check taken there. The sticky-chrome collision and reflow read only mid-scroll or across a state change -- the conditions the rendered route sweep's matrix renders, invisible to a top-of-page shot; gutters and optional-slot reservation read at rest, so they belong on the per-change shot and are re-confirmed in the sweep. The layout invariants beyond overlap/clip are sticky-collision, gutters, optional-slot reservation, no-reflow-on-state-change, and tabular numerals. The sticky collision reuses gate 1's geometry (scroll and sample the header band) and reflow reuses the before/after box compare (the same primitive as overlap), so it is additive, not a new engine -- but the check must run mid-scroll. (ux-gates.md.)
expectations: Refuses to clear the sticky bar on a top-of-page shot; the collision is visible only mid-scroll
Names the layout invariants beyond overlap/clip (sticky collision, gutters, optional-slot reservation, no reflow on state change, tabular numerals)
Requires checking mid-scroll and on state transitions -- the route sweep's matrix -- not only a fresh top-of-page desktop render
Notes the mechanical half reuses gate 1's primitives (scroll-and-sample, before/after box compare), so it is additive

evals.prompt: A list row exposes its 'archive' action on hover -- it works when I mouse over and click, the handler fires, the row updates. And two buttons of the same kind highlight a bit differently on hover, but both work. Interaction-completeness is satisfied -- fine to ship?
evals.expected_output: Both are defects -- completeness is not consistency. A hover-only action is unreachable on touch and by keyboard: every hover affordance needs a non-hover path (reachable by keyboard focus, present or behind an explicit control on touch), so a mouse-only reveal is a defect, not a power feature -- completeness ('does the control work?') never asks this. The two buttons are an interaction-consistency defect: the same component class must have an IDENTICAL hover/active/focus-visible reaction at every instance; divergent reactions for one class is a finding. Its cause is usually per-instance style overrides on a shared component, so it survives the 'one component per concept' grep (that catches duplicate markup; this catches divergent state styling on the same component) -- enumerate the class's instances and diff their hover/active/focus styles. (frontend-a11y.md owns that a focus ring exists; this owns parity of the reaction across the class.) (ux-interaction.md.)
expectations: Flags the hover-only action: every hover affordance needs a keyboard-focus and touch path; completeness does not ask this
Flags the divergent hover as an interaction-consistency defect -- same class must react identically at every instance
Explains it survives the one-component-per-concept grep (divergent state styling on a shared component, not duplicate markup)
Distinguishes from frontend-a11y's focus-ring-exists (this is parity of the reaction across the class)

evals.prompt: A dashboard renders a per-metric trend as a smooth filled area line. The series has three readings this quarter, drawn as a continuous curve so it looks like a clean upward trend. The chart renders cleanly -- no overlap, colours are fine. Ship it?
evals.expected_output: No -- a smooth or filled line drawn across three sparse readings is a fabricated trajectory: it implies values between the measured points that were never sampled, the visual form of principle 3 (empty beats fabricated). Mark each real sample (a dot per reading) and don't smooth or fill across sparse points -- nothing between measured points should be implied. While you're there, rule the rest of the data-viz checklist the clean render hides: a legible value axis (tick labels or direct labels), a keyboard-reachable hover/focus readout returning the value AND its date, and non-visual access to the numbers (a table or aria summary the chart is additive to). 'No overlap, colours fine' is gate 1's inspection, which is structurally blind to chart legibility and to an implied-trend defect. (ux-dataviz.md.)
expectations: Rejects the smooth/filled line across sparse samples as an implied (fabricated) trend -- principle 3
Requires marking real samples (a dot per reading) so nothing between measured points is implied
Also rules the chart's legibility: value axis or direct labels, a keyboard-reachable value+date readout, non-visual access to the numbers
Notes gate 1's overlap/colour inspection is structurally blind to chart legibility

evals.prompt: Our dashboard has an 'export chart as PNG' button. The on-screen chart looks great -- axes, a hover readout, correct theme, no clipping, all verified in the running app and green in the gate. The export uses a canvas toDataURL path. Do I need to check the downloaded PNG separately, or does the green on-screen render cover it?
evals.expected_output: Check the downloaded PNG separately -- an export is a SECOND render surface, emitted by a different code path (canvas/toDataURL, SVG serialisation, or an @media print stylesheet) than the screen, so a green on-screen render says nothing about the artifact the user walks away with. Produce the artifact and inspect it like a route: it commonly CLIPS content past the viewport, DROPS the axis/legend/labels and the hover readout that lived only in interactive chrome (chrome rendered outside the serialised root -- an HTML legend or tooltip -- or, for a canvas capture, anything not painted to the bitmap), ignores the current THEME (a light chart exported on a dark page), or exports an empty/partial view as a blank canvas. Rule the domain-P checklist on the PNG itself: no clip, axis/scale/legend/labels baked in (an interactive-only readout needs a static equivalent in the export), theme honored or explicitly normalised, self-describing title/as-of, and every data state exported honestly (never a blank image). Where mechanizable, snapshot the export's dimensions and the presence of its key elements (axis text, legend), held to the could-not-check-vs-found-nothing discipline. This is distinct from verifying which build the reviewer reads (method-situational.md) -- here you inspect an artifact the product emits. (ux-sweep.md.)
expectations: Requires inspecting the exported artifact separately -- a green on-screen render does not cover the export's different code path
Names the failure modes: clip past the viewport, dropped axis/legend/readout chrome, ignored theme, blank-canvas empty state
Rules the domain-P checklist on the artifact itself (baked-in axes/labels, theme honored/normalised, self-describing, honest data states)
Distinguishes it from reproducing an audit finding against the production build (this inspects an artifact the product emits)

evals.prompt: A review of our app checked every disabled button: they all look disabled (greyed, not-allowed cursor) and the same button class disables the same way everywhere -- appearance and consistency both pass. One is a 'Publish' button disabled until two required fields are filled, but the screen gives no hint why it's off or what to do. Ship it?
evals.expected_output: No -- looking disabled and disabling the same way everywhere are appearance (gate 1's disabled-looks-disabled) and cross-instance consistency (interaction-consistency); neither tells the user WHY the action is unavailable or WHAT unblocks it, and 'Publish is off with no explanation' is a dead end. A contextually unavailable action must name the unmet prerequisite and a concrete next step ('Publish needs a title and a summary', ideally pointing at the empty fields). Crucially, don't put that in the button's own tooltip: a native `disabled` element may receive no hover or focus events, so a tooltip on it is unreachable -- use nearby text or a focusable wrapper/popover the user can actually reach (keyboard included). Separately, an action permanently unavailable to this user's role should be hidden or replaced with an attainable alternative rather than shown as a permanent dead control, unless its discoverability is explicitly wanted. This is the recoverability axis, distinct from appearance and from the disabled-control contrast exemption frontend-a11y.md owns. (ux-interaction.md.)
expectations: Refuses to ship: passing disabled-appearance and consistency does not cover reason + recovery
Requires naming the unmet prerequisite and a concrete next step for a contextually-disabled action
Flags that a tooltip on the disabled element is unreachable (no hover/focus events) -- put the explanation in nearby text or a focusable wrapper/popover
Distinguishes the separate permanent-role case (hidden or replaced with an attainable alternative) from this contextual one

evals.prompt: I delegated a review's fixes to three lanes; each lane reported back 'done' and I compiled the report saying all seven findings are resolved. The owner then asked me to double-check that everything actually landed. I re-read the three lane reports and confirmed each said done -- should I report back that yes, all seven are resolved?
evals.expected_output: No -- re-reading the lane reports re-confirms what they claimed, not what landed; a report of 'done' is not the artifact. Reconcile the seven claims against the COMMITTED DIFF: enumerate the seven as a list and join each to the hunk, test, or file that proves it, marking every one present, partial, or absent, and surfacing your own misses, not only confirming hits. Trust the diff over any lane's say-so -- independent verification (a lead's own read of the code) outranks self-report, and a delegate's 'done' is self-report. And this audit should have run BEFORE you closed, unprompted -- an owner asking 'did you actually do all of it?' is a process incident, the signal the completeness check was owed earlier, not a trigger for it; it is cheap because the claim list and the diff are both already in hand. This set-completeness pass (is every claimed fix present at all) precedes per-claim verification (is each backed by a real surface, not a favorable proxy). (method.md.)
expectations: Rejects re-reading the lane reports as reconciliation -- a 'done' report is not the delivered artifact
Requires enumerating the claim set and joining each claim to the committed diff (hunk/test/file), marking present/partial/absent incl. own misses
Reconciles against the committed diff, not the delegates' reports of what they did
Flags that the audit must run unprompted before close; the owner's challenge is the signal it was owed earlier, and it is cheap

evals.prompt: A redesign made a feed page render only user-posted items, and our test store is kept empty on purpose, so the overlay-open spec that used to run from the feed has nothing to click. We rewrote it to open the overlay from a content-populated page instead; it's green. The comment explains the move. Good to merge?
evals.expected_output: Not yet -- the rewrite is correct but it silently drops what the feed spec covered: the overlay could open from the feed, and no test asserts that anymore. A later change that removes the feed's wiring (its import of the shared overlay-link component) would break the feed overlay while the whole suite stays green. Three things are owed before merge: (1) name the retired coverage as a gap -- an unrecorded dropped assertion reads as coverage (an absence is evidence only after a positive control fires), and a commit comment is not where coverage is tracked; (2) state that the feed path is now unverifiable via a browser test without seeding the intentionally-empty store, so the gap is a decision, not an accident; (3) add a source-level structural gate -- a unit assertion that the feed component still imports and uses the shared overlay-link component, matching the pattern the codebase's other overlay-wiring tests already use. That fallback is WEAKER than the browser scenario it replaces -- it proves the component is referenced, not that the interaction works -- so it is a named fallback for the retired check, never a substitute that trades rendered coverage for an import check. (testing-ui.md.)
expectations: Does not pass the rewrite on its new-surface green; flags the silently-dropped feed coverage as a finding
Requires naming the retired coverage as a gap (an unrecorded absence reads as coverage; principle 2), not just a commit comment
Requires a source-level structural fallback that pins the wiring (import/use of the shared component), matching the codebase's existing pattern
States the fallback is weaker than the browser coverage -- pins wiring, not the interaction -- a named fallback, never a substitute

evals.prompt: A static audit lane (browser skipped, memory pressure) reports two gaps with file-level confidence: 'interactive SVG elements have no focus ring -- keyboard users are invisible; build an SVG focus overlay' and 'gaps have no per-item route to land on -- add one.' It grepped for ring-* and for a route segment. Should I brief a lane to build both?
evals.expected_output: No -- not on a static grep. Both are ABSENCE findings, and an absence is unfalsifiable from the report: it claims nothing exists anywhere, but the report can only show what the searcher looked FOR, so anything written in an idiom they didn't try reads as missing. A focus ring can be ring / outline / stroke / box-shadow / a rendered overlay; grepping ring-* alone misses an SVG-native stroke ring (e.g. group-focus-visible:stroke-...). A per-item destination can be a route / query param / hash / id-keyed overlay; a route-segment search misses /issues?focus=<id>. Before any of this becomes a build brief: (a) search by behaviour -- grep every encoding, not one; (b) confirm the absence at RUNTIME (an absence is evidence only after a positive control fires) -- render it and look; the browser was skipped, fine for presence checks but not for absence, so these are unverified / unconfirmed-absent, not gaps; (c) if you do brief a lane, instruct it to re-confirm the gap and report back before building, because an absence finding is a work order and a false one builds a second, competing mechanism next to a working one. (method.md.)
expectations: Treats both as absence findings a static grep cannot establish; refuses to authorize construction on them
Requires searching every encoding of the behaviour (ring/outline/stroke/box-shadow/overlay; route/param/hash/id-keyed), not one idiom
Requires runtime confirmation for absence (positive control / principle 2); downgrades unconfirmed absence to unverified, not a gap
A downstream build brief must re-confirm the gap before building -- an absence finding is a work order; a false one builds a competing implementation

evals.prompt: Our audit:ux gate uses scripted focus() at a 320px-tall viewport and reports 26 routes failing keyboard focus. A teammate manually tabbed through at a normal viewport and found 196 clean Tab stops. We've argued for hours over which is right so we can put one 'focus' verdict in the report. Which is correct?
evals.expected_output: Neither is 'wrong,' and there is no single aggregate verdict to report -- these are two different experiments that share the label 'focus.' A behavior claim is only meaningful with the procedure that produced it: scripted focus() vs native Tab is a different INTERACTION METHOD, and 320px-tall vs a full viewport is a different VIEWPORT, and both change what focus does (scripted focus() can land on off-screen or programmatically-focused nodes a Tab sequence never reaches; a short viewport changes what scrolls into view). Two results contradict only when method and viewport match; here they differ, so the honest report preserves BOTH, each labeled with its method + viewport + route coverage (scripted focus() @ 320px: 26 routes fail; native Tab @ full viewport: 196 clean stops), and refuses a flat 'focus passes' or 'focus fails.' To reconcile, run a controlled follow-up that changes one variable at a time (native Tab at 320px; scripted focus() at full height) until the responsible variable is isolated. Both are true experiments, but for the keyboard-USER question the canonical instrument is native Tab (what a real user actually does), not scripted focus(), so once the variable is isolated the native-Tab result is the one that reflects the user's real experience. (report-format.md.)
expectations: Refuses a single aggregate 'focus passes/fails' verdict; preserves both results as method-sensitive, not contradictory
Identifies the differing interaction method (scripted focus() vs native Tab) and viewport (320px vs full) as why both can be true
Requires each claim to carry its method + viewport (+ route coverage) so results are comparable
Reconciles by a controlled follow-up changing one variable at a time, not by declaring a winner

evals.prompt: On our app's home and weekly pages, the Add comment / Submit update / Ask AI buttons render disabled for the first few seconds on a cold load, then go live once the page finishes loading. They read from a client-side useSession hook. A reviewer filed it as a 'disabled control needs an explanation' issue. Is that the right call, and how do we gate it?
evals.expected_output: No -- this is a different class from the contextually-disabled control that owes an explanation. That control STAYS disabled; these WILL enable themselves once the client bundle hydrates and useSession resolves. During the SSR -> hydration window they are in the LOADING data state, so they must LOOK loading -- a skeleton or spinner affordance -- not a bare dead-looking disabled button. The fix is a loading affordance, or optimistic-enabled ONLY if the click is captured and replayed after hydration so the handler is never a no-op; an enabled button whose pre-hydration click is silently dropped is the dead-control / no-op-handler trust defect, not a fix. Gate it as an unverified LEAD, not a finding: the static disabled={!session} pattern with no loading sibling is confirmed only by a pre-hydration render (a snapshot before the client bundle runs); where the harness cannot capture one, report could-not-check and fail open, never a silent pass. (ux-interaction.md.)
expectations: Reclassifies as the LOADING data state during the SSR -> hydration window, not the permanent contextually-disabled class that owes an explanation
Requires a loading affordance (skeleton/spinner) or optimistic-enabled with the click replayed after hydration; a dropped pre-hydration click is the no-op-handler defect
Treats the static disabled={!session} pattern as an unverified lead confirmed only by a pre-hydration render; missing capture is could-not-check / fail-open, not a pass
Does not conflate it with the permanent-disabled-needs-explanation rule

evals.prompt: Our repo's required browser/UX jobs are gated behind a cost label so they don't run on every PR -- the forge reports them SKIPPED/Success, which satisfies branch protection. But our own merge-preflight script refuses to pass any PR where those jobs are SKIPPED if the diff touches app code. An agent can't add the label (owner-only) or trigger the manual dispatch. Local gates are all green. Is the preflight right to hold?
evals.expected_output: No -- the preflight is stricter than the required check it stands in for, and it deadlocks anyone without the owner-only lever. The forge already accepts SKIPPED/Success as green; a local gate that refuses that verdict, whose only unblock is a label or a dispatch the agent is barred from, is a gate stricter than the standard it enforces (the same gate-vs-standard rule ux-gates.md / frontend-a11y.md apply to UI) -- a catch-22, not a safety check. The fix is not to weaken the cost gate: it is to make the preflight DIAGNOSE why the job is absent -- policy-declined (the cost gate: work exists, a human must grant the run) vs nothing-to-run (a path filter: no in-scope change) -- and name the owner action, rather than refuse blindly and push the agent toward the forbidden label. Report the local green as the proof it is, flag the config as an agent-unmergeable deadlock (a High config gap, not a flake), and route the run-grant to the owner. (merge-operations.md.)
expectations: Identifies the local preflight as stricter than the forge's own SKIPPED/Success verdict -- a gate stricter than the standard (gate-vs-standard rule)
Names the deadlock: the only unblock is an owner-only label / dispatch the agent cannot use
Fix is to diagnose policy-declined (cost gate) vs nothing-to-run (path filter) and name the owner action, not to weaken the cost gate or add the label
Treats it as a config gap to route to the owner (High), not a flake to wait out

evals.prompt: A review found a broken auth guard -- disabled={!member} -- on one composer button, where member is briefly undefined so the control dead-ends. We fixed that callsite. Ship the finding as a single-site fix?
evals.expected_output: No -- disabled={!member} is a copyable idiom, so a single callsite is almost never the whole finding. Before calling it single-site, grep the idiom across the tree (the same guard shape, sibling identity flags) in the SAME pass: the search result IS the blast radius, and the finding is reported as one class-finding with its full instance set -- how many sites, and where -- not the first callsite alone. Fixing one and stopping under-scopes the finding and leaks a second fix into a later increment (and a third instance no lane encountered stays broken). This is the review analogue of the one-component-per-concept duplicate-twin sweep (ux-components.md), for a bug pattern rather than a duplicated component: land every instance in one increment, then a single follow-up verifies none remain. (method.md.)
expectations: Refuses the single-site framing; treats the guard as a copyable idiom with a multi-site blast radius
Requires grepping the idiom across the tree in the same pass, the search result defining the instance set
Reports it as one class-finding with its full instance set (count + locations), fixed in one increment
Connects to the duplicate-twin / one-component-per-concept sweep, but for a bug pattern not a duplicated component

evals.prompt: Our LLM review flagged 'user-controlled input reaches this SQL sink -- SQL injection' on one line, and 'the aws-sdk version here is vulnerable' on a dependency. Both sound right. Post them as findings?
evals.expected_output: Not as asserted findings -- corroborate each against the deterministic proof the LLM cannot itself generate, or mark it unverified. 'Input reaches this sink' is a taint/data-flow claim: confirm it against a CodeQL (or equivalent) source->sink path; a claim with no path is unverified, not a finding. 'This version is vulnerable' is an exact version<->CVE match: check osv-scanner / Trivy / Grype against the machine-readable affected-version ranges rather than trusting the model's recall of ranges (error-prone). Running the project's wired scanners is already Phase 1 and re-verifying against source is already the fan-out discipline; this is the security-specific rule that a class a deterministic engine can PROVE is corroborated against that proof (ingested via SARIF / OSV JSON), the LLM layering judgment on top, not asserting the proof. A verified-live secret (TruffleHog Verified) and reachability (Semgrep Supply Chain: importing != executing) are the same pattern. (security-appsec.md.)
expectations: Does not post either claim as a confirmed finding on the model's say-so; corroborates against a deterministic proof or marks unverified
Maps the taint claim to a CodeQL source->sink path and the version claim to an exact OSV/Trivy/Grype version<->CVE match
Names SARIF / OSV JSON as the ingestion format and frames the LLM as layering judgment on a proof it cannot generate
Reuses the existing run-scanners (Phase 1) + re-verify (fan-out) discipline rather than restating it; adds the tool-proof corroboration

evals.prompt: We imprinted our review standards into AGENTS.md so our agents pick them up. But the team also uses Anthropic's managed GitHub Code Review and the local /code-review command, and neither applies our review-specific severity tuning. What should the Phase-6 imprint do?
evals.expected_output: Imprint a review-SCOPED rules block, not just the all-tasks AGENTS.md, and state the surface split. Two consumers read a review-only surface: OpenAI Codex reads a `## Code Review Rules` section of AGENTS.md (root = repo-wide, nested = service-scoped), and Anthropic's MANAGED GitHub Code Review reads a root REVIEW.md (severity recalibration, skip rules, verification bar, nit caps). Map all six severities to the de-facto markers so they agree -- the markers are coarser than the six-level rubric, so map by is-it-a-real-bug (Blocker/Critical/High/Medium -> Important, a Medium is a real defect not a Nit; Low/Nit -> Nit; a pre-existing bug -> Pre-existing). The catch to state in the block: the managed reviewer reads REVIEW.md but the LOCAL /code-review command reads CLAUDE.md ONLY (not REVIEW.md) -- so a rule you need on both goes in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, and REVIEW.md carries managed-only tuning. Same idempotent-additive imprint discipline; author each rule as rule -> bad -> good -> reasoning. (docs-and-dx.md.)
expectations: Adds a review-scoped block (## Code Review Rules in AGENTS.md and/or REVIEW.md), distinct from the all-tasks AGENTS.md context
States the surface split: managed Code Review reads REVIEW.md, local /code-review reads CLAUDE.md only
Maps all six severities to the de-facto markers, Medium -> Important (a real defect, not a Nit), Low/Nit -> Nit, pre-existing -> Pre-existing
Keeps the idempotent-additive imprint discipline and the rule->bad->good->reasoning format

evals.prompt: A PR adds an autonomous agent that can call external tools and spend from a budget. The team says 'we already did a STRIDE threat model of the app last year.' Is that covered, and what do we check?
evals.expected_output: Not covered -- name the method that fits and check coverage, not ceremony. A year-old STRIDE model of the app does not model an AUTONOMOUS AGENT with tool-calling and spend authority: that introduces new trust boundaries, a new principal (the agent acting on a user's behalf), and new state transitions the old model never considered, so the model is stale relative to the diff -- a finding. The fitting method here is MAESTRO (the agentic-AI threat-modeling method, complementary to the OWASP ASI / MITRE ATLAS catalogs), not general STRIDE; LINDDUN if privacy threats are in scope; PASTA if threats must tie to business impact; attack trees to decompose one attacker goal. The review lens is: does the change introduce a trust boundary / principal / transition the existing model didn't cover (here, yes), and is an agentic surface modeled with an agent-specific method (here, no). Maturity frames (SSDF/SAMM/BSIMM) measure the org's program, not this diff. (appsec-design.md.)
expectations: Flags the change as outrunning the existing model (new trust boundary/principal/transition) -- a stale model is a finding, not covered
Names MAESTRO as the fitting method for an agentic system (not general STRIDE), and names LINDDUN(privacy)/PASTA/attack-trees for their cases
Frames the lens as coverage (does the diff outrun the model / is the agentic surface modeled), not threat-model ceremony
Does not treat naming a maturity frame (SSDF/SAMM/BSIMM) as covering this diff

evals.prompt: A PR adds a custom tab component: divs with role='tab' and role='tablist', click handlers switch panels, and each tab is in the tab order so you can Tab to it. Accessibility looks handled. Sign off?
evals.expected_output: No -- 'Tab reaches it' is not 'operable.' Check the custom widget against its ARIA Authoring Practices (APG) pattern: a tablist has a prescribed keyboard map -- Arrow keys move between tabs, Home/End jump to first/last, and only the active tab is in the tab order (roving tabindex), not every tab. This implementation is missing arrow-key navigation and likely puts every tab in the tab order, so a keyboard user can't operate it as a tablist -- a finding, even though each tab is Tab-reachable. Also verify the states reflect (aria-selected on the active tab, aria-controls to its panel). The rule order still holds: prefer native elements first; the APG pattern applies because this is a hand-built widget. (a11y-focus.md.)
expectations: Rejects 'Tab-reachable = operable'; checks the widget against its APG pattern's full keyboard map
Names the tablist pattern's specifics (Arrow between tabs, Home/End, roving tabindex / only the active tab in the tab order)
Requires the states to reflect (aria-selected / aria-controls), not just roles present
Keeps the native-element-first rule; APG applies because it's a hand-built widget

evals.prompt: A PR is clean -- tests pass, no bugs, good style. The linked ticket says 'let users export their data as CSV.' The diff adds a JSON export instead. Everything works. Approve?
evals.expected_output: No -- correctness and intent-conformance are different lenses. The code is correct, but it does not do what was CLAIMED: the ticket asked for CSV export and the diff ships JSON. A flawless implementation of the wrong thing is a finding, cited to the stated intent (the linked ticket's 'export as CSV'). This is distinct from any domain-audit finding (those ask 'is it correct,' not 'does it satisfy the request'), and is the review-side counterpart to the delivery spec gate. Flag it as an intent-conformance finding -- the diff does X (JSON) while the ticket asked for Y (CSV) -- and route to the owner to confirm whether the ticket or the diff is authoritative rather than silently approving. Where a PR states no intent, say so rather than infer one. (method.md.)
expectations: Separates correctness (code is right) from intent-conformance (does it do what was claimed) -- clean code does not make it approvable
Cites the stated intent (ticket: CSV) vs what the diff does (JSON) as the finding
Frames it as a lens the correctness/domain audits miss; the delivery-spec counterpart
Routes the mismatch to the owner rather than approving; where no intent is stated, says so rather than inferring

evals.prompt: A reviewer wants to file three High findings: 'possible DoS -- this endpoint has no rate limit', 'possible resource exhaustion -- this loop could be large', and 'this input isn't validated'. None traces a concrete exploit path; they're pattern-spotted. File them as High?
evals.expected_output: Not as High on suspicion -- these are chronically-noisy classes (DoS, rate-limiting, resource-exhaustion, generic input-validation) where pattern-spotting without a demonstrated impact path produces false alarms. The anti-slop / mechanism-unproven rule applies: a finding in these classes with no reached sink or concrete exploit/exhaustion path is held 'unverified' or dropped to Nit, not posted as a High. To promote one, show the path: for the input-validation item, does untrusted input actually reach a dangerous sink (injection/SSRF/traversal)? for the DoS/exhaustion items, is there a concrete attacker-controlled unbounded amplification with no upstream limit? A proven impact path re-promotes the finding to its real severity; absent that, it is noise that costs the author a round trip. Not every security class -- secrets, authz/IDOR, and data-loss keep their severity; this bar is for the suspicion-prone classes. (method.md.)
expectations: Refuses to post the three as High on suspicion; applies the proven-impact / mechanism-unproven bar to the noisy classes
Names what a real impact path looks like (untrusted input reaches a sink; attacker-controlled unbounded amplification with no limit)
Holds them unverified / Nit absent a path; a proven path re-promotes to real severity
Does not relax the bar for secrets / authz / data-loss classes

evals.prompt: Eight PRs targeting our 'development' integration branch all show a required check as SKIPPED and merge_preflight refuses them; a ninth PR just failed a 'parity' gate. The team is adding the 'full-ci' label and re-running, guessing flakes. What's the right diagnosis order?
evals.expected_output: Stop guessing labels/flakes -- read the workflow config first, in order. For the no-run/Pending required check on PRs targeting 'development': (1) is 'development' in the workflow's on.pull_request.branches -- the filter that matches the PR's BASE/target branch? A pull_request workflow that doesn't list 'development' never fires for PRs targeting it, so the required check never reports on their heads -- a structural no-run/Pending block (the #262 no-status case), not a cost-gate or a flake. Fix: add 'development' to on.pull_request.branches -- THIS unblocks the PRs. (Separately, listing 'development' in on.push.branches stamps its own HEAD green via a push run after merge, but that does NOT unblock the open PRs.) Only after that: (2) a job-level cost-gate if:, (3) a path filter (OK), (4) then rerun/flake. For the ninth PR's 'parity' failure (and any time N PRs fail the SAME gate at once): check git log HEAD..origin/main --oneline for a STALE BASE before triaging each PR -- a gate that diffs against origin/main turns one additive main commit the integration branch hasn't pulled into a whole-queue failure with no real regression; one git merge origin/main on development clears them all. Sync the integration branch on each additive main merge, and new gates should baseline on the PR base, not origin/main. (merge-operations.md.)
expectations: Reads the workflow on: block FIRST and names the right key -- target branch absent from on.pull_request.branches (the base-branch filter) = structural no-run/Pending; fix = add the target branch to on.pull_request.branches (on.push.branches only stamps the branch HEAD post-merge, does not unblock the PRs)
For N PRs failing the same gate, checks stale-base (git log HEAD..origin/main) before triaging individual PRs; one merge clears the queue
Names the root cause of the whole-queue failure: a gate diffing against origin/main + a drifted integration branch (additive main commit)
Does not reach for the label / rerun / flake hypothesis first

evals.prompt: A Playwright shard has been in_progress for 70 minutes (normal is ~15) during a merge-critical run. Someone already triggered two reruns; all three are running in parallel. What should we do?
evals.expected_output: Stop the rerun-storm -- three parallel instances multiply runner spend for zero new signal. Past ~2x a shard's normal duration, READ THAT SHARD'S LOG before acting (< 60s): look at the last-output timestamp and whether a test started but never finished. Diagnose hang vs timeout: a HANG (no new output for minutes -- a deadlocked browser, a port that never opened) should be cancelled and root-caused before any rerun; a TIMEOUT (the log shows a test hitting its per-test/suite limit) should be left to fail cleanly, then the specific timed-out test triaged. Rerun at most once, and only after diagnosis -- a rerun with no known root cause is spend with no expected change; if a second run reproduces the same hang/timeout, that IS the bug -- file it, don't rerun again. Cancel the extra parallel runs now, and cancel with a note naming the evidence (last log line, elapsed) so the next reader knows it was a hang, not a flake or a stale push. (merge-operations.md.)
expectations: Reads the shard's log before acting; diagnoses hang (no output) vs timeout (log shows a test at its limit)
Names the rerun-storm anti-pattern (parallel reruns = spend, no new signal) and passive-wait as the mirror error
Reruns at most once and only after diagnosis; a reproduced hang/timeout is the bug to file, not to rerun
Cancels a hang with evidence (last log line, elapsed) so it isn't mistaken for a flake

evals.prompt: Our team keeps a committed .review-calibration file of nits we've decided we don't care about (e.g. 'we allow console.log in scripts/'). This PR re-introduces a console.log in scripts/ AND has an unscoped SQL query that could leak another tenant's rows. The calibration file says 'ignore console.log in scripts/'. What does the reviewer post?
evals.expected_output: Suppress the console.log nit, post the SQL finding. The review-calibration record legitimately silences a SETTLED STYLE/PREFERENCE nit the team has already declined -- the console.log in scripts/ is exactly that, so re-raising it is noise (anti-slop: a finding that changes no owner action). But the record NEVER suppresses a security, logic, null-deref, or data-validation/data-loss finding: the unscoped SQL query is a cross-tenant data leak (a security + data finding), so it is raised at full severity regardless of any calibration entry -- a calibration file that silenced it would be a dangerous misuse. Calibration is a committed, path-scoped record of style/preference decisions read to cut repeat noise, not a hosted memory service and not a mechanism to dismiss correctness or safety. (method.md.)
expectations: Suppresses the settled style nit (console.log) per the committed calibration record -- cuts repeat noise
Posts the unscoped-SQL cross-tenant leak at full severity -- calibration NEVER suppresses security/logic/data findings
Frames calibration as a committed path-scoped style/preference record, not a hosted memory service and not a way to dismiss correctness/safety
Does not let a calibration entry override a security/data finding

evals.prompt: A PR titled 'add a 7th item to the anti-slop checklist' changes exactly one file. Before the diff the checklist had 6 top-level bullets; after it, it still has 6, and one existing bullet's first line now reads differently. Lint, formatting, and the test suite all pass. What does the reviewer post?
evals.expected_output: Flag it: an 'add' that leaves the item count unchanged is a silent REPLACE, not an add. The claimed 7th bullet was spliced into an existing bullet's opening line -- fusing two rules into one and deleting the original's subject -- so the count stayed 6, not 7. Verify mechanically: `git show <base>:<file> | grep -cE '<bullet shape>'` against the working copy must rise by the one item claimed; a delta of zero on a claimed add is the tell. The fusion leaves every byte valid, so lint, formatting, and tests all pass over it -- only the count delta or a human read catches the lost rule. This is an intent-conformance finding (Phase 2): the diff did not do what its title claimed, and an existing rule was silently lost. (method.md.)
expectations: Identifies the unchanged count (6 -> 6) as the tell that a claimed add was actually a replace/fusion, not a genuine add
Names the mechanical check -- base-vs-working-copy item count via git show must rise by the number claimed
Notes the fusion keeps all bytes valid, so lint/format/tests pass over it -- gates do not catch it, a count delta or human read does
Frames it as intent-conformance (the diff did not do what its title claimed) and that an existing rule was silently lost, not merely nothing-added

evals.prompt: A review found two files with equally tangled, over-complex code (the same cyclomatic complexity). File A (src/legacy/report_export.py) has 2 commits in the last two years; file B (src/checkout/pricing.py) has 40 commits in the last three months. Neither has a correctness bug. How does the reviewer prioritize the maintainability debt?
evals.expected_output: Lead with file B. Both are equal structural debt, so rank them by team behavior -- change-frequency x complexity, the hotspot lens: B is churned constantly (40 commits in 3 months), so its complexity taxes the team on every change, while A is near-dormant (2 commits in 2 years) and its ugliness rarely bites. Flag B's debt first and keep A low. This is a RANKING decision, not a severity bump -- neither file is a Blocker/High merely for being complex, and A's low churn does not erase its debt, it only deprioritizes it. Compute churn from the repo's own git history (e.g. git log --format= --name-only | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn); if history were absent (shallow clone, fresh import), say so and fall back to complexity alone rather than invent a churn number. This ranks maintainability debt by where the team works, distinct from Phase-0 blast-radius which ranks the audit scope. (domain-h.md.)
expectations: Ranks the high-churn file B (40 commits/3mo) above the equally-complex low-churn file A -- hotspot = change-frequency x complexity from git history
Treats it as a ranking/prioritization decision, not a severity bump -- does not inflate either complex file into a Blocker/High
Keeps the low-churn file's debt low priority without erasing it (deprioritized, not dismissed)
Computes churn from the target's own git history and, if history were absent, says so or falls back to complexity rather than inventing a churn number

evals.prompt: Our orchestrator sheds load under memory pressure by running `pkill -f node` to stop the heaviest lane. Each lane runs a Node build in its own git worktree. What does the reviewer flag?
evals.expected_output: Flag the `pkill -f node` load-shed as a cross-lane collateral kill. pkill -f selects by command line, so it kills EVERY node process -- the other lanes' builds, a shared dev server, the reviewer's own tooling, even the orchestrator itself -- not just the heaviest lane. Kill by OWNERSHIP instead: start each lane in its own process group (setsid / a new pgid; a Job Object on Windows), record the pgid with the lane's claim, and terminate that group (kill -TERM -<pgid>) so the tool and every child it forked die together and nothing unrelated is selected.
