Besides the >=3:1 contrast between focused/unfocused states (met here), the indicator's AREA must be at least that of a 2 CSS px thick perimeter of the unfocused component (or sub-component). A uniform 1px outline traces the same perimeter at half the reference band-width, so roughly half the required area — it fails the area prong even though its contrast is fine (the rule is total area, not a 2px thickness minimum: a differently-shaped indicator with equivalent area can pass). Fix: make the indicator's area meet the 2px-perimeter equivalent (a >=2px outline, a thick underline of equivalent area, or a large-enough shape), not just clear the contrast floor. (Contrast alone is 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, AA; 2.4.13 adds the size requirement on top and is AAA, so scope the finding accordingly.)
expectations: Identifies that 2.4.13 has two requirements and a 1px ring meets the contrast prong but fails the AREA prong (at least a 2 CSS px thick perimeter of the unfocused component or sub-component)
Prescribes making the indicator's area meet the 2px-perimeter equivalent (thicker outline / equivalent-area shape), not merely clearing the contrast floor
Correctly separates 2.4.13's area+contrast (AAA) from 1.4.11 contrast-only (AA), scoping the finding as AAA

evals.prompt: A download endpoint serves `res.sendFile(path.join(BASE_DIR, req.query.name))`. A reviewer says 'it joins under BASE_DIR, so files outside are safe.' A request arrives with `?name=../../../../etc/passwd`. What happens, and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: `path.join(BASE_DIR, '../../../../etc/passwd')` normalizes the `..` segments and resolves OUTSIDE BASE_DIR, so `sendFile` serves `/etc/passwd` — classic path traversal (CWE-22). `path.join` does not confine to the base; it concatenates-and-normalizes, and `../` walks up. 'It joins under BASE_DIR' is false. Fix: after resolving, verify the canonical result is still within the base — `const p = fs.realpathSync(path.resolve(BASE_DIR, name)); if (!p.startsWith(BASE_DIR + path.sep)) reject;` (realpath follows symlinks; a lexical `path.resolve` alone would miss a symlink escape, and note the trailing `path.sep` — a bare `startsWith('/base')` also matches `/base-evil`) (canonicalize/`realpath` BEFORE the check; also block absolute-path overrides and symlinks that escape). A denylist of literal `../` is insufficient — bypassable via URL-encoded `%2e%2e` or `....//`. Test with `../`, an absolute path, and an encoded traversal.
expectations: Identifies that path.join/concatenation with `../` resolves OUTSIDE BASE_DIR (path traversal, CWE-22) and serves an arbitrary file — 'joins under BASE_DIR' is false

Prescribes resolving to a canonical realpath (symlink-following) then verifying it is a TRUE SUBPATH of the base — compared against base + its trailing separator, or a real is-subpath check, not a bare `/base` prefix (which also matches `/base-evil`) — plus rejecting absolute-path overrides and escaping symlinks
Notes a literal `../` denylist is bypassable (encoded `%2e%2e` / `....//`); test with `../`, an absolute path, and an encoded traversal

evals.prompt: An accessibility audit flags every interactive element under 24×24 CSS px as a WCAG 2.2 Target Size (2.5.8) failure — including inline 'Terms' / 'Privacy' text links inside a paragraph, and a small 'edit' icon with several px of clear space on every side. A reviewer says 'anything under 24px fails 2.5.8.' Is that right?
evals.expected_output: No — 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum, AA) has FIVE exceptions, and both flagged items likely qualify. (1) The inline 'Terms'/'Privacy' links are covered by the **Inline** exception: 2.5.8 does not apply to targets within a sentence or sized by the line-height of non-target text. (2) The spaced 'edit' icon is covered by the **Spacing** exception: an undersized target is exempt if a 24 CSS px diameter circle centred on each intersects neither another target nor another undersized target's circle (so two adjacent small icons still fail when their circles overlap). The other exceptions are **Equivalent** (another control does the same function at full size), **user-agent-controlled**, and **essential**. 'Anything under 24px fails' over-flags: an undersized target meeting any of the five exceptions is not a finding. Fix the audit to apply the exceptions (especially Inline and Spacing) before reporting.
expectations: Identifies that 2.5.8 has exceptions and that flagging every <24px target over-flags — an undersized target meeting an exception is not a finding

Names the Inline exception for the in-sentence text links (2.5.8 doesn't apply to targets in a sentence / sized by non-target line-height) and the Spacing exception for the spaced icon (24px-circle non-intersection)
Notes the remaining exceptions (Equivalent / user-agent-controlled / essential) and prescribes applying the exceptions before reporting

evals.prompt: A page reflects the `X-Forwarded-Host` header into an absolute URL in its HTML (a `<link>`/redirect), and the response is cacheable at the CDN. The CDN's cache key is just path + query — it does not include `X-Forwarded-Host`. A reviewer says 'that header is from our own load balancer, not user input, so it's fine.' What's the risk?
evals.expected_output: Web cache poisoning. `X-Forwarded-Host` is an attacker-settable request header (an attacker can send it directly, and it is often not stripped end-to-end), and it shapes the response body while NOT being part of the cache key — so an attacker sends one request with a malicious `X-Forwarded-Host`, the poisoned response (a `<link>`/script-src/redirect pointing at attacker infrastructure) is cached under the normal URL and then served to EVERY subsequent visitor: a reflected issue becomes a stored, mass-distributed one (XSS, malicious script load, open redirect). 'From our LB / not user input' is false — the header is client-settable. Fix: every input that can change the response must be in the cache key or stripped/normalized at the edge before caching; never reflect an unkeyed header into a cacheable response; census the cache key against every response-affecting input. (Distinct from a shared-cache identity leak, which serves one real user's private body to another.)
expectations: Identifies that `X-Forwarded-Host` is attacker-settable and, being unkeyed, its reflected value is cached and served to every subsequent visitor — a reflected issue becomes stored/mass-distributed (cache poisoning)
Rebuts 'from our LB / not user input' — the header is client-settable and often not stripped end-to-end

Prescribes: every response-affecting input must be in the cache key or stripped/normalized at the edge before caching; don't reflect an unkeyed header into a cacheable response; census the cache key vs response-affecting inputs

evals.prompt: A login form blocks paste into the password field (to 'prevent shoulder-surfing') and its password input has `autocomplete="off"`. There's no puzzle or CAPTCHA. A reviewer says '3.3.8 Accessible Authentication is about not requiring a puzzle — there's none here, so it passes.' Is that right?
evals.expected_output: No. 3.3.8 (AA) is broader than 'no CAPTCHA': it requires an auth step not to demand a cognitive-function test WITHOUT an alternative or a mechanism to complete it — and the canonical mechanism is a password manager. Blocking paste and setting `autocomplete="off"` defeat password managers, forcing the user to recall and manually type the password (a cognitive-function test) with no assisting mechanism — a 3.3.8 failure even with no puzzle. Fix: allow paste into password/OTP fields, set correct `autocomplete` tokens (`current-password`/`new-password`/`one-time-code`), and don't intercept clipboard events, so a password manager / OTP autofill works. ('Prevent shoulder-surfing' is not a valid basis to block paste — it defeats the very mechanism 3.3.8 requires.)
expectations: Identifies that 3.3.8 is broader than 'no CAPTCHA' — blocking paste + autocomplete=off defeats the password-manager MECHANISM, forcing manual recall/typing (a cognitive-function test) with no assisting mechanism = a 3.3.8 failure
Prescribes allowing paste, correct autocomplete tokens (current-password/new-password/one-time-code), and not intercepting clipboard events so password managers / OTP autofill work
Rejects the 'prevent shoulder-surfing' rationale for blocking paste

evals.prompt: A banking login uses an image-recognition CAPTCHA ('select all the buses') as a step. A reviewer says it's fine because 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) explicitly allows an object-recognition test as an exception. For a high-stakes financial flow, is that sufficient?
evals.expected_output: It passes 3.3.8 (Minimum, AA) — object-recognition IS one of that SC's allowed exceptions — but for high-stakes auth the bar is 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced, AAA), which permits ONLY the Alternative and Mechanism exceptions and drops object-recognition and personal-content. So the 'select all the buses' image CAPTCHA passes Minimum but FAILS Enhanced. For a banking/health flow, hold it to 3.3.9: provide a non-cognitive alternative (a hardware key / passkey / email-or-SMS link / accessible 2FA) rather than an image-recognition puzzle, which also excludes users with visual or cognitive disabilities. 'It's an allowed 3.3.8 exception' is true but insufficient at the AAA tier a high-stakes flow warrants.
expectations: Identifies that object-recognition is an allowed 3.3.8 (Minimum) exception so the CAPTCHA passes 3.3.8 — but 3.3.9 (Enhanced) drops that exception, so it FAILS 3.3.9
States that a high-stakes (banking/health) flow warrants the 3.3.9 / AAA bar, not just Minimum
Prescribes a non-cognitive alternative (hardware key / passkey / accessible 2FA) instead of an image-recognition CAPTCHA

evals.prompt: A review filed a Critical: 'the export endpoint returns other tenants' rows.' The author replies: 'that endpoint is internal-only, behind the VPN, so it's not exploitable — please drop it or downgrade to Nit.' The reviewer could drop it, or keep it Critical. What should the reviewer do, and how should they get there?
evals.expected_output: Neither (a) nor (b) reflexively — run a hold-or-concede loop. First genuinely re-weigh the claim: is 'internal-only, behind the VPN' actually true and sufficient? Check it — is the origin reachable off-VPN, and is 'internal' enforced by code or just asserted? If the author is right that it's truly unreachable by any attacker, drop or rescope the finding and say so. If it still stands (a VPN is not an authorization boundary; an internal actor or a compromised internal host still crosses tenants; 'internal' is often unenforced), restate with evidence (the missing tenant predicate at file:line, a two-principal test) and HOLD the severity — a cross-tenant leak's consequence doesn't shrink because the author objects, so it does not become a Nit under pressure. Stay civil. If deadlocked, escalate to a named owner / Decisions-needed entry and record the resolution so the rationale isn't lost in the thread. Caving to avoid friction buries a real risk; digging in on ego is equally wrong — the deciding factor is the evidence, not who pushed.
expectations: Rejects both reflexive options (cave-to-keep-peace and insist-on-ego) — the decision turns on re-weighing the evidence, not on the pushback itself
Prescribes genuinely re-checking the author's claim (is the VPN/'internal' actually an enforced authorization boundary?) and dropping/rescoping only if the finding is truly wrong
If it stands: restate with evidence + HOLD the severity (a real cross-tenant leak doesn't become a Nit under pressure), stay civil, escalate to a named path + record the resolution if deadlocked

evals.prompt: A reviewer writes: 'This auth code is sloppy and whoever wrote it clearly doesn't understand sessions — obviously broken.' The finding underneath (a session token not invalidated on logout) is correct. Is the comment acceptable because the finding is right?
evals.expected_output: No — a correct finding delivered as a judgment of the author is still a defective review comment. Comment on the code, not the person: state the defect, its impact, and the fix ('logout deletes the cookie but does not invalidate the server-side session, so a captured token stays valid until expiry — invalidate the session / advance a per-user not-before on logout'), with no 'sloppy' / 'doesn't understand' / 'obviously.' The severity (a real auth defect) rates the code's consequence, not the author's competence — and phrasing it as an attack makes a valid Critical easier to dismiss and erodes the working relationship while adding no technical information. Keep the finding and its severity; rewrite the register. (This is tone/register, not the finding's substance — the substance is correct and stays.)
expectations: Identifies that a correct finding is still a defective comment when it judges the author ('sloppy'/'doesn't understand'/'obviously') rather than the code
Rewrites to comment on the code — defect + impact + fix — keeping the finding and its severity (consequence, not competence)
Notes the attacking register adds no technical information, makes a valid finding easier to dismiss, and harms the relationship — fix the register, keep the substance

evals.prompt: A DIFF adds a new pure function `prorate(amountCents, periodDays, usedDays)` for mid-cycle billing. No existing test reaches it. The reviewer reads it and the arithmetic 'looks right.' Is a careful static read enough to mark this changed logic sound, or is there a stronger move?
evals.expected_output: A static read is the weaker claim — for changed correctness-bearing logic no test reaches, author a minimal, disposable probe test that calls `prorate` at its boundary conditions (usedDays = 0, usedDays = periodDays, usedDays > periodDays, periodDays = 0, negative/overflowing amounts) inside the throwaway worktree at START_SHA (the same containment as the planted-defect probe; never the working tree). A red result — e.g. a divide-by-zero at periodDays = 0, or a value exceeding the full amount when usedDays > periodDays — is a finding with a real repro attached. A green result is recorded as 'no defect at the inputs probed,' with the probe and the exact inputs listed; it is NOT an invariant on its own — one passing example does not prove the property. Promote it to a `checked_sound` / Invariants-verified-to-hold row only if the test actually pins the property across the input class (e.g. a property/fuzz test over the whole domain), not a single example. Either way it is a stronger, evidence-grounded claim than the read alone.
expectations: Says the static read is the weaker claim and prescribes authoring a minimal disposable probe test at boundary conditions in the throwaway worktree at START_SHA
RED = a finding with a real repro attached; names plausible boundary bugs (e.g. periodDays=0 divide, usedDays>periodDays over-charge, negative/overflow)
GREEN is only 'no defect at the inputs probed' (record probe+inputs), NOT an invariant — promote to checked_sound / Invariants row only if the test pins the property across the class, not one example

evals.prompt: To probe changed logic, a reviewer wants to author a test that calls `chargeAndSummarize(order)` — a handler that hits a live payment API and a paid LLM, then writes the result to the production database. There is no existing test. Should the reviewer author a probe test that runs it to exercise the new branch?
evals.expected_output: Not one that fires the real calls. The throwaway worktree bounds filesystem blast radius, not outbound effects — running `chargeAndSummarize` as written would POST a real charge, burn paid model spend, and write prod, which the confirm-before-billable/side-effect rule forbids for a reviewer's own probe. Isolate first: stub/mock the payment client, the model call, and the DB writer, then probe the pure decision logic (the new branch, the amount computation) against the stubs. If the changed logic genuinely cannot be exercised without the real outbound/paid/stateful call, do not run it — skip and record `could-not-check` (distinct from found-nothing: it is an explicit gap, not a clean result), and fall back to the static read plus a note that dynamic verification was blocked on un-stubbable side effects. Never fire a real side effect to get a probe result.
expectations: Refuses to run the probe as-is because the throwaway worktree bounds filesystem, not outbound/paid/stateful effects (real charge / model spend / prod write) — the confirm-before-billable/side-effect rule
Prescribes stubbing the payment, model, and DB boundaries and probing the pure decision logic against the stubs
If it can't be isolated: skip and record could-not-check (distinct from found-nothing) + fall back to static read — never fire a real side effect for a result

evals.prompt: A PR says 'canary rollout with automatic rollback if error rate regresses.' The deploy config does split 5% of traffic to the new build. The telemetry stamps `service.name` on every metric but no version and no cohort tag. Is the canary's automatic rollback actually implementable as described?
evals.expected_output: No — the halt metric as described cannot be computed. Automatic rollback 'on regression' means comparing the canary cohort's error rate against the baseline's, but with only `service.name` (no `service.version` or cohort tag) on the telemetry, the 5% canary traffic and the 95% baseline are merged into one undifferentiated metric — there is no dimension to split them by, so 'canary error rate vs baseline' is not a query you can run. The traffic split is real but the measurement is not: a canary that is 100% broken only moves the blended error rate by ~5%, which may not cross a threshold at all. Fix: stamp a stable resource identity that includes `service.version` (OpenTelemetry `service.version`, Stable) or an explicit canary cohort tag, and partition the halt metric by it so the canary cohort is compared against baseline; a named halt metric that reads an unpartitioned series is measuring a blend and can never regress-check. (observability.md telemetry resource identity + release-engineering.md canary.)
expectations: Says the rollback is NOT implementable as described because with only service.name (no version/cohort dimension) canary and baseline traffic merge into one metric that can't be split
Notes the consequence: a badly-broken 5% canary barely moves the blended rate, so the threshold may never fire
Fix: stamp service.version (or a canary cohort tag) and partition the halt metric by it so canary is compared against baseline — an unpartitioned series can't regress-check

evals.prompt: A service computes multi-window burn-rate SLOs from its telemetry. Staging and production both emit with `service.name=frontend` to the same metrics backend; there is no environment attribute. A reviewer is told 'staging traffic is tiny, so it can't matter.' Is that reasoning sound?
evals.expected_output: No — this is a correctness defect, not a volume question. Per the OpenTelemetry spec, `deployment.environment.name` 'does not affect the uniqueness constraints defined through the service.namespace, service.name and service.instance.id resource attributes,' so `service.name=frontend` in production and in staging 'MUST be considered to be identifying the same service' — the two environments are, by default, one identified resource. Staging errors, deploys, and load tests therefore land in the production SLO's error budget: a staging incident or a load test burning errors can trip a production burn-rate alert (false page) or silently consume budget, and 'staging is tiny' is irrelevant because a deliberately-failing staging run is unbounded. This collision is the default behavior, not an edge case. Fix: add `deployment.environment.name` (or `service.namespace`) as a resource dimension and scope every SLO/burn-rate query to `production`, so staging and prod are distinct series. (observability.md telemetry resource identity + role-coverage.md SRE burn-rate.)
expectations: Rejects the 'staging is tiny' reasoning — the defect is identity collision, not volume; a deliberately-failing staging/load run is unbounded

Grounds it in identity collision — same service.name with no environment/namespace dimension is one identified series, so staging errors land in the prod SLO/error budget (bonus: names the OTel rule that deployment.environment.name does not affect uniqueness)
Fix: add deployment.environment.name / service.namespace and scope every SLO/burn-rate query to production so the environments are distinct series

evals.prompt: A RAG pipeline retrieves the top-8 chunks, concatenates them in retrieval-score order, and if the concatenation exceeds the model's limit it trims the tail by character count to fit, then sends it. Retrieval quality is separately measured and good, and the team already caps `max_tokens` on the response and believes that covers the model's limits. Is the assembly step sound?
evals.expected_output: No — two assembly defects sit between good retrieval and the answer. (1) Budget must be measured with the model's ACTUAL tokenizer, not a character/word estimate (chars-per-token varies by content and model, so a char-trim both over- and under-shoots the real limit). (2) On overflow, drop WHOLE lowest-ranked chunks, never truncate mid-content: a character tail-trim can cut a fact or citation in half, and the model then completes or misattributes the fragment — a silent wrongness. Also (3) placement: concatenating in raw retrieval-score order can bury the single most-relevant chunk in the middle, where models use context markedly worse ('Lost in the Middle,' Liu et al. 2023) — position the top chunk at the start or end. Fix + test: compute the budget with the real tokenizer; on overflow drop whole lowest-ranked chunks (assert no partial chunk reached the prompt, the dropped ones were lowest-ranked, and the drop was counted/logged); order so the most-relevant chunk is at an edge. This is per-call prompt assembly — distinct from an output max_tokens cap (bounds what comes out) and from a long-running agent's conversation compaction (security-ai-agents.md). (testing-ai-evals.md.)
expectations: Flags char/word budgeting instead of the model's actual tokenizer

Flags mid-chunk truncation (drop whole lowest-ranked chunks instead; a mid-cut fact/citation is silently completed or misattributed) and prescribes the overflow test (no partial chunk, lowest-ranked dropped, counted)
Flags placement — most-relevant chunk buried mid-concatenation ('lost in the middle') should sit at start/end; and distinguishes this per-call assembly from an output cap / agent compaction

evals.prompt: An eval scores output quality with an LLM-as-judge: it shows the judge two candidate answers (the system-under-test's answer always presented first), asks which is better, runs at temperature 0, and reports a high win rate. The judge is the same model family as the system under test. Is this a trustworthy quality measurement?
evals.expected_output: Not yet — temperature 0 only makes the judge deterministic, not unbiased, and self-consistency is not precision. Three known judge biases are untested here (Zheng et al. 2023): (a) POSITION — always presenting the SUT's answer first invites positional bias; run each comparison twice with the two answers' positions swapped and treat a flipped verdict as positional bias (two calls, zero human labels). (b) SELF-PREFERENCE — the judge shares a model/vendor family with the system under test, so self-enhancement bias is a live risk; flag it explicitly and prefer an independent judge family. (c) VERBOSITY — check the judge's score against answer length on a labeled cohort; a strong positive correlation with no length-normalized rubric means it may be rewarding length, not quality. And validate against a frozen, human-labeled cohort with a named agreement bar (strong judges reach roughly >=80% agreement with human preference), re-checked when the judge model version changes — an unpinned judge is as unreliable as an unpinned embedding model. The reported win rate is uninterpretable until at least the order-swap and independence checks are done. (testing-ai-evals.md.)
expectations: Says temp-0/high-win-rate is not trustworthy yet — determinism and self-consistency are not precision/validity
Prescribes the order-swap test for positional bias (SUT always first) and flags self-preference bias from the judge sharing the SUT's model/vendor family

Adds verbosity-correlation check + validation against a human-labeled cohort with a defined agreement threshold (bonus: strong judges reach ~>=80% agreement, Zheng et al.), re-checked when the judge model version changes

evals.prompt: After a CSRF incident on `/transfer`, the team added an Origin check to that one endpoint. Other cookie-authenticated mutating endpoints (`POST /settings`, `POST /delete-account`) were not touched, and the shared JSON body parser also accepts `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. Is the CSRF fix complete?
evals.expected_output: No, on two counts. (1) A CSRF guard on one route is not a guard on the class: grep every cookie-authenticated MUTATING route (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) and confirm the guard is wired into all of them — `/settings` and `/delete-account` are still exposed, the same one-callsite-instead-of-the-whole-class miss the review scopes to its full instance set (Phase 4). (2) The shared parser accepting `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` (or `text/plain` / `multipart/form-data`) is reachable by the classic HTML-form-to-JSON CSRF — a cross-site `<form>` can POST those content-types with no CORS preflight, so 'we only take JSON' is false unless the parser enforces `Content-Type: application/json` and rejects a mismatch. Fix: census every mutating route × {guard present?, parser content-type-gated?}; put the guard on the whole class and make the parser reject non-JSON content-types (and/or add a real anti-CSRF token). (security-appsec.md.)
expectations: Flags that the guard must cover the whole class of cookie-auth mutating routes (grep them all — /settings, /delete-account still open), not just /transfer (Phase 4 full-instance-set)
Flags the form-urlencoded/text-plain-accepting parser as an HTML-form-to-JSON CSRF bypass (cross-site form, no preflight) — require Content-Type: application/json and reject a mismatch
Prescribes the census (every mutating route × {guard present, parser content-type-gated}) rather than a single-route patch

evals.prompt: An admin endpoint admits when `timingSafeEqual(req.header('x-admin-token'), process.env.ADMIN_TOKEN)` returns true — a constant-time comparison. In one deployment `ADMIN_TOKEN` is set to `admin123`. The compare is correct and constant-time. Is the gate sound?
evals.expected_output: No — constant-time compare and secret strength are separate properties, and this fails the second. The token gates ADMISSION, so a short/low-entropy value like `admin123` is brute-forceable no matter how the comparison is written; `timingSafeEqual` only closes a timing side-channel, it does not make a weak secret strong. Enforce a minimum length AND entropy where the secret is USED (reject a too-short/low-entropy value at load and fail closed) — not only where a generator would create it, since a strong generator doesn't stop a hand-set env value in one deployment. This is admit-direction weakness, which outranks an exclude-direction gap (a weak admit secret grants access; a weak exclude filter only over-blocks). Detect it by grepping for the floor itself (a length/entropy check at the compare site), not the secret's name — the guard was never written. (security-appsec.md.)
expectations: Says constant-time compare is not sufficient — a short/low-entropy admit secret (admin123) is brute-forceable regardless; strength and timing are separate properties
Prescribes an enforced length AND entropy floor at the point of use (reject weak value at load, fail closed), not only at generation
Notes admit-direction outranks exclude-direction, and detection is grepping for the floor constant/check at the compare site, not the secret's name

evals.prompt: A PR titled 'refactor: rename UserService methods' is 1,800 lines. Most of it is the mechanical rename, but buried in the diff is a brand-new `POST /admin/export` route. How should the reviewer scope this DIFF — and does the 'refactor' framing set the depth?
evals.expected_output: No — the PR's title and size are not the depth budget; classify each hunk by kind and route each at matched depth. The renames are **mechanical**: fast confirm-it-is-mechanical read (verify no behavior rode in — a moved guard, a flipped default, a widened type — on the renamed call sites). The `POST /admin/export` route is **new-surface** (a new endpoint/trust boundary), so it gets the **full Phase 3 adversarial opener set regardless of the 'refactor' title**: anonymous-GET/route sweep (is it reachable unauthenticated?), two-principal object-swap (can principal A export B's data?), dual-surface every caller of the loader (API vs SSR/RSC — one redacting while another does not), then injection/SSRF/traversal on its inputs — and, since it's an export, the export-is-a-sharper-leak-surface check (`security-appsec.md`). A new endpoint buried in a refactor PR is both the highest-risk change and the easiest to wave through at face value; the bucket, not the PR framing, sets the depth. (This is depth classification, distinct from Phase 0's blast-radius ordering, which only ranks what to review first.) (method.md Phase 2.)
expectations: Rejects letting the 'refactor' title/1800-line size set the depth — classify hunks by kind and route each at matched depth

Identifies POST /admin/export as new-surface → the FULL Phase 3 opener set (anon/route sweep, two-principal object-swap, dual-surface caller check, injection/SSRF) — every opener, not a subset — regardless of the PR title; notes export = sharper leak surface belonging in the dual-surface census
Treats the renames as mechanical (fast confirm no behavior rode in — moved guard/flipped default), and distinguishes this depth-classification from Phase 0 blast-radius ordering

evals.prompt: A 2,000-line DIFF is almost entirely a repository-wide formatter run (whitespace/quote style), plus one 12-line change to the session-authentication path. The reviewer has limited time. How should they spend it?
evals.expected_output: Not by spreading attention evenly across 2,000 lines. Classify by kind: the formatter hunks are **mechanical** — a fast confirm-it-is-mechanical pass (spot-check that it is truly format-only: no logic, no moved guard, no changed default rode in under the reflow — a real risk when a formatter run is used to camouflage a behavioral edit), which can lean on a format-only tool/diff view. Nearly all the depth goes to the **behavioral** 12-line auth-path change: full domain audit (domain B), the failure-direction (fail-open vs fail-closed) weighing, and a Phase 3 probe if it touches a guard/precondition. The 2,000-line size is not the depth budget — the 12 behavioral lines on the auth path carry essentially all the risk. Confirm the formatter didn't also smuggle a behavioral change (the mechanical bucket's whole job is to be sure it's mechanical). (method.md Phase 2.)
expectations: Rejects uniform attention across 2,000 lines — classify by kind; the size is not the depth budget
Routes nearly all depth to the 12-line behavioral auth-path change (full domain-B audit + fail-open/closed + a Phase 3 probe if a guard/precondition changed)
Gives the formatter bulk a fast mechanical-confirm pass that verifies no logic/guard/default rode in under the reflow (formatter-as-camouflage risk)

evals.prompt: A dashboard renders three <section> panels for 'Recent Orders', 'Recent Refunds', and 'Recent Disputes' via a shared <DashboardPanel> component. The first two pass an aria-label prop; a later contributor copy-pasted the JSX for the disputes panel and dropped the aria-label prop. All three render as visually identical bordered panels with headings. Is there an accessibility problem, and would a visual review catch it?
evals.expected_output: Yes, and a visual review would miss it. An HTML <section> is exposed to assistive tech as an ARIA region landmark only when it has an accessible name (aria-label, aria-labelledby, or title); the disputes <section> with no name maps to no landmark role at all -- it is not a badly-labeled region, it is simply absent from landmark/rotor navigation. A screen-reader user browsing by region reaches 'Recent Orders' and 'Recent Refunds' but never 'Recent Disputes', with no visual cue anything is missing, because the three panels render identically. Fix: pass the same aria-label (or aria-labelledby) prop the other two instances already receive. Detection is a landmark/rotor list pulled from the accessibility tree, not the DOM or a screenshot -- the difference between the three instances is a single missing prop, easy to miss by eye across separate call sites.
expectations: Identifies that the unnamed <section> maps to no ARIA landmark role at all (not merely an unlabeled one) and is therefore absent from landmark/rotor navigation
States that a visual/screenshot review cannot catch this because all three panels render identically -- the gap only shows up in the accessibility tree / landmark list
Prescribes passing the same aria-label/aria-labelledby the sibling instances already receive, and detecting via the landmark/rotor list rather than the DOM

evals.prompt: A combobox-style filter dropdown opens a listbox on click; pressing Escape or clicking outside closes it via a single isOpen boolean, with no other focus handling. QA confirms the modal dialog elsewhere in the app correctly returns focus to its trigger button when it closes. Is the dropdown's focus handling adequate?
evals.expected_output: No. The restore-focus-to-the-trigger rule the modal correctly implements is not modal-specific -- it applies to any dismissible overlay: popover, dropdown/select menu, combobox listbox, flyout, or click-triggered tooltip. A bare isOpen boolean plus an Escape/outside-click handler with no captured trigger ref and no .focus() call back onto it means that on close, focus falls to <body> -- a keyboard user who opened the filter is dumped at the top of the page with no sense of where they were, even though the identical bug is already fixed for the modal elsewhere in the same app. Fix: capture the trigger element's ref when the dropdown opens and call .focus() on it from every path that closes the dropdown (Escape, outside-click, and item-selection alike) -- the same shape the modal's close function already uses.
expectations: States that restore-focus-to-the-trigger is not modal-specific -- it applies to the whole dismissible-overlay class (popover, dropdown/select menu, combobox listbox, flyout, tooltip)
Identifies the tell: a bare boolean open/close state with an Escape/outside-click handler that never captures a trigger ref or calls .focus() back on close

States the consequence -- focus falls to <body> on close, disorienting a keyboard user -- and prescribes restoring focus in every dismiss path (Escape, outside-click, selection), mirroring the modal's already-correct pattern

evals.prompt: A shared-services quality dashboard shows a 'check failure rate' per team. A shared internal library has no single owning team, so it is excluded from every team's `checks_total` (denominator) -- ownerless entities aren't attributed to anyone. But when the shared library fails a check, the alerting rule fans the failure out to every team that imports it, incrementing each importing team's `checks_failed` (numerator). Team Falcon's and Team Osprey's failure rates both spiked this week this week even though neither team's own code regressed. What's the review finding?
evals.expected_output: The numerator and denominator use different attribution rules for the same shared entity. The numerator attributes the shared library's failure under a broad fan-out rule (every importing team gets charged), while the denominator attributes membership under a strict single-owner rule (the ownerless library has no owner to credit, so it is in no team's checks_total). That charges the failure to every importing team's numerator while it sits in no team's denominator -- inflating the ratio for every team that imports the library, and making it undefined (divide-by-zero) for any team whose entities are all shared/ownerless. Each team's own row-level increment is individually correct, which is why no single-row check catches it -- and this is distinct from denominator integrity's entity-type-eligibility case, since every row here is the right type. Fix: derive the numerator and the denominator from the same membership/attribution rule for the same entity -- both fan-out, or both single-owner, never mixed.
expectations: Identifies that the numerator (fan-out to every importing team) and the denominator (strict single-owner, excludes the ownerless library) apply different attribution rules to the same shared entity
States the shared library's failure is charged to every importing team's numerator while counted in no team's denominator -- inflating, or making undefined, every affected team's ratio
Prescribes the fix: numerator and denominator must derive from the same membership/attribution rule for the shared entity, not a mismatched pair

evals.prompt: A metrics pipeline renders `attainment_pct` with this guard before appending a '%' sign: `if (value < 1) { value = value * 100 }` -- meant to catch an analyst who passed a raw 0-1 fraction instead of an already-converted percent. A downstream dashboard now shows one key result at '5000%'. What's the review finding?
evals.expected_output: The guard is asymmetric by construction: it checks only a lower bound (value < 1) and has no upper bound, so any value that lands above 1 sails through unchanged with no error. Here a value already expressed as a percent (e.g. 0.5 meaning 50%) was run through the conversion twice -- 0.5 * 100 * 100 = 5000 -- and nothing caught it because the guard only ever asks 'is this below 1', never 'is this an implausible percent'. The same hole lets a metric that can legitimately exceed 100% (an attainment or index over par) render correctly by accident but leaves no way to distinguish that from a real double-conversion bug. Fix: extend the guard to a plausible range check with a sane upper bound sized to what this specific metric can actually take -- the question 'can this metric legitimately exceed 100%?' sets the bound -- and fail loud (flag it) rather than silently clamping or rendering whatever number falls out.
expectations: Identifies the guard as asymmetric -- it checks only a lower bound (value < 1) and has no upper bound
Explains a value above 1 (here, a double *100 conversion producing 5000) passes through rendered wrong (it shows the wrong value, no error) with no error
Prescribes extending the guard with a plausible upper-bound range check sized to the metric's own semantics, failing loud instead of silently clamping

evals.prompt: Our monorepo's CI only runs migration-safety checks when migrations changed. The change-detection step runs `git diff origin/release-v2...HEAD --name-only | grep -q '^db/migrations/'`. `release-v2` was cut eight months ago; our long-lived `integration` branch is hundreds of commits ahead of it now, and the migration-check step reports 'changed' on every PR, even ones touching only `docs/`. Separately, in a shallow-clone CI job (`fetch-depth: 1`) that never fetched `release-v2`, that same `git diff origin/release-v2...HEAD` step errored (`fatal: bad revision`) and the `grep -q` swallowed the failure, so the migration check silently reported 'unchanged' and never ran on a PR that genuinely added a migration. What's wrong, and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: The change-detection diff is pinned to a hardcoded, stale ref (`release-v2`) instead of the branch's actual base -- its configured upstream `@{u}`, the PR's declared target branch, or a computed `git merge-base <base> HEAD`. That stale constant drifts both ways: once `integration` runs far ahead of it, the diff spans the branch's entire history since the cut, so every push false-positives as 'changed' -- noise/cost, not a correctness issue by itself. The silent (dangerous) direction is not positional: a three-dot/merge-base diff correctly reports a branch's downstream commits even against a stale-but-resolvable ref. The false-green comes from the literal ref failing to RESOLVE -- in a shallow/partial checkout that never fetched `release-v2`, `git diff origin/release-v2...HEAD` errors and a naive `grep -q` reads the empty/failed output as 'unchanged', so the migration job silently skips with nothing turning red. Fail closed: a change-detection diff that errors or can't resolve its base must run the job (or fail the run), never skip. Fix: derive the base at run time (never a literal branch/tag name) and have the gate name the base it actually diffed against in its output, so a spurious result is diagnosable. This is distinct from a PR opened against the wrong target branch -- that's PR targeting; this is the diff-base a local change-detection script uses to decide scope.
expectations: Identifies the change-detection diff as pinned to a hardcoded, stale ref (`release-v2`) instead of the branch's actual base -- @{u}, the PR's declared target, or a computed `git merge-base <base> HEAD` -- and requires deriving it at run time instead of hardcoding a release-branch constant

Explains both failure directions: a branch running ahead of the constant balloons the diff to the branch's whole history so every push false-positives as 'changed' (noise/cost); and the dangerous silent direction is the literal ref failing to RESOLVE in a shallow/partial checkout (not a positional 'behind' -- merge-base/three-dot correctly detects downstream commits), so the diff errors and a naive grep swallows it as 'unchanged' -> the job skips. Requires failing closed on an errored/unresolved base.

Requires the gate to name the base ref it actually diffed against in its output so a spurious 'changed'/'unchanged' result is diagnosable, and distinguishes this from a PR opened against the wrong target branch (PR targeting) -- a different mechanism sharing the same hardcoded-constant-instead-of-computed-base root cause

evals.prompt: A support-ticket list component fetches `{ tickets, total }` for the current filter. The header reads `${total} open tickets` (currently "47 open tickets", a correct separate count query). The body renders `tickets.slice(0, 10)` with no page control, footer link, or "+N more" text -- it just stops after 10 rows. Separately, whenever `tickets.length === 0` the component renders "No tickets match -- try adjusting your filters," and that same branch is what renders on a fetch error, on a 403 from a permission check, and on a genuinely empty filtered result -- the component does not distinguish them. Sign off this list view as done?
evals.expected_output: No, two separate defects. First: the "47 open tickets" header being correct does not prove the 10 rendered rows are the whole set -- the count and the sliced list are two independent reads of the same data, and a user has no way to know 37 more exist. Add an explicit remainder indicator ("+37 more", a page control, or "Show all 47") whenever `total > shown`. Second: "No tickets match -- try adjusting your filters" asserts a specific cause (an over-narrow filter) and is only honest when a filtered-to-zero query is the *only* way the empty branch renders -- here a fetch error and a permission denial reach the same branch, so a permission-denied user is wrongly told to change filters, and a fetch failure reads as "no matches." Enumerate every path that reaches `tickets.length === 0` and either branch the copy per cause or fall back to a cause-neutral empty state, rather than trust one hardcoded string for all of them. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Flags the missing remainder indicator: a correct top-line count (47) does not prove the sliced list of 10 is complete, and requires an explicit "+N more"/pagination/"show all" affordance whenever total exceeds shown
Flags the hardcoded empty-state copy as a fabricated cause because the same zero-rows branch is reachable via a fetch error and a permission denial, not only the filtered-empty case the message names

Requires enumerating every path that reaches the empty branch and either branching the copy per cause or falling back to a cause-neutral empty state, rather than trusting one hardcoded string for all paths

evals.prompt: A PR against a private repository changes a dashboard's layout. The PR body's "Screens-changed evidence" section contains only `![dashboard after](https://raw.acme-vcs.example/AcmeWidgets/app/main/artifacts/dashboard-after.png)`, and the status line reads "Screenshot attached -- dashboard renders correctly at 390/1440." A teammate opens the PR cold to review it and sees a broken-image icon where the screenshot should be. Does the screens-changed gate pass?
evals.expected_output: No. A markdown image tag pointing at a private raw-content host is not evidence unless it actually renders for the reviewer -- that host requires an authenticated session or an auth header a plain `` fetch cannot supply, so it renders for the PR's author (who is signed in) and shows broken for a cold reviewer on a private repo. The tag existing in the PR body is not the same as the evidence existing (existence is not content, full-map.md principle 2) -- the author has verified a link, not a screen. Gate on visibility, not presence: re-attach the image as an uploaded attachment served through the review platform's own proxy, or commit an in-repo diff-able image file; a raw-content-host link does not satisfy the bar even when the file behind it is a real, correct screenshot. (ux-gates.md.)
expectations: Answers no / gate not satisfied -- a markdown image linking to a private raw-content host is not valid screens-changed evidence

Explains the mechanism: the raw host needs auth a reviewer's plain image fetch can't supply, so it renders broken for a cold reviewer on a private repo even though the markdown tag exists (existence is not content)
Requires the fix to be an uploaded attachment or an in-repo diff-able image file, not re-verifying the same raw-content-host link

evals.prompt: An SSE dashboard's clients each implement exponential backoff on reconnect, correctly capped and doubling after every failed attempt. The service does a rolling restart that drops all 4,000 open connections within the same second. Thirty seconds later, the newly healthy service falls over again under a spike of reconnect traffic. The per-client backoff logic is verified correct in isolation. What's missing?
evals.expected_output: Jitter. Every client's exponential backoff is anchored to the same drop instant (the rolling restart), so every client computes the same wait and they all retry at the same instant — a synchronized reconnect storm the service, barely back up, cannot absorb. Backoff alone only protects against one client's own repeated failures; it does nothing when the correlation source is external (the server's own restart), because every client was driven into the same state at the same time. Fix: randomize each client's wait inside its backoff window (jitter) so reconnects spread out instead of clustering. This is not the same jitter as a single caller's own retry policy (reliability-error-handling.md) or a cache-key expiry stampede (performance-db-cost.md) — both of those correlate independent callers on a shared key or a shared failure; here a server-side mass-disconnect event is the synchronizer correlating otherwise-unrelated clients on a shared instant. (api-contracts.md, Streaming transports.)
expectations: Identifies missing jitter as the cause — correct per-client exponential backoff still retries in lockstep when every client's schedule is anchored to the same server-side drop instant

Distinguishes this from per-request retry jitter (reliability-error-handling.md) and cache-stampede jitter (performance-db-cost.md): those correlate on a shared key/failure, this correlates on a shared drop instant caused by the server's own restart
Fix is randomizing each client's wait inside its backoff window so reconnects spread out, not just widening or capping the backoff further

evals.prompt: A chat service keeps subscriptions in a single Map<userId, WebSocket> inside each server process. It works perfectly in staging (one instance). In production, it runs behind a load balancer at 6 replicas with round-robin routing, and users intermittently stop receiving messages sent by other users — no errors in the logs, no dropped connections, no crash. What's the mechanism, and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: The registry is process-local. Each of the 6 replicas has its own private Map that only knows the sockets it personally accepted; a publish handled by the replica that received the sender's request has no way to reach a recipient whose WebSocket happens to be held open on a different replica, so the message is silently dropped — no exception, because from that replica's point of view the recipient was simply never connected. This is a scope mismatch, not the lifetime mismatch that governs most in-process shared-state bugs (the Map's lifetime is fine — it's that it never sees the other 5 replicas' connections that's wrong), and it's a wrong-answer/silent-delivery-loss bug, not a backpressure, liveness, or DoS issue. Fix: move fan-out through a layer shared across processes — a pub/sub adapter (e.g. Redis pub/sub, NATS) every replica subscribes to, so a publish on any replica reaches every replica's local sockets — or route each user's traffic to the one replica holding their socket with sticky/session-affinity routing. (concurrency-shared-state.md, In-process races.)
expectations: Identifies that the in-process Map<userId, socket> is scoped to one replica — a publish handled by replica A never reaches a socket held on replica B, with no error or exception

Names this a scope mismatch distinct from the file's lifetime-mismatch bugs (the registry's lifetime is fine; it's cross-process scope that's wrong), and distinct from backpressure/liveness/DoS findings
Fix is a shared fan-out layer (pub/sub adapter such as Redis pub/sub or NATS) or sticky/session-affinity routing to the replica holding the socket — not a lock or in-process fix

evals.prompt: A gRPC client opens a long-lived server-streaming RPC that receives a new message only every few minutes. To detect a dead connection quickly, an engineer sets the client's keepalive ping interval (KEEPALIVE_TIME) to 10 seconds. In production, against a server running gRPC's default settings, the stream gets torn down every few minutes with a GOAWAY frame carrying debug data 'too_many_pings' — even though the network and both processes are healthy. What's happening, and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: The client's aggressive keepalive is the problem, not a symptom of a dead peer: gRPC's own keepalive guide states that if the service does not support keepalive, the first few keepalive pings will be ignored, and the server will eventually send a GOAWAY message with debug data equal to the ASCII code for too_many_pings. The server's default minimum-allowed gap between pings carrying no data (PERMIT_KEEPALIVE_TIME) is 5 minutes; a 10-second client ping interval on an RPC that isn't otherwise sending data blows through that default many times over, so the server's keepalive policy rejects the pings and tears the connection down with GOAWAY — the opposite of what the client intended. This is a different failure than a missed WebSocket pong (that's each side detecting the other is gone); here the client's own liveness probe is what gets it disconnected by a healthy, default-configured peer. Fix: raise the client's keepalive interval to something the server's PERMIT_KEEPALIVE_TIME allows, or explicitly raise the server's PERMIT_KEEPALIVE_TIME / enable PERMIT_KEEPALIVE_WITHOUT_CALLS to match the client's intended policy — both sides' keepalive configuration has to agree. (api-contracts.md, Streaming transports.)
expectations: Identifies that the client's own aggressive keepalive pings — not a dead network or dead peer — lead the server's keepalive policy to reject them with GOAWAY(too_many_pings), because the server's default PERMIT_KEEPALIVE_TIME (5 minutes) is far looser than the client's 10-second interval

Distinguishes this from liveness detection (e.g. a missed WebSocket pong detecting the peer is gone): here the prober itself gets disconnected by a healthy peer enforcing its own keepalive-cadence policy

Fix requires matching both sides' keepalive policy (raise the client interval, or raise the server's PERMIT_KEEPALIVE_TIME / allow PERMIT_KEEPALIVE_WITHOUT_CALLS) rather than treating it as a network problem

evals.prompt: A profile-editing PR does two things. (1) The API's `PATCH /api/profile` mutation now requires a `timezone` field; the fix updates the Quick-Edit modal, which builds its payload via `buildProfilePayload(fields)`, to pass `timezone`. The Full-Profile page also calls `PATCH /api/profile`, building its own field list through the same `buildProfilePayload` helper, but the PR does not touch it. (2) The same PR adds a compact Team Roster row showing each member's avatar. Everywhere else, initials are computed by the shared `getInitials(fullName)` helper, which returns only a first-and-last initial (e.g. "Jane Smith" -> "JS") so the compact UI never renders a full surname. The new roster row instead adds its own local helper, `shortName(fullName)`, returning the first initial plus the full last name ("J. Smith"), because it fit the column better. Is this PR done?
evals.expected_output: No — both changes are lockstep-adapter drift, and one of them is worse than a style nit. (1) The timezone fix landed only at the call site the ticket named; the Full-Profile page calls the same mutation through the same buildProfilePayload helper but was never re-checked, so it still sends the pre-fix field set and the PATCH will now fail (or the field silently defaults) for that caller. Closing the fix requires grepping every other call site of PATCH /api/profile / buildProfilePayload and diffing the field set each one actually sends, not just the one the bug report pointed at. (2) shortName is a divergent copy of the initials/short-label family, found by grepping the family of derived-name helpers (any function computing a short display form of a full name), not by grepping the one name getInitials. Because the canonical helper's one-initial-plus-one-initial shape is a deliberate data-minimization cap — it exists specifically so the compact UI never discloses a full surname — the roster row's version discloses more of the user's name than the design intends: that is a privacy/compliance gap, not a cosmetic inconsistency, and should be raised at that severity, not filed as a UI-consistency nit.
expectations: Requires grepping every other call site of the shared mutation/body-builder and diffing the field set each one sends, rather than treating the ticket's one named call site as the whole fix
Finds the divergent shortName helper by grepping the initials/short-label helper family, not the single name getInitials
Identifies the divergence as a privacy/compliance gap because the canonical helper's short form is a deliberate data-minimization cap — not merely a visual/style inconsistency

evals.prompt: An ingestion service validates incoming analytics events against a hand-maintained constant, ALLOWED_KIND_CATEGORY_PAIRS, a list of (kind, category) tuples; any event whose pair isn't in the list is dropped and counted as rejected_unknown_pair. The events themselves are produced by a code-generated client, built from a schema file a separate team owns; the schema recently gained a new pair, ("refund", "partial"), and the generated client now happily emits it. Nobody updated ALLOWED_KIND_CATEGORY_PAIRS. rejected_unknown_pair has been quietly climbing for a week and nobody has looked at it. Is the hand-maintained allow-list just tech debt, or is there an active bug, and what should the review require?
evals.expected_output: There's an active bug, and it's a generated-vs-source lockstep failure, not ordinary tech debt: ALLOWED_KIND_CATEGORY_PAIRS is a manually-maintained enum/allow-list coupled to whatever the schema's generated client actually emits, and the two have drifted — the generator can now produce ("refund", "partial") but the hand-written list doesn't have it, so every one of those events is silently dropped as rejected_unknown_pair. That counter climbing is the drift already firing in production, not a hypothetical. The review should require: (1) enumerating every (kind, category) combination the schema/generator can actually emit (walk the schema, or run the generator against its full domain) and diffing that set against the allow-list, not just the pairs seen in current tests or sample data, and (2) closing the gap by deriving the allow-list from the same schema the client is generated from — one generated source — rather than re-approving pairs by hand each time the schema changes, so the next new pair can't silently regress the same way.
expectations: Identifies the allow-list as a generated-vs-source pair coupled to the schema/generator's output, not merely an out-of-date list to refresh
Requires diffing the allow-list against every combination the generator/schema can actually emit, not just pairs seen in current tests or sample data

Ties the climbing rejected_unknown_pair counter to the missing ("refund","partial") pair as the live drift, and prescribes deriving the allow-list from the same generated source instead of hand-maintaining it

evals.prompt: An end-to-end test shells out to a headless Chromium binary to render a page and capture a screenshot. It starts with `which chromium && run-render`, treating the binary as available whenever that line succeeds, and only skips when `which` itself fails. In a fresh CI container (the image's default root user, no extra setup beyond installing the browser package), `which chromium` passes — but the render step then crashes before producing an image. A teammate says: 'We already handle the missing-binary case with `which`; a crash after that must be a real product bug, not an environment problem.' Evaluate that reasoning and the test's design.
evals.expected_output: The reasoning is unsound. `which`/`command -v` only proves the binary is present on `PATH` — CI is 'present but different/broken,' not 'absent,' so a presence check passing tells you nothing about whether the binary can actually do what the test needs. A headless-Chromium binary run as root in a container commonly needs its sandbox configured explicitly (a non-root user, or an explicit launch flag) or the launch itself crashes before it renders anything — exactly the kind of environment-specific failure a `which` check cannot see, so the crash is at least as likely to be a container/launch-config defect as a product bug, and the team cannot tell which without more evidence. The test's design is the real problem: (1) it must gate on a functional smoke — actually invoke the binary on a trivial real case and confirm it produced output — and skip loudly with the captured error on ANY failure, not just a missing `which`; (2) it should supply its own required launch configuration explicitly (a non-root container user, or the flags its environment needs) instead of inheriting whatever the CI image's ambient defaults happen to be, so the failure is prevented rather than merely reclassified after the fact.
expectations: Identifies that which/command -v only proves PATH presence, not functional success — CI is 'present but different/broken,' not 'absent,' so a crash after a passing presence check is not evidence of a product bug over an environment defect

Names the concrete mechanism: a headless-Chromium binary run as root in a container commonly needs explicit sandbox configuration (a non-root user or an explicit launch flag) or it crashes before rendering — a failure a PATH check cannot detect

Prescribes fixing the test: gate on a functional smoke (a real invocation checked for actual success) that skips loudly with the captured error on any failure, and have the test supply its own required launch configuration explicitly rather than depend on the runner ambient setup

evals.prompt: A service reads a DynamoDB item with GetItem, increments a counter field in application code, and writes the whole item back with a plain PutItem that has no ConditionExpression. Under concurrent requests hitting the same item, the counter periodically loses increments even though every individual PutItem call succeeds. What is the root cause, and what is the fix?
evals.expected_output: The plain PutItem always overwrites whatever is currently stored, regardless of what the preceding GetItem returned -- with no ConditionExpression there is nothing tying the write to the value that was read, so two concurrent get-then-put cycles both succeed and the second silently clobbers the first's increment. Unlike a SQL read-modify-write, there is no wrapping transaction or row lock available for a single-item DynamoDB operation to fall back on -- the conditional clause on the write itself is the only guard that exists. Fix: add a ConditionExpression that repeats the value or a version attribute read in the GetItem (e.g. the counter equals the value just read, or a version number equals the value just read), so a write that raced against another writer fails with a conditional-check error instead of overwriting, and the caller re-reads and retries.
expectations: Identifies the missing ConditionExpression (or equivalent optimistic-write guard) as the root cause -- the plain PutItem always overwrites whatever is currently stored, regardless of what GetItem returned

States that unlike a SQL read-modify-write, there is no wrapping transaction or row lock to fall back on for a single-item DynamoDB operation -- the conditional clause on the write itself is the only guard available

Fix names a ConditionExpression keyed on the previously-read value or version attribute so a stale write fails with a conditional-check error instead of silently overwriting, and the caller re-reads and retries

evals.prompt: Right after a service successfully writes a new order item to a DynamoDB table (HTTP 200 from PutItem), it queries a Global Secondary Index on that table to build a confirmation page listing the order. In staging this always works; in production the confirmation page intermittently shows the order missing from the list, even though a GetItem against the base table for the same order always succeeds immediately after the write. Why, and what should the review flag?
evals.expected_output: DynamoDB Global Secondary Index reads are always eventually consistent and the index is populated asynchronously from the base table -- a successful base-table write (HTTP 200) durably persists the item but does not guarantee the GSI already reflects it. Unlike the base table or a local secondary index, a GSI has no strongly-consistent read option at all: ConsistentRead is not supported on GSI queries, so there is no read-your-writes escape hatch on that path. Staging masks the bug because propagation is normally sub-second and staging's low concurrency/load rarely exposes the tail; production sees real, if occasional, longer propagation delays. Fix: read the base table (or a strongly consistent LSI) for the just-written item on the confirmation path instead of querying the GSI, or explicitly design the caller to tolerate and retry across a bounded staleness window.
expectations: Identifies that Global Secondary Index reads are always eventually consistent and asynchronously propagated from the base table -- a successful base-table write does not guarantee the GSI already reflects it

States that, unlike the base table or a local secondary index, a GSI has no strongly-consistent read option at all (ConsistentRead is not supported on GSI queries) -- there is no read-your-writes escape hatch on that path

Fix routes the just-written item's read through the base table (or explicitly handles bounded staleness) instead of assuming the GSI is read-after-write consistent, and notes that a low-latency/low-load staging environment can mask lag that surfaces intermittently in production

evals.prompt: A Cassandra table enforces a uniqueness invariant on a partition using a lightweight transaction: INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS. Separately, an operator cleanup script issues a plain (non-conditional) DELETE and a plain INSERT against rows in the same partition to 'fix' some bad data. After the cleanup script runs, the uniqueness invariant is occasionally violated again, even though every application code path still writes exclusively through the IF NOT EXISTS guard. What is going on?
evals.expected_output: Cassandra lightweight transactions use the Paxos protocol and a timestamping/ballot mechanism that is distinct from normal reads and writes. DataStax's own documentation warns that lightweight transactions use a timestamping mechanism different from normal operations and that mixing LWTs and normal operations on the same partition can result in errors -- once a partition is guarded by an LWT, only LWTs (for both reads and writes) should touch it. The cleanup script's plain DELETE/INSERT bypasses the Paxos round entirely, so it can race past the guard and reintroduce a duplicate the IF NOT EXISTS check was meant to prevent. This is the same 'a guard must intercept every mutation primitive' shape as an application-level CAS check bypassed by a direct, unconditional write -- just enforced at the storage-engine level instead of the application level. Fix: the cleanup script must also use conditional operations (IF EXISTS / IF NOT EXISTS) against that partition, with no unconditional write path left for ops/cleanup tooling to take.
expectations: Identifies that Cassandra lightweight transactions (Paxos-based) use a different timestamping/consensus mechanism than normal writes, and that mixing LWT and non-LWT operations on the same partition is documented to be able to produce errors or violate the guarded invariant

States the fix as: once any row in a partition is guarded by a lightweight transaction, every writer and reader touching that partition -- including one-off ops/cleanup scripts -- must also use the conditional (IF / IF NOT EXISTS / IF EXISTS) path, not just the normal application write path

Frames this as the same 'a guard must intercept every mutation primitive' shape as an application-level CAS/version check bypassed by a direct unconditional write -- just enforced at the storage-engine level rather than the application level

evals.prompt: `<PromoBanner />` lives in `src/components/PromoBanner.tsx`, is exported from the components barrel file, and has a unit test (`PromoBanner.test.tsx`) that renders it directly and asserts the discount copy shows. Lint and the test suite are green. A grep across every route file, page, and layout in the app turns up zero imports of `PromoBanner` outside its own test file. Is this component fine to leave as-is since it's tested and lint-clean?
evals.expected_output: No -- this is a dead-render candidate. A unit test that does `render(<PromoBanner />)` mounts the component directly, so the suite being green proves the component behaves correctly in isolation; it proves nothing about whether any real route ever shows it to a user. Exported + tested + lint-clean makes the file look alive, but with zero mount paths from any router entry, page, or layout, nothing in the running app puts it in front of anyone. This is the proactive counterpart of 'fix the surface that renders' (which disambiguates which of several live surfaces a grep hit belongs to) -- here the trace finds no live surface at all. Detection: walk the router/page tree inward from every entry; a component reachable from no entry, only from its own test, is the tell. Flag it to wire it up (find or add the missing mount) or retire it -- retirement is an owner call under 'Decisions needed,' not a unilateral delete. (ux-components.md.)
expectations: Identifies PromoBanner as a dead-render candidate despite a green unit test and clean lint/export, because a test that renders the component directly proves isolated behavior, not that any router/page entry mounts it; and flags the zero-import result as a CANDIDATE / unverified pending a check for React.lazy()/dynamic import()/a component registry/runtime-built route config, not an auto-confirmed dead component (retirement is an owner call).

Requires tracing from every router/page/layout entry inward to confirm zero mount paths, distinguishing this from the 'which live surface renders a grep hit' check (there is no live surface at all here)
Recommends flagging the component to be wired up or retired as an owner decision, not deleting it unilaterally

evals.prompt: A security dashboard has two panels fed by separate API calls. Panel A, "You might also like," is a supplementary recommendations rail; when its fetch throws, the catch block logs the error and renders the same empty state as a genuine zero recommendations: a muted "Nothing to show." Panel B, "Account access log," lists every login and permission change; its fetch is wrapped the same way -- on a fetch error it also falls through to render "No access events," identical to what a genuinely-clean account shows. Is this pattern -- one shared catch-to-empty fallback -- fine for both panels?
evals.expected_output: No, not for both -- the two panels carry different stakes and that changes what's acceptable. Panel A is a low-stakes, supplementary value: a wrong read (the user thinks there are no recommendations when the fetch actually failed) costs little, so degrading a fetch failure straight to the ordinary empty render is a reasonable simplification, not a defect worth its own error-and-retry UI. Panel B is a value the user reads as a definitive statement about history: "No access events" means, to a reader, "confirmed: nothing happened" -- exactly what an attacker or an auditor needs to be false. Swallowing a fetch error into that same empty branch manufactures a false all-clear that no copy wording can fix, because the defect is architectural (no distinguishable error path), not lexical. Panel B must surface a distinct, retryable error state instead of falling through to empty. This is a third axis, independent of whether the empty copy honestly names its coverage or its cause -- the stakes of misreading empty-as-confirmed-none. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Distinguishes the two panels by stakes: accepts that the low-stakes recommendations rail (Panel A) may acceptably degrade a fetch failure into its ordinary empty state

Requires the audit/access-log panel (Panel B) to surface a distinct, retryable error state on fetch failure rather than falling through to the same empty branch as a genuine zero, because empty reads there as confirmed-none / a false all-clear

Frames this as an architectural requirement (a separate error path), not something fixable by rewording the empty-state copy, and as an axis distinct from whether the copy honestly names its coverage or cause

evals.prompt: A login bug where 'Jane' and 'jane' were treated as different accounts got fixed: the signup/write path now runs every username through a shared normalizeUsername() (NFC + Unicode case-fold) before storing it, and a backfill migration re-normalized every existing row. The team calls the bug closed. The login lookup was left untouched: db.users.findOne({ username: input.trim().toLowerCase() }). Is the fix complete?
evals.expected_output: No -- the write/index side was fixed but the login lookup was not, so the bug is still live at that call site. input.trim().toLowerCase() is an ad-hoc inline canonicalization that diverges from the shared normalizeUsername(): ASCII lowercasing is not the same as Unicode case-folding (e.g. Turkish İ/ı break a naive toLowerCase()), and this call performs no NFC either. A user whose stored, correctly-normalized username differs from the naively-lowercased login input fails to match -- the row is there, but this specific query never reaches it, so it looks like 'user not found' (missing data) rather than a comparison bug, and the write-side fix plus backfill makes the bug look closed. The reviewable property is symmetry: the write/index path and every read/query path must call the SAME shared normalization function. Fix: replace the inline .trim().toLowerCase() with normalizeUsername(input), then sweep every other lookup/compare against the username field itself -- not just ones matching this exact .trim().toLowerCase() pattern, since a lookup that normalizes not at all is the same defect -- one converted call site does not imply the rest were. (i18n-l10n.md.)
expectations: Identifies the login lookup's inline .trim().toLowerCase() as diverging from the shared normalizeUsername() -- not the same function

Explains the failure signature: the row exists but this query misses it, presenting as missing data / user-not-found rather than a comparison error -- and a write-side fix plus backfill can look complete while this call site still drifts

Requires the write/index path and every read/query path to call the same shared normalizer, and to sweep every other lookup against the normalized field itself (not just call sites matching this exact pattern -- a lookup with no normalization at all is the same defect) rather than treating the one reported call site as the whole fix

evals.prompt: A Lambda function is triggered by an SQS queue with a batch size of 10. Inside the handler, each record is processed in a try/catch; on failure the catch block logs the error and continues to the next record. The handler returns nothing (an implicit success) either way. The event source mapping has no FunctionResponseTypes configured. A teammate says the try/catch already makes this safe against a poison message. Review this design.
evals.expected_output: The teammate is wrong: the per-item try/catch only stops one bad record from crashing the whole invocation — it does not tell the platform which records actually failed. Because the handler returns a bare success and ReportBatchItemFailures is not enabled on the event source mapping, Lambda sees a clean invocation and deletes the entire batch, including the records that hit the catch block and were never actually processed successfully — silent data loss with no error, no retry, no dead-letter entry. The fix needs both halves: the handler must collect failed message IDs and return them as a batchItemFailures list, and the event source mapping's FunctionResponseTypes must include ReportBatchItemFailures so Lambda actually reads that list instead of treating the invocation's mere return-without-exception as complete success. Either half alone is insufficient — code that reports failures is ignored if the config flag is off, and the config flag does nothing if the code never reports which items failed.
expectations: States that per-item try/catch bounds what the code does but does not control the platform's retry/delete unit — that is decided by the invocation's response shape plus the event-source-mapping config, not the code's control flow

Identifies the specific failure in the scenario: catching and logging errors internally while returning a bare/implicit success causes the platform to treat the whole batch as fully successful and delete it, so the caught failures are silently dropped (data loss), not retried or dead-lettered

Requires both fixes together — the handler must return a per-item failure list (e.g. batchItemFailures) AND the event source mapping must enable partial-batch reporting (e.g. ReportBatchItemFailures) — and states that neither change alone is sufficient

evals.prompt: A Lambda function has a DynamoDB Streams trigger on the Orders table: on every INSERT or MODIFY event it computes a derived 'shippingEta' field and writes the updated item back to the same Orders table. Code review of the function shows solid per-item error handling and no recursion in its own source. Overnight, the account's Lambda concurrency and DynamoDB write costs spike 40x with no corresponding rise in real order volume. Diagnose.
evals.expected_output: This is a self-amplifying recursive invocation loop, not a code bug the function's own source can show: writing the derived field back to the Orders table is itself a MODIFY event, which the same DynamoDB Streams trigger delivers back to the function, which writes again, forever — each invocation causing another, with no call stack and no depth counter, so a generic recursion-depth-cap review of the function's code finds nothing wrong (and didn't, per the prompt). The cycle lives in the trigger wiring between the table and the function (the event source mapping / stream trigger defined in IaC), a different artifact from the function's source, which is why a code-only review missed it. This matches the concurrency/cost-spike signature exactly: an unbroken loop burns spend and can consume the account's available Lambda concurrency. Some platforms (e.g. AWS Lambda) ship on-by-default recursive-loop detection, but it currently covers only loops between functions, SQS, S3, and SNS (stopping the chain at roughly its 16th hop via trace metadata) — a loop mediated by DynamoDB is a documented gap that detection does not currently cover, so nothing here would have auto-stopped it. Fix: break the cycle (write the derived field to a separate table/attribute the stream trigger ignores, filter the stream so a system-authored write doesn't re-trigger, or compute the field on read instead of writing it back), and add the review habit of tracing the resource-to-trigger graph (what each function writes to, and what triggers each function) for cycles, not just reading each function's source in isolation.
expectations: Identifies the mechanism as a recursive event-source invocation loop (the function's own write to the Orders table re-triggers itself via the same DynamoDB Streams trigger), not a bug visible in the function's code, and explains why: no call stack, no depth counter, so a generic recursion-depth review of the source finds nothing

States that the cycle lives in the trigger wiring / event-source mapping defined in IaC (a separate resource-to-resource wiring), not in the function's source, and connects it to the observed concurrency/cost-spike symptom

Names the platform detection gap as an example rather than assuming universal protection — e.g. AWS Lambda's recursive-loop detection covers function/SQS/S3/SNS cycles but not one mediated by DynamoDB — and prescribes tracing the resource-to-trigger graph for cycles plus breaking this one (e.g. writing to a separate table/attribute, filtering the stream, or computing the field on read) as the review action

evals.prompt: A bug fix needs the OrderSummary UI component to read the current shipping status. The fastest fix imports the DB client straight into the component (`import { db } from '../../infra/db-client'`) and queries the table inline.
