CI's `no-restricted-imports` layering rule -- UI code must not import the DB client, only the service layer may -- fails on the new import, so the PR adds `// eslint-disable-next-line no-restricted-imports` above it to get CI green. Is that the right fix?
evals.expected_output: No -- the layering rule is correctly calibrated (UI/DB separation is a real architectural boundary this rule exists to hold, not an accidental over-strict pattern), so the fix is what's wrong, not the gate. Suppressing it with eslint-disable trades a real defect -- an inline DB import from the presentation layer, which couples the component to schema, bypasses whatever the service layer enforces on that read (access checks, caching, error mapping), and re-opens the same hole at the next call site -- for a green CI run: a design problem wearing a gate problem's clothes. Getting the shipping status to the UI and keeping the UI off the DB client are both correct constraints in only apparent tension: the reconciling design is to add or extend a service-layer function (e.g. `getShippingStatus(orderId)` in the existing service module) that the component calls, landing the fix without touching the boundary rule at all. Never widen the eslint-disable or add an exception to the rule's allow-list to unblock one call site; if a reconciling design genuinely does not exist, that is an owner trade-off on the architecture, not a unilateral suppression. (method-situational.md.)
expectations: Identifies the import/layering rule as correctly calibrated -- the fix is wrong, not the gate
Rejects the eslint-disable (or widening the rule's exception list) as an acceptable fix

Prescribes the reconciling design -- add or extend a service-layer function the UI calls -- satisfying both the boundary rule and the bug fix, with any genuine no-reconciling-design case routed as an owner trade-off

evals.prompt: A shopping cart's total is computed as `total = sum(item.amount for item in items)`, where `item.amount` is a bare integer in minor units (cents) and each item carries its own `item.currency` field (some sellers on the marketplace list in USD, others in EUR). A `convert_to_usd(amount, currency)` helper exists, but it is only called when displaying the total to a US-based buyer -- the `total` used everywhere else, including a `total >= free_shipping_threshold_cents` check where `free_shipping_threshold_cents = 5000`, is the raw sum. Review this pricing path.
evals.expected_output: Applies the multi-currency-correctness lens (billing-correctness.md): summing item.amount across items of differing currencies is a type error, not a rounding nuance -- amount and currency are one inseparable value (Money value-object pattern), and a plain numeric sum silently treats 50 EUR and 50 USD as the same 50. The free-shipping threshold check compounds the bug by comparing that already-corrupted mixed-currency sum to a bare USD constant with no conversion. Converting only at display time is too late -- the total is wrong before it's ever shown, and every downstream decision (threshold check, tax base, reporting) that consumes the raw total inherits the error. Fix: give amounts a currency-aware type that refuses cross-currency arithmetic, or convert to one pinned currency before any sum/compare.
expectations: Flags summing item.amount across differing currencies as a type error, not a rounding nuance
Applies or names the Money value-object principle -- amount and currency travel together, never a bare number
Flags the free-shipping threshold compared directly against the mixed-currency sum with no conversion, and notes display-time-only conversion is too late

evals.prompt: A wallet/credits system tracks each user's spendable balance in a `wallets.balance` integer column, updated in place: `UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance + :delta WHERE user_id = :id`. Every top-up and spend also inserts a row into an append-only `wallet_transactions` table (id, user_id, delta, created_at), which today is used only to render the user's activity-history UI. Support periodically gets tickets where a user's displayed balance doesn't match what adding up their transaction history would give, especially after a burst of concurrent requests or a deploy that crashed mid-request. Review this design.
evals.expected_output: Applies the ledger-integrity lens (billing-correctness.md): wallets.balance is a mutable running-total column, not derived from the entry log, so nothing keeps it in agreement with wallet_transactions -- the UPDATE and the INSERT are two separate writes, not one atomic operation, so a crash or a race between concurrent requests can commit one and lose the other with no detection. wallet_transactions is being treated as a side audit trail instead of the source of truth. The fix is the double-entry-bookkeeping invariant: every transaction's debits sum to its credits and net to zero, and the balance must be derived as SUM(credits) - SUM(debits) over the append-only log rather than stored as a separately-updated column at all -- making the two writes atomic would only close the crash window, it would not stop the column from being a second, independently-wrong source of truth. The concurrent-mutation mechanics (compare-and-set) belong to concurrency-shared-state.md, not restated here.
expectations: Flags the mutable balance column as the defect -- balance must be derived (SUM(credits) minus SUM(debits)) from the append-only entry log, not updated in place
Explains the drift mechanism: the balance UPDATE and the transaction INSERT are not atomic, so a crash or race lets them disagree with no detection
Names or applies double-entry bookkeeping (debits sum to credits) as the correctness invariant, treating the entry log as the source of truth over the mutable column

evals.prompt: A nightly sync job upserts rows into a `subscribers` table keyed on `email` (the natural key; there is no surrogate id in the sync path). For each batch it: (1) SELECTs the emails already present, (2) in application code splits the incoming batch into `toInsert` (email absent from the SELECT) and skips the rest, (3) runs a single batch `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING` over `toInsert` as a safety net in case two sync runs overlap, and (4) logs and returns `inserted: toInsert.length`. During a deploy window, two sync runs are accidentally triggered concurrently and overlap in execution for the same source file. Both runs' logs show `inserted: 500` for the same 500 new emails, and both exit with no errors. The table gained only 500 rows total, not 1000. On-call is confused because both jobs reported full success. Review the upsert/reporting logic and explain what happened and what to fix.
evals.expected_output: The reviewer identifies that ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING is doing exactly its job as a race backstop -- one of the two concurrent runs' inserts is a genuine no-op at the database layer because those rows already exist by the time it executes -- but the code never checks whether the clause actually fired. The reported `inserted: 500` comes from `toInsert.length`, the size of the batch the app decided to insert before the write ran, not the statement's actual affected-row count, so the losing run reports full success while its insert was silently dropped. Fix: read the statement's actual affected-row count (driver rowcount / `RETURNING`) and reconcile it against the intended count, surfacing any mismatch (re-read and reconcile, report the delta, or fail) instead of reporting the pre-write batch size as the result.
expectations: Identifies that ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING correctly prevented a duplicate-key failure as a race backstop, and that the race it exists for is exactly what fired here (both runs read the same emails as absent before either inserted)

Explains that the reported inserted count came from the app-side toInsert array length decided before the write, not from the statement's actual affected-row count, so the DB-level no-op on the losing run went unnoticed

Prescribes reading the write's actual affected-row count (rowcount / RETURNING) and reconciling it against the intended count, treating a mismatch as the race outcome to surface rather than accepting the pre-write batch size as truth

evals.prompt: A workspace search endpoint serves three content kinds from one path -- `docs`, `boards`, and `snippets` -- merged into a single results list. Callers may narrow results with an optional `team` query parameter. Matching is generic: `SCHEMAS[kind].teamKeys(row).includes(requestedTeam)`. `docs` and `boards` are team-scoped, so their `teamKeys` reach into each row's `sharing.teams` array. `snippets` are personal and were never team-scoped by design, so `SCHEMAS.snippets.teamKeys` is `() => []`, with a comment above it reading `// snippets aren't team-scoped`. QA reports: searching with no `team` param returns the user's snippets fine; searching with `?team=growth` returns zero snippets even though the user's own snippets clearly match the text query. Review the filter and explain the bug.
evals.expected_output: The reviewer identifies that `SCHEMAS.snippets.teamKeys() => []` is a deliberate 'not applicable' signal from the author, backed by the comment, not a bug in reaching a nested field. The generic filter can't distinguish that intent from 'this row has no matching teams': `[].includes('growth')` is `false` either way, so passing any `team` filter silently drops every snippet from the merged results with no error. The fix is to represent inapplicability explicitly -- bypass `snippets` from the team filter's domain entirely, or use a sentinel the filter special-cases -- rather than relying on an empty array that a generic `.includes()` reads as exclusion.
expectations: Recognizes that the failure is type-wide -- every snippet disappears under any team filter regardless of its own content, not just snippets that happen to lack a matching team -- because SCHEMAS.snippets.teamKeys always returns [] independent of the row, which is the tell that distinguishes this from an ordinary per-row filter mismatch

Explains that the generic filter's .includes(requestedTeam) check on an empty array is indistinguishable from a row that simply has no matching teams, so passing any team filter silently excludes every snippet from the merged results

Prescribes representing inapplicability explicitly -- bypassing snippets from the team filter's domain, or a sentinel the filter special-cases before calling .includes() -- rather than leaving () => [] for a generic membership check to misread as exclusion

evals.prompt: A finance-ops tool at a fictional company, Acme Capital, lets a human approve a vendor payout in a dashboard. On approval, the backend mints a compact `<payload>.<signature>` bearer credential -- HMAC-signed, carrying the payout id and a 4-minute expiry -- and hands it to an unattended worker process, which calls `POST /payouts/execute` with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. The handler verifies the HMAC signature and checks that `exp` hasn't passed; nothing else. Three days later, the finance team finds the same payout was executed twice, four seconds apart, both calls carrying byte-for-byte the same bearer token, both inside the token's original 4-minute window. A shared debugging proxy in front of the worker was found to have logged full request headers, including `Authorization`, for that time range. Diagnose the vulnerability class, explain why the existing signature/expiry check didn't catch it, and give the fix plus a cheap regression test that would have caught this before it shipped.
evals.expected_output: The credential is replayable: capture-replay, where a captured, still-valid bearer token is resubmitted to redo the same privileged action. Checking the HMAC signature and exp only proves the token is authentic and not yet expired -- it says nothing about whether it has already been used. Once the debugging proxy logged the Authorization header, the token became a reusable secret for the rest of its 4-minute life; anyone (or anything) with access to that log could resubmit the identical token, and the handler had no way to tell the second call apart from the first. Fix: give the token a unique id (jti) at mint time, record consumed ids in a server-side store keyed by that id with a TTL at least as long as the token's own max lifetime, and reject any token whose id has already been recorded; fail closed (refuse the action) if that consumption-tracking store is unreachable, rather than allowing the action through unverified. Regression test: mint one token, call the endpoint once and confirm it succeeds, then replay the byte-for-byte identical still-unexpired token and assert the second call is rejected -- cheap, deterministic, and specific to this class of bug, since a test that only checks expiry/signature would still pass on the broken code.
expectations: Identifies the defect as capture-replay of a captured, still-valid bearer token, not a signature-forgery or expiry bug -- states that checking signature + exp proves the token is authentic and fresh but says nothing about whether it has already been used

Prescribes a server-tracked single-use control: a unique token id (jti or equivalent) recorded in a consumed-id store with a TTL at least as long as the token's own lifetime, reject on reuse, and fail closed (deny the action) if that store is unreachable rather than allowing an unverifiable reuse
Gives a concrete regression test: mint one token, use it successfully once, replay the identical still-unexpired token, and assert the second call is refused

evals.prompt: An API endpoint `POST /transfers/execute` accepts a short-lived bearer token minted right after a human approves a funds transfer (HMAC-signed, 5-minute expiry, verified for signature and expiry only). The endpoint also requires an `Idempotency-Key` header on every call: the server stores the response for each key for 24 hours, and a repeated call with a previously-seen key returns the stored result instead of re-executing the transfer. Someone flags that the bearer token was captured, still valid, in a support ticket's pasted curl command. A colleague responds: 'We're covered -- the endpoint already has idempotency keys, so a duplicate call can't do anything.' Evaluate that response, and say what, if anything, still needs to change.
evals.expected_output: The colleague is wrong: the idempotency key protects against a different failure than the one described. It only collapses a retry that reuses the same idempotency key -- a decision the calling client makes, not a property of the token -- into a single execution; it says nothing about the bearer token itself being replayed. Someone who captured the token from the support ticket controls the entire request, including a brand-new Idempotency-Key value they generate themselves; the server sees a call with a valid signature, an unexpired token, and a key it has never seen before, and executes the transfer again. The two mechanisms solve orthogonal problems: the idempotency key stops the same caller's own retry (e.g. a network timeout and resend) from double-applying, while stopping a different party who captured the credential from using it at all requires single-use enforcement on the token itself. Nothing about the idempotency-key mechanism substitutes for that. Fix: add token-level single-use enforcement -- mint the approval token with a unique id, record it as consumed on first use, and reject the token itself, independent of whatever Idempotency-Key accompanies the call, on any subsequent presentation.
expectations: Rejects the colleague's claim that idempotency keys cover this case -- states or clearly implies that an attacker who captured the token can supply a fresh/unseen Idempotency-Key of their own choosing, so the idempotency mechanism does not stop the replayed token from executing

Explains the two controls are orthogonal / solve different problems: the idempotency key dedups the same caller's own retry of a request it controls, while stopping a captured token from being reused by a different party requires single-use enforcement on the token itself

Prescribes adding token-level single-use enforcement (e.g. a unique token id marked consumed on first use and rejected on reuse) independent of, and in addition to, the existing Idempotency-Key mechanism

evals.prompt: A CSV-import endpoint parses 200 rows and applies whatever validates, returning `{ parsed: 200, applied: 178, skipped_duplicate: 14, unresolved: 3, error_count: 5, errors: [...] }` from the same pass. The client-side response type used to parse it is `{ parsed: number; applied?: number; skipped_duplicate?: number; unresolved?: number }` -- no `error_count`, no `errors`. The UI renders three badges (applied / skipped / unresolved) and nothing else. QA ran a batch with 5 rows in a bad date format, got back a 200, and the three badges summed to 195 out of 200 with no error indicator anywhere on screen. Is the defect here a missing render branch for a top-level request error?
evals.expected_output: No -- the request succeeded (200) and every individual state the UI does render is handled correctly, so a missing top-level error branch is the wrong diagnosis. The gap is one layer earlier, at the type boundary: the server computes real failure detail (`error_count`, `errors`) from the same pass that produced the success counters, but the client's declared response type never includes those fields, so no render branch could exist for them -- there is nothing to forget to render. The visible symptom is the tell: success badges (178+14+3=195) summing to less than the operation's own total (200) with no failure indicator is what a dropped field looks like from the outside. Fix: widen the client-side type to declare `error_count`/`errors` and render them (a count, or the first/aggregate reason), not just add an error-state branch to the existing fields. Detection: diff the route handler's actual `return`/response shape against the client type that parses it -- any server field absent from the client type, especially a count or array of failure reasons, is a candidate silent drop; confirm by checking whether the success counters can ever sum to less than the total. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Identifies the gap as the client's response type declaring only the success fields -- narrower than what the endpoint actually returns -- rather than a missing render branch for a top-level request error
States the fix as widening the client-side type to include the failure fields (error_count/errors) and rendering them, not just adding an error branch to the existing fields

Names the diagnostic: visible success counters summing to less than the operation's own total (195 of 200) with no failure indicator is the symptom of a field dropped at the type boundary, found by diffing the route handler's actual response against the client type

evals.prompt: A reactions feature exposes `useReactionCounts(postId)`, shared via context so a post page's header chip and its comments-sidebar chip both read one fetch instead of firing two. The hook returns `{ countFor(id), ready, loadError }`, and on a failed fetch it sets `loadError` and leaves counts empty rather than backfilling zeros. The header chip does: `if (!tally.ready) return <Skeleton />; if (tally.loadError) return <ErrorDot />; return <Badge count={tally.countFor(postId)} />`. The sidebar chip, reading the exact same context instance, does only: `return <Badge count={tally.countFor(postId)} />`. A reviewer checks the hook's contract, checks the header chip, confirms both handle the failure case correctly, and signs off the reactions feature as done. Is that sign-off complete?
evals.expected_output: No. The reviewer verified the hook's contract plus one consumer, and treated that as proof the feature is handled -- but a correct contract on a shared hook says nothing about whether every consumer of it actually reads the contract's signal. The sidebar chip destructures only `countFor` and never touches `ready`/`loadError`, so on the identical fetch failure the header shows a skeleton or an error dot while the sidebar renders a confident '0' -- indistinguishable from genuinely zero reactions. One correct consumer does not imply the rest are. Fix: grep the hook/context name itself (not just the file already reviewed) to enumerate every consumer of the shared instance, check each one independently for whether it branches on the readiness/error field, and verify by forcing the shared fetch to fail and loading every surface that consumes it -- not only the one already known to be correct. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Rejects the sign-off as incomplete -- verifying the hook's contract plus one consumer is not the same as verifying every consumer

Names the concrete defect: the sidebar chip destructures only the count and never reads ready/loadError, so the same fetch failure the header discloses renders on the sidebar as a confident false zero

Requires enumerating and independently checking every consumer of the shared hook/context (e.g. by forcing the fetch to fail and loading each surface), not inferring correctness from the one consumer already checked

evals.prompt: A route-lookup service at a fictional logistics dispatcher, Aurora Freight, ships a latency SLO: '99% of route-lookup requests complete under 300ms.' The service instruments request duration with a Prometheus client library's histogram using the library's out-of-the-box default bucket list -- no custom `buckets=` argument was ever set. The on-call dashboard's SLO panel runs `sum(rate(route_lookup_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.3"}[5m])) / sum(rate(route_lookup_duration_seconds_count[5m]))` and has rendered completely blank, with no data point, for the three weeks since launch -- the team's working theory is 'the query must have a typo, but requests feel fast so it's low priority.' Separately, a second Grafana panel titled 'p99 latency across pods' computes `avg(route_lookup_duration_seconds{quantile="0.99"})` over all 12 running pods and shows a smooth, populated line the team trusts as the real p99. Review this observability setup.
evals.expected_output: Applies the metric type & shape correctness lens (observability.md): the SLO panel is blank not because of a query typo but because the histogram only has the client library's default bucket boundaries, none of which sit at exactly 0.3 -- a fixed-bucket histogram query for a specific threshold like le="0.3" returns no result at all when no bucket matches that boundary (and would return an incomplete result with no warning if only some instances had it). The fix is an explicit bucket configured at or near the SLO threshold, or switching to native/exponential histograms. Separately, the 'trusted' p99 panel is actually wrong in a different way: averaging a quantile-labeled series (quantile="0.99") across pods is statistically invalid because a percentile does not average -- the smooth, populated line is a false confidence signal, not a correct number. The fix there is to recompute the quantile once from the summed raw histogram buckets, never by averaging already-computed per-pod quantiles.
expectations: Identifies that the histogram's default bucket list lacking a boundary at the SLO threshold (0.3s) is why the SLO query returns no data at all -- not a query-syntax bug
Recommends an explicit bucket boundary configured at or near the threshold (or a native/exponential histogram) rather than accepting the client library's default buckets

Separately flags the avg()/mean() over the quantile-labeled p99 series across pods as statistically invalid despite looking populated and trustworthy, and recommends recomputing the quantile from the summed raw histogram buckets instead

evals.prompt: A fictional password manager backend, Ironclad Vault, tracks `failed_login_attempts_total` as a monotonically-incrementing in-process counter, exported as a Prometheus counter metric. A nightly cron job re-initializes the counter's stored value back to 0 at midnight local time, 'to keep the fraud dashboard tidy for the new day' -- the process itself is never restarted. The fraud team's paging alert is `rate(failed_login_attempts_total[5m]) > 50`. Separately, the same backend tracks concurrently active sessions with an OpenTelemetry UpDownCounter named `active_sessions`: the code calls `active_sessions.add(1, {"region": r})` when a session starts, and `active_sessions.add(-1, {"region": r, "auth_method": m})` when it ends, where `auth_method` is only known once the session's logout flow completes. Review this metrics design.
evals.expected_output: Applies the metric type & shape correctness lens (observability.md): re-initializing failed_login_attempts_total to 0 on a nightly schedule -- rather than only on process restart -- is invalid counter usage; rate()'s reset-compensation logic assumes a counter only resets on process restart, so a scheduled reset outside that assumption produces miscounted or spurious rate values right around midnight, silently corrupting the fraud-alert threshold with no error thrown. The fix is to never reset a counter on anything other than process restart -- use a gauge instead if a periodically-resettable value is genuinely needed. Separately, active_sessions forks into two never-reconciled time series because the increment and decrement calls use different attribute sets (region-only vs. region+auth_method) -- per the OpenTelemetry UpDownCounter consistency guidance, mismatched attributes on increment vs. decrement produce independent series, one that only rises and one that only falls, so the 'current active sessions' reading is permanently wrong. The fix is to use the identical attribute set on every increment/decrement pair, deferring any attribute only known at end-of-session to a different signal (e.g. a counter or log line), not to the UpDownCounter's attributes.
expectations: Flags the nightly re-initialization of failed_login_attempts_total to 0 as invalid counter usage, explaining that rate()'s reset-compensation logic assumes resets happen only on process restart and that a scheduled reset outside that assumption produces miscounted or spurious rate values
Flags the UpDownCounter's mismatched attribute sets between increment (region only) and decrement (region + auth_method) as forking active_sessions into two independent, never-reconciled time series

Recommends concrete fixes for both: never reset a counter on anything other than process restart (use a gauge instead if a resettable value is genuinely needed), and use an identical attribute set on every increment/decrement pair for an UpDownCounter

evals.prompt: A fictional payment processor, Northwind Pay, increments `payment_declined_total{reason="insufficient_funds"}` (among other reason label values) only at the moment a decline with that specific reason actually occurs -- the label value is never initialized in advance. During a spike investigation, an analyst runs an alert query, `sum(rate(payment_declined_total{reason="insufficient_funds"}[1h])) / sum(rate(payment_attempts_total[1h]))`, and it pages 'no data,' which the on-call engineer logs as 'monitoring is broken, ignore.' Separately, a background worker fleet is meant to be watched by a deadman/absence alert, `absent(worker_heartbeat_total) == 1`, intended to fire if a worker crashes and stops emitting -- but `worker_heartbeat_total` is also only created lazily, the first time a worker completes a tick, rather than exported at process startup. Review this alerting design.
evals.expected_output: Applies the metric type & shape correctness lens (observability.md): payment_declined_total{reason="insufficient_funds"} and worker_heartbeat_total are both lazily-created time series -- they do not exist as a zero until the labeled event or first tick actually happens, they simply do not exist as a series at all before that. This means the decline-rate ratio genuinely returns no data (not a true zero) whenever that reason hasn't fired recently, which is exactly why the on-call engineer's 'monitoring is broken, ignore' read is the wrong conclusion -- the query is correct, the metric's existence is the problem. The deadman check is worse than merely noisy: it is defeated outright, because a healthy-but-quiet worker (hasn't ticked yet) and a genuinely crashed worker both present as 'no series' -- absent() cannot distinguish them. The fix for both is the same: export a default value of 0 at startup for every metric and label combination known in advance, so a ratio reads a real zero and an absence check's silence is a meaningful signal again.
expectations: Identifies that payment_declined_total{reason="insufficient_funds"} and worker_heartbeat_total are lazily-created series that do not exist at all (not present-and-zero) before their first occurrence

Explains that this makes the decline-rate ratio return no data rather than a true zero, and specifically rejects the on-call engineer's 'monitoring is broken, ignore' conclusion as the wrong read of a correct query

Flags that the absent()-based deadman check is defeated by the same lazy-creation pattern -- a healthy-but-quiet worker and a crashed worker both read as 'no series' -- and recommends exporting a default 0 at startup for any metric/label combination known in advance

evals.expected_output: `fetchCustomer(order.customerId)` is a genuine dependency -- it needs `order.customerId`, which only exists after `fetchOrder` resolves, so it correctly stays sequential; that is not a bug to flag. `fetchShippingOptions()` is the accidental serialization: it reads nothing produced by either prior call, yet the natural top-to-bottom order makes it run last, so the loader pays the sum of all three latencies instead of the max, adding an unnecessary round-trip to time-to-first-byte. The fix is not to wrap all three in one blind `Promise.all` (that would incorrectly race `fetchCustomer` before `order.customerId` exists) -- it is to start `fetchOrder` and `fetchShippingOptions` together (e.g. `Promise.all([fetchOrder(orderId), fetchShippingOptions()])`) and await `fetchCustomer(order.customerId)` afterward, once `order` has resolved.
expectations: Identifies fetchOrder -> fetchCustomer as a genuine data dependency (customer fetch needs order.customerId) that correctly stays sequential -- does not flag it as a bug
Identifies fetchShippingOptions as independent of both order and customer, and flags it as the accidental serialization with no data reason to run last

Prescribes running fetchShippingOptions concurrently with fetchOrder (e.g. via Promise.all over just the independent pair) and awaiting fetchCustomer afterward -- rejects or avoids a naive blind Promise.all over all three calls

evals.expected_output: No, the teammate is wrong. Importing `labelForSku` still imports the whole `catalog.ts` module at runtime, and because `index` is built by processing the entire `CATALOG_DATA` import into one object at module load time, a bundler cannot tree-shake around it -- the whole 4,000-product JSON dataset ships into the product-badge component's client bundle, not just the small function. This is invisible to typecheck, lint, and tests, and shows up only as an oversized bundle-analyzer entry or a slow page load. Because the label renders on first paint for every card rather than behind an interaction gate, deferring the import with React.lazy or a dynamic import() does not fix it -- the data is still needed immediately. The real fix is architectural: resolve the label server-side and pass only the resolved string down as a prop, or refactor to a structural-parameter form (`labelForSku(sku, index)`) living in a dataset-free module, so the client component supplies its own narrow slice instead of importing the module that holds the full dataset.
expectations: Rejects the teammate's claim -- explains that importing the helper still imports the whole module, and because the module builds its index over the entire dataset at load time, the bundler cannot tree-shake it, so the full dataset ships to the client bundle, not just the small function

Recognizes that deferring the import (React.lazy / dynamic import) does not fix it here because the label is needed on first paint for every card, not gated behind an interaction -- ruling out lazy-loading alone as the fix

Prescribes an architectural fix: resolving the lookup server-side and passing the resolved value as a prop, or refactoring the helper to take the dataset as a parameter so it lives in a dataset-free module -- not merely shrinking, renaming, or lazy-loading the helper

evals.prompt: A fictional freight-dispatch company, Acme Freight, runs a fleet-dispatch service where multiple worker processes compete to claim and update a shipment record stored in a shared Postgres table. Workers coordinate through a Redis-based distributed lock (a standard SET NX PX with a 10-second TTL) before writing the shipment's status. A teammate, worried about a worker pausing (a long GC pause, a suspended container, a slow disk write) past the lock's TTL, adds a safety check: immediately before the worker writes the new status to Postgres, it re-reads the Redis key and confirms the lock is still held by its own client id, and only then proceeds with the write. The teammate says this closes the gap, because the write now only happens if the lock is confirmed valid at that moment. Evaluate whether this actually prevents two workers from writing conflicting shipment statuses, and say what, if anything, still needs to change.
evals.expected_output: The teammate is wrong: re-checking the lock immediately before the write does not close the gap, because the exact same kind of pause that motivated the check in the first place (a GC pause, a suspended container, a slow disk write) can land between the recheck and the write it guards -- there is no code position that is immune to an arbitrarily-placed pause. A worker can pass its own recheck, then stall, have its lock expire and get reassigned to a second worker, and still complete its write afterward; both writes land on Postgres with nothing to stop the second (stale) one. This is not a smaller or different bug than the one the teammate was trying to fix -- it is the identical race, just moved a few lines later. The real fix has to live at the resource being written, not in another client-side check: give each lock acquisition a monotonically increasing fencing token (e.g. incremented in Redis on each successful acquire), include it with every write to Postgres, and have Postgres itself reject (via a conditional update against a stored token/version column) any write whose token is not higher than the last one it accepted. That way a stale worker's late write is refused by the database regardless of when it arrives, instead of relying on the worker correctly judging its own state beforehand.
expectations: States that re-checking the lock right before the write does NOT close the race, because the same kind of pause that motivated the check can land between the recheck and the write itself -- explicitly rejects the teammate's claim that the recheck fixes it, rather than treating it as a partial or acceptable mitigation

Identifies this as the identical race as before (not a new or lesser bug) -- a worker can pass the recheck, then stall, lose the lock to a second worker, and still write afterward, so both writes can land

Prescribes moving the guarantee to the resource itself via a fencing token: a monotonically increasing value issued per lock acquisition, included with the write, and enforced by Postgres (e.g. a version/token column checked on write, rejecting any write whose token is not the highest seen) -- not another pre-write check performed by the client

evals.prompt: A checkout service takes a ZooKeeper distributed lock, keyed by order id, before calling a third-party carrier's shipping-label API (operated by an unrelated external vendor, Meridian Carrier) to purchase a shipping label for that order -- the lock exists so that if one worker stalls past the lock's TTL, a second worker retrying the same order won't also purchase a label, double-charging the merchant's carrier account. During review, a colleague says: 'The lock alone isn't quite enough if a worker can stall -- just add a fencing token like we did for the Postgres writes, and a stale worker's label purchase will be rejected.' Evaluate whether adding a fencing token is a workable fix in this situation, and if not, say what actually is.
evals.expected_output: The colleague's suggestion does not transfer to this case. A fencing token only works when the protected resource itself validates the token on every write and rejects one that is lower than the highest it has already accepted -- that requires control over the resource's write path. Here the resource is Meridian Carrier's shipping-label API, a third party the checkout service does not operate and cannot modify to add token validation; there is nowhere to enforce 'reject a write with a stale token,' so 'add a fencing token' is not actionable advice for this call, even though it worked for the earlier Postgres example. The underlying problem the colleague raised is still real, though: the ZooKeeper lock by itself gives no exclusivity guarantee against a stalled worker, so a second worker can still legitimately acquire it and call the carrier API concurrently with the first. Since fencing isn't available, the fix has to make the purchase call itself safe to run twice: use the carrier API's own idempotency mechanism if it offers one (e.g. a client-supplied idempotency or request key the carrier deduplicates on), or its conditional/compare-and-set semantics if offered (e.g. 'only issue a label if none exists yet for this order'); if the API offers neither, the fallback is a compensating check-before-purchase plus reconciliation/refund-on-duplicate after the fact, not a bare assumption that the lock alone prevents the double purchase.
expectations: States that a fencing token requires the protected resource to validate the token on every write and reject stale ones, and that this is not implementable here because the team does not control the third-party carrier API's write path -- explicitly rejects 'just add a fencing token' as actionable for this specific call

Agrees that the colleague's underlying concern is still valid: the ZooKeeper lock alone gives no exclusivity guarantee against a stalled worker, so a second worker can still call the carrier API concurrently

Prescribes the correct narrower fix instead of fencing: make the third-party call itself idempotent (e.g. an idempotency/request key the carrier API deduplicates on) or use its compare-and-set/conditional semantics if available

evals.expected_output: Yes, and it is worse than 'less randomness' -- it is a forgery vulnerability. `IV` is a module-level constant, so every call to `encryptMessage` reuses the exact same nonce under the exact same key -- the fact that the 12 bytes were drawn from a CSPRNG once does not help, because the requirement is uniqueness *per encryption*, not just randomness at generation time. For AES-GCM, repeating a (key, IV) pair lets an adversary who sees two ciphertexts under that pair recover the GHASH authentication subkey from them, then construct a ciphertext forgery -- and because GCM's underlying encryption is Counter-mode, once authentication is broken the adversary can go further and control the decrypted plaintext of a forged message, not merely read leaked bits of the original. This is CWE-323 (Reusing a Nonce, Key Pair in Encryption); its severity is pinned by the exposure-boundary discriminator, not a flat default — Critical here specifically because it is the sole encryption path for every message the service sends. Fix: move `crypto.randomBytes(12)` inside `encryptMessage` so a fresh IV is drawn immediately before every single `createCipheriv` call, and return/store that per-message IV alongside its ciphertext (the IV need not be secret, only unique per key) -- never at module scope, never cached, never reused across calls.
expectations: Flags the module-level IV as broken specifically because it is reused across every encryption call under the same key -- not because 12 bytes or a CSPRNG source is insufficiently random

States the AES-GCM-specific consequence of nonce reuse: recovery of the authentication subkey enabling ciphertext forgery, and -- because the underlying cipher is Counter-mode -- attacker control over decrypted plaintext, not merely a confidentiality leak

Prescribes moving IV generation inside the function so a fresh CSPRNG-drawn IV is produced immediately before each encryption call, with the per-message IV carried alongside its ciphertext (not secret, but never reused)

evals.prompt:
Review this two-factor login handler for cryptographic failures (OWASP A04):

```python
def verify_otp(user_id, submitted_code):
    expected_code = get_otp_for_user(user_id)  # 6-digit string, from secrets.choice
    if submitted_code == expected_code:
        consume_otp(user_id)
        return True
    return False
```

The OTP is generated with `secrets.choice` (a CSPRNG), is exactly 6 digits, and expires after 5 minutes. Given that, is `verify_otp` safe as written?
evals.expected_output: No. The OTP's generation and expiry are fine -- the bug is in the comparison, not the value being compared. `submitted_code == expected_code` is a plain, short-circuiting string equality: it returns as soon as it hits the first mismatched character, so a correct-so-far prefix takes measurably longer to reject than a completely wrong guess. That is CWE-208, Observable Timing Discrepancy -- an attacker who can send enough requests (even within a nominal rate limit, over enough samples) can use the timing signal to recover the code digit-by-digit far faster than brute-forcing all 10^6 combinations blind. This is the same underlying bug as comparing an HMAC signature or a session token with `==` or `.equals()` -- a hand-rolled compare of a secret-derived value -- just surfacing here on an OTP instead. Fix: replace the `==` with a constant-time comparison -- `hmac.compare_digest(submitted_code, expected_code)` in Python (Node: `crypto.timingSafeEqual`; Java: the static `MessageDigest.isEqual`) -- and make sure both arguments are the same fixed length before comparing, since these constant-time primitives only give their guarantee across equal-length inputs (Node's `timingSafeEqual` throws outright on a length mismatch).
expectations: Identifies the defect as a timing side channel in the comparison itself (`==` / string equality on a secret value), explicitly distinguishing it from the OTP's generation and expiry, which it notes are already fine

Names the general mechanism -- a short-circuiting equality leaks the position of the first mismatched character via response timing (CWE-208 Observable Timing Discrepancy) -- and identifies it as the same class of bug as an insecure HMAC-signature or session-token comparison, not an OTP-specific issue

Prescribes a constant-time comparison function (e.g. hmac.compare_digest / crypto.timingSafeEqual / MessageDigest.isEqual) in place of `==`, and notes both inputs must be the same fixed length for the constant-time guarantee to hold

evals.prompt:
A teammate says: 'Our password storage already passed security review -- we use bcrypt, a memory-hard KDF, not a fast hash like SHA-256.' Here is the actual call:

```javascript
async function hashPassword(password) {
  return bcrypt.hash(password, 4); // approved: uses bcrypt per the security checklist
}
```

Does using bcrypt clear the password-storage check on its own?
evals.expected_output: No. Bcrypt is the right algorithm family, but `4` is the work-factor argument, and it is far below any currently-recommended floor -- OWASP's Password Storage Cheat Sheet calls for bcrypt work factor 'as large as verification server performance will allow, with a minimum of 10.' A work factor of 4 hashes fast enough that it largely defeats the point of choosing a memory-hard KDF in the first place: an attacker with an offline copy of the hash table can brute-force it at close to fast-hash speed. The earlier review checked *which function* was called and stopped there; it never checked *how expensive* that call actually was -- those are two separate checks, and passing the first proves nothing about the second. Fix: raise the work factor to at least the current OWASP floor. Do not treat '10' as permanent doctrine, though -- OWASP's own guidance is that the number should rise as hardware gets cheaper, so the right fix is to re-check the live cheat sheet at review time (and add a lint/regression check that fails the build if the work-factor argument drops below whatever that current floor is), not to hard-code today's number forever.
expectations: Rejects 'we use bcrypt' as sufficient by itself -- explicitly separates the algorithm-name check (already passed) from the cost/work-factor check (not done), and refuses to treat the algorithm name alone as proof of adequate protection

Names the concrete defect: a work factor of 4 sits far below the current floor (reasons toward a minimum around 10 for bcrypt per current OWASP guidance) and hashes fast enough to undercut the purpose of choosing a memory-hard KDF

Frames the fix as re-checking against current published guidance rather than hard-coding today's number permanently -- treats the cost floor as a moving target that must be re-verified at review time, not a fixed constant

evals.expected_output: The teammate is wrong. `seen` is a hash table, and a hash table's amortized O(1) insert/lookup holds only when keys don't collide into the same bucket. The 5,000-item count cap bounds how many items are processed, but it does nothing to bound which tracking_id values the caller sends -- an attacker who can predict or influence the hash function's collision pattern can choose 5,000 tracking_id strings that all collide into the same (or very few) buckets. Every insert then degrades from O(1) to O(n), so the loop's total cost degrades from O(n) to O(n^2) -- entirely within the existing 5,000-item cap, which never fires and provides no protection because the count is fine; it's the key values that are the attack. Lowering the cap further only shrinks n, it doesn't remove the O(n^2) degradation or the attacker's ability to trigger it. The actual fix is to reduce the attacker's control over which keys land in the structure or verify the runtime's hash-map is already collision-hardened (e.g. confirm hash-seed randomization is on for this language/runtime) before assuming a count limit alone is sufficient.
expectations: Identifies that the dict insert loop can degrade from amortized O(1) to O(n) per insert (O(n^2) total) when the attacker chooses colliding tracking_id key values -- names this as a hash-collision/hash-flooding attack distinct from a large item count

Explicitly rejects 'the 5,000-item cap already bounds this' -- explains the cap never fires and provides no protection because the count stays within the limit while only the key values change; a model that says the count cap already handles it, or that the fix is simply to lower the cap further, fails this expectation

Prescribes addressing the hash-collision surface itself (e.g. verifying/hardening the keyed structure's collision resistance against attacker-chosen keys, such as confirming hash-seed randomization) rather than treating a numeric item-count limit as sufficient on its own

evals.prompt: A fictional company, Acme Ledger, runs a public `/webhooks/ingest` endpoint that accepts a JSON body up to 256 KB (enforced by the framework's body-size limit) and parses it with the language's standard JSON library at its default settings. Separately, Acme Ledger's outbound client code -- which calls a third-party payment partner's API -- already validates the partner's response against a schema and enforces a size and recursion bound before trusting any of it. A reviewer says: 'We're covered: the outbound client already bounds size and recursion for anything we parse, and the inbound endpoint has a 256 KB body cap, so a stack-exhaustion crash isn't possible here.' Evaluate that claim specifically for `/webhooks/ingest`.
evals.expected_output: The reviewer is wrong about `/webhooks/ingest`. Two separate gaps hide behind the claim. First, the outbound client's 'bound size and recursion' check only runs when Acme Ledger consumes the payment partner's response -- it is scoped to that outbound/client code path and says nothing about the app's own inbound request-parsing path; `/webhooks/ingest` is a different code path entirely and is not covered by it. Second, the 256 KB body cap bounds byte size, not nesting depth: a payload of a few KB -- well under the 256 KB ceiling -- can nest brackets or objects thousands of levels deep (e.g. `[[[[[...]]]]]`), and a recursive-descent JSON parser at default settings consumes one call-stack frame per nesting level, exhausting the stack long before the byte-size cap is ever approached. The fix is not to lower the byte-size cap (it does not bound depth at any size) -- it is to verify what the JSON library's actual default max-nesting-depth behavior is on this inbound path, and set or confirm an explicit max-depth option (or add a fail-closed recursion counter) for the `/webhooks/ingest` parse specifically.
expectations: Identifies that the outbound 'bound size and recursion' check on the payment-partner response covers only the app-as-client/outbound direction and provides no protection for the inbound /webhooks/ingest request-parsing path -- a distinct code path

Identifies that the 256 KB body-size cap bounds byte size, not recursion/nesting depth, and explains that a small, deeply-nested payload well under that cap can still exhaust the call stack -- rejects the idea that the byte cap substitutes for a depth guard

Prescribes verifying the JSON library's actual default max-nesting-depth behavior on the inbound path and setting or confirming an explicit max-depth limit or recursion counter, rather than asserting a specific library's default depth number from memory or proposing to shrink the byte-size cap

evals.prompt:
A fictional photo-processing service, Glimmer Photos, uses a two-phase upload: the client first POSTs a small JSON descriptor (capped at 10 KB by the gateway) declaring the image's `width` and `height`, then a second call streams the actual pixel bytes. The handler for the first call reads:

    descriptor = parse_json(request.body)  # <= 10 KB, enforced by the gateway
    buffer = allocate_pixel_buffer(descriptor.width * descriptor.height * BYTES_PER_PIXEL)

A teammate says: 'The gateway already caps the request body at 10 KB, so this can't be used to exhaust memory.' Assess that claim, and compare this bug to a classic integer-overflow-before-malloc bug in C -- are they the same failure?
evals.expected_output: The teammate is wrong. The 10 KB gateway cap bounds the size of the JSON descriptor document itself, not the width/height values declared inside it. A tiny JSON body, far under 10 KB, can declare `width: 2000000000, height: 2000000000`, and the handler multiplies those attacker-declared values and pre-allocates a buffer of that size before any real pixel byte has arrived or been validated -- a small request can still claim a multi-gigabyte (or larger) allocation, entirely independent of how small the request body was. This is not the same bug as integer-overflow-before-malloc: that classic C bug is an *undersized* allocation, where a wrapped/overflowed size calculation produces a buffer smaller than intended, and a later write past that too-small buffer causes memory corruption (a buffer overflow). Here the allocation is *oversized* exactly as the attacker requested -- there is no overflow in the arithmetic -- and the failure mode is memory exhaustion / process crash (an availability problem), not memory corruption. The fix is to clamp the declared width/height (or any similar declared count/size field) to an application-level sane ceiling before allocating, independent of the wire-level body-size cap, or to allocate incrementally as real pixel bytes arrive in the second phase.
expectations: Identifies that the 10 KB gateway cap bounds the size of the JSON descriptor document, not the width/height values declared inside it -- rejects 'the body-size cap already prevents this' and explains a tiny request can still declare an enormous width x height

Correctly distinguishes this from integer-overflow-before-malloc: recognizes this allocation is oversized exactly as requested (no arithmetic overflow), whose consequence is memory exhaustion/availability, versus the classic bug's undersized allocation whose consequence is buffer overflow/memory corruption

Prescribes clamping the declared width/height (or count/size) fields to an application-level ceiling before allocating -- independent of the wire-level request-size cap -- or allocating incrementally as real bytes arrive, rather than treating the existing 10 KB cap as sufficient

evals.prompt: A reviewer flags that a paginated endpoint's page token is a raw, readable string like `offset=40&tenant_id=5`, letting any client see and edit the pagination internals. The team's proposed fix is to base64-encode that same string before returning it, so the token now reads like `b2Zmc2V0PTQwJnRlbmFudF9pZD01`. Does base64-encoding the token resolve the reviewer's concern? What, if anything, still needs to change?
evals.expected_output: No — base64 is a reversible encoding, not an obfuscation or opacity mechanism: any client can decode the string right back to `offset=40&tenant_id=5`, edit a field, and re-encode it, so nothing about the client-visible contract has actually changed (base64-encoding an otherwise-transparent page token is not a sufficient obfuscation mechanism). The pagination internals (the offset scheme, the field names) are still exposed and still editable, so they remain a de-facto part of the public API that can't be changed later without breaking whoever decoded the format — and because tenant_id rides inside the token, an edited token could also be used to try to page through another tenant's data. The real fix is two things, not one: make the token genuinely opaque (an opaque server-issued reference, or an encrypted/signed payload the client cannot parse or tamper with), and independently verify authorization/tenant scope from the authenticated request context on every page — never from whatever the token itself claims — so even a decoded or replayed token cannot grant access on its own.
expectations: States that base64 is a reversible encoding, not opacity/obfuscation — the decoded content and structure are unchanged and still editable by the client
Explicitly rejects base64-encoding alone as fixing the exposed-internals/tamperable-token problem, not accepting it as sufficient

Requires both a genuinely opaque/tamper-resistant token AND that authorization (e.g., tenant scope) be re-checked against the authenticated principal on the request, independent of the token's content

evals.prompt: A team paginates a reporting table with `SELECT * FROM events LIMIT 50 OFFSET 100` — no `ORDER BY` clause. The table is loaded once overnight and is never written to during the day, when users page through it. A developer argues: 'nothing is being inserted or deleted while people are browsing, so plain OFFSET pagination is safe here.' Evaluate that argument.
evals.expected_output: The argument is wrong. With no `ORDER BY` that constrains rows to a unique order, SQL makes no promise about row order at all — this isn't only a concurrent-write problem. The query optimizer takes LIMIT/OFFSET into account when building a plan, so it is free to pick a different plan — and therefore a different physical row order — for different LIMIT/OFFSET values against the exact same query text and the exact same, unchanged data. So even on a table nobody is writing to, page 3 can duplicate a row already seen on page 2, or skip one, purely because the query never pinned down an order and the planner isn't obligated to reuse the same plan for every OFFSET. The absence of writes has nothing to do with it. Fix: add an `ORDER BY` on a column set that is unique/total (e.g. a primary key, or a `(sort_key, id)` tiebreak) — that is what makes result order deterministic and pagination correct; it's required whether or not concurrent writes are also happening.
expectations: Rejects the 'no concurrent writes means OFFSET pagination is safe' reasoning as false

Explains the mechanism as the query planner being free to choose a different plan/row order for different LIMIT/OFFSET values absent a fully-discriminating ORDER BY — not framed as merely a concurrent-write row-shift
Prescribes a total, unique ORDER BY (not just 'add any ORDER BY') as the fix, independent of whether concurrent writes are occurring

evals.prompt: A shared `<LoadingPanel label="Loading results…" />` component used across a fictional analytics app (Northwind Analytics) renders `<div aria-busy="true" aria-label={label}>` around a skeleton graphic, with no `role` and no `aria-live` anywhere on it or an ancestor. A teammate says this is already accessible: 'aria-busy tells assistive tech it's loading, and aria-label gives it a name -- screen reader users are covered.' Evaluate that claim and say what, if anything, is missing.
evals.expected_output: The teammate is wrong. `aria-busy="true"` marks the element as a state property assistive tech can query -- it does not cause an unprompted announcement. A plain `aria-label` is exposed only as the element's accessible name, which is spoken if the element is focused (or is itself an auto-announcing role) -- not proactively spoken when nothing is focused. With neither a `role="status"`/`role="alert"` nor an `aria-live` region anywhere on the element or an ancestor, a screen-reader user gets complete silence through the entire loading window, and again at the swap to the loaded result, even though the JSX looks finished. Fix: add `role="status"` to the region (it carries an implicit `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, so a separate `aria-live` attribute is not required) so the label is announced automatically on mount and again when the content changes; keep `aria-busy` alongside it only as a supplement -- e.g. to suppress reads of partially-updated content -- never as a substitute for the live-region role. A regression test should assert `getByRole('status')` resolves and contains the expected text, not just snapshot the DOM.
expectations: Rejects the teammate's claim -- explains aria-busy is a state property (queryable, not announced) and a plain aria-label is only an accessible name (spoken on focus or via an auto-announcing role), so neither causes a screen reader to announce anything unprompted

Identifies the concrete fix as adding role="status" (or an equivalent aria-live="polite" live region) so the label is announced on mount and again when the loading state resolves to the loaded content -- not merely keeping aria-busy + aria-label as they are
Does not accept 'aria-busy + aria-label' (or either alone) as sufficient; treats aria-busy as a valid supplement only alongside the live-region role, never a replacement for it

evals.prompt: In a fictional reporting app, Lumen Reports, a button shows the visible text 'Export SVG'. To make the screen-reader experience more informative, a developer adds `aria-label="Export the report as a PDF file (summary only)"` to the same button, leaving the visible text unchanged. A voice-control user reports that saying 'Click Export SVG' no longer activates the button. Explain why, and name the WCAG success criterion implicated.
evals.expected_output: A static `aria-label` overrides the visible text as the element's accessible name. Voice-control software matches a spoken command against the accessible name, not the rendered DOM text, so once the label is rewritten to 'Export the report as a PDF file (summary only)' -- which drops the words 'Export SVG' entirely -- the command 'Click Export SVG' has nothing to match against, even though the button still visibly reads 'Export SVG'. This fails WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.3 Label in Name (Level A): 'for user interface components with labels that include text or images of text, the name contains the text that is presented visually.' The fix is to either drop the aria-label (the visible text is already a reasonable name) or, if extra context is genuinely needed, lead the label with the visible text verbatim and append the context after it, e.g. 'Export SVG — exports as PDF, summary only' -- never compose an unrelated sentence that omits the visible words.
expectations: Names WCAG SC 2.5.3 Label in Name (Level A) and states its rule accurately: the accessible name must contain the text that is visually presented, not merely be a reasonable-sounding label

Explains the mechanism: voice-control software matches a spoken command against the accessible name (the aria-label, which overrides the visible text), so a rewritten name that drops the visible words breaks that match even though the visible button text is unchanged

Prescribes a fix that preserves the visible words verbatim in the accessible name (e.g. leading with 'Export SVG' before appending extra context, or removing the aria-label if the visible text already suffices) rather than accepting the descriptive rewrite as-is

evals.prompt: A fictional file-browser app, Cascade Files, has a folder-tree row whose toggle button renders an `onClick` handler, a conditional icon (`chevron-right` / `chevron-down`), and a conditional `aria-label` (`'Expand ' + name` / `'Collapse ' + name`), all keyed off the same `open` boolean. A reviewer who tested with a screen reader says it sounds fine -- it announces 'Expand Invoices' or 'Collapse Invoices' correctly on first read. Is this a fully accessible disclosure widget? What, if anything, is missing, and how would you detect it across a codebase with many similar rows?
evals.expected_output: It is not fully accessible despite sounding correct on a first read. Swapping the aria-label changes the button's accessible NAME, which is why a screen reader announces a sensible 'Expand' or 'Collapse' the first time it lands on the control. But the ARIA disclosure pattern also requires the accessible STATE, exposed via `aria-expanded` on that same control, and this component never sets it. Assistive technology that reports state changes rather than re-announcing the full name on every interaction never gets one, and state-aware tooling -- axe, or Testing Library's `getByRole('button', { expanded })` -- will not recognize the row as a disclosure widget at all. Fix: add `aria-expanded={open}` (paired with `aria-controls` naming the toggled region) on the same button whose label/icon already swap. To detect this across a codebase, grep for the icon/label-swap tell (a conditional icon name and aria-label keyed off the same boolean) and check whether the same element also carries `aria-expanded`; diffing several similar tree/list/accordion row components against each other -- most having `aria-expanded` and one not -- is strong evidence of a single overlooked component rather than a deliberate omission.
expectations: States the component is NOT fully accessible despite sounding correct on a first read -- the swapped aria-label changes the accessible NAME, but the ARIA disclosure pattern also requires the accessible STATE via aria-expanded on the same control, which this component never sets

Explains the consequence: assistive tech that reports state changes (rather than re-reading the full name on every interaction) never gets one, and state-aware tooling (axe, getByRole with an expanded option) will not recognize the row as a disclosure widget

Prescribes adding aria-expanded={open} (plus aria-controls naming the toggled region) on the same button, and describes a cross-component detection method (diffing aria-expanded usage across the codebase's similar tree/list/accordion rows to spot the one outlier missing it)

evals.expected_output: The teammate is wrong. assertSizeAllowed only runs after `await request.arrayBuffer()` has already read the entire request body into memory -- by the time that call throws and the 413 is produced, the full oversized payload has already been buffered, so the memory allocation the cap exists to prevent has already happened. The eventual rejection does not undo the resource consumption; a handful of concurrent oversized uploads can still exhaust server memory regardless of the fact that each one is eventually rejected. The Content-Length pre-check above it does not save this either: `request.headers.get('content-length')` returns `null` when the header is chunked or simply omitted, and `Number(null ?? '')` evaluates to `Number('')`, which is `0` -- `0 > MAX_BYTES` is false, so the pre-check silently passes an arbitrarily large body straight through to the unbounded `arrayBuffer()` read. A real fix has to bound the read itself: read the body through a streaming loop that sums bytes as they arrive and cancels/aborts the read the instant the running total crosses MAX_BYTES, so worst-case memory use is capped independent of what the client declares (or fails to declare) and independent of a post-hoc check on an already-fully-read value.
expectations: Rejects 'assertSizeAllowed already protects us' as sufficient -- explicitly identifies that the check runs only after `request.arrayBuffer()` has already buffered the full body into memory, so the resource-exhaustion damage has already occurred by the time the 413 fires

Independently flags the Content-Length pre-check as a no-op for a missing/chunked header -- explains that a null/absent header coerces to a value (e.g. via `Number(null ?? '')` = 0) that trivially passes the `> MAX_BYTES` comparison regardless of the true body size, rather than accepting the pre-check as protective on its own

Prescribes enforcing the cap via a bounded/streaming read -- a running byte counter over chunks that aborts/cancels the read once MAX_BYTES is crossed -- rather than a post-hoc check performed on the result of an already-completed unbounded read

evals.expected_output: No, only half the problem is fixed. Running the check earlier is necessary but not sufficient, because the check still trusts a client-declared header rather than the real byte stream. A request sent with chunked transfer-encoding legitimately has no Content-Length header at all, so `request.headers.get('content-length')` returns `null`; the `declared !== null` guard is then false, the whole `if` is skipped, and execution falls straight through to the unbounded `request.arrayBuffer()` read with no size enforcement applied whatsoever -- an attacker who simply omits the header (or a client using chunked encoding for a legitimate reason) sails past the 'fix' entirely. Content-Length is also just a claim the client makes; nothing stops a sender from understating it. Ordering the check before the read is the right direction, but the only reliable bound is a hard ceiling enforced against bytes actually received as they stream in -- a running byte counter that aborts the read once it crosses MAX_BYTES -- independent of whether Content-Length is present, absent, or honest.
expectations: Rejects 'moving the check earlier fixes it' as sufficient on its own -- recognizes the check still only inspects the client-declared Content-Length header rather than the real byte stream

Identifies the specific bypass: a chunked-encoded or Content-Length-omitting request makes `declared` null, so the guard is skipped entirely and the code falls through to the unbounded `arrayBuffer()` read with zero size enforcement applied
Prescribes a real streaming/hard byte-ceiling enforced against bytes actually received (not the declared header) as the fix, regardless of whether Content-Length is present or what value it claims

evals.prompt: A fictional subscription service, Northwind Media, renews subscriptions with a job that (1) calls the payment processor to charge the customer's card for the renewal period, and (2) on success, runs a compare-and-swap update on the subscription row -- `UPDATE subscriptions SET status = 'active', version = version + 1 WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2` -- moving it from `renewal_pending` to `active`. The job can run twice for the same subscription: once from the scheduled cron pass, and again from an operator-triggered manual retry a few minutes later if the first run's status looks stuck. A teammate reviewing a related bug report says: 'the compare-and-swap on `version` already makes this safe -- only one of the two runs can win that update, so we can't double-charge.' Evaluate the teammate's claim, and say what you'd change, if anything.
evals.expected_output: The teammate is wrong. The CAS on `version` only decides which of the two runs gets to record the subscription as `active` -- it does nothing about the charge, which already happened, in full, at step (1), before either run reaches the CAS. Both the cron pass and the manual retry can each call the payment processor and each succeed in charging the card; the CAS only decides which one's status write survives, not whether both charges fired. Whichever run loses the CAS still charged the customer, and that charge is now unrecorded -- the losing branch has no field or log entry saying 'I also charged the card.' Fix: reorder so the job claims the renewal (a CAS/reservation on the row moving it out of `renewal_pending`, or a per-period claim record) before calling the payment processor, so only the winner ever charges; or, if the processor must be called first, make the charge idempotent by passing a per-period idempotency key so a second call for the same subscription/period is a no-op at the processor; or, at minimum, record the charge's result as part of the same write that updates status so a losing run's charge is still discoverable and refundable rather than silently lost.
expectations: Rejects the teammate's claim that the version-checked CAS makes the flow safe -- states explicitly that the CAS only governs which run's status write survives, not whether the charge already fired
Explains that both the cron pass and the manual retry can each independently charge the card before either reaches the CAS, so the losing run's charge still happened even though its CAS update failed

Prescribes reordering to claim/reserve the renewal before charging, or making the charge idempotent via a per-period idempotency key at the payment processor, or recording the charge outcome atomically with the status write -- not accepting the existing CAS as sufficient

evals.prompt: A fictional customer-support platform, Meridian Helpdesk, escalates an unresolved ticket through a bot that (1) sends a Slack direct message to the ticket's account manager summarizing the escalation, and (2) then runs a compare-and-swap on the ticket row's `claimed_by`/`version` columns to mark the escalation as delivered. A bot instance holds a 20-second processing lease on a ticket while it works it; if the lease expires before the bot finishes, the escalation becomes eligible for another bot instance to pick up and process from the start. Slack API responses have occasionally taken longer than the lease window during vendor slowdowns. A teammate reviewing an unrelated flakiness report says: 'the compare-and-swap on the ticket already stops two bot instances from double-claiming the same escalation, so there's nothing else to check here.' Evaluate the teammate's claim, and say what you'd change, if anything.
evals.expected_output: The teammate is wrong. The CAS decides which bot instance's delivery is recorded on the ticket, but by the time either instance reaches the CAS, both may have already sent their own Slack DM to the account manager -- the CAS runs after the side-effect, so it cannot prevent or undo a message that already went out. If the lease expires mid-send during a Slack slowdown, a second bot instance is free to pick up the same ticket and independently send its own DM before either instance's CAS resolves; only one CAS succeeds, but nothing stops the DM send that preceded it. Whichever instance loses the CAS still sent its message, and that send is now unrecorded -- the losing branch's result has no field saying 'I also sent a DM.' This is not the lease-liveness race by itself (a paused/slow holder losing exclusivity) -- even a lease that behaved perfectly would still let both instances observe it as valid at the moment they each decide to send, because the send happens before either checks in with the CAS. Fix: claim the ticket (win the CAS/lease) before sending the DM, not after, so only the winner ever sends; or make the send idempotent/keyed by ticket id so a duplicate is suppressed at the Slack API; or, failing both, record that a send happened as part of the same write that updates the ticket, so a losing instance's DM stays discoverable and can be reconciled.
expectations: Rejects the teammate's claim that the CAS makes the flow safe -- states that the CAS governs which bot instance's delivery is recorded, not whether a DM already went out

Derives that a lease expiring mid-send lets a second bot instance pick up the same ticket and independently send its own DM before either instance's CAS resolves, so both DMs can go out even though only one CAS succeeds -- and distinguishes this from the lease-liveness/paused-holder race alone

Prescribes claiming (winning the CAS/lease) before sending, or making the send idempotent/keyed so a duplicate is suppressed, or recording the send's outcome atomically with the ticket state so a losing instance's send stays discoverable -- not accepting the existing CAS as sufficient

evals.prompt: In a fictional multi-agent delivery pipeline for Wavelength Drop, Lane A opens PR #482 and adds a `Verify: pending` gate checklist to the body by running `gh pr edit 482 --body-file checklist.txt`. Ten minutes later, Lane B -- reviewing the same PR for accessibility -- wants to add its own findings, and runs `gh pr edit 482 --body "$(cat a11y-notes.txt)"`. When Lane A's gate later reads the PR body to confirm the checklist marker, the marker is gone and the gate fails, even though Lane A never touched the PR again. What went wrong, and what should Lane B have done instead?
evals.expected_output: Lane B's `gh pr edit --body` call replaced PR #482's entire body -- `--body`/`-b` sets the body outright; it does not append to or merge with whatever is already there. Lane A's `Verify: pending` checklist marker lived only in the old body, and Lane B's call overwrote the whole body with just the a11y notes, so Lane A's own gate (which reads the body for that marker) now sees content that never mentions it and fails -- despite Lane A's own work being unchanged. This is the same blind-overwrite mechanism that lets a mistyped or stale PR number clobber a completely unrelated PR's body: `gh pr edit --body` is a last-writer-wins replace with no diff, no merge, and no ownership check. Lane B should have read the current body first (`gh pr view 482 --json body`), merged its a11y notes into that existing content, and re-posted the combined text -- or, since it was only adding, posted a `gh pr comment` instead of touching the body at all. Any process that batch-edits many PR bodies carries this same clobber risk on every single call.
expectations: Identifies that `gh pr edit --body` fully replaces the PR body rather than appending or merging -- Lane B's call wiped Lane A's checklist marker instead of adding to it
Explains why the failure lands on the wrong lane: Lane A's own work is unchanged, but the body its gate depends on was silently overwritten by a different lane's edit

Prescribes the fix: read-verify-write (`gh pr view --json body` before any `--body` edit, merge, then re-post the combined text) or use `gh pr comment` when only adding -- never a blind `--body` replace on content you didn't author

evals.prompt: A fictional platform team at Rustling Leaves Cloud dispatches four parallel agent lanes: three edit application code, and one -- Lane D -- edits `.github/workflows/ci.yml` to parallelize a slow test job. Lane D edits the YAML, runs the workflow-sensitive test suite locally, and commits cleanly. At `git push` it gets: `refusing to allow an OAuth App to create or update workflow .github/workflows/ci.yml without workflow scope`, and the push fails. The other three lanes push and merge without issue. The team lead assumes Lane D just needs to retry the push. Is that right, and what should the lead have done differently?
evals.expected_output: No -- retrying will not help, because this is not a flaky or transient failure. It is the pushing credential's `workflow` OAuth scope being absent, and every retry with that same token fails identically. GitHub requires the `workflow` scope on the token/`gh` auth used to push before it will accept any commit that adds or updates a file under `.github/workflows/`; a token without that scope is rejected at push time no matter how correct or well-tested the change is. Because the restriction is credential-wide, it silently blocks a whole CLASS of lanes -- any lane editing a workflow file -- not just this one; had the lead dispatched three workflow-editing lanes instead of one, all three would fail identically at the same step, each only after doing all of its own work first. A lane cannot self-heal this: granting the scope needs a human's browser device-auth (e.g. `gh auth refresh --scopes repo,workflow,read:org,gist`). The lead should have checked `gh auth status` for the `workflow` scope BEFORE dispatching any lane that touches `.github/workflows/`, kept CI-workflow edits in a separate batch from app-code lanes so a scope gap fails closed on only that slice, and -- since Lane D's commit is already good -- banked it locally and pushed it once the scope is granted, rather than rebuilding the change.
expectations: Rejects 'just retry the push' -- identifies the failure as the token/gh auth lacking the `workflow` OAuth scope required for any push touching `.github/workflows/*`, not a transient/flaky error
Recognizes the failure blocks a whole class of lanes (any workflow-editing lane) identically and cannot be fixed by the lane itself -- granting the scope needs the human's browser device-auth

Prescribes checking `gh auth status` for the `workflow` scope before dispatching a workflow-editing lane, separating such lanes from app-code lanes, and preserving (not rebuilding) the already-good local commit once the scope is granted

evals.prompt: A dashboard has a single 'Search' input pinned above three tabs (Orders / Shipments / Returns); only the active tab's panel is mounted. The Orders tab renders 300 rows. Its component builds each row's view-model inline in the render body — joining the order, its latest shipment status, and a computed 'days late' flag — and passes the result into `<OrderRow>`. The search input's `onChange` updates local `queryText` state synchronously (so typing feels instant) in the same parent that renders the active tab; a `useEffect` on `queryText` debounces 300ms before calling `fetchResults(debouncedQuery)`. Profiling shows all 300 Orders rows re-render on every keystroke, even before the debounce timer fires and even though Orders' underlying data hasn't changed. An engineer proposes bumping the debounce to 800ms. Will that fix the jank, and what actually will?
