Addresses the objection that forks do not receive repo secrets: GitHub does withhold secrets from a fork `pull_request` job, but the harm comes from sharing the machine with a secret-bearing job, so residue-harvest and cache-poisoning route around the withholding.

Explains why the review and tooling passed without touching the bug: each workflow is correct on its own; the actions really are SHA-pinned (a genuine but orthogonal positive) and the tests really are green, and neither those nor the runner's speed says anything about whether the runner is single-use or shared across trust tiers. May note that the speed is itself a tell in the wrong direction -- it is fast because the runner is reused and warm, the same property that makes the residue and the poisonable cache exist.

Prescribes the fix: run untrusted work on runners created fresh for a single job and destroyed after it, so nothing survives to the next job, and segregate runner pools by trust tier so fork/public-PR jobs never share a runner with jobs that hold deploy secrets. Concretely -- move `pr-check.yml` off `ci-box` onto GitHub-hosted runners or a dedicated single-use pool that carries no secrets, reserve `ci-box` (or its replacement) for privileged jobs, and gate fork-PR runs behind maintainer approval; if a self-managed runner must serve PRs it must be provisioned per-job and torn down, never a persistent shared host.

Prescribes detection for the class and bounds the claim: for every workflow read `runs-on`; a value that is not a standard GitHub-hosted image (`ubuntu-latest`, `windows-latest`, ...) is a lead rather than a verdict, since a custom label may resolve to a self-managed runner or to a GitHub-hosted larger-runner / runner group (the latter are hosted and rebuilt per job, so not this finding) -- confirm it is self-managed and persistent, then enumerate the workflows sharing that label and check each trigger, and if any is reachable by untrusted input (a fork `pull_request`, or `pull_request_target`/`workflow_run`) while another on the same label is privileged (push to a protected branch, or consumes `secrets.*`/deploy tokens), the shared persistent runner is the finding. Bounds it: the SHA-pinning and the passing tests are real positives and not the problem, and the broader risk of running untrusted PR code at all is a separate adjacent axis -- this finding is specifically that a reused, non-single-use runner is shared between an untrusted-trigger workflow and a privileged one.

evals.expected_output:
No -- the approval is sound for the three things the reviewer checked (the query is correct, it returns the newest row per metric, it is indexed and fast) but it misses the defect, which is not in the read query at all. The defect is that this read path exposes no signal of *how current* the number is, and the job that keeps it current can die without anyone noticing -- so once it does, the dashboard serves an arbitrarily old number that looks exactly like a live one.

Mechanism: `recompute_summary.py` wraps its whole body in `try/except`, logs the error, and exits 0 -- a reasonable choice on its own (one bad night should not crash the box or page anyone). But it means that if `recompute()` starts failing every night (an upstream schema change, an expired credential, a bug in `count_active_accounts()`), the job stops inserting new rows while the process still exits cleanly and the only trace is a log line nobody watches. The read query -- `ORDER BY computed_at DESC LIMIT 1` -- then keeps returning the last night that *did* succeed: a perfectly valid, indexed, fast query that now returns a value from an arbitrarily old row. The table even records `computed_at`, so the age is *available*, but `/api/summary` returns only `value`; the response and the tile are byte-identical whether the number was computed six hours ago or three weeks ago. There is no user-facing distinction between "this just recomputed" and "the writer has been dead for days."

Why the review passed is why the bug survives: the read path really is correct -- the query is right, the index is right, it is fast, and the test passes -- but none of those properties says anything about whether the row it returned is current or how a reader would know if the writer stopped. The seeded-row test actually hides the failure mode: it proves the read works when a fresh row exists, never that the system notices when new rows stop arriving.

Fix, on two surfaces. (1) Reader side -- surface the currency of the value: return `computed_at` alongside `value` and render a "data as of HH:MM" cue, and/or assert a bound at read time -- if the newest row is older than roughly 2x the nightly cadence, stop rendering a confident number and show a warning/degraded state instead. That is the one bit the current response throws away. (2) Operator side -- alarm when the job has not succeeded within about 2x its schedule (time since the last successful run), so a dead refresher pages someone instead of only writing a log line; record a real success marker (a heartbeat row or a last-success metric), not just "the process exited." The two are complementary: the operator alarm gets the pipe fixed, but until it is fixed the reader is still owed a visible signal that the number on screen is not live.

Bound the claim: the catch-log-continue resilience is fine to keep -- the defect is that its failure is invisible at the point of read, not that it swallows the error. This is about the *pipe's* liveness (did the recompute actually run), which is a different question from how old the underlying business data is; a per-record date the rows might carry does not answer "is the summary still being refreshed." And it is distinct from a cache stampede or a cached error/not-found -- there is no visible expiry here at all, precisely because a background job owns the refresh and its death goes unobserved.
expectations: Identifies that the defect is not in the read query (which is genuinely correct, newest-row-per-metric, indexed, fast) but in the read path exposing no signal of how current the value is: the response returns only `value` and drops `computed_at`, so the rendered number is byte-identical whether it was just computed or computed weeks ago.

Explains the silent-death mechanism: `recompute_summary.py` catches, logs, and exits 0, so if the nightly recompute starts failing it simply stops inserting new rows with no crash and no page -- and `ORDER BY computed_at DESC LIMIT 1` then keeps returning the last row that succeeded, an arbitrarily old value that looks live. Recognizes the catch-log-continue is a reasonable resilience choice; the problem is that the failure is unobservable at read.

Explains why review and tests passed without touching the bug: the query/index/speed are real but orthogonal positives, and the seeded-row test proves the read works when a fresh row exists rather than that the system detects new rows no longer arriving.

Prescribes the reader-side fix: surface the value's currency -- return `computed_at` and render a "data as of" cue, and/or assert a read-time bound (if the newest row is older than ~2x the nightly cadence, show a degraded/warning state instead of a confident number).

Prescribes the operator-side fix and bounds the claim: alarm when the job has not succeeded within ~2x its schedule (time since last successful run / a real success marker, not just process exit) so a dead refresher pages someone (cross-ref observability). Bounds it: the resilience is fine to keep; this is about the pipe's liveness, distinct from how old the business data itself is and distinct from a cache stampede or a cached error.

evals.prompt: A repository's release runs from `.github/workflows/release.yml`, which triggers on a tag push, has `permissions: write-all`, and can read the signing key and registry credentials from repository secrets. A branch-protection rule requires a review from the platform team before any merge that changes a file under `.github/workflows/`; changes under `scripts/` need one approval from any engineer on the repo. The one meaningful step in `release.yml` is `run: ./scripts/release.sh`. A pull request modifies `scripts/release.sh`, adding a line that pipes a remote script into `sh` before the build runs. A reviewer approves the PR: "This only touches a shell script, and the release workflow file itself is unchanged and still needs platform-team sign-off, so the protected path is intact." One engineer's approval merges it. Is the reviewer's reasoning sound?
evals.expected_output: No. The workflow *config* is protected, but the file it executes is not, and the release job runs whatever `scripts/release.sh` contains -- with `write-all` permissions and access to the signing key and registry credentials. The next tag push runs the attacker's `sh` pipe inside that privileged job: it can exfiltrate the secrets, publish a backdoored release, or tamper with the build, all without ever editing `release.yml`. "The workflow file is unchanged" is exactly why the platform-team gate never fired -- but that gate protects only the YAML, while the pipeline's real trust boundary is the transitive closure of everything it executes: the build script, any `Makefile`/`Dockerfile` it calls, hook and linter configs, `package.json` scripts. Whatever a privileged pipeline runs can act with the pipeline's privileges, so gating the config while leaving its executed files on a one-generic-approval path just relocates the attack one file over. Fix: put every file the release pipeline executes under the *same* enforced review gate as the workflow file (extend the required-review rule to `scripts/`, `Makefile`, `Dockerfile`, hook/linter configs, and the `package.json` scripts the pipeline invokes), and keep the privileged workflow's permissions and secret scope minimal so a script edit can't reach the signing key. The finding is not that `release.yml` is misconfigured -- it's that protecting the config without protecting its executed files leaves the privileged path open.
expectations: Concludes the reasoning is NOT sound: the protected workflow config still `run:`s `scripts/release.sh`, which is not under the same enforced review gate, so editing that script runs attacker code inside the privileged release job (write-all + signing key + registry credentials) on the next tag push -- without touching `release.yml`. NOT that `release.yml` itself is misconfigured.

Names the concrete impact: secret/credential exfiltration, a backdoored or tampered release, executed with the pipeline's privileges; and identifies that "the workflow file is unchanged" is precisely why the platform-team review never fired, so gating only the config relocates the attack one file over rather than closing it.

States the general principle: a privileged pipeline's trust boundary is the transitive closure of everything it executes (build scripts, a Makefile/Dockerfile it calls, hook/linter configs, package.json scripts), not just the workflow YAML.

Prescribes the fix: put every file the pipeline executes under the SAME enforced review gate as the workflow file, and minimize the privileged workflow's permissions/secret scope -- NOT merely re-confirming that the workflow file is protected.

evals.prompt: A CI pipeline has three jobs that run in order. `build` compiles the binary, then saves it with `actions/upload-artifact` and also writes the compiler's output directory to `actions/cache` under a key shared across branches. `test` restores that cache and runs the suite. `release` runs `actions/download-artifact` to pull the compiled binary, signs it with cosign, generates a provenance attestation, and publishes both alongside the binary. A security reviewer signs off on the release process: "Every published binary carries a valid cosign signature and a provenance attestation that verifies against our identity, so a consumer can prove the artifact came from our pipeline -- the chain of custody is covered." Is that conclusion sound?
evals.expected_output: No -- the signature and attestation are produced by the `release` job over whatever bytes reached it, so they prove custody only from that last step onward, not for the two handoffs that fed it. Nothing checks the binary as it passes from `build` to `release` via `download-artifact`, and nothing checks the compiler output restored from `actions/cache`, so anyone who can write that cache entry can seed a tampered entry that `test`/`build` restores and nothing between stages would catch it. If the bytes are altered before `release` signs them, the pipeline faithfully signs and attests the tampered artifact: the attestation comes out green over poisoned input, and the consumer's verification passes because provenance answers "did this come from our pipeline," not "were the inputs that built it untampered." Attestation at the promotion step is necessary but does not extend integrity backward over every handoff that produced the signed thing. Fix: validate integrity at *each* handoff, not only at the end -- attest or pin+digest-check the inter-job artifact before `release` consumes it, scope cache keys so they can't be written from an untrusted branch and verify the restored cache against an expected digest, and treat a missing or mismatched check between stages as fail-closed. The signature isn't wrong; it just covers a narrower span than "chain of custody" claims.
expectations: Concludes NOT sound: the cosign signature/provenance is generated by the `release` job over whatever bytes reached it, proving custody only from that step onward -- nothing verifies the binary handed from `build` via `download-artifact` or the compiler output restored from `actions/cache`, so tampering before `release` signs is signed faithfully and the attestation is green over poisoned input. NOT that the signature/attestation mechanism itself is wrong.

Identifies the unverified inter-job artifact and restored cache as a concrete tampering vector -- anyone who can write that cache entry seeds a tampered entry that `build`/`test` restores, or the inter-job artifact is altered before `release` consumes it -- and that provenance answers "came from our pipeline," not "the inputs were untampered."
Distinguishes end/promotion attestation from per-handoff integrity: signing at the final promotion step does not extend integrity backward over the earlier handoffs that produced the signed artifact.

Prescribes the fix: verify integrity at EACH handoff -- attest or pin+digest-check inter-job artifacts before a downstream job consumes them, scope and verify cache keys (no untrusted-branch writes; check the restored cache against an expected digest), and fail closed on a missing/mismatched between-stage check -- not only at promotion.

evals.prompt:
Review this migration, scheduled to run online against a 400M-row, high-write `events` table:

```sql
ALTER TABLE events ADD COLUMN ingested_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp();
```

The PR description says: "Adds an ingestion-time column. This is safe to run in business hours: it has a DEFAULT, so there's no backfill step and no long lock -- it's the fast, metadata-only ALTER path." Is that reasoning correct?
evals.expected_output: No -- the review must reject "it has a default, so it's the fast metadata-only path." clock_timestamp() is evaluated per row (a different value each call), so this default is not stored once as catalog metadata; it forces the entire table and its indexes to be rebuilt, holding a blocking table-level lock for the duration on a 400M-row hot table -- an outage, the opposite of what the author claims. The review should note that a constant/non-volatile default WOULD be metadata-only and fast, but this one is not, and give a safe path: add the column nullable, backfill in bounded batches, then set the value and enforce -- or use a genuinely constant default if one fits.
expectations: Rejects the author's 'it has a default, so it is fast / metadata-only / no long lock' reasoning rather than endorsing it
Identifies that this particular default is computed per row and therefore forces a full table-and-index rebuild, not a metadata-only change
Notes the rebuild runs under a blocking table-level lock on a large hot table (an availability/outage risk)
Contrasts with a constant/non-volatile default (which would be metadata-only) and prescribes a safe path (nullable column + bounded backfill, then enforce)

evals.prompt:
Review this migration. It ships in the same rolling deploy as the application change that starts reading the new name:

```sql
ALTER TABLE accounts RENAME COLUMN signup_ts TO created_at;
```

The PR says: "Trivial cleanup -- brings the column to our naming convention. It's an instant catalog-only change: no table lock, no data copied, so it's safe to ship any time." Anything to flag before this merges?
evals.expected_output: The review should agree the statement itself is cheap and fast at the database level, then flag that speed is not the risk. During a rolling deploy the previous application version is still running and still selects and writes `signup_ts`, which no longer exists once the statement commits, so those instances error until every pod has rolled to the new code. The fix is a phased, backward-compatible sequence rather than a single rename: add the new name alongside the old (e.g. a new column kept in sync, or a view/synonym), migrate all readers and then writers across separate deploys, and only drop the old name once nothing references it. "Catalog-only / no lock / no data copied" does not make it safe to ship in one step.
expectations: Does NOT treat 'fast / catalog-only / no lock / no data copied' as evidence the change is safe to ship as-is
Identifies that old application code still running during the rolling deploy references the old column name and will error once it is gone
Recommends a phased add-new / migrate-readers-then-writers / drop-old sequence across separate deploys
Frames the rename as a backward-incompatible interface change, not a cosmetic cleanup

evals.expected_output: The rollback mechanics are correct, and that is the trap — the finding is the message path, not the revert. `saveProfile` (and, by the wrapper's design, the whole app) renders failures through `toUserMessage(err)`; the new toggle handler instead reads `(err as Error).message` directly, so this one write is the single place that skips the shared mapper — an inconsistency (the app now speaks two error languages) and a leak. The reason it passed review and the author's 500 test is that a non-2xx response is the safe case: `apiFetch` reaches `if (!res.ok)` and throws a curated `ApiError` whose `.message` is already a clean sentence, so the direct read looks identical to the mapped one. The gap is a transport-level failure — offline, DNS, CORS, server unreachable — where `fetch()` itself rejects before `if (!res.ok)` ever runs, so the thrown value is a browser-native `TypeError` whose text is UA-specific ("Failed to fetch" / "Load failed" / "NetworkError when attempting to fetch resource"). `toUserMessage` maps that non-`ApiError` to the fixed fallback; the direct `.message` read shows the raw browser string verbatim, and because the toast host is an `aria-live="assertive"` region it is read aloud to a screen-reader user. Fix: route the toggle's `onError` through the same `toUserMessage(err)` the rest of the app uses — one mapping boundary for every user-facing failure, reverted writes included. Acceptance: a test that makes `fetch` reject with a raw `TypeError` (not a mocked 500) asserts the toast/announced text equals the fixed fallback, not the raw message; the author's 500-only test cannot catch it because the curated path is exactly the one that already looks right. (ux-writes.md.)
expectations: Identifies that the toggle's onError reads (err as Error).message directly while the sibling saveProfile and the rest of the app route failures through the shared toUserMessage mapper, and names that one path's inconsistency/leak as the defect rather than the rollback logic (which is correct)

Explains why the author's 500 test passes but the bug survives: a non-2xx throws a curated ApiError with a clean .message, whereas a transport-level fetch rejection is a browser-native TypeError (UA-specific, e.g. 'Failed to fetch' / 'Load failed') shown verbatim
Notes the leaked string is announced aloud because the toast renders into an aria-live region
Fix routes the revert path through the same toUserMessage mapper (one mapping boundary); acceptance test makes fetch reject with a raw TypeError and asserts the fixed fallback, not the raw message

evals.prompt: A feature asks the model to extract a shipping address and return it as JSON. The handler does `const addr = JSON.parse(resp.choices[0].message.content); order.city = addr.city;` and writes the order — no `try`/`catch`, no other checks. In review a colleague approves: 'We set the model to JSON mode, so the content is always valid JSON — parsing it directly is fine.' Is the colleague right, and what would you flag?
evals.expected_output: No. The colleague is wrong that JSON mode makes direct parse-and-use safe. A model's reply is a frequently-malformed input class, not a guaranteed clean string: even in JSON mode it can wrap the JSON in prose or a fenced code block, hit the token limit and return TRUNCATED (unparseable) JSON, or return a safety refusal that is itself well-formed JSON but carries none of the expected fields. Three gaps: (1) nothing validates the PARSED object against the expected shape — a successful parse proves syntax, not that `city` exists, so a missing/renamed field silently writes `undefined`; (2) there is no `try`/`catch` around the parse and no repair-once-then-deterministic-fallback, so a fenced or truncated reply throws and 500s the request; (3) a refusal / off-shape reply has no branch of its own — it is either thrown as a 500 or written to the order as a blank address as if it succeeded. Fixes: validate the parsed object against the shape; wrap the parse, repair at most once (e.g. strip a fence / re-ask) then fall back to a deterministic default or a surfaced error; and give the refusal / off-shape case its own branch that is surfaced to the user or the consuming logic, not mapped to a 500 and not stored blank-as-success. JSON mode constrains syntax only, so approving on that basis is the defect. (security-ai-agents.md.)
expectations: Rejects the 'JSON mode ⇒ safe to parse-and-use directly' reasoning and names the model reply as a frequently-malformed class — prose/fenced wrapping, token-limit truncation, and a well-formed safety refusal carrying none of the expected fields
Requires validating the PARSED object against the expected shape (a successful parse proves syntax, not that the fields exist), not just that JSON.parse succeeded
Requires a try/catch with repair-once-then-deterministic-fallback AND a distinct branch for a refusal / off-shape reply that is surfaced — not mapped to a 500, not stored blank-as-success

Requires the production credential to be scoped to the deploy job that needs it — bound to a protected deployment environment whose secrets only that job can read (with an approval / wait / branch restriction before deploy) — not left readable workflow- or repository-wide
Flags that a secrets-bearing pull_request_target job runs in a context influenced by untrusted contributor code and must not be able to read the production deploy credential

evals.expected_output: No — the loader returns correct data but pays an unnecessary round-trip on every render, and the one-line diff plus the concurrent pair already in the function is exactly why the review missed it. `getProfile` and `getRecentOrders` are both started before either is awaited (start timestamps t+1ms / t+2ms), so those two overlap correctly — that is the "fetches concurrently up top" the reviewer saw. `getPromoBanner()` takes no argument and reads nothing either prior call returns (a global promo, independent of the user), yet it is `await`ed on its own line and does not start until both prior reads have resolved (t+341ms, with the first two finishing ~t+338ms). It has no data reason to run last; it does only because it was appended at its point of use. So the loader pays the sum (~340ms for the pair + ~114ms for the banner ≈ the 455ms render) instead of the max (~340ms) — a full extra round-trip on the critical path, every request. The tell is structural: a group of reads kicked off together and then, immediately below it, a lone `await` whose arguments reference nothing the group produced. A correct concurrent pair already in the function is not proof the whole loader is concurrent — the trace (does this `await`'s input come from a prior `await`'s result?) has to run on the `await`s after the group too, and `getPromoBanner` fails it. Provenance confirms the shape: the concurrent pair and `getPromoBanner` land in different commits — the pair was written concurrent, and a later "seasonal banner" change added read k+1 at its natural spot without reopening the top-of-function group. That is why the diff is one line and the review waved it through: the group it should have joined is unchanged context (often outside the hunk), and "already fetches concurrently up top" reads as done. Fix: start `getPromoBanner()` with the other two — hoist it (`const pBanner = getPromoBanner()` beside `pProfile`/`pOrders`, then `await pBanner` at its point of use) — so all three overlap and the loader pays the max. One caveat on the fix: `getPromoBanner` is a non-critical read (a global promo), yet as a bare `await` today its failure already throws the whole loader — after profile and orders have resolved. Blindly widening a fail-all group does not fix that and, worse, discards the profile/orders results (which may still be in flight) whenever the banner rejects. Keep the fix resilient: hoist `getPromoBanner()` to its own promise with a `.catch` fallback (or use `Promise.allSettled`) and `await` it at its point of use, so a promo-banner outage degrades to no banner instead of failing the page. Acceptance: all three independent reads start within one tick, and the banner's failure does not fail the page. (performance-db-cost.md, Concurrency — the Sequential-`await`s bullet's batch-drift extension.)
expectations: Identifies `getPromoBanner` as independent of both prior reads (takes no argument, consumes nothing they return) and flags that it is awaited on its own line and does not start until both resolve though it has no data reason to run last — reads the timestamps as the pair overlapping (t+1/t+2ms) and the banner starting only afterward (t+341ms), so the loader pays the sum (~455ms) instead of the max (~340ms): a full extra round-trip on the critical path

Prescribes folding the third read INTO the existing concurrent group — start `getPromoBanner()` alongside `getProfile`/`getRecentOrders` (e.g. hoist to a promise variable and `await` it at its point of use) so all three overlap — not appending it after the group and not adding a second group beside it

Surfaces the batch-drift / provenance angle: a correct concurrent group already present is NOT proof the whole loader is concurrent, the argument-trace must run on the `await`s after the group too, and the group vs the trailing read land in different commits (a later change appended read k+1 past the top-of-function group) — which is why the diff is one line and the group it should have joined is unchanged context

Rejects the reviewer's "already fetches concurrently up top — LGTM": the existing group is the camouflage, and a diff-only pass that reads a correct group as "concurrency handled" misses an independent read appended past it

Notes a resilience caveat on the fix (beyond timing): `getPromoBanner` is a non-critical read whose failure should not fail the page, and a fail-all group rejects as a whole on any member's failure (discarding the sibling results), so it should be hoisted with its own `.catch`/fallback (or moved to `Promise.allSettled`) to degrade to no banner. Does not depend on the false premise that the current bare `await` already fails soft — today a banner rejection throws the whole loader

evals.expected_output: No. The strip is made focusable the same way on every row, but on the common rows whose two or three tags already fit within the column there is nothing to move: focus lands on a group that scrolls nothing and, because it is named, is announced to a screen reader for no reason. Because the strip renders once per dataset row, this adds a focusable target to nearly every row of a long list, lengthening keyboard traversal (WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order) on exactly the view meant to be scanned fastest — and the keyboard test still "passed" only because focus does land and a ring does show; the test never checks whether the stop has a purpose. The fix is to make the strip focusable only when it can actually scroll: gate the focusability (and the role and accessible name that exist to explain it) on a live measurement of whether the content exceeds the box — a ResizeObserver / resize-aware hook comparing the strip's scroll size against its client size (scrollWidth vs clientWidth) — instead of a constant prop, so only the rare rows that really scroll become focus targets. Recompute on mount and resize but not while the strip holds focus: removing focusability from the element that is currently focused drops focus to the document body, a worse Focus Order break than the empty stop it was fixing. On the rows that do scroll, keeping the group role plus an accessible name is correct — that is what tells an assistive-tech user why the strip is focusable and what the arrow keys will do.
expectations: Rejects the approval: identifies that because the strip is made focusable by a constant prop set the same way on every row, on the rows whose tags already fit within the column the focused group scrolls nothing — a purposeless focus target (announced by its name for no reason), repeated once per row, that lengthens keyboard traversal (Focus Order); and notes this is why a keyboard-only smoke test still passed (focus lands, a ring shows) without proving the stop has a purpose.

Requires making the strip focusable only when it can actually scroll — deriving the focusability from a live overflow measurement (a ResizeObserver / resize-aware hook comparing scroll size to client size, e.g. scrollWidth vs clientWidth) rather than a static prop on every instance — so only the rows that truly need sideways scrolling become focus targets.

Keeps the group role and an accessible name for the rows where the strip IS focusable, so assistive tech can explain why it is a focus target and what the keys do — the defect is the empty stop, not focusability itself; it does not tell the team to simply drop the role/name or the keyboard-scroll support outright.

evals.expected_output: No. The four inactive panels are never mounted, but their charts are already built before `<Tabs>` ever runs. `content: renderTrendChart(...)`, `renderCohortGrid(...)`, and `renderFunnel(...)` are function calls, and they are evaluated when `MetricsPanel` builds the `tabs` array literal in its own render — before that array is handed to `<Tabs>`. A prop value is an ordinary argument computed by the parent, so the container's rule of rendering only `tabs[active].content` gates which element is placed in the DOM, not which charts are computed: all five heavy builds run on the initial render. Worse, `active` is state inside `MetricsPanel`, so every tab click re-renders `MetricsPanel` and rebuilds all five charts again — the one interaction the tab set was meant to make cheap pays for every chart each time. The reviewer conflated "only the active panel is mounted" with "only the active chart is built." Memoizing the array (`const tabs = useMemo(() => [...], [metrics])`) does not fix it: it still builds all five on the first compute and on any `metrics` change, and the four never-opened charts still run — the problem is which branches execute, not how often they recompute. The fix is to move each panel's work to the moment it is shown: store a function or a component reference instead of a pre-computed element (`content: () => renderTrendChart(metrics.revenue)`, rendered as `tabs[active].content()`), or pass each panel its raw inputs and let the mounted panel compute its own chart. Then only the panels a user actually opens pay. Acceptance: the number of chart builds equals the number of tabs opened — zero for a tab never visited, one for a first visit — not the five defined. (A bare element such as `content: <TrendChart data={metrics.revenue}/>` would not be the problem: the element descriptor is cheap and nothing heavy runs until it mounts; it is the call in prop position, and the work inside it, that runs early.)
expectations: Rejects the sign-off and identifies the mechanism: `content: renderTrendChart(...)` / `renderCohortGrid(...)` / `renderFunnel(...)` are function CALLS evaluated when `MetricsPanel` builds the `tabs` array in its own render — before `<Tabs>` receives it — so all five heavy builds run regardless of which panel is mounted; the container's "render only `tabs[active].content`" gates which element enters the DOM, not which charts are computed.

Names the re-render amplifier: because `active` lives in `MetricsPanel` state, every tab switch re-renders `MetricsPanel` and re-runs all five builds, so the very interaction the tab set was meant to make cheap rebuilds every chart each time — and calls out that the reviewer conflated "only the active panel mounts" with "only the active chart is built."

Rejects a memoization-only patch: `useMemo` on the `tabs` array still builds all five on the first compute (and on any `metrics` change) and never skips a never-opened panel — the axis is which branches run, not how often they recompute, so memoization cannot cure it.

Prescribes moving the work to mount time — store a function / component reference / children the container invokes only for the panel it shows (`content: () => renderTrendChart(...)` rendered as `tabs[active].content()`), or pass raw inputs and let the mounted panel derive its own chart — so only opened panels pay.

States a render-count acceptance (chart builds equal tabs actually opened: zero for an unvisited tab, one for a first visit, not the five defined) and does not misfire on a bare element like `content: <TrendChart data={metrics.revenue}/>`, whose descriptor is cheap — it is the call, or an eagerly-computed inner prop, that is the defect.

evals.prompt: Review this list endpoint from an internal analytics API. The handler reads a `limit` query parameter and passes it straight through as the SQL `LIMIT` for the query that returns dataset rows; when the parameter is absent it defaults to 50, and when present the caller's value is used as given. A reviewer signs off: "Good — the endpoint paginates, so clients pull data in pages instead of all at once. Approved."
evals.expected_output: The review rejects the sign-off: supporting a `limit` parameter is not the same as bounding it. Because the caller sets the row count and the server enforces no maximum, one request can ask for — and this endpoint will return — every row in the table, so the response side is the amplifier: the memory to materialize and serialize the rows, plus DB work and egress, all scale with an attacker-chosen number, and a few such requests can degrade or take down the service (an availability risk, not merely a slow query). It requires a server-side hard maximum that clamps the requested size to a ceiling regardless of what the client asks for, and treats a sensible default paired with a missing (or far-too-high) maximum as still vulnerable — the limit is set inappropriately, not merely absent. The cap and cursor mechanics themselves live in the performance reference; the finding here is that the result-set size is client-settable and unbounded.
expectations: Rejects "the endpoint paginates / it takes a limit" as sufficient — identifies that the client sets the row count and the server enforces no upper bound, so a single request can return the entire result set (the whole table)

Frames it as a server-side availability / resource-amplification risk driven by an attacker-controlled parameter (memory to materialize and serialize the rows, DB and egress cost), not only a latency or over-fetch nit

Requires a hard server-side maximum that clamps the requested size to a ceiling regardless of the client's value, and notes that a sensible default with a missing or too-high maximum is still the defect (a limit set inappropriately, not just a limit missing)

evals.prompt: Review this reporting endpoint. It runs a synchronous multi-table aggregation whose running time depends on the date range the caller supplies — a few seconds for a narrow range, several minutes for a very wide one — and the handler holds the request open until the query returns before responding. It runs on the same fixed-size pool of request handlers that serves the rest of the API. A reviewer approves: "The numbers come back correct and the slow path is rare — ship it."
evals.expected_output: The review rejects the sign-off: "correct and rare" does not address availability. Because a single request can run for minutes and nothing bounds how long the handler may execute, each of the slowest requests holds one handler in the shared fixed-size pool for the whole duration, and a few concurrent ones occupy the entire pool — so every other caller, including cheap requests, is denied service. Correctness of the numbers and rarity of the slow path are not defenses: a caller can send the wide-range request deliberately and repeatedly. It requires a server-side wall-clock ceiling on how long a single inbound request may run, after which the server aborts the request and frees the handler; moving the heavy job to a background/queued job the client polls is a complementary fix but is not itself the per-request ceiling.
expectations: Rejects "correct and rare — ship it" as missing the availability risk — identifies that nothing bounds how long a single inbound request may execute

Explains that because the handler is synchronous and runs on a shared fixed-size pool, a few slow/expensive concurrent requests occupy the whole pool and deny service to other callers, and that a caller can send the expensive request deliberately so rarity is not a defense

Requires a server-side per-request time limit (a wall-clock ceiling that aborts the request and frees the handler); may note offloading to a background/queued job as complementary, but not as a substitute for the inbound ceiling

evals.prompt: Acme ships Concierge, a customer-support chat assistant that makes one LLM call per user message. On every turn the client builds the request by concatenating, in this fixed order: a long system prompt (the assistant's role, a formatting contract that says always answer as a JSON object, and a hard rule to refuse anything outside billing questions), then the full conversation history oldest-first, then the current user message. It sends the joined string to the model. The provider SDK is configured so that if the assembled input is larger than the model will accept, it automatically keeps only the most recent portion that fits and sends that. Short chats work perfectly. On long threads, testers report that Concierge starts replying in prose instead of JSON and will happily answer off-topic questions it is supposed to refuse. A reviewer signs off on the assembly code, reasoning: 'Those input-budgeting and placement checks are a RAG concern -- we do no retrieval, so there is nothing to rank or bound here.' Is the sign-off right?
evals.expected_output: No -- the reviewer has mis-scoped a general check to RAG. Retrieval ranking is only one instance of context assembly; the check applies to any prompt assembler, and Concierge is one. Look at the order: the system prompt (the JSON formatting contract and the refuse-out-of-scope rule) is concatenated FIRST, then oldest-first history, then the user message last. The SDK's 'keep only the most recent portion that fits' behavior drops from the FRONT on overflow -- so on a long thread the first thing silently discarded is the system prompt itself, then the earliest turns. That is exactly the reported symptom: with its instructions no longer in the input the model stops emitting JSON and stops refusing off-topic asks, and no error is raised because nothing failed -- the load-bearing text was simply dropped. The fix is to give the assembler an explicit input budget measured with the model's actual tokenizer (not a character estimate) and an explicit drop-priority that protects the load-bearing parts: pin the system prompt and the current user message, shed the OLDEST turns first, and drop whole messages rather than clipping one mid-content. Force the overflow in a test and assert the system prompt is still present in the assembled request and only oldest turns were dropped. This is per-call prompt assembly -- distinct from a RAG retrieval seam (there are no chunks to rank here) and from a long-running agent's conversation compaction; and a max_tokens cap bounds the response, not the input, so it does nothing for this. 'No retrieval' does not mean 'no budget': any assembler that concatenates parts without a budget and a protect-the-system-prompt drop order has this failure.
expectations: Rejects the sign-off AND the reviewer's premise itself -- that the absence of retrieval removes the obligation: the input-budget / drop-priority check is not RAG-specific, retrieval is only one instance of prompt assembly and this single-call chat assembler is another, so 'no retrieval' does not mean 'nothing to bound.' A response that reaches the right verdict but leaves the RAG-scoping premise standing (e.g. treats it as a one-off bug rather than naming the obligation as belonging to any assembler that concatenates parts) has not caught the fold.

Traces the concrete failure: because the system prompt is concatenated first and the SDK keeps only the most recent portion that fits, on a long thread the earliest text -- the system instructions (the JSON contract and the refusal rule) -- is silently dropped from the front with no error, which is exactly why the assistant stops emitting JSON and answers off-topic questions.

Prescribes an explicit input budget plus an explicit drop-priority that PROTECTS the load-bearing input: pin the system prompt (and the current user message) and shed the oldest turns instead of the front, dropping whole messages rather than clipping one mid-content; and verifies with a forced-overflow test that the system prompt survives assembly.
Distinguishes this per-call assembly from a RAG retrieval seam and from long-running-agent conversation compaction, and notes a max_tokens / output cap does not address an input-side overflow.

evals.prompt: Acme runs an internal project wiki. Every page has a free-text description that users frequently paste in from release notes, chat messages, or other tools, so a description often already contains some HTML, including anchor tags. Before a description is saved and later shown to every viewer, it runs through a shared helper, linkify(text), that turns any bare https:// URLs in the text into clickable anchors. Because a description flows through several formatting helpers and linkify sometimes runs on the same text more than once, its author made it safe to re-run: the very first thing linkify does is check whether text already contains an `<a ` tag, and if so it returns text exactly as it received it. Only when no anchor is present does it take the other path -- HTML-encode the text, find the bare URLs, confirm each one begins with http:// or https://, and wrap those matches in `<a href="...">`. The helper's output is stored and later inserted into the page with the framework's raw-HTML rendering call. A reviewer signs off on linkify: 'every URL it emits is scheme-checked and the surrounding text is encoded first, so whatever a user puts in a description is safe to render.' Is the sign-off right?
evals.expected_output: No. The sign-off describes only the second path. linkify's first action is an early return: if text already contains an `` tag (a harmless one is fine) alongside a hostile payload -- a raw `` or ``, or an anchor whose own href is a javascript: scheme. Because an `
expectations: Rejects the sign-off and names the specific hole: the 'already contains <a>' early return sends the text on to the reader WITHOUT the HTML-encoding and the http(s) scheme check, which run only on the URL-building branch -- so the reviewer validated a path the malicious input never takes.

Constructs the exploit itself rather than being handed it: observes that because descriptions are routinely pasted in already containing anchors, an attacker need only include any tag together with a payload (a raw

Names why it survived review: the safe-to-re-run short-circuit is deliberate and typically locked in by a run-it-twice unit test, which pins the very branch that omits the security checks; a reviewer reading only the link-building path sees correct escaping and a scheme check and signs off.

Prescribes making the safety step unconditional rather than just 'escape output': scope the re-run guard to the link transform and always encode/scheme-check, OR re-validate the pre-existing content (including the scheme of any anchor already present) on the skip branch instead of trusting it; and adds sink-side defense -- the raw-HTML renderer enforces its own scheme/tag allowlist regardless of upstream, ideally via one shared audited sanitizer.

evals.prompt: A React app has a shared <Modal> component that every dialog in the codebase renders through: it moves keyboard focus onto the dialog when it opens, keeps the keyboard confined to the dialog while it is open, hides the rest of the page from the screen reader, and returns focus to the trigger on close. Last week a new full-screen 'Session expired -- sign in to continue' gate was added. It is not rendered through <Modal>: it is a raw <div> mounted as a sibling of the app root that copies the same dialog role and the other ARIA attributes <Modal> sets, and visually covers the whole viewport with a dimmed backdrop. But nothing moves keyboard focus onto the gate when it appears; pressing Tab from the gate's last button moves the focus ring onto the navigation links on the page behind the backdrop; the content behind the backdrop is still announced by the screen reader and its buttons still respond to it; and dismissing the gate leaves the focus ring wherever it happened to land. A reviewer approved the PR: 'Looks good -- it has a dialog role and the same accessibility attributes as our real modals, and it covers the whole screen.' Do you agree with the sign-off?
evals.expected_output: The sign-off should be rejected, and so should its premise. A dialog role plus the modal ARIA attributes (role="dialog" + aria-modal="true") is not a description AT reads back but an instruction it acts on -- it tells assistive tech to confine the user to the dialog and treat the background as removed from perception. The hand-rolled gate delivers none of it: focus never enters it, Tab escapes to the background, the background is neither inert nor hidden from the screen reader, and focus is not restored on close -- so the copied aria-modal="true" is a false claim that is worse than omitting the attribute, because it sends a keyboard/AT user into background it swore was gone. The fix is to render the gate through the shared <Modal> primitive (or native <dialog>.showModal()), or, only if bespoke is unavoidable, to call the same focus-in / focus-trap / background-inert / focus-restore helpers -- not to keep a hand-rolled copy that merely carries the attributes. It is an instance of bypassing the shared accessible component and must be gated by a keyboard/DOM test, since an 'is it mounted?' test cannot catch it.
expectations: Rejects the sign-off AND the reviewer's premise that a dialog role plus the modal ARIA attributes is sufficient: those attributes assert modal semantics assistive tech acts on (confine the user to the dialog, treat the background as inert/removed), so their mere presence is not the bar -- the behavior must actually be delivered.

Names the concrete defect: because focus never moves into the gate, Tab escapes to the background, the background is neither inert nor aria-hidden, and focus is not restored on close, the copied aria-modal="true" asserts a containment the code does not provide -- a false claim that is worse than omitting the attribute, since a keyboard/AT user is sent into background the attribute said was gone.

Prescribes routing the gate through the shared modal / focus-trap / inert primitive (or native <dialog>.showModal()) rather than a hand-rolled sibling -- and, only if a bespoke overlay is unavoidable, calling the same focus-in / focus-trap / background-inert / focus-restore helpers; bolting the ARIA on without the behavior is explicitly not the fix.

Treats it as an instance of the bypass-the-shared-accessible-component family, not a one-off, and requires a keyboard/DOM regression test (focus lands inside on open, Tab wraps within, background is inert, focus returns on close) -- an 'is it mounted?' or source-text assertion cannot catch a missing trap.

evals.prompt: Acme's web app has a sign-in page. After a successful login it returns the user to wherever they started: the sign-in link carries a `next` query parameter holding a path, and on success the server reads `next` and issues a redirect to that value in the `Location` header, which the browser then follows. To keep `next` from bouncing a freshly-authenticated user to some other website, the handler validates it first. The check is two conditions: the value must begin with a `/` (so it is a path on this site), and it must not begin with `//` (a value like `//other-site.example/...` would be read by the browser as a reference to another site, so that form is rejected); a `next` that fails either condition is dropped and the user is sent to the dashboard instead. A reviewer approves the PR: 'Good -- it only lets `next` be a path on our own origin and explicitly rejects the `//other-site` form, so a crafted `next` cannot send anyone off our site.' Is the sign-off right?
evals.expected_output: No. The check reasons about the string, but the browser reasons about the URL, and the two disagree on one character. A browser's URL parser treats a backslash as equivalent to a forward slash in the authority position of an http/https URL, so a `next` of `/\evil.example` -- a leading `/` followed by a `\` -- satisfies BOTH conditions: it begins with `/`, and it does not begin with `//` (its second character is `\`, not `/`). Yet when the browser follows `Location: /\evil.example` it resolves the `\` to `/`, reads `//evil.example` as a reference to another site, and navigates to `https://evil.example`. The same holds for `\/evil.example` and `\\evil.example`. So the guard blocks the exact form the reviewer checked (`//host`) while passing its equivalents, and the redirect that was meant to stay on-origin sends the freshly-authenticated user off-site -- link spoofing / phishing, and a token-leak vector when the destination is trusted after auth. It clears review because the double-slash case is the well-known one and is usually the only one tested; the backslash equivalent is spec-mandated browser behavior a hand-rolled string check rarely accounts for. There is a mirror in the wild: a check that treats ANY value beginning with `/` as a safe relative path -- with no second condition at all -- is fooled the same way by `/\evil.example`. Fix: stop matching on the string prefix, which is not a structural test. Resolve `next` against a fixed base on your own origin with the platform URL parser and allow-list the resulting origin -- redirect only when the parsed origin equals your own -- rather than pattern-matching the raw string. If a prefix check is truly unavoidable, reject a leading `/` or `\` followed by another `/` or `\`: a negative lookahead that excludes BOTH characters (`/^\/(?![/\\])/`), not only the second slash (`/^\/(?!\/)/`). And when a codebase has more than one 'is this URL safe' filter -- a link target here, an image or iframe source there -- diff them against each other, not only against their own unit tests: a hardening that excludes both characters in one filter and only `/` in its twin is a gap, and a test scoped to a single filter never surfaces the divergence.
expectations: Rejects the sign-off and names the exact hole: a `next` beginning with `/` and then a backslash (e.g. `/\evil.example`) satisfies both conditions -- it begins with `/` and does not begin with `//` -- yet a browser resolves a backslash as a forward slash in an http/https URL's authority position, so `Location: /\evil.example` navigates to `evil.example`; the guard blocks only the specific `//host` form it was written against.

Constructs the bypass itself rather than being handed it and covers the variants: `/\host`, `\/host`, and `\\host` all clear a check that rejects only a leading `//`, and identifies the concrete outcome -- the freshly-authenticated user is redirected to an attacker origin (link spoofing / phishing, and a post-auth token-leak vector) -- plus the mirror case where a bare 'begins with `/` means safe' check (no second condition) is fooled by `/\host` too.

Prescribes replacing the string-prefix test with a structural one: resolve `next` against a fixed same-origin base using the platform URL parser and allow-list the resulting origin (redirect only when the parsed origin matches your own); and, if a prefix check must remain, excludes BOTH characters after the leading slash (a negative lookahead such as `/^\/(?![/\\])/`), not only a second `/`.

Generalizes beyond the one handler: names why it survives review (the double-slash case is the tested one; the backslash equivalent is spec-mandated browser behavior a hand-rolled regex rarely accounts for) and calls for diffing every 'is this URL/path safe' filter (link href vs image/iframe src vs redirect) against one another -- a hardening present in one filter but not its twin is a gap that per-filter unit tests never surface.

evals.prompt: A team runs an LLM-backed support-reply feature in production. For every call, their dashboards record the model name and the exact model build that served it, the token counts, latency, cost, and whether the call succeeded, errored, refused, or returned empty. Last Tuesday an engineer reworded the standing instruction the feature feeds the model -- a routine copy edit, pushed straight to prod with the app code. Over the next few days the replies got noticeably worse: more off-topic answers and more user complaints. No model upgrade happened in that window -- the dashboards show the same model and build the whole time. The team wants to find what changed and undo it, but when they slice the recorded call data, every field reads the same before and after the drop, so they can't line the regression up against anything they recorded. A reviewer looks at the setup and says the logging is fine: 'we already record the model and its exact build on every call, so any regression is attributable.' Do you agree?
evals.expected_output: Reject the sign-off. Recording the model and its build makes a *model* regression attributable, but the model is only one of the two inputs that decide an LLM call's behavior -- the instruction it is given (the prompt) is the other, and here it is the input that changed. A reworded prompt pushed to prod is exactly the kind of change that can degrade output quality, yet nothing on the call record identifies which revision of the prompt served each request, so the drop cannot be lined up against the change that caused it: model, build, tokens, latency, and outcome all read identical before and after, and the regression is unattributable even though the record looks complete. Fix: stamp each call with the prompt's identity alongside the model build -- a prompt version tag from wherever prompts are stored, or a hash of the prompt *template* (not of the rendered prompt: a hash of the filled-in text takes a new value on every request and is derived from payload you should not be logging) -- so a quality regression traces to the exact prompt revision that shipped it, the same way model + build already lets you trace a model change. The identifier is a version/hash, i.e. metadata, not the prompt text, so it does not reintroduce the raw-payload/PII risk that keeps prompts out of logs. This is the production-traceability counterpart of the pre-merge accuracy gate that already fails a build when a prompt or model change drops quality (`testing-ai-evals.md`): the gate stops a bad prompt change before merge; the prompt id on the call record localizes one that reaches prod. (`observability.md`.)
expectations: Rejects the sign-off: logging model + build makes a MODEL regression attributable, but the prompt/instruction is the other input that changes an LLM call's behavior and is the one that changed here, so 'we record the model build' does not make a prompt-caused regression attributable.

Names the concrete gap: nothing on the call record identifies which revision of the prompt served each request, so with model, build, tokens, latency, and outcome identical before and after, the drop can't be lined up against the change that caused it.

Fix: stamp each call with a prompt version tag or a hash of the prompt TEMPLATE alongside the model build, so the regression traces to the exact prompt revision -- and specifies the identifier is metadata (a version/hash), NOT the raw or rendered prompt text, so it does not reintroduce the payload/PII risk (a hash of the filled-in prompt is per-request and useless as a grouping dimension).

Frames it as the production-traceability counterpart of the pre-merge accuracy/eval gate on prompt/model changes (`testing-ai-evals.md`), not a restatement of it -- the gate blocks a bad change before merge; the prompt id on the call record localizes one that reached prod.

evals.prompt: A React web app reads the signed-in member through a `useUser()` hook that many components call. The hook is written so that no matter how many components call it while a screen renders, the app makes a single `GET /api/user` request and every caller reads the same result from it. The top navigation bar -- which is part of the app shell and stays mounted on every screen -- needs the member's avatar and an unread-notifications count; it calls a helper `fetchUser()` directly inside its own `useEffect` when it mounts, and re-runs that helper on a 30-second timer so the badge stays fresh. Users report that for a few seconds after the page settles, the nav's unread count and the count shown elsewhere in the app sometimes disagree. A reviewer approves the navigation change: 'I grepped every `useUser()` call site and they all read the same cached result -- we only fetch the member once.' Do you agree?
evals.expected_output: Reject the sign-off. The reviewer's grep proves the wrong thing: it confirms every *`useUser()` caller* shares one request, but the nav does not call `useUser()` -- it calls `fetchUser()` directly -- so it never appears in a grep of the hook's call sites, and it issues its *own* `GET /api/user` when it mounts plus another on every tick of its 30-second timer. The member is therefore fetched at least twice per load, not once, and the reviewer's method structurally cannot see the second fetcher. To actually enumerate the consumers, grep the *endpoint* (`/api/user`), not the hook name, and reconcile every hit against the hook's callers; the leftover hit is the nav. (A claim that the data is 'already cached so we fetch once' is a cue to audit for another consumer, not proof the caching is complete.) The disagreeing counts are the tell that this is not just wasted bytes: because the nav fetches and polls on its *own* timer, independent of the hook's data, its unread-count badge drifts out of sync with the count the rest of the app derives from the hook until each happens to refresh. Fix: route the nav through the same `useUser()` source it should have used -- delete its direct `fetchUser()` call and its private 30-second timer, and read the hook -- so a single request and a single refresh loop feed both the nav and the rest of the app. Guard it with a test that *mounts the nav together with an ordinary hook consumer* and asserts exactly one `/api/user` request; a test that mounts only a hook consumer passes while the nav still double-fetches, so it would not have caught this. (`web-fetch.md` -- the always-mounted consumer left outside an existing shared hook/Provider, the sibling of the identity fan-out bullet where the shared instance does not yet exist.)
expectations: Rejects the sign-off and identifies why the reviewer's grep is insufficient: it confirms only that `useUser()` callers share one request, but the always-mounted top nav calls `fetchUser()` directly and never calls the hook, so it does not appear in a grep of `useUser()` call sites and still issues its own `GET /api/user` -- the member is fetched at least twice per load, not once.

Gives the detection fix: because the nav holds a raw fetch rather than a hook call, a hook-name grep structurally cannot find it; enumerate consumers by grepping the ENDPOINT/URL (`/api/user`) and reconciling the hits against the hook's callers to surface the leftover consumer -- and/or notes that 'already cached so we fetch once' is a cue to audit for another consumer, not proof the caching is complete.

Names the CONSISTENCY consequence behind the disagreeing counts, not only the wasted request: the nav fetches and polls on its own timer independent of the hook, so its unread-count badge drifts out of sync with the count derived elsewhere until each refreshes.

Fix: migrate the nav onto the same hook/source -- delete its direct `fetchUser()` call and its private timer, read the hook -- so one request and one refresh feed all consumers; AND the regression test must mount the nav together with an ordinary consumer and assert a single request, because a test scoped to a hook consumer alone passes while the nav still double-fetches.

evals.prompt: A web app stores each user's chosen start date as the exact string the API returns -- values like `2026-03-14`, year-month-day and nothing else. To display it, the code runs `new Date(theString)` and formats the result with the browser's local formatter (`toLocaleDateString()`). A tester in London sees the correct day. A teammate in California files a bug: every start date renders as the day *before* the one that was saved. A reviewer investigates and concludes: 'The stored string is correct and `new Date()` is the standard parser, so this is a display-locale quirk, not a date bug -- the fix belongs on the formatting side.' Is that conclusion right?
evals.expected_output: No -- the defect is in the PARSE, not the formatter. `new Date('2026-03-14')` -- a date with no time component -- is parsed at midnight UTC (MDN: a date-only ISO string "will imply UTC time because it's date-only"). `toLocaleDateString()` then renders that instant in the viewer's own zone: for California (UTC-7/-8) midnight UTC is still the previous evening locally, so the formatter shows the previous calendar day; for London (UTC, or +1 in summer) it lands on the same day, which is exactly why the bug is invisible there. The wrong instant was produced before any formatting ran, so a formatting-side change cannot fix a value that is already the wrong moment. The reviewer also missed the trap that makes this subtle: the *same* calendar day written WITH a time and no offset -- `'2026-03-14T00:00:00'` -- is parsed in LOCAL time instead (MDN: "set to ... in the local timezone of the system, because it has both date and time"), so merely adding a time flips the behavior; and any non-ISO spelling (`'03/14/2026'`, `'2026/03/14'`) is, per MDN, "implementation-defined and may not work across all browsers," so `new Date(str)` on a non-ISO string is unportable, not reliably local either. Fix: keep a calendar day as a calendar day, parsed and formatted in one frame -- compare/format the `YYYY-MM-DD` string directly, or parse it explicitly as UTC and format with `timeZone: 'UTC'`, or hold it in a date-only type -- never round-trip a bare day through `new Date(str)` and a viewer-local formatter. (`time-date-correctness.md`, `lang-js-ts.md`.)
expectations: Rejects the 'display-locale quirk, fix on the formatting side' conclusion and locates the defect in the PARSE: a date-only string like `2026-03-14` is parsed at midnight UTC, so a viewer-local formatter in a zone behind UTC renders the previous calendar day -- the wrong instant exists before formatting runs

Explains why London sees the correct day while California does not -- a viewer at or ahead of UTC lands on the same day, a viewer behind UTC lands one day earlier -- i.e. the defect is zone-dependent, not a formatter setting

Names the asymmetry trap: the same day written WITH a time and no offset (`2026-03-14T00:00:00`) parses in LOCAL time instead, and any non-ISO/slash spelling is implementation-defined and unportable -- so neither 'add a time' nor 'use slashes' is a reliable fix

Prescribes keeping a calendar day in one frame: compare/format the `YYYY-MM-DD` string as-is, or parse explicitly as UTC and format with an explicit UTC zone, or use a date-only type -- never `new Date(str)` plus a viewer-local formatter

evals.prompt: A records system stores every user's date of birth in a column typed as a timestamp -- the same type used for `created_at` -- writing the birth date at midnight. Dates of birth are entered and checked by a data team working in central Europe. A support agent in Hawaii opens an account and the date of birth shows one day earlier than the identity document on file; some users on the US west coast report the same thing on their own profiles. The stored row is exactly what was entered. A reviewer says: 'The value we stored is correct, and we already store all times in UTC, so nothing is wrong here -- the readers just need to format consistently.' Do you agree?
evals.expected_output: No. A date of birth is a CALENDAR DATE -- the same date everywhere, with no moment in time attached -- so "store everything in UTC," which is the right rule for an instant like `created_at`, is the wrong rule here. Putting it in a timestamp column FORCES a moment: midnight was recorded in *some* zone (whether the data team's central-European zone or UTC), and every read then converts that moment to the reader's zone. For a reader behind the storage zone -- Hawaii (UTC-10) and the US west coast (UTC-7/-8) are behind both central Europe and UTC -- midnight crosses back over the date boundary into the previous calendar day, so a DOB of `1990-05-01` displays as `1990-04-30`. "Format consistently" cannot fix it, because the value is a MOMENT, not a DAY, and any zone-aware rendering of a moment is legitimately allowed to move it; the defect is the TYPE, not the formatter. Note it fails the same way whichever zone stamped the midnight (central Europe or UTC), which is what makes it a type-level bug rather than a mis-set zone. Fix: store the value in a date-only TYPE that carries no moment to convert -- a SQL `DATE` column, a `LocalDate`, or `Temporal.PlainDate`, which MDN defines as "a calendar date (a date without a time or time zone) ... an event on a calendar which happens during the whole day no matter which time zone it's happening in." The same applies to invoice dates, holidays, and all-day events. (`time-date-correctness.md`, `data-quality.md`.)
expectations: Rejects 'stored in UTC + format consistently' and identifies the TYPE as the defect: a date of birth is a calendar date with no moment attached, so a timestamp column forces a midnight in some zone that every read then converts

Explains the shift directionally: a reader behind the storage zone (Hawaii, US west coast) sees the stored midnight fall into the previous calendar day, so the DOB displays one day early -- and because a moment legitimately moves under zone conversion, consistent formatting cannot remove it

Distinguishes this from the legitimate 'store an instant in UTC' rule (correct for a point-in-time event like `created_at`, wrong for a value that is a calendar date everywhere) and notes it fails the same way whichever zone stamped the midnight -- a type-level bug, not a mis-set zone
Prescribes a date-only type end to end (SQL `DATE`, `LocalDate`, `Temporal.PlainDate` -- a type with no moment to convert) and generalizes to invoice dates, holidays, and all-day events

evals.prompt: A React product-search page renders `<Results>`, which re-fetches whenever the search box changes. Every change calls one shared helper, `runSearch(query)`: it switches a spinner on, `await`s `GET /api/search?q=<query>`, and — in a completion step wired to run no matter how the request ends — switches the spinner off and hands the returned rows to `setResults(rows => [...rows, ...page])`. A shopper types `lap`, which fires a search; before it returns they finish typing `laptop`, firing a second search through the same helper. The earlier `lap` request comes back first — while the `laptop` request is still outstanding — its completion step runs, the spinner switches off, and its rows are handed to the setter; the `laptop` response lands a moment later and its rows go to the same setter. On a fast local connection everything looks fine and the spinner always ends up off. QA on a throttled connection reports two things: the spinner sometimes disappears while the results the shopper is actually waiting on are still loading, and the list occasionally shows a block of loosely-matching rows for a half-typed query sitting above the ones that belong. A reviewer signs off: 'Both entry points go through the one helper, and its completion step always switches the spinner off, so it can never get stuck spinning — I typed a query and watched it clear. Ship it.' Do you agree?
evals.expected_output: Reject the sign-off. 'Always switches the spinner off' is the defect, not the safeguard. The completion step is shared by both searches and runs unconditionally, so it fires for whichever request happens to settle — including the earlier `lap` request, which the shopper's later typing already superseded. Because `lap` comes back while the current `laptop` request is still outstanding, its completion step switches the spinner off even though it does not own the current operation: the search the shopper is actually waiting on has not settled, so the spinner reads 'done' while those results are still in flight. The same unconditional completion also hands the superseded `lap` rows to the shared `setResults(rows => [...rows, ...page])`; nothing clears them and the reducer only appends, so the later `laptop` rows pile on after the leftover `lap` rows — the block of loosely-matching rows QA saw. The fix is to establish operation identity before the completion is allowed to act: stamp each request with a monotonic id/sequence (or wire an `AbortController` per search), and let only the *current* request's completion switch the spinner off and only the current response feed the setter — drop or abort a superseded one instead of clearing the indicator or merging its rows. (Equivalently, give each in-flight operation its own indicator so one cannot clear another's; and a fresh search should *replace*, not append.) The reviewer's evidence — 'I typed a query and watched it clear' — is a single-path check that structurally cannot see this: it never overlaps two requests. Guard it with a test that fires two searches, lets the superseded one settle while the current one is still outstanding, and asserts both the spinner state and the rendered list; a one-query test passes while the superseded completion still clobbers the indicator and merges the wrong rows. (`web-fetch.md` — a cleanup arm shared by two async operations clearing a loading flag it does not own, here the cross-generation variant where a superseded request's settle flips off the flag the current one still needs.)
expectations: Rejects the sign-off and identifies why 'always switches the spinner off' is the bug rather than the safeguard: the completion step is shared and unconditional, so the earlier `lap` request — already superseded by the shopper typing `laptop` — settles while the current `laptop` request is still outstanding, and its completion switches the spinner off even though it does not own the current operation, so the spinner reads 'done' while the search the shopper is waiting on is still in flight.

Explains the loosely-matching block as the same defect in the reducer: the unconditional completion hands the superseded `lap` response to the shared `setResults(rows => [...rows, ...page])`, which merges it and lets the later `laptop` rows append after the leftover `lap` rows — a superseded response must be dropped, not merged (and a fresh search should replace, not append).

Gives the identity-gating fix: stamp each request with a monotonic id/sequence (or wire an `AbortController`) and let ONLY the current request's completion switch the spinner off and ONLY the current response feed the setter, dropping or aborting a superseded one — or give each in-flight operation its own indicator so one cannot clear another's.

Names the test gap: the reviewer's single-path check ('typed a query and watched it clear') cannot reproduce this because it never overlaps two requests; the regression test must fire two overlapping searches, let the superseded request settle while the current one is still outstanding, and assert both the spinner state AND the resulting list.

evals.prompt: Our CI security-audit step reads an ignore file listing advisories we've accepted, each row carrying a comment explaining why it's safe to skip. A dependency-bump PR regenerates that file; the generator re-emitted every existing row unchanged, including `# safe: false positive, upstream patch pending (ISSUE-42)` next to a suppressed high-severity advisory. The audit is green, the file now has 40 rows (it was 31 two quarters ago), and a reviewer approves it because every row still has a documented reason. Sign off?
evals.expected_output: A documented reason is not a current fact. Each suppression row's comment (here 'false positive, upstream patch pending, ISSUE-42') is a falsifiable claim to re-verify against current source and ticket state before it is trusted, not settled truth carried forward: check ISSUE-42's real status and grep the code for the flagged path, because if the upstream fix has since shipped (or the false positive became real) the row now hides a live high-severity finding while the audit stays green -- so the regenerated file must not be approved on the strength of its documented reasons. The review asks that each entry carry an expiry or a re-verification trigger (a date, a linked-issue state check, a periodic sweep) rather than a permanent documented reason, and flags that a passing audit plus a count that only ever grows (31 -> 40, nothing ever removed) proves only that the accepted set is still accepted (no new unaccepted finding), never that any row's reason still holds -- so the set must be diffed across regenerations to confirm entries actually leave, not just arrive. Dropping the row merely because it 'looks old,' without re-verifying ISSUE-42 against current source, does not satisfy this.
expectations: Treats the row's 'upstream patch pending (ISSUE-42)' comment as a claim to re-verify against current ticket and source state, not a fact carried forward because it is documented
Warns the suppression can now hide a live high-severity finding if the upstream fix already shipped or the false positive became real, while the audit stays green
Calls for a per-entry expiry or re-verification trigger, not a permanent documented reason

Flags that a green audit proves only that the accepted set is still accepted (no new unaccepted finding), never that any row's reason still holds; and that an only-growing, never-shrinking set shows the suppression never tightens, so it must be diffed across regenerations to confirm entries actually leave

evals.prompt: A teammate asks whether feature X has shipped to production. A reviewer runs `git log --all --grep` for it, finds the commit, sees the feature's PR is marked merged, and concludes "yes -- it's live in prod." Context: the team develops on a long-lived `development` branch that is about 1,500 commits ahead of `main`; production deploys only from `main`, and the open PR meant to reconcile `development` into `main` is currently conflicting. Is the reviewer's "it's live" conclusion sound, and if not, what would actually settle it?
evals.expected_output: The "it's live" conclusion is rejected as unproven: a `git log --grep` hit and a "merged" PR status only establish that the change is on `development` (or some branch), not on `main`, the branch production deploys from. What settles it is a containment check against `main` specifically -- `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> origin/main` -- and, because a squash/rebase merge makes the original SHA a non-ancestor even when the content shipped, corroboration via `main`'s tree (git grep / git show on the `main` ref) or the forge record of the merge into `main`. "Merged to development" (integration milestone) and "promoted to main" (shipped) are kept distinct, and the ~1,500-commit divergence with a conflicting reconcile PR is flagged as a release-readiness risk in its own right.
expectations: Rejects "it's live" as unproven -- a commit-grep hit and a merged-PR status establish presence on development / some branch, not that the change reached main, the branch prod deploys from

Names a containment check against main specifically (e.g. git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> origin/main, or grepping/reading main's own tree) as what would settle it -- not a repo-wide or current-branch grep, and not the merged status

Handles the squash/rebase false-negative: a preserved-SHA ancestry test can read "not shipped" for work that did ship, so corroborates via main's tree (git grep / git show on the main ref) or the forge record of the merge into main

Distinguishes merged-to-integration (development) from promoted-to-release (main), and/or flags the large divergence plus conflicting reconcile PR as a release-readiness risk rather than treating grep-visible work as live

evals.prompt: A data table renders its rows sorted by a status column. Months ago, to keep not-yet-started work out of the way, someone added a rule to the row-sorting logic: any row whose status is `Pending` is pushed to the bottom, and every other row is ordered by comparing its status text. Last week a separate feature shipped a new status, `Draft`, for rows a user has started but not submitted; that change added the status and its badge but did not touch the sorting code. Reviewing the table now, you see `Pending` rows correctly at the bottom, but `Draft` rows appear scattered among the active rows rather than grouped down with `Pending`. The engineer who wrote the diff approved it with the note "placeholders sort last -- looks right." Is that approval sound? Explain what is actually happening to the `Draft` rows, and how you would fix the ordering so it does not break again the next time a status like this is introduced.
