evals.expected_output: The approval is not sound. The sorting rule hard-codes exactly one placeholder: it forces `Pending` to the bottom and routes everything else -- `Draft` included -- through the status-text comparison, so `Draft` rows sort by the raw string `Draft` into wherever it falls among the active statuses instead of dropping to the bottom. "Placeholders sort last" holds only for the one placeholder the rule names; the ordering covers a subset of the placeholder set, and the newly added `Draft` was never given a rule. The order is still internally consistent (a valid total order), which is why nothing looks broken except the misplaced rows -- a monotonicity / total-order check would pass and miss it. Fix by keying the decision on a positive predicate -- "is this a real, user-facing status?" -- and forcing every non-real status to the bottom in the else branch, so any placeholder added later is covered by construction with no list to maintain. If an explicit list is unavoidable, derive it from the single enum/type that defines the statuses (so a new member is included automatically) and add a test that fails when a new placeholder status is added with no ordering rule -- a test pinning only the currently handled placeholders proves non-regression, not completeness.
expectations: Rejects the approval: the rule pushes only `Pending` to the bottom and sends every other row -- including the new `Draft` -- through the ordinary status-text comparison, so `Draft` sorts by its raw value into the active rows instead of to the bottom

Identifies that the ordering handles only one of several placeholder statuses -- the placeholder set has more than one member and the later-added one has no rule -- rather than treating it as a generic sort bug

Prefers a positive "is this a real value?" predicate whose else branch forces every current or future placeholder to the end by construction (no per-value list to keep complete); or, as a fallback, deriving the placeholder set from the single enum/type that defines it so a new member is included automatically

Calls for a test that fails when a new placeholder status is added with no ordering rule, noting a test pinning only today's handled placeholders proves non-regression, not completeness -- and/or notes the result stays a valid total order, so a monotonicity check would not catch the misplacement

evals.prompt: An Android banking app keeps the user signed in across launches by saving the auth token and a cached copy of the last account balance so the home screen renders instantly, even with no network. The developer writes both values with the standard app-preferences API into the app's own private data directory. In review the developer signs off: "These live in the app's private sandbox that only our own app can read, and every phone sold in the last decade encrypts its storage at rest, so a lost or stolen phone is already covered and there's nothing more to do here." Is that sign-off sound for a security review, and if not, what would you require before approving it?
evals.expected_output: The sign-off is rejected. The 'private sandbox' guarantee holds only on a non-compromised device: a rooted or forensically-imaged phone, a device or cloud backup, or an instrumented process (e.g. a hooking framework on a controlled device) can all read the app's private data directory, so a plaintext long-lived token and the cached account data walk off a lost, stolen, or seized device. 'Encrypted at rest' does not cover this: full-disk / file-based encryption protects a LOCKED or powered-off device, but once the device is unlocked and the app can read its own files, a privileged local adversary (root, a restored backup, instrumentation) can read them too -- it is device-versus-outsider isolation, not app-level protection of the secret, so 'the phone encrypts storage' is not a reason to store a secret in plaintext. What is required before approval: store the credential in the platform hardware-backed secure store (Android Keystore-wrapped storage, or on iOS the Keychain with a this-device-only, when-unlocked protection class), ideally hardware-backed and bound to a user-authentication requirement; encrypt any local database or preferences with a Keystore/Keychain-managed key instead of writing plaintext app preferences; exclude the data from device and cloud backups; and prefer a short-lived, server-revocable token over a long-lived plaintext one. The mobile threat model -- physical device access, other installed apps, and backups -- is named as the reason server-side 'secrets in env' reasoning does not transfer to a value sitting on the user's device.
expectations: Rejects the 'private sandbox = safe' claim: the app-private data directory is readable on a rooted / compromised device, via a device or cloud backup, or through forensic / physical extraction -- the mobile threat model (physical access, other installed apps, backups) is not the server-side model, so a plaintext long-lived token there is extractable

Rejects 'encrypted at rest = covered' on the mechanism: names that full-disk / file-based encryption only protects a LOCKED or powered-off device and does NOT isolate the app's own data from a privileged on-device adversary (root / restored backup / instrumentation) once the device is unlocked

Requires the secret move into the platform hardware-backed secure store -- Android Keystore-wrapped storage, or iOS Keychain with a device-only, when-unlocked protection class (hardware-backed and user-auth-bound where warranted) -- or at least a local store encrypted with a Keystore/Keychain-managed key, rather than plaintext app preferences
Treats the cached balance as PII with its own leakage path (exclude it from device and cloud backups) and/or calls for a short-lived, server-revocable token instead of a long-lived plaintext one

evals.expected_output: No -- the approval misreads WHEN the params are read. The handler snapshots the query string into `params` at the moment each keystroke schedules the write (outside the setTimeout), so the write still waiting when the user clicks the status chip holds the params as they were BEFORE that click -- `q` only, no `status`. The chip's immediate write sets `?q=invoice&status=open`; then the waiting search write fires 300ms later, rebuilds the URL from its already-read `params` (which never saw `status`) and calls `router.replace('/reports?q=invoice')`, overwriting the newer status write -- so a change made for an unrelated reason while the write was waiting is reverted the moment the stale write lands. 'It spreads the existing params' is true, but the spread captured a set that is now out of date; it preserves only the params that existed at schedule time. It is invisible per-control because it needs the overlap -- a second write landing between the search write's schedule and its fire -- so every single-control test passes. Fix: read current state at fire time instead of replaying a captured set. Build the payload INSIDE the setTimeout from the live URL (read `new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)` when the timer fires) or via a functional/merge update, so it merges over whatever `status` is current; move the delayed write into an effect keyed on the search value whose cleanup cancels the still-waiting write on each change and on unmount; and route every delayed URL writer through one shared write hook so they all merge over current state rather than each holding its own copy. Add a test that schedules the search write, issues a different param's write before it fires, lets it fire, and asserts the other param survives. Distinct from a loading-flag clobber (that clears a boolean a concurrent operation does not own) and from request de-duplication (how many requests fire) -- here the question is which write wins.
expectations: Identifies that `params` is read at schedule time (outside the setTimeout), so the still-waiting search write holds a set captured before the status click and, when it fires, rebuilds the URL without `status` and overwrites the newer immediate write -- a concurrent change reverted by a stale delayed write

Rejects 'it spreads the existing params so it preserves status': the spread captured the params as they were at schedule time, not at fire time, so it preserves only what existed before the status click; notes it is invisible per-control because it requires the overlap of a second write landing before the delayed write fires

Fix reads current state at fire time -- build the payload inside the timer from the live URL or a functional-merge update (not a set captured at schedule time), key the delayed write to an effect with cleanup that cancels the still-waiting write, and share one delayed-write hook; plus a test that issues a different param's write before the delayed one fires and asserts it survives
Distinguishes it from a loading-flag clobber (a boolean a concurrent op does not own) and from request de-duplication (how many requests fire) -- here it is which write wins

evals.expected_output: No -- the approval misses the ordering. `db.comments.findTree` runs at the top of the handler, BEFORE the `if (!req.viewer)` guard, so the signed-out path -- the majority of traffic -- executes the full comment-tree query and then returns `{ post, comments: [] }` without ever reading `comments`. The endpoint therefore issues and throws away that query on its most frequent path. 'It's needed for signed-in viewers' is true, but it is positioned so it runs for EVERYONE; 'a single indexed query' does not make a per-request read whose result the common branch drops free -- at endpoint scale it is one wasted round-trip plus its DB load on every signed-out hit. The fix is to relocate the call, not to cache it: move `await db.comments.findTree(...)` BELOW the `if (!req.viewer) return` so only the signed-in branch that consumes it issues it (fetch `post` first, branch, then fetch comments), or make it lazy behind a thunk/promise the signed-in branch awaits. Caching does not fix it -- a cached read is still a needless lookup on a path that ignores the result; the lever is WHERE the call sits, not how often it recomputes. Detect by checking, for each `await`, whether its result is read on every branch that can return after it -- a value consumed only past an earlier return is the finding. Acceptance: `findTree` executes zero times on the signed-out path after the fix. Distinct from over-fetching columns/rows (which trims a result the branch DOES use), from parallelizing independent awaits or reading a twinned source once (reads that are all used, just serialized or duplicated), and from dead code (an unreferenced function nobody calls -- here the call runs on every request and only its result goes unused on the hot branch).
expectations: Identifies that `findTree` runs above the `if (!req.viewer)` guard, so the signed-out majority executes the full comment-tree query and returns `comments: []` without reading its result -- the endpoint issues and throws away the query on its most frequent path

Rejects the sign-off: 'needed for signed-in viewers' is true but the call is positioned to run for everyone, and 'a single indexed query' does not make a per-request read whose result the common branch drops free at endpoint scale

Fix relocates the call rather than caching it: move the await below the guard (fetch post, branch, then fetch comments only on the signed-in branch) or make it lazy; notes caching does not help because a cached read is still a needless lookup on a path that ignores the result -- the lever is where the call sits, not how often it recomputes

Gives detection (for each await, is its result read on every branch that can return after it?) and acceptance (findTree runs zero times on the signed-out path); distinguishes from over-fetch, from parallelize/read-once (reads that are used), and from dead code (an unreferenced function)

evals.prompt: A webhook order-import handler receives a payload of up to a few thousand line items and persists them like this: `for (const item of payload.items) { await db.orders.insertOne(item); }`. The reviewer runs the linter's no-floating-promises rule, confirms every database call is properly awaited with no dangling promise, checks that each insert is individually correct, and signs off: 'every write is awaited, no floating promises, correct.' Review the persistence path.
evals.expected_output: The review flags that writing one row per network round-trip inside the loop issues one database call per item -- N sequential round-trips that scale with the payload size, so throughput collapses and a large import times out. It notes why the await-correctness / floating-promise check cannot see it: the promise IS awaited (that is exactly why the missing-await scan passes) and the cost is the round-trip count, not a dangling promise; and there is no prior query result being looped, so a read-N+1 grep does not match either. It recommends collapsing the loop into a single bulk/batched write (insertMany / a multi-row INSERT / COPY / the ORM's createMany), chunked to a bounded number of round-trips if the driver caps batch size, in one transaction where atomicity matters. It explicitly rejects wrapping the same per-row writes in Promise.all as a non-fix (still N round-trips, can exhaust the connection pool) and preserves per-row error attribution when partial success matters.
expectations: Identifies N sequential single-row writes (one round-trip per item, scaling with input size) as the defect -- not a correctness or missing-await bug
Explains why an await-correctness / floating-promise scan misses it: each write is correctly awaited and the cost is the round-trip count, not a dangling promise
Recommends a single bulk/batched write (insertMany / multi-row INSERT / COPY / createMany), rejects Promise.all-over-N-single-writes as a non-fix, and keeps per-row error handling

evals.prompt: A reviewer scanning a pricing module files a Critical performance finding: 'nested loop -- O(n^2) -- rewrite with a hash map before this ships.' The code iterates the application's supported currencies and, for each, loops the same list again to find a matching rounding rule: `for (const a of SUPPORTED_CURRENCIES) { for (const b of SUPPORTED_CURRENCIES) { ... } }`. SUPPORTED_CURRENCIES is a hard-coded constant of 12 entries defined in the module's config. Assess the finding.
evals.expected_output: The review rejects (or downgrades) the Critical: the collection is a compile-time constant of fixed size (12 entries), so the nested scan is a small constant times a small constant with no growth term and no measurable cost -- the hash-map rewrite is churn with no win. It states the discriminator: a nested-loop / quadratic finding is warranted only when the collection's size scales with request input, dataset size, or an attacker-controlled count (unbounded / request-scale), not when it is bounded by config, an enum, or a schema. It notes that the same shape over a request-sized or attacker-controlled collection WOULD be a real finding (and a denial-of-service lever), so the discipline is to check what bounds n before filing, not to pattern-match the loop shape.
expectations: Recognizes the collection is bounded by a compile-time config constant, so the nested loop is a fixed small constant -- not a real quadratic-growth problem
Rejects or downgrades the Critical rather than endorsing the hash-map rewrite; names it a false positive
States the discriminator: reserve the quadratic finding for unbounded or request/attacker-scale n, where growth (and possible denial of service) is real

evals.prompt: A login rate limiter keys its per-client counter on the client IP, derived as `const ip = req.headers['x-forwarded-for'].split(',')[0].trim();`. The app sits behind a CDN and one reverse proxy. The reviewer writes a test: an honest client hits the endpoint, the derived IP equals the client's real address, the counter increments, and after 5 attempts the limiter blocks. The reviewer confirms the code handles the comma-separated list and trims whitespace correctly, and signs off: 'client IP extracted correctly, limiter works.' Review the IP derivation.
evals.expected_output: The review flags that the leftmost X-Forwarded-For entry is written by the original client, so it is fully attacker-controlled -- as forgeable as any client-sent header. An attacker sends a crafted X-Forwarded-For and mints a new 'IP' per request, resetting the counter and defeating the limit; the same inversion breaks an IP allow/deny, a geo decision, or an audit trail built the same way. It explains why the happy-path test still passed: for an honest client the leftmost entry happens to be the real address, so every functional test is green and only a crafted header exposes the flaw -- confirming the parse is correct never reaches the question of which end is trusted. Fix: pin the number N of trusted proxies in front of the app (or a trusted-CIDR set) and take the (N+1)th entry from the right -- the address the app's own outermost trusted proxy observed and appended -- via the platform's proven primitive (Express trust proxy plus req.ip, WSGI ProxyFix, nginx set_real_ip_from), never a fixed left index; if the origin is reachable directly the header is unusable and the decision must bind to an authenticated principal instead. Cites CWE-348 (Use of Less Trusted Source) / CWE-807 (Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision).
expectations: Identifies the leftmost X-Forwarded-For entry as client-controlled and forgeable, so the limiter (and any IP allow-deny / geo / audit built the same way) is bypassable by a crafted header -- not merely a parsing question
Explains why the happy-path test passed (for an honest client the leftmost entry is the real IP; only a crafted header reveals the inversion), so parse-correctness is not the property under review

Fixes by counting trusted proxies N and trusting the (N+1)th-from-the-right entry via a proven platform primitive (not a fixed left index), or binding to an authenticated principal when the origin is directly reachable

evals.prompt: Fictional issue-tracker app, Beacon. A select-only combobox (a button that opens a popup with role="listbox") is built by hand. Its dismiss handling: a keydown on the listbox closes it on Escape; a document pointerdown listener closes it when the click is outside both the button and the popup; and choosing an option closes it. Focus uses roving tabindex -- while the popup is open only the highlighted option is focusable, and the combobox button is the single tab stop for the whole widget (the options are not in the page tab order). QA verified that Escape closes it, clicking elsewhere closes it, and selecting an option closes it. The reviewer approved: "Every way to dismiss this popup is handled -- Escape, click-away, and selection all close it; there is no dismissal path we have missed." Do you agree with the sign-off?
evals.expected_output: No. The widget has a fourth, independent dismiss path the sign-off misses: keyboard focus leaving the widget. Because the popup and its options are excluded from the page tab order (the WAI-ARIA APG combobox keeps the combobox a single tab stop), pressing Tab or Shift+Tab moves focus to the next page control -- which fires no pointer event (so the outside-click listener never runs) and is not the Escape key (so that handler never runs). Wired only for Escape + outside-click + selection, the popup is left open and orphaned -- floating over the page while focus sits on a later control -- a WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order break. A keyboard-only smoke test that opens, arrows, and Escapes never presses Tab while the popup is open, which is why it passes. Fix: add the focus-exit dismiss -- a focusout/blur handler on the widget container that closes when relatedTarget falls outside the trigger+popup subtree (or handle Tab/Shift+Tab in the keydown before focus moves), then let focus land naturally on the next control. A non-modal popup must NOT trap focus, so do not add a focus trap. Regression test: render the popup open, move focus to a control outside the widget, and assert the listbox is gone (queryByRole("listbox") is null), not only that Escape closes it.
expectations: Identifies that focus leaving the widget by keyboard is a distinct dismiss path, separate from Escape (a keydown) and outside-click (a pointer listener), that the sign-off does not cover

Explains the consequence: the popup is left open/orphaned with focus on a later page control -- a WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order defect -- and notes that a roving-tabindex / non-tabbable-popup design guarantees Tab moves focus out of the widget

Prescribes a focusout/blur close (relatedTarget outside the trigger+popup subtree) or Tab handling in the keydown, WITHOUT trapping focus (a non-modal popup must not trap), letting focus land on the next control

Notes why a keyboard smoke test misses it (it never presses Tab while the popup is open) and gives a regression test asserting the popup closes when focus moves to an outside control, not only on Escape

evals.prompt: Fictional dashboard app, Meridian, ships a shared design-system component library. A reviewer is asked whether the design system is fully adopted -- whether any screen has drifted by re-creating a component the library already provides. Their method: grep the tree for duplicated component names, copy-pasted JSX blocks, and repeated user-facing literal strings, on the theory that a drifted screen will look like a copy of the shared component. The search comes back clean. They conclude: "No duplication anywhere -- every surface renders through the shared components; design-system adoption is total." Is that conclusion safe, and if not, what higher-signal search would close the gap?
evals.expected_output: The conclusion is not safe. A structural search keyed on resemblance to the shared component -- duplicated names, copied JSX, repeated strings -- is blind to a call site that reimplemented the component from scratch: a from-scratch version shares no literal with the shared one, so it never matches the duplicate search, and a clean result proves only that no one copy-pasted, not that everyone reused. The higher-signal search is to read the code's own comments for admitted deviations: a developer who deliberately bypassed the shared component very often records why in a comment ("not using the shared Select, it can't do X", "hand-rolled instead of the DS modal", "inlined this, the shared client doesn't fit"). Grep for those tells (instead of / not using / not the shared / can't use / rather than / hand-rolled / workaround) near an import or a shared symbol name. Each hit is a pre-verified finding worth two things at once: (1) this call site has drifted and may have lost the correctness the shared version bakes in (an a11y behavior, a guard, a dedup), and (2) the shared component has a real gap the author already hit, so the root-cause fix is usually to close that gap at the source, not to bless the workaround. It is higher-confidence than a cold duplicate search because the author pre-verified the deviation. Confirm each match at source (the workaround still bypasses the shared thing at HEAD) rather than trusting the comment on its face.
expectations: Rejects the 'adoption is total' conclusion: a structural/duplicate search is blind to a from-scratch reimplementation that shares no literal with the shared component, so a clean result does not prove reuse

Proposes mining the code's own comments for admitted deviations (grepping tells like 'instead of' / 'not the shared' / 'hand-rolled' / 'workaround' near an import or shared symbol) as the higher-signal search
Explains each hit is worth two findings: local drift that may have lost the shared version's baked-in correctness, AND a real gap in the shared component whose root-cause fix belongs at the source
Notes the technique is higher-confidence because the author pre-verified the deviation, but each match must still be confirmed at source, not trusted on its face

evals.prompt: Fictional analytics app, Lumen. A reviewer checks whether a newly added StatTile matches the rest of the design system. On screen it is pixel-identical to its sibling tiles -- same padding, same accent colour, same corner radius -- and a visual-regression snapshot against a sibling shows no difference. Reading the source, the reviewer notes the sibling tiles set padding: var(--space-4) and color: var(--brand-600), while the new StatTile sets padding: "16px" and color: "#2563eb"; the design system's --space-4 currently resolves to 16px and --brand-600 currently resolves to #2563eb. The reviewer signs off: "Renders identically to its siblings and the snapshot is clean -- visually consistent and design-system-conformant." Do you agree with the sign-off?
evals.expected_output: No -- it renders identically today only by coincidence, and that coincidence is the defect. The new tile writes literals (16px, #2563eb) chosen to equal what --space-4 and --brand-600 resolve to right now, so it has forked those values instead of referencing them. Every check that compares the rendered result -- the screenshot, the visual-regression snapshot, the eyeball pass -- agrees "consistent" because the pixels match at this moment. But the drift is latent: when either token's value changes for any reason (a rebrand, a density pass, a dark-theme remap, a grid migration), every sibling that references the token moves and this tile silently stays behind, so the surface that looked most conformant becomes the lone off-brand element -- discovered only by the next snapshot after the token change. It is therefore NOT design-system-conformant despite matching now. Detection can't grep the token name (the literal never names it); use the siblings as the oracle -- most tiles reference the token and this one writes a literal equal to the token's current value, which marks it as a bypass rather than a deliberate one-off. Fix: reference the token (var(--space-4), the brand colour token) so the value has one source and the next token change reaches this tile too. If the value genuinely must not track the token, mark it (a named constant or a comment) so it reads as chosen, not drifted.
expectations: Rejects the sign-off: the tile renders identically only because the literals equal the tokens' CURRENT values, so 'consistent now' is not 'conformant' -- it has forked the values by hardcoding them

Explains why every rendered-result check (screenshot, visual-regression snapshot, eyeball) passes yet the drift is latent: a token change moves the token-referencing siblings and leaves the hardcoded tile behind, making it the lone off-brand element after the change

Gives the detection: you cannot grep the token name (the literal never names it), so use siblings as the oracle -- most reference the token, this one writes a literal equal to the token's current value
Prescribes referencing the token so the value has one source, and treats a genuine intentional one-off as a marked exception (named constant/comment), not a silent literal

evals.prompt: Fictional repo, Tessellate. The pre-commit hook runs three steps in this sequence: (1) the full Jest suite (about 4 minutes), (2) a Docker image build (about 3 minutes), (3) a commit-message-format lint (about 50 milliseconds). A contributor keeps fumbling the message format, and each attempt re-runs the whole suite and the image build before finally reaching the message check. The reviewer signs off: "The hook runs the format lint, the test suite, and the image build -- every gate a commit has to pass is present and enforced, so the hook is solid." Do you agree with the sign-off?
evals.expected_output: No. The gates are all present but in a self-defeating sequence: the ~50ms message-format lint runs last, behind ~7 minutes of suite plus image build, so every retry of a trivial message typo pays the entire expensive tier for a mistake the instant check would have caught first. The fix is a free re-ordering -- put the cheap, decisive checks (message format, lint, formatter) first so the common cheap failure fails fast before the slow test/build tier ever starts. 'All gates present' is not the same as 'gates in the right order'; the reviewer graded presence and missed cost.
expectations: Names the sequencing as the defect: the cheap message/format/lint check must run before the expensive test/build tier, not after it
Explains the wasted cost -- every retry of a trivial mistake re-pays the slow tier that the instant check would have rejected in milliseconds
Fix is a free re-ordering (cheapest-decisive check first, fail fast), not accepting the hook merely because every gate is present

evals.prompt: Fictional graph editor, Weaver. A test builds a scene graph in which each node holds a reference back to its parent and references to its neighbour nodes, then asserts the whole tree with assertEqual(rootNode, expectedRoot, "scene mismatch"). In CI the test intermittently exceeds the 5-second per-test timeout and gets marked flaky. A developer proposes raising the per-test timeout to 30 seconds. The reviewer agrees: "The graph is large, so the comparison is just slow -- bumping the per-test timeout to 30 seconds is the right fix." Do you agree?
evals.expected_output: No. The time is not spent comparing large data -- it is the assertion library trying to serialize and format rootNode to build a failure diff. Because each node references its parent and neighbours, the graph is self-referential, and traversing it to render a message does not terminate cheaply; that formatting step is what blows the timeout, and it is triggered on the failure path (the values differ), which no green run exercises. Raising the timeout only moves or hides the wall and still yields no usable diff. Fix: assert on a small scalar drawn from the object -- a node id, a child count, a status flag -- or snapshot a bounded, acyclic projection, never the whole live node.
expectations: Identifies the cause as the assertion library deep-traversing/serializing the large self-referential node graph to build a failure diff, not slow application logic
Notes the cost lands on the failure path (and is aggravated by the cyclic references), so a larger timeout hides rather than fixes it and still gives no usable diff
Fix asserts on a small scalar or a bounded acyclic projection drawn from the object, not the entire live node

evals.prompt: Fictional static-site generator, Quill. It separates a Markdown file's YAML frontmatter from the body by reading lines from the top until it reaches the first line equal to ---, which it treats as the close of the frontmatter. Two posts render wrong: one whose body opens with a horizontal rule written as ---, and one whose frontmatter has a multi-line description value that itself contains a line of ---. The reviewer signs off: "The splitter locates the closing --- and separates the two sections; it passes on every post in our fixture set." Do you agree?
evals.expected_output: No. Matching the first line equal to --- assumes --- only ever appears as the real closing fence, but --- can appear legitimately as content before it -- a body horizontal rule, or a --- line inside a multi-line frontmatter value. On those posts the scan stops early and mis-splits, silently handing a truncated header or a swallowed body downstream instead of raising. The fixtures pass only because none of them happened to contain an interior ---, so a green fixture set is not evidence. Fix: use a real YAML/frontmatter parser, or, if hand-rolling, require the block to both open and close with the fence (a lone opener is an error), count the paired fences rather than matching the first, and raise on the ambiguous/malformed case rather than returning a best-effort split.
expectations: Names the failure: matching the first --- ends the span early whenever --- occurs legitimately as content before the true closing fence
Rejects the green fixtures as evidence -- they pass only because none contained an interior ---, and the bug needs content that does
Fix uses a real parser or requires open+close / counts fences and raises on the ambiguous case instead of silently splitting

evals.prompt: Fictional inventory service, Palletdb. A reconciler compares the declared stock count against a separately computed count for six attributes (onHand, reserved, damaged, inTransit, returned, quarantined) and logs a discrepancy per attribute. It is six near-identical blocks, one per attribute. Reading them: five of the blocks begin with the line `if declared is None: continue` and then run the comparison; the quarantined block starts straight at the comparison with no such line. The suite is green -- its fixtures set every attribute on every row. The reviewer signs off: "I read all six reconciliation blocks; each one is present and reads correctly on its own, so reconciliation coverage is complete." Do you agree?
evals.expected_output: No. Reading each block in isolation is exactly what hides this. Five copies skip rows where `declared is None` and the quarantined copy dropped that precondition, so on a legacy/unset row it will log a spurious discrepancy the other five would not. 'Each reads correctly on its own' is the wrong check: the defect exists only relative to the siblings, and it surfaces only when you diff the copies' guard conditions against each other -- the block with one fewer precondition than the rest is the finding. The green suite proves nothing because its fixtures populate every attribute and never exercise the None branch. Fix: collapse the six into one parameterized reconciliation so there is a single guard set, or restore the `is None` skip in the quarantined block and add a test over a row where that attribute is unset.
expectations: Catches that the quarantined block dropped the `declared is None` precondition the other five share -- drift in one of N parallel copies
Rejects 'each reads correctly on its own' as the wrong test; the defect is visible only by diffing the copies' guard conditions against each other
Fix parameterizes the six into one check (or restores the missing guard) and adds an unset/legacy-row test; notes the all-populated fixtures never exercise the dropped branch

evals.prompt: Fictional timeline UI, Chronoline. Each event bar's pixel width is first computed as w = Math.max(w, 4) so that zero-duration events stay visible as a 4px sliver. Later, in the layout pass, w = Math.min(w, trackEnd - x) so a bar cannot extend past the right edge of its track. A zero-duration event whose start x lands within 4px of trackEnd renders with width 0 and disappears. The reviewer signs off: "Both lines are standard -- one keeps tiny bars visible, the other prevents overflow, and each is correct on its own; the vanishing bar is probably bad input data." Do you agree?
evals.expected_output: No -- it is not the data. Each line is correct alone, but their composition is the bug. When x is within 4px of trackEnd, trackEnd - x is less than 4, so the later Math.min re-bounds the width back down to that remaining room -- below the 4px minimum the earlier Math.max established, here to 0. The minimum-width guarantee holds everywhere except within 4px of the far edge, which ordinary test data rarely hits. Fix: re-assert the minimum after the edge bound (w = Math.max(Math.min(w, trackEnd - x), 4), then decide explicitly whether the bar overflows or the track grows, since you can no longer have both), or bound x first so at least 4px of room remains.
expectations: Identifies composition as the defect -- the later Math.min re-bounds width below the 4px minimum the earlier Math.max set, not bad input
Gives the exact trigger: start x within 4px (the minimum) of trackEnd, so trackEnd - x is below the minimum
Fix re-asserts the minimum after the edge bound, or bounds x first so remaining room stays at or above the minimum -- not 'blame the data'

evals.prompt: Fictional monorepo, Larkspur. A CI job named route-checks decides which test suites to run by listing the files changed since the PR base: it runs `git fetch origin "$BASE_SHA"` and then `git diff --name-only "$BASE_SHA"...HEAD`, maps the changed paths to suites, and runs only those suites. The repo's checkout step fetches only the last two commits to keep CI fast. When a PR's base commit is older than that, the fetch prints `fatal: remote error: upload-pack: not our ref` and the script's fallback `|| { echo 'no files changed'; SUITES=''; }` then runs zero suites, so route-checks reports success. The author defends it: 'the full fetch was slow, and if we cannot read a diff there is nothing to test anyway, so a clean pass is the safe default -- worst case we skip one run.' Do you agree?
evals.expected_output: No. Two defects. (1) Resolving the base by its exact commit SHA cannot work on a checkout that fetched only the last two commits -- a base older than that is not in the fetched history, so `git fetch origin <sha>` fails. Resolve the base by ref instead: fetch the base branch by name (`git fetch origin <base-branch>`), or deepen/unshallow the checkout, so the commit is actually obtainable. (2) The fallback is a false pass: it treats 'could not compute the diff' as 'nothing changed' and skips every suite, so any PR whose base is out of range merges with no suites run while CI shows green. A changed-files router is a detective check -- its job is to find what changed -- so an unreadable diff is could-not-check (unknown), not empty. It must fail open conservatively: emit a distinct could-not-check status and run the suites as if everything is in scope; it must never fabricate an empty diff that silently skips them, and never (the opposite error) hard-fail the PR as if a violation were found. Contrast a security, secret, or authz gate, which fails closed when its input is missing. 'Found nothing because it could not look' must not read as 'found nothing.'
expectations: Names the exact-SHA base resolution as the root cause -- a commit older than the two-commit checkout is absent, so fetch the base by ref (branch name) or deepen/unshallow instead
Flags the fallback as a false pass: an unreadable diff is treated as 'no files changed' and silently skips all suites while CI reports success

Says a changed-files/diff detector must fail open on an unreadable diff -- emit could-not-check and run suites conservatively -- not skip them and not hard-fail, unlike a security gate that fails closed

evals.prompt: Fictional web app, Marigold, in a private repo. A required CI check named pr-evidence fails unless the PR body contains a screenshot, and it rejects image embeds whose URL points at an external file host. A contributor's PR shows an image embed linking to a file on their own object-storage bucket; pr-evidence is red, but the image loads fine in the contributor's own browser. The contributor also ran the repo's `scripts/pr-evidence.sh` from their branch locally and it exited 0. They ask a maintainer to `--admin` merge past the red check: 'it is broken -- the screenshot is right there, and the same script passes on my machine, so CI is just flaky.' Do you agree?
evals.expected_output: No -- do not override. Two separate claims are being conflated. (1) The evidence requirement is about what the reviewer can see, not whether a URL is present. An image embed pointing at an external or private object-storage host loads for the author -- who is authenticated to that host, or whose browser carries the right origin and cookies -- but shows a broken image to reviewers reading the PR cold, so the linked file is not evidence even when it is a real, correct screenshot. The check rejects exactly that link and is behaving correctly; the fix is for the contributor to upload the image as a platform attachment served through the forge's own proxy, or commit an in-repo image file -- gate on what renders for the reviewer, not on mere presence, and the failure text should name that exact fix. (2) 'The same script passes on my machine' is not evidence that CI is wrong. A local copy of a gate, run from the contributor's own branch, can be an older copy that has fallen behind the CI definition, and even a current one is self-reported and bypassable -- the only trusted control is the forge run pinned to the reviewed commit. A red required check with a local green means investigate why the two disagree and single-source the gate so the local entry point runs the same script CI runs -- not `--admin` past it. Overriding here merges a PR whose evidence no reviewer can actually see.
expectations: Says the external/object-storage image link is not evidence because it does not display for reviewers (only for the author), and the fix is a platform attachment or an in-repo image file, not any present URL
Says pr-evidence is behaving correctly and its failure message should name the exact fix, rather than being overridden

Rejects 'it passed on my machine' as grounds to --admin override: a local gate copy can be behind CI and is self-reported; only the forge run on the reviewed commit is trusted, and the gate should be single-sourced so local matches CI

evals.prompt: Fictional settings dashboard, Cobalt. The team ran a migration to move every segmented control (the little grouped button strips used for view toggles) onto one shared <SegmentedControl> recipe backed by design tokens, replacing the older one-off implementations. A reviewer audits completeness like this: they list every file that imports <SegmentedControl>, open each, and confirm it renders correctly with the new tokens. Every importer checks out, and on screen every segmented control they can find looks right. They sign off: "Every call site of the shared control is on the new recipe and renders correctly -- the migration is complete, nothing is left on the old styling." Is that conclusion safe?
evals.expected_output: No -- listing the shared control's importers cannot prove the migration reached every segmented control, because the ones most likely to be missed import the shared control nowhere. Two classes are invisible to an importer census: (a) a segmented control built later or in a parallel branch that was simply never migrated -- it still carries the OLD recipe's markup and class signature and imports the new shared component not at all, so it never appears in the importer list; and (b) a control that CANNOT use the shared component -- a state-toggle that is not a real navigation link, or one needing a different role -- which gets a hand-rolled copy of the styling and likewise imports nothing shared. Both render correctly today, so a per-screen look and a snapshot approve, and the drift is latent: when the shared recipe or a token moves, every migrated instance follows and these lag into the lone off-recipe controls. Audit by the control CLASS, not the importer set: grep the OLD recipe's signature (its distinctive class names, its markup shape, the literal values it inlined) and any newer variant of the same visual control, enumerate that whole population, and diff it against the migrated/importer set -- each member that does not resolve to the shared recipe is a candidate straggler to confirm renders. The importer list answers 'which files use the shared thing', not 'which controls of this type exist'.
expectations: Rejects the sign-off: an importer/call-site census of the shared control cannot establish migration completeness, because un-migrated or can't-use-it controls import the shared component nowhere and never appear in that list

Names the two missed classes: (a) a control built later/in parallel, still on the old recipe, never migrated; (b) a control that cannot use the shared component at all (wrong role -- a state-toggle, not a link) and got a hand-rolled copy

Prescribes enumerating by the control TYPE -- grep the old recipe's signature / markup shape / inlined values across the whole tree and diff that population against the migrated set -- rather than by importers
Notes the drift is latent (renders identically now; diverges when the shared recipe or token moves) and that each candidate straggler is confirmed by rendering it, not by grep alone

evals.prompt: Fictional job-board app, Harbor. Active search filters render as a row of dismissible chips; clicking a chip removes that filter. Each chip is a single button whose content is the filter label followed by a small close glyph, so a chip reads visually as `Location: Berlin x` (the trailing x is the close glyph). A reviewer runs an accessibility pass: every chip is a real button, is keyboard-focusable and operable, and has a non-empty accessible name computed from its visible text. They sign off: "Every remove-chip is a real, focusable button whose accessible name is present and matches what is shown on screen -- the accessible-name requirement is met, this is accessible." Do you agree with the sign-off?
evals.expected_output: No. The button has a role and a non-empty name, but the name is computed from the visible content to the filter's VALUE -- 'Location: Berlin' (plus the trailing glyph) -- so a screen-reader user hears the filter that is set and is never told the button's PURPOSE is to remove it. A label that describes the value but not the action fails WCAG 2.4.6 Headings and Labels (AA: a label must describe the control's purpose), and leans on 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value; the trailing close glyph is decorative with no reliable spoken form (read as 'times', as its Unicode name, or skipped), not a dependable 'remove' cue. It slips through because a name does exist and even reads as descriptive, so a presence check (if (!name)), a first-read screen-reader pass, and a sighted click-through (the glyph looks like 'remove') all approve. Fix: give the button an aria-label stating the action and target -- aria-label='Remove filter: Location Berlin' -- and mark the close glyph aria-hidden='true' so it is not announced. Note the interaction with Label in Name (2.5.3): since the button has visible text, the action label you add must still contain that visible text (lead with the action, keep 'Location: Berlin' in the string) so the fix does not itself break 2.5.3. A name being present and matching the visible text is necessary but not sufficient -- here the visible text names the value, not the action.
expectations: Rejects the sign-off: a present, visible-text-matching accessible name is not sufficient here because it names the filter VALUE, not the button's purpose (to remove/clear the filter) -- a WCAG 2.4.6 Headings and Labels failure (with 4.1.2)
Flags the trailing close glyph as a decorative mark with no reliable spoken equivalent (read as 'times' / its Unicode name / skipped), not a dependable 'remove' cue
Prescribes an aria-label stating the action AND target (e.g. 'Remove filter: Location Berlin') and aria-hidden on the glyph
Notes the Label-in-Name (2.5.3) interaction: because the button has visible text, the added action label must still contain that visible text, so the fix does not break 2.5.3

evals.prompt: Fictional metrics dashboard, Pulse. Each KPI tile shows its change as a plain badge span: an up- or down-pointing triangle character followed by the magnitude (for example a green up-triangle with `3.2%`, a red down-triangle with `1.1%`), the colour keyed to whether the move is good. A reviewer checks it for colour independence: because the triangle's DIRECTION (up vs down) is a distinct shape, the meaning survives with the colour removed -- it still reads with colour stripped out. They sign off: "Direction is carried by the arrow shape, not colour alone, so this is colour-blind-safe and accessible." Do you agree with the sign-off?
evals.expected_output: Not for a screen-reader user. The arrow shape does clear the colour-blind test -- a sighted user without colour perception sees the triangle's direction -- but that shape channel is VISUAL only. The badge is a bare Unicode symbol character in a span, and a bare symbol has no reliable spoken form: assistive tech announces an up-triangle as 'black up-pointing triangle', as 'up arrow', or skips it entirely, depending on the AT and its verbosity. So to a screen-reader user the direction rides on the glyph plus the colour, and neither is dependable -- WCAG 1.1.1 Non-text Content (the glyph is not a dependable text alternative) and 1.4.1 Use of Color (colour is unspoken). The trap is that a Unicode arrow LOOKS like text -- it is a character -- so it is assumed accessible and no alternative is added. Fix: put the direction in a WORD the accessibility tree exposes -- visually-hidden (sr-only) text inside the badge ('up ' / 'down '), which joins the computed name, or an aria-label on a labelable host ('up 3.2 percent versus last month') -- and mark the decorative triangle aria-hidden='true'. The arrow reinforces; the word carries. Passing the colour-removed test is necessary but does not clear the screen-reader axis.
expectations: Accepts that the arrow SHAPE clears the colour-blind / colour-removed axis, but rejects the leap to 'accessible': that shape channel is visual-only

Explains a bare Unicode arrow character has no reliable spoken form (announced as its Unicode name, as 'up arrow', or skipped by AT), so it is not a dependable text alternative -- WCAG 1.1.1, with colour unspoken (1.4.1)
Names the trap: a Unicode arrow looks like text (it is a character), so it is wrongly assumed accessible and no alternative is added
Prescribes a direction WORD in the accessibility tree (sr-only text joining the name, or an aria-label) plus aria-hidden on the decorative glyph

evals.prompt: Fictional docs site, Atlas. An automated UX audit renders each page and grabs a full-page screenshot with page.screenshot({ fullPage: true }), then a checker scans the image for layout problems. On the long article pages -- which have a position: sticky top nav and a position: fixed 'back to top' button -- the audit reports the nav bar appearing several times down the page and the button showing up in three places. A reviewer looks at the full-page screenshots, sees the repeated bars, and files a High layout bug: "Sticky nav and the fixed button are duplicating down the page on long articles -- confirmed in the full-page screenshots. Needs a fix." Is that the right call?
evals.expected_output: No -- that is almost certainly a capture artifact, not a page defect, and it must be reproduced against the live page before it is filed. fullPage: true does not photograph the page in one shot; it scrolls the viewport and stitches the segments into one tall image. A position: sticky or position: fixed element is painted in EVERY segment, so the stitched result shows it repeated down the page (or displaced) even though the live product renders it exactly once, correctly pinned. The stitched image looks authoritative, which is exactly why a 'duplicated nav' / 'button in three places' reads as a real bug and burns a fix cycle chasing something no real viewport shows. Verify first: open the running page and scroll it, or take per-viewport captures at specific scroll offsets (which do not stitch), and file only what survives that check. This is the inverse of a genuine sticky-chrome collision (real content painting UNDER sticky chrome, seen mid-scroll) -- here the capture INVENTS a defect for a correctly-pinned element -- and an instance of reproducing a suspected finding against the right instrument (the live render or a non-stitched per-viewport shot), not the full-page stitch, before trusting it.
expectations: Rejects filing it as-is: a fixed/sticky element repeated or displaced in a fullPage screenshot is a stitching capture artifact (fullPage scrolls and stitches, painting the pinned element in every segment), not a defect the live page has
Says to reproduce against the live DOM (scroll the running page) or per-viewport / non-stitched captures BEFORE filing, and file only what survives
Notes the cost of not verifying: the stitched image looks authoritative, so it burns a fix cycle chasing a bug no real viewport shows
Distinguishes it from a real sticky-chrome collision (content under sticky chrome) -- this is the inverse, an invented defect -- and frames it as reproducing a finding against the right instrument

evals.prompt: A web application puts an authentication middleware in front of every route, with a short allow-list of paths the middleware skips. One allow-listed path is `POST /session/exchange`: it reads a third-party identity-provider token from the request body, makes a server-side HTTPS call to that provider to validate the token and look up the user, and on success issues a local session cookie. It is on the allow-list because it has to run before any session cookie exists. The outbound provider call has a 3-second timeout, and the handler rejects any token larger than 4 KB. A colleague reviews it: 'The allow-list entry is correct -- this has to work before login -- and the provider call is hardened with a timeout and a size cap on the token, so there is nothing left to harden here.' Do you agree?
evals.expected_output: No. The allow-list entry being correct for access control is exactly what creates the problem: an authenticated route carries an implicit throttle because a caller must first obtain a session -- itself a scarce, mint-limited credential -- but skipping the auth gate removes that implicit throttle along with the auth, so this endpoint is reachable by anyone, pre-session, at any rate. The 3-second timeout and 4 KB token cap bound a SINGLE outbound call; they do nothing about the NUMBER or CONCURRENCY of calls. With no limit of its own, unbounded inbound requests fan out to unbounded server-side calls to the provider: the app's own outbound worker/connection pool saturates (a self-inflicted denial of service that starves every other caller), and the provider's per-tenant quota is exhausted so it starts refusing the app -- breaking login for everyone. The damage is availability (and provider-quota exhaustion), not a per-message bill, so a spend ceiling or billing alert is not the fix and does not apply here. This is OWASP API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption: an unauthenticated, auth-gate-exempt endpoint whose per-request outbound call is the amplified resource -- distinct from the metered-spend sub-case where the damage is the bill. Fix: treat this unauthenticated endpoint as a resource-consumption surface in its own right and add a limit specific to it, independent of the auth gate it is exempt from -- key it per-IP and per-token-subject for honest callers but back that with a global per-endpoint ceiling, since both an IP and an unverified token subject are attacker-mintable -- and cap the concurrency of the outbound leg with a bounded pool or semaphore so a single burst cannot saturate it. Not 'the timeout and size cap already cover it,' and not merely confirming the allow-list entry is correct.
expectations: Rejects the 'timeout + token-size cap = nothing left to harden' sign-off -- states those bound a single outbound call, not the number or concurrency of calls, and identifies that placing the endpoint on the auth middleware's allow-list removed the implicit throttle authenticated routes rely on, leaving it reachable pre-session at any rate

Frames the damage as availability -- the app's own outbound pool saturating (a self-inflicted DoS starving other callers) and/or the provider's per-tenant quota being exhausted so login breaks for everyone -- and identifies it as OWASP API4:2023's outbound-amplification case, explicitly NOT the metered-spend/billing sub-case (a spend ceiling or billing alert is not the fix here)

Prescribes a limit specific to this endpoint and independent of the auth gate it is exempt from (per-IP plus per-token-subject, backed by a global per-endpoint ceiling because both keys are attacker-mintable) AND an outbound-concurrency cap (bounded pool or semaphore) -- not merely relying on the per-call timeout/size cap or on the allow-list entry being correct

evals.prompt: Fictional analytics product, Kestrel. A recurring 'no rows match the active filters' empty state (a heading plus a 'Clear filters' button) had drifted across several list views, so a team extracted a shared FilteredEmptyState component (it takes an onClear client callback) and adopted it at the client-side list pages. In the PR that introduced it, one file carries the comment: `// the reports page (server-rendered) still hand-rolls its own version; migrating it onto FilteredEmptyState is a tracked follow-up`. A reviewer doing a consistency pass greps for imports of FilteredEmptyState, finds it used at every client list page, reads that comment, and signs off: "Empty-state is unified -- every client list imports the shared component, and the one server-rendered leftover is a tracked follow-up, so there's nothing more to do here." For reference: the reports page, on zero filtered rows, renders a muted line reading 'No matching reports -- clear a filter to widen the results.', and its filter-chip row elsewhere on the page has a working 'Clear all' control. A separate search page on the same product shows, depending on state, 'Type to search', 'Keep typing...', 'No reports match "X"', and -- when a status filter removes the text matches -- 'No reports match the current status filter.' Is the sign-off right?
evals.expected_output: No. The sign-off trusts two things it should have checked. First, 'tracked follow-up' is a claim in a code comment, not evidence: confirm a real open issue actually names that migration. If none exists, the claim is false and the reports-page copy is untracked duplication -- nothing forces the consolidation, so the next accessibility fix or copy change lands on FilteredEmptyState and silently not on the hand-rolled reports version, and the two drift. Second, the importer grep is structurally blind to the reports page precisely because it imports nothing shared: it is server-rendered and cannot pass the client onClear callback, so it hand-rolled an action-LESS empty state whose copy is a prose instruction ('clear a filter to widen the results') pointing at a 'Clear all' control that lives elsewhere on the page and is not wired to this empty state. Grepping importers can never surface a site that adopts nothing; enumerate the concept, not the component's call sites. The fix belongs at the component: give FilteredEmptyState an action-descriptor form (an href/action alternative to the bare onClear callback) so a server caller is not structurally forced to hand-roll. Third, the search page hides one real survivor among legitimately-distinct siblings: 'Type to search', 'Keep typing...', and 'No reports match "X"' are genuinely different empty states and must stay separate, but 'No reports match the current status filter' IS the shared filtered-to-zero concept and should adopt (or at least be classified/commented as) the shared component. A concept-grep over-matches the distinct branches, which is exactly why a reviewer sees 'several empty states for good reasons' and stops. When closing an 'extract shared component X' ticket, enumerate the call sites excluded and why (framework boundary, multi-branch conditional) rather than closing on 'every match of the old pattern I found is gone.' Note this is not the 'we avoided the shared component because...' technique (a comment stating a reason NOT to use a primitive, i.e. a pre-found bug) -- this is a comment PROMISING to finish a migration, and the action is to verify the promise was kept.
expectations: Rejects the sign-off and treats 'tracked follow-up' as an unverified claim -- confirm a real issue exists; if not, the leftover is untracked duplication that will drift as fixes land on the shared component and not the hand-rolled copy

Identifies the server-rendered reports page as a leftover the importer grep cannot see because it imports nothing shared: it cannot pass the client onClear callback so it hand-rolled an action-less, prose-instruction empty state; prescribes extending the shared component to accept an href/action-descriptor

Identifies that only the 'status filter removed the matches' branch of the search page is the shared filtered-to-zero concept, while 'type to search' / 'keep typing' / 'no text match' are legitimately distinct and must stay separate -- and explains the reviewer stopped because a concept-grep over-matches the distinct branches
Names the completeness step (enumerate excluded call sites and why at ticket close) and/or distinguishes this from the avoidance-comment 'we avoided X because...' technique

evals.expected_output: No. Three of the four reads have a fallback; profile is the one left bare, and it is awaited unguarded. If fetchProfile's pool.query rejects -- a transient DB blip, a timeout, a rotated credential -- that rejection propagates straight out of loadDashboard, past the try/catch the docstring's own promise means nobody added, and crashes the ENTIRE page, taking down activity, alerts, and usage, each of which would have degraded to its own fallback. So the loader violates its own stated contract exactly under the failure the contract exists to handle. It is invisible on the happy path because every test resolves, and it hides from a quick read because the eye sees .catch repeated three times and pattern-matches the whole block as safe -- the way to find it is to diff each read's error handling against the stated 'every read degrades' contract and spot the one that diverges from its siblings, not to trust the repeated shape. Before filing, the fact that fetchProfile is a bare pool.query with no guard down its own chain confirms it genuinely can reject (not one already fail-soft two levels down), and profile is consumed. Fix: give fetchProfile the same treatment as its siblings -- `.catch(e => { log(e); return null; })`, a safe fallback matching the consumed type -- and add a regression test that stubs fetchProfile to reject and asserts loadDashboard still resolves with a degraded result instead of throwing. (Chaining .catch after the await would not be enough if the same promise were also awaited unguarded elsewhere.)
expectations: Rejects the sign-off and identifies profile / fetchProfile as the one read with no fallback, awaited unguarded, so its rejection propagates out of the loader and crashes the whole page (not just its own panel), contradicting the docstring's every-read-degrades contract
Notes it is invisible on the happy path (all tests resolve) and is found by diffing each read's error handling against the stated contract, not by pattern-matching the three repeated .catch calls

Prescribes adding the same .catch(fallback) (a safe value matching the consumed type) the siblings use, plus a regression test that makes that read reject and asserts the loader resolves degraded instead of throwing
Confirms the read genuinely can reject (bare pool.query, no guard down its chain) before filing, or notes a .catch after the await is insufficient if the promise is awaited unguarded elsewhere

evals.expected_output: No. The revert is a bare reset to a value captured when THIS drag started, with no check that the card is still where this drag left it. Sequence: drag 1 moves the card to column B, captures prev = A, and fires a slow save; before it returns, the user drags the same card to column C -- drag 2 captures prev = B (the current optimistic value), moves to C, and fires a save that succeeds, correctly leaving the card at C. Drag 1's save then fails and its .catch unconditionally sets the column back to A (its captured prev), clobbering the confirmed C and snapping the card back to A, with a 'Move failed -- reverted' toast for a move the user has long since moved past. Both writes target one key and neither checks that it still owns the value it is about to overwrite. A single-drag unit test -- drag once, reject the save, assert the revert -- passes every time; the defect exists only in two overlapping drags on one card resolving in the order first-fails-after-second-succeeds, which the missing pending guard makes an ordinary interaction, not an exotic one. Fix: capture a per-card request token (or the value this call wrote) at drag time and only let the async continuation mutate state if the current token/value still matches this call -- a client-side compare-and-set -- and/or disable re-dragging a card while its save is pending. Regression-test two overlapping drags on one card, the first failing after the second succeeds, asserting the card ends at C. This is not the debounced-write case (a timer replaying a schedule-time snapshot on its own late fire); here it is an error-path revert to a captured previous value under a second write. And it is not the reverted-write-message case (routing the failure's error TEXT through a shared safe-message mapper); here the defect is the state WRITE clobbering a newer confirmed one.
expectations: Rejects the sign-off and traces the two-drag sequence where drag 1's failure revert resets the card to its captured previous column and clobbers drag 2's already-succeeded new column

Explains why review and tests miss it: each handler is correct alone and a single-call test passes; the defect is only in two overlapping calls on one key resolving out of order, made ordinary by the missing disable/pending guard

Prescribes a per-call identity/token check (client-side compare-and-set) so only the latest write's continuation may mutate state, plus a regression test with two overlapping calls where the first fails after the second succeeds

Distinguishes it from the debounced schedule-time-snapshot revert and/or from routing the revert's error message through the shared safe-message mapper -- a different defect on the same kind of handler

evals.prompt:
Fictional model-registry app, Ledger. A model detail page renders a diagram section only when the model has a graph: `{model.graph ?
...
: null}`. A separate models table elsewhere in the app shows each row's coverage as an 'N of M' cell that links into that section: `{covered} of {total}`, rendered for every row; when a model has no graph the cell reads '0 of 0' and is styled red. A reviewer checks both components: the detail page correctly avoids drawing an empty diagram, and the table always links a row to its detail page. They click the link on a model that has a graph and it scrolls to the diagram. They sign off: "Both components are correct in isolation -- the detail page shouldn't draw an empty diagram, and the coverage cell always points at the model's detail. Nothing to fix." Do you agree with the sign-off?
evals.expected_output: No. The two components are individually reasonable and the bug lives only in their combination, under the empty case the reviewer never tested. When model.graph is falsy the detail page renders null -- so not just the diagram but the <section id="diagram"> wrapper, and its id, are gone. The coverage cell is built unconditionally off the same 0/0 numbers that mean 'no graph', so for exactly those models it still renders a link to #diagram (in red), and clicking it navigates to a fragment that resolves to nothing: no scroll, no error, no explanation -- indistinguishable from a broken control. It survives review because each file reads fine alone and the click test used a model that has a graph, never the empty record where the target disappears; it hides further if sibling views (a card, a preview drawer) render the no-graph state with an honest placeholder, so the lone null looks consistent. There are really two defects in one: a dead cross-view anchor AND a blank region with no honest 'no graph yet' message. Fix -- keep the wrapper and its id always mounted and render an honest inline empty-state inside it: the region is never blank and the anchor always resolves to a real, in-viewport element. Alternatively gate the link too -- don't render a clickable fragment into a section this model won't have, or point it at /models/{id} with no fragment. Detect generally: for any element conditionally rendered on a data-presence check that carries a DOM id, grep every href/router-push building a fragment that matches that id; an unconditional link (or one gated on a count that can legitimately be 0) into a conditionally-rendered id is a guaranteed dead anchor in the empty case. This is not the same-component 'header rendered above a filtered-empty row' defect -- there the break is within one component; here it is a cross-component contract: one component's link depends on an id another component drops.
expectations: Rejects the sign-off and identifies that the bug exists only in the combination under the empty (model.graph falsy) case the reviewer did not test: the detail page renders null, so the <section id="diagram"> wrapper AND its id disappear

Explains the coverage cell is built unconditionally off the same 0/0 numbers, so for a model with no graph it still links to #diagram and the click resolves to nothing -- a dead anchor indistinguishable from a broken control, and also a blank region with no honest empty-state message

Prescribes keeping the wrapper and its id always mounted with an honest inline empty-state inside (or, failing that, gating the cross-link / dropping the fragment) so both the blank region and the dead anchor are closed at once

Gives the cross-component detection (grep href/router-push fragments against any conditionally-rendered id-bearing element) and distinguishes it from a same-component header-over-empty-row defect -- here it is a cross-view anchor contract

evals.prompt: Fictional data-catalog tool, Index. A user can edit a dataset's description. The flow used to be 'submit -> a steward reviews -> it goes live', and the button read 'Submit for review'. A recent change relabelled it: the button now reads 'Apply', and on success a toast says 'Applied -- your change is live, no review needed.' Under the hood the write is unchanged: it commits to a Git-backed content repo by automatically opening a pull request, and the dataset's public page that displays the description is a statically generated site that is rebuilt only when a maintainer merges that PR. A reviewer takes the success screenshot ('it now says Applied') and signs off: "The new copy is accurate and clearer than the old 'submit for review' language -- the edit is applied immediately now. Ship it." Do you agree with the sign-off?
evals.expected_output: No. The success copy was strengthened to 'Applied -- live, no review needed' but the publish path was never collapsed to match: the write still lands in an intermediate store (an auto-opened pull request) and the description becomes visible only after a separate, out-of-band step -- a maintainer merging the PR and the static site rebuilding. The read surface the user then looks at (a statically generated page) is a different plane the write does not touch until that step runs, so it is not eventually-consistent-in-seconds, it is not connected. A user who 'applied' an edit and reloads the dataset page sees the old description with no diff, no 'publishing' state, and no pending indicator, directly under a message claiming it is live -- making a successful write indistinguishable from a dropped one, so they may re-edit (duplicate PRs) or stop trusting the tool. It ships because the copy change and the pipeline are reviewed separately: the 'waiting for a steward' affordance was removed from the submit surface without checking that the display surface still depends on that human step to ever update; often the same change also deletes a 'pending review' badge that keyed off the old status enum, removing the one honest signal as it removes the caveat. Giveaway: a slower flow in the same product -- e.g. the steward's own acceptance screen -- likely still states the real caveat honestly; the regression is that the fast flow dropped language the slow one keeps. Fix, either closes it: (A) make the read surface reflect the write -- revalidate/refetch the value in the same session and keep a 'pending -- live once merged and rebuilt' indicator until the merge+rebuild actually completes; or (B) make the copy match reality -- 'Recorded; a change request was opened automatically -- live once it is reviewed and published' -- rather than reusing 'Applied/live' from a faster path. This is not an optimistic-UI race (a newer write clobbering an older one, or a leaked raw error string); it is a process/pipeline mismatch -- the completion claim outran the unchanged async publish step.
expectations: Rejects the sign-off: the 'Applied -- live, no review needed' copy was strengthened while the publish path (auto-opened PR, merged out of band, static site rebuilt) was left unchanged, so the claim outruns what the read surface can show

Identifies that the write plane (the PR / content repo) and the read plane (a statically generated page) are different and not connected until a separate merge+rebuild step, so the user sees the old value with no pending/publishing indicator under a message asserting it is live -- a successful write looks identical to a dropped one

Prescribes either making the read surface reflect the write (revalidate + keep a 'not yet live' indicator until merge/rebuild completes) or making the copy state the real caveat -- and notes the giveaway that a slower sibling flow likely still carries honest language, and that a pending affordance was likely removed with the status enum
Distinguishes it from an optimistic-UI race (clobbered write / leaked error message) -- this is a process/pipeline mismatch where completion copy outran an unchanged async publish step

evals.prompt: Fictional analytics dashboard, Prism. An automated UX-audit agent screenshots each page and scores it against a fixed checklist: does every view have an empty state, a loading state, a focus ring, an aria-label on icon buttons, AA text contrast? On the main dashboard every item passes, and the agent reports 'No defects found.' A designer glancing at the same screenshots immediately notes the KPI tiles are crammed together with inconsistent gaps, a column of status badges does not share a right edge, and ten full-width panels are stacked with no overview so nothing is scannable. The audit report mentions none of this. A reviewer reads the audit output and signs off: "The UX audit passed with no defects across every checklist item, so the dashboard meets the bar -- no UX work needed this release." Do you agree with the sign-off?
evals.expected_output: No. A clean checklist pass is a floor, not proof the surface is acceptable, and here it is being read as the latter. Every checklist item is individually true, but the problems the designer sees in seconds -- cramped and inconsistent spacing, badges that do not share a right edge (ragged alignment), and ten stacked panels with no scannable hierarchy -- are composition quality: a relational judgment across everything on the screen at once, not a yes/no property of any one component, so a binary checklist has no line item that can express it and returns 'no defects' by construction. That clean report is the default output of a shallow pass (a short 'no defects' is cheaper than prose that must justify each finding), not evidence of quality; 'found nothing' with no written critique should be treated as the audit not having looked closely enough -- unverified, not a pass. The fix is not a longer checklist: require the audit to actually read the rendered screenshots and produce a written per-surface composition critique against a named best-in-class bar -- 'would a senior designer at a top product org ship this?' -- covering spacing rhythm, alignment, density, hierarchy, chrome consistency, and overlap. Also capture multiple real-viewport screenshots at the scroll positions a user lands on rather than one full-page stitch, which both hides composition problems and can fabricate a fixed/sticky overlap. Note the adjacent trap in the other direction: a full-page stitch can invent a false overlap on a fixed/sticky element (verify against the live DOM before filing) -- but that 'it is a capture artifact' reasoning must not be inverted into an excuse to wave away a real composition problem unverified. A checklist that exists and is consulted can still rubber-stamp, because composition does not reduce to line items.
expectations: Rejects the sign-off: every checklist item passing does not mean the surface is acceptable -- the cramped/inconsistent spacing, ragged badge alignment, and unscannable stack of panels are real composition defects a human catches at a glance

Explains why a checklist structurally misses them: composition quality is a relational judgment across the whole screen, not a yes/no property of one component, so no fixed line item expresses it; a bare 'no defects found' is the default of a shallow pass and should be treated as unverified, not a pass

Prescribes not a longer checklist but a written per-surface composition critique against a named best-in-class bar (spacing/alignment/density/hierarchy/chrome/overlap), plus multiple real-viewport scroll-position screenshots instead of one full-page stitch

Notes the opposite-direction relationship to the fixed/sticky full-page-stitch false positive, and warns the 'capture artifact' reasoning must not be inverted into an excuse to discard a real finding unverified

evals.prompt: Fictional project-tracker, Cadence, built on an in-house design system with a <Button> and <Link> primitive and a correct keyboard focus ring. Users say it 'feels like a mediocre prototype.' Two concrete complaints reproduce: (1) on several screens some clickable elements show the default arrow cursor and their hover colour snaps instantly with no easing -- these turn out to be written as raw <button>/<a> rather than through <Button>/<Link>; (2) the marketing landing page, which is server-rendered, appears blank for over a second before its hero fades in, even though 'view source' shows the hero HTML is already in the server response -- the hero is styled `opacity: 0` and a useEffect sets it visible after hydration. An engineer proposes: open a ticket per screen to add cursor and transition CSS to each raw element, and add a loading spinner to the landing page while it 'loads'. They sign off: "We'll fix the prototype feel by cleaning up each screen one at a time, starting with the worst offenders." Is that the right plan?
evals.expected_output: No -- both complaints are single shared-primitive roots, each fixed once at the base layer, and the per-screen plan will never converge (and the spinner is wrong). Root 1: the raw <button>/<a> elements bypass the design system's <Button>/<Link>, so they do not inherit the base affordances the primitive bakes in -- cursor: pointer and a hover/focus transition. Fixing it per element is endless whack-a-mole; fix it once globally: `button:not([disabled]) { cursor: pointer; }` and a shared `transition` on `a, button, [role="button"], [role="tab"]`. Two mechanics matter: use the attribute selector :not([disabled]), not the pseudo-class :not(:disabled), whose lower specificity lets a per-instance cursor utility get out-specified back to the base rule; and exclude box-shadow from the transitioned properties (do not use transition: all), because focus rings are often a box-shadow and easing one in reads as laggy, unresponsive keyboard navigation -- an a11y regression. Add a prefers-reduced-motion: reduce zero-out. Root 2: the landing page is not slow to load -- the server already sent the hero; it is hidden by opacity: 0 until JS hydrates and reveals it, so a fast render reads as a multi-second blank. A spinner makes it worse (more delay theatre).
