Fix: play the reveal as a pure CSS @keyframes that starts at first paint (animation: fadeIn 300ms ease-out), or drop the opacity: 0 initial state above the fold and reserve reveal-on-scroll for below-the-fold content. Do not over-fix: the primitives and focus ring are already correct, so audit for bypass sites (raw <button>/<a> outside the primitive), do not rewrite <Button>/<Link>. Verify: getComputedStyle(el).cursor and .transitionProperty on a real bespoke element, and curl the route with no JS to confirm the hero HTML is present with visible styling, not opacity: 0. Distinct from a shared component whose hover reaction merely diverges across instances (here the element never went through the primitive at all) and from a control disabled/blank pre-hydration (here it is already-rendered non-interactive content whose visibility was gated on hydration).
expectations: Rejects the per-screen plan: both complaints trace to one or two shared-primitive roots, each fixed once at the base layer, so a symptom-by-symptom pass never converges (and adding a landing-page spinner is wrong)

Root 1: raw <button>/<a> bypass the <Button>/<Link> primitive and so lack base cursor: pointer and a hover/focus transition; fix globally with `button:not([disabled]) { cursor: pointer; }` and a shared transition -- using the attribute selector :not([disabled]) not :not(:disabled), excluding box-shadow so focus rings do not lag, with a prefers-reduced-motion zero-out

Root 2: the SSR page is not slow -- the hero HTML shipped but is hidden by opacity: 0 until hydration reveals it, so it reads as a blank multi-second load; fix with a pure-CSS @keyframes reveal at first paint or by dropping opacity: 0 above the fold, not a spinner

Says to audit for bypass sites rather than rewrite already-correct primitives, and to verify via getComputedStyle and a no-JS curl of the raw HTML; distinguishes the roots from a shared component diverging across instances and from a control disabled/blank pre-hydration

evals.prompt: Fictional collaboration app, Loom Desk, on a React Server Components stack (Next.js App Router). A module request-id.ts has no directive at the top of the file; at module scope it does `export const requestId = crypto.randomUUID()` and it also exports a `<RequestBadge>` component that renders that id in the page footer. The intent: one stable id per page load, generated on the server, printed in the footer so a user can quote it on a support ticket. It behaved that way in early builds. After a refactor, a toolbar component that starts with the `'use client'` pragma began importing `<RequestBadge>` and rendering it directly. Now support says the footer id changes as the user clicks around and differs between two people viewing the same shared page, and a teammate spots the id value sitting in the JavaScript shipped to the browser. Typecheck, lint, and the unit tests -- which import the module directly and assert the id is generated once -- are all green. What happened, and what is the fix?
evals.expected_output: The module stopped being server-side the moment a client component imported it. In this framework render location is decided by the import graph, not by whether a file carries a client pragma: a module with no pragma is shared, so importing and rendering `<RequestBadge>` from inside a client-pragma toolbar pulls request-id.ts into the client and runs it in the browser, re-executing on every client render. So `crypto.randomUUID()` at module scope now runs per client rather than once per request on the server -- its value differs between users (each browser makes its own), it changes across client re-renders and navigations, and it is now present in the shipped JavaScript. The 'generated once' assumption -- and any module-load singleton, one-time side effect, or server-only secret/env read written on that same assumption -- breaks silently. The green tests prove nothing here: they import the module in a plain Node context where it does run once, exactly the context that never exercises the bug. Fix: do not infer render frequency from file content -- enforce the boundary. Add a build-time server-only import to request-id.ts so the build fails if any client module pulls it in; generate the per-request id in a request-scoped server construct (a server component or layout, or a request context) and pass it down as a prop instead of holding it in module scope; if the badge itself must live inside a client component, hand it the server-generated id as a prop rather than importing the server module. Then verify the real import graph, not the pragma. This is the opposite direction from the plain-value-proxied-across-the-boundary defect (a client value becoming a client-reference proxy when a server component imports it, which breaks rendering); here a pragma-less module is pulled into the client and re-run, breaking a render-once / server-only assumption.
expectations: Identifies that render location and frequency follow the import graph, not the file's client pragma: a pragma-less module imported and rendered by a client component is pulled into the client and runs in the browser, re-executing per client render

Explains the concrete breakages: the module-scope crypto.randomUUID() now runs per client (not once per request), so the footer id differs between users and changes across re-renders, and the value is exposed in the shipped JavaScript -- generalizing to any module-load singleton, one-time side effect, or server-only secret read made on the same assumption
Notes the green typecheck/lint/unit tests miss it because the unit tests import the module in a plain Node context where it does run once -- only a real client-side render exposes it

Prescribes enforcing the boundary rather than trusting file content: a build-time server-only guard, generating the id in a request-scoped server construct and passing it down as a prop, and verifying the real import graph; distinguishes this from the opposite-direction proxied-plain-value boundary defect

evals.prompt: Fictional helpdesk, Beacon. A security fix just landed on the shared markdown renderer that turns `[text](url)` into an `<a href>`: it now rejects `javascript:` and `data:` URLs and escapes the link text, closing a stored-XSS hole. The author closes the ticket as fixed and the renderer's unit tests are green. Reviewing, you notice the app also produces links in two places that do not go through that renderer: a hand-written autolinker that runs when composing outbound notification emails, and a helper in a legacy ticket-export path that builds `<a>` tags by string concatenation. Neither was touched by the PR. Is the XSS class actually closed, and what should the review require before the ticket is closed?
evals.expected_output: No -- the class is not closed; the fix hardened one implementation of the link transform and left two siblings bare. Blocking the scheme and escaping the text on the shared markdown renderer closes the hole only on that path. The email autolinker and the concatenation helper in the export path are independent implementations of the same `[text](url)` -> `<a href>` transform, and each is its own sink: if either accepts a javascript:/data: href or fails to escape the link text, an attacker-controlled URL or label reaches HTML unescaped there just as it did in the renderer before the fix. These siblings are exactly what a fix sweep misses, because they share the renderer's behavior but none of its code: grepping for the renderer's function name or its parsing regex will not find a hand-rolled concatenation or a different autolinker, and the renderer's unit tests say nothing about them. Require, before closing: for each vuln class fixed in the primary parser (scheme allowlist, text escaping, and rel/target hardening on the produced anchor), find the other implementations of the same transform by what they produce -- grep the sinks (`<a`, `href=`, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, setAttribute('href')) and the link-shaped source pattern (a bracketed label immediately followed by a parenthesized URL) rather than by matching the fixed code's shape -- and confirm each carries the same guard, with a test per sibling. The durable fix is to collapse the three into one shared, audited linker so the scheme allowlist and escaping have a single home; until then, each unguarded sibling is a live finding, not a closed class.
expectations: Rejects 'fixed': the scheme-block/escaping fix hardened only the shared markdown renderer, while the email autolinker and the export-path concatenation helper are independent implementations of the same link transform and each is a separate XSS sink that can still accept javascript:/data: or emit unescaped text

Explains why a fix sweep misses the siblings: they share the renderer's behavior but not its code, so grepping the renderer's function name or regex does not find a hand-rolled or different implementation, and the renderer's unit tests do not cover them

Requires finding every implementation of the transform by what it produces (grep the href/anchor sinks and the link-shaped source pattern, not the fixed code's shape) and confirming each carries the same guard for each vuln class fixed, with a test per sibling
Recommends collapsing the implementations into one shared, audited linker so the guard has a single home, and treats each still-unguarded sibling as a live finding until then

evals.prompt: Fictional routing engine, Meridian. A function takes a directed cycle of N stops indexed 0..N-1 and splits it into sub-cycles by adding 'backward chord' edges, each chord closing off a sub-cycle back to an earlier stop; every sub-cycle must contain at least MIN stops. A validity check runs afterward to confirm the decomposition is well-formed before the engine uses it. QA reports that a decomposition the domain team hand-verified as correct is being rejected as invalid: it is the case where the final sub-cycle -- the one that closes back to stop 0 -- has exactly MIN stops. Decompositions whose last sub-cycle is larger than MIN validate fine. What is the bug, and how should the check and its tests change?
evals.expected_output: The validity check has a boundary bug at the terminal sub-cycle. Interior sub-cycles all have their length derived the same way, but the last one is computed from what remains -- the span that closes back around to stop 0 -- so its size comes from a different expression (a remainder, or an index that must wrap with `% N`). The check was written and tested against the interior form and is one step too strict at the terminal position: most likely it tests each piece with a strict `len > MIN` where the true contract is `len >= MIN`, so a final sub-cycle of exactly MIN is rejected as too short; or it computes the closing index as `i + 1` without `% N`, so the wrap onto stop 0 runs off the end. Either way a genuinely valid decomposition is falsely rejected -- the mirror of the usual off-by-one that lets one too many through. It slipped past tests because the fixtures used uneven splits where the last piece sat comfortably above MIN; the boundary only bites when the terminal piece lands exactly at the floor. Fix: make the terminal comparison inclusive (matching the interior contract's `>=`), compute every ring index modulo N so the close onto stop 0 stays in range, and assert the partition invariant directly -- the sub-cycle lengths sum to N and each one, the last included, is at least MIN. Add tests for the degenerate boundaries the current suite skips: N (and N-1); the all-minimal decomposition where every sub-cycle including the last is exactly MIN; and a decomposition whose only MIN-sized piece is the terminal one. This is a single comparator one notch too strict at the terminal position -- distinct from a floor that is undone by a later clamp, which is two individually-correct bounds whose composition violates the floor.
expectations: Identifies a terminal-boundary bug: the last sub-cycle's size is derived differently (a remainder or an index that must wrap onto stop 0), and the check is one step too strict there -- a strict `len > MIN` where it should accept `len` equal to MIN, or a closing index computed as `i + 1` without a modulo-N wrap

States the consequence: a genuinely valid decomposition is falsely rejected when the final sub-cycle is exactly MIN (the mirror of the usual off-by-one that admits one too many), and explains it survived because fixtures used uneven splits where the last piece exceeded MIN
Fix: make the terminal comparison inclusive, compute ring indices modulo N, and assert the partition invariant (lengths sum to N and each piece including the last is at least MIN)

Adds the degenerate-boundary tests: N and N-1, the all-minimal decomposition (every sub-cycle including the last exactly MIN), and one whose only MIN-sized piece is the terminal one; distinguishes this single-comparator bug from a floor undone by a later clamp

evals.prompt: In Aperture, a project dashboard, every team gets a 'Checklist complete' tile computed as `pct = totalItems > 0 ? Math.round(doneItems / totalItems * 100) : 0` and shown as `{pct}%`. A team that was created this morning and has not added any checklist items yet shows a red '0%' tile sitting next to teams reading 60-80%. An engineer says the tile is fine: the guard stops a divide-by-zero, and zero done out of zero really is zero progress. Is the tile correct, and what should the new team's tile show?
evals.expected_output: No. For a team with zero items the tile should not read 0%. 0% reads as 'this team has completed none of its work' and gets the alarming/red treatment, when the truth is there is nothing to complete yet -- a not-applicable state, not zero attainment. The `: 0` fallback avoids a NaN but picks a sentinel that renders as a real percentage, so it conflates an empty population with 'none done'. Show a non-numeric state for the empty case (N/A, a muted dash, or 'nothing to do') and reserve 0% for a team that has items but has done none of them (totalItems > 0 && doneItems === 0), which is a real, actionable zero.
expectations: Says the 0% tile is wrong for a zero-item team and rejects 'zero of zero is zero progress'
Identifies that 0% reads as 'none done' while the truth is 'nothing to do' (a not-applicable state)
Recommends a non-numeric rendering (N/A, dash, 'nothing to do') for the empty-population case, not 0%
Distinguishes the empty-denominator case from a genuine totalItems > 0 && done === 0 zero
Does not accept 'the guard prevents a divide-by-zero' as making the tile correct

evals.prompt: In Meridian, an issue list, each row is rendered as a flexbox: a title cell with `flex: 1`, then three fixed-width status chips (priority, assignee, state). Each individual row looks tidy and the chips sit neatly at its right end. But scanning down the whole list, the three chips do not line up with one another from row to row -- on each row they begin at a different horizontal position, so the right side of the list looks ragged. A developer says nothing is broken: the chips are right-aligned inside every row and it is only the titles that vary in length. What is the root cause, and how should the row layout be changed so the chips line up from row to row?
evals.expected_output: Root cause: each row is its own flex container, so the `flex: 1` title takes whatever width that row's title leaves, and the fixed-width chip cluster therefore starts at a different x on every row -- flexbox aligns children within one row, never across rows, so there is no shared column. The developer's 'right-aligned within each row' does not create alignment from row to row. Fix: give the list container a shared column structure -- CSS Grid on the list with one grid-template-columns (for example `1fr max-content max-content`), each row a grid row (or display: contents / subgrid for a nested row component) -- so every row's chip column shares the same track boundaries and the chips align down the list.
expectations: Identifies the root cause as each row being its own flex container with a growing cell, so no column is shared across rows
Explains that flexbox aligns within a row but not across rows
Recommends a shared column structure on the container (CSS Grid template / subgrid), not a per-row styling tweak
Rejects 'right-aligned within each row' as producing alignment from row to row

evals.prompt: In Halcyon, category badges appear on five screens. During review a colleague points out that the team already extracted `resolveCategoryColor(key)` into a shared util and every one of the five screens imports it, so the color logic has a single source and is fully DRY. On that basis they mark the item 'category badge: unified -- one source of truth' and move on. Reading the five screens, each writes its own JSX around the call: screen A renders `<span className={cx('dot', resolveCategoryColor(k))}>`, screen B a `<div className={cx('pill', resolveCategoryColor(k))}>`, screen C wraps the same in an extra icon, and so on. Is the colleague right that the badge is unified? If not, what is still wrong and how would you fix it?
evals.expected_output: No. Only the value (the color) is centralized; the render around it -- the element, the class scaffolding, the a11y attributes, the icon, the sizing -- is hand-rolled independently on each of the five screens, so the badge's markup still drifts screen to screen even though the color logic is DRY. A DRY check on the resolver gives a false 'unified' signal because it inspects only the value, not the render. The concept is unified only when the render is one shared component (for example `<CategoryBadge category={k}/>`) that owns both the resolver call and the markup, with its one legitimate per-site difference (size/variant) as a prop. Audit the markup at each call site, not just whether the value is centralized.
expectations: Answers No: a shared color/value resolver does not make the concept unified while the surrounding render is duplicated per screen
Identifies that the markup (element, a11y, icon, sizing) drifts across the five screens despite the shared resolver
Notes the DRY-on-the-resolver check gives a false 'unified' signal because it inspects only the value
Recommends consolidating the render into one shared badge component owning both the lookup and the markup

evals.prompt: In Solstice, a UX consistency audit is comparing how the same components render across screens. It has drafted two items to file as inconsistencies to fix: (1) the status badge is a solid filled pill on the active-projects board but an outline-only badge on the archived-projects view; (2) the main action is a prominent solid button on the create form but a small subdued text link on the read-only detail page. The reviewer is about to file both as 'same component rendered two different ways -- unify them.' Before filing, what should the reviewer check for each item, and are these two actually defects to fix?
evals.expected_output: Before filing, check each difference rather than assume every cross-surface difference is accidental. Ask: are these the same concept? do they mean the same thing in each context? does the visual difference carry meaning? Both examples look like intentional, meaning-bearing differences, not accidental drift: an outline badge signals 'archived' against the active board's filled badge, and the subdued link versus the solid button reflects that the action is primary on create but not really available on a read-only page. Filing those as inconsistencies and 'unifying' them would erase a real signal -- a net-negative change. So neither is an automatic defect; at most, if the reviewer thinks a distinction is wrong, raise it as an owner decision, never a blocker. File as an inconsistency only when it is the same concept, the same intended meaning, and the difference carries no meaning.
expectations: Says to check/classify each difference before filing, not to file both as inconsistencies automatically
Applies a test of same-concept / same-meaning / does-the-difference-carry-meaning (or equivalent)
Recognizes both examples as intentional, meaning-bearing differences (archived vs active; action available vs not), not drift
Warns that unifying a meaning-bearing difference erases a real signal / is a regression
Concludes they are not automatic defects -- at most an owner decision, not a blocker

evals.prompt: A component renders with class="grid-cols-3 gap-4" -- the class string is confirmed present in the live DOM -- but the three-column grid never appears: no build error, no lint warning, no console message. The identical utility classes work in a sibling component under src/legacy/. A teammate's test greps the component file, confirms the class strings are present, and marks it passing. What do you check before assuming a CSS-specificity or JIT-syntax bug, and is that grep test sufficient?
evals.expected_output: The file most likely sits outside the build tool's configured source/content scan scope, so those utility classes compile to no CSS at all -- zero emitted rule, no error, the class is just an inert string on className. Confirm it: read getComputedStyle for the property the utility should set (grid-template-columns) and walk the compiled stylesheet (document.styleSheets, recursing nested @media/@supports) for any rule matching the class; if the class rides the DOM but no rule exists anywhere, the scanner never saw the file (or its extraction missed the syntax). Rebuild fresh first to rule out a stale cache. The grep test is NOT sufficient and proves nothing here: the string is present but maps to no emitted rule, so a source-text-presence check must never stand as proof a utility renders an effect -- assert the produced effect (a computed-style value) instead. Fix going forward: keep the scan scope a superset of the source dirs (add a directory's entry in the same change that adds the directory), add a CI guard that fails the build when a dir with recognizable source files is outside the configured scope, or a computed-style canary per top-level source dir. (reliability-error-handling.md.)
expectations: Checks whether the file is inside the build tool's configured source/content scan scope before assuming a specificity/JIT bug
Verifies via computed style and the compiled stylesheet that no rule for the class exists anywhere, and rebuilds fresh to rule out a stale cache
Rejects the grep/source-text test as proof the utility renders -- requires asserting the produced effect, because the class string being present maps to no emitted rule
Prescribes keeping the scan scope a superset of source dirs / a CI coverage guard / a computed-style canary per top-level source dir

evals.prompt: Our pre-commit gate greps every *.ts, *.js, *.md, *.json, *.sh, *.yml, and *.txt file for banned tokens and secrets. It just ran in CI and printed 'clean', exit 0. The repo also commits *.py scripts and *.ipynb notebooks. Can I record this boundary as clean?
evals.expected_output: No. The gate selects files by an include-list of extensions that omits committable types (*.py, *.ipynb), so those files were never scanned -- a banned token or secret in one is invisible and the gate still exits 0. The green means 'clean within the subset I scanned,' not 'clean'; this is false confidence, and worse than no gate because it trains the team to trust a no-op. It is not the same as a skipped scope from a missing pattern-list: the single scan ran, but its input file-set is a subset of what the repo can commit. Fix: make the scanned set a superset of the committable surface -- derive it from git ls-files (scan-all-then-exclude / deny-list) rather than a hand-maintained include-list; and because this is a secret/identifier gate, treat an unrecognized committable type as could-not-check and fail closed, never a silent pass. Prove it with a negative control per committable type: plant a banned token in a throwaway file of each type the repo commits and assert the gate catches every one; a gate with no such self-test is unverified, not clean. (reliability-error-handling.md.)
expectations: Refuses to record the boundary clean: the extension include-list omits committable types (*.py, *.ipynb) that were never scanned, so exit 0 covers only the scanned subset
Names it false confidence -- worse than no gate -- and distinguishes an under-covering input file-set from a skipped scope caused by a missing pattern-list
Requires coverage be a superset of the committable surface (git ls-files / scan-all-then-exclude), and fail-closed / could-not-check on an unrecognized committable type for a secret/identifier gate
Requires a negative-control self-test that plants a banned token in every committable file type and asserts the gate catches each

evals.prompt: A README states: 'the human read always wins over the model's estimate.' In the code, the human read is written into a 'read' column; the row's 'status' -- the field the shortlist and the exported report act on -- is computed in a branch that consults only the model/research signals. One row shows status='keep' next to a read of 'do NOT -- regulated, hard pass.' Is the stated precedence actually implemented, and what's the rule?
evals.expected_output: No -- the precedence is nominal only. The senior source (the human read) is written to a side 'read' column, but the decision field 'status' is computed purely from the junior (model) branch and never consults the read, so the field a reader acts on contradicts the override: status='keep' beside a read that says hard pass. For any stated precedence (A outranks B), grep the field that encodes the acted-on decision and confirm A is consulted first in the branch that sets THAT field -- not merely written somewhere on the row. Fix: in the branch computing status, consult the human read first and let it win; test the conflict case explicitly (a row where override and base disagree must render the override's verdict in the acted-on cell). Also never truncate a caveat-bearing field to a length that can cut the disqualifying clause ('do NOT -- regulated' clipped to a positive stub is how the reason gets lost) -- clip low-information display fields instead. Distinct from which store holds the field (a dual-registered write-target) and from a compare-and-swap guarding the wrong column: here one record, the write reaches the row but the decision branch ignores it. (data-scoring.md.)
expectations: Concludes the precedence is not implemented: the override is written to a side column while the acted-on decision field is computed only from the junior branch and never consults it
States the rule: for a stated precedence, confirm the senior source is consulted first in the branch that sets the decision field -- not merely written somewhere on the row

Requires testing the conflict case (override vs base disagree -> the acted-on cell shows the override's verdict) and warns against truncating a caveat-bearing field so it cuts the disqualifying clause
Distinguishes it from a dual-store write-target and from a CAS guarding the wrong column -- one record, the write lands but the decision branch ignores it

evals.prompt: We join a survey overlay onto a company snapshot by name using: if a in b or b in a. In the human-facing export, a fund named 'AV' picked up a confidential revenue note that actually belongs to a company named 'Haven'. A teammate proposes fixing it by switching to a strict exact string match. Sign off on that fix?
evals.expected_output: No -- to both the current join and the proposed fix. The bidirectional substring test (a in b or b in a) with no word-boundary or length guard makes the short name 'AV' a substring of 'Haven', so the fund inherits an unrelated entity's confidential row and it lands in a human-facing output -- a privacy leak, not just a quality defect. But strict exact string match over-corrects: rows whose names differ only trivially (a legal suffix like 'Inc' or 'gmbh', punctuation, case) stop matching and drop out silently. Fix both directions at once: match on a normalized key (case/whitespace/unicode-NFC/suffix-folded) or a resolved stable id; when overlaying, emit every overlay entry as a matched-or-unmatched row so a name mismatch is a visible unmatched row, never a silent drop; and verify the join both ways on real data -- sweep for false positives (a wrong row attached) AND false negatives (an expected row missing). A join is unproven until both counts are seen. (data-quality.md.)
expectations: Rejects both the unguarded substring join (it inherits a confidential row from an unrelated entity -- a privacy leak) and the naive exact-string fix (it silently drops rows differing only by suffix/case/punctuation)
Requires matching on a normalized key or a resolved stable id rather than an unguarded substring
Requires surfacing every overlay entry as a matched-or-unmatched row so a mismatch is visible, never a silent drop
Requires verifying the join both directions on real data -- false positives AND false negatives -- before trusting it

evals.prompt: A shared dashboard's server loader starts eight independent section reads in parallel; each read is wrapped as .catch(err => { log(err); return [] }) so one failing read cannot take the page down. The team added these guards after an earlier incident where a single rejected read crashed the whole dashboard. Sign off on the loader?
evals.expected_output: No. Every read is now guarded so the page will not crash -- but returning [] on failure makes a failed read render identically to a section that genuinely has no rows: a transient DB/upstream failure shows as '0 items / nothing here', and neither a viewer nor any downstream count/total can tell a failed load from a real empty. On a shared multi-viewer dashboard that silent false-empty under-reports live data as absence -- worse than the loud crash it replaced. The fallback must carry a distinguishable failed/degraded signal: a tagged result or sentinel the renderer maps to an error-or-stale marker, or last-good behind a stale badge, reserving the empty state for a read that succeeded with no rows. Test both paths -- a rejected read must render the error/stale marker and a resolve-empty read the empty state, and the two must diverge. (reliability-error-handling.md.)
expectations: Confirms the added guards fix the crash but flags that returning an empty value on failure renders a failed read identically to a genuinely-empty section
Names the harm: no viewer and no downstream count can tell a failed load from a real empty, so a shared dashboard shows the same '0' to everyone and under-reports live data as absence
Requires the fallback to carry a distinguishable failed/degraded signal (an error or stale marker, or last-good), reserving the empty state for a successful read with no rows
Requires testing that a rejected read and a resolve-empty read produce different rendered states
Distinguishes it from the missing-guard crash bug (the guard is present here) and from writing an empty artifact over last-good bytes (this is a display defect, not a write-path one)

evals.prompt: In a Next.js App Router dashboard, a Server Component builds five section bodies -- each is itself a Server Component that runs its own database reads and joins -- and passes them to a Client Component <Tabs> as an array of { id, node }. <Tabs> keeps activeTab in useState and renders only the active section's node, hiding the rest, so only one tab's data is visible at a time. Is this an efficient way to keep the hidden tabs' data off the client until they are opened?
evals.expected_output: No -- the design does the opposite of what is assumed. Because the parent is a Server Component that builds all five nodes, every section body executes its reads and joins on the server on each request, and each rendered node (plus any data serialized into the RSC payload) is sent to the client before <Tabs> picks one. activeTab only chooses which pre-computed node to reveal; it cannot prevent the other four from having run. Result: five sections' worth of server work and queries to display one, and the hidden tabs' data is present in the payload the browser receives -- readable in the network response regardless of the CSS that hides it -- a cost and a leak, not isolation. It passes typecheck and looks right in the browser, so only the RSC/network payload or the query log exposes it. Fix: make an inactive section's body not run until it is chosen -- give each tab its own route/segment so navigation triggers the read, or defer the body behind a boundary that only renders on activation and fetches on demand; pass the inputs a tab needs (an id or query key), never the pre-built node of an unopened tab. (lang-js-ts.md.)
expectations: Rejects the assumption: all five section bodies execute their server-side reads/joins on every request because the Server Component parent builds every node before any client tab state exists
Explains that client activeTab state gates only which pre-built node is displayed and cannot stop the other sections from having run
Names both consequences: wasted server work / repeated queries for unshown tabs, and hidden-tab data serialized into the client payload (readable despite the CSS that hides it)
Requires making an inactive tab's body not run until chosen -- a per-tab route/segment or an activation-gated boundary that fetches on demand, passing inputs rather than a pre-built node

Distinguishes it from a directive-less module whose run-location follows its import site -- here the sections legitimately run once on the server and the fix is to defer execution, not to relocate them off the client

evals.prompt: A shared helper gates every 'is this integration usable' code path: isConnected = i => i.hasApiKey && i.hasWebhook. A dashboard shows a 'Connected: N of M' stat computed separately as integrations.filter(i => i.hasApiKey).length. QA reports the stat sometimes shows a higher connected number than the feature that relies on isConnected will actually enable. Review the stat.
evals.expected_output: The stat re-derives 'connected' by hand and tests only hasApiKey, dropping the hasWebhook condition the shared isConnected helper also requires. Every field it reads is real, so it looks correct in isolation, but it counts integrations the actual gate treats as not-connected -- so the user-facing 'N of M' over-counts and silently disagrees with the behavior isConnected controls. Fix: call the shared helper -- integrations.filter(isConnected).length -- and never re-express a check the codebase already centralizes; a count over the helper cannot diverge from the gate. To find the class, start from the shared helper, enumerate the fields it reads (hasApiKey, hasWebhook), and search every site that reads any of them in a boolean/count/filter context, flagging any that tests fewer conditions than the helper. (method.md.)
expectations: Identifies that the stat tests only hasApiKey and omits hasWebhook, which the shared isConnected helper also requires
Explains the symptom: every field read is genuine so the code looks right, but the user-facing count over-counts and silently disagrees with the behavior the shared helper gates
Requires calling the shared helper (filter(isConnected)) rather than re-expressing a check the codebase already centralizes
Gives the detection technique: start from the shared helper, enumerate the fields it reads, and search sites that read any of them but test fewer conditions

Distinguishes it from N drifting sibling copies of a guard with no single source of truth -- here a shared helper is the source of truth and the bug is one narrower hand-rolled check that omits a condition

evals.prompt: In Beacon (a form-heavy dashboard), the primary submit button uses `disabled={isSubmitting}`: the click handler sets isSubmitting = true, fires the request, and the button greys out until it resolves; a small confirmation banner renders elsewhere on the page. A keyboard user tabs to the button and presses Enter to submit. QA drove the mouse path and the visible states looked correct. Is there an accessibility problem specific to the keyboard user, and if so how would you fix it while keeping the guard that stops a double submit?
evals.expected_output: Yes. A native `disabled` element cannot hold focus, so the instant isSubmitting flips the button to disabled it is pulled out of the focus/tab order and the browser moves focus to <body> -- the keyboard user is silently dumped to the top of the page mid-submit, with nothing restoring their place and no announcement (WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order, Level A). The mouse path hides it because a mouse user's focus was never on the control in a way they track, and a render test asserts the button is disabled, not document.activeElement. Fix, keeping the double-submit guard: at or before the disable, move focus to a sensible target -- a role=status result/toast region (which also announces the outcome), the next control, or a results region -- so focus is placed rather than dropped; OR drive the busy state with aria-disabled=true plus a guarded handler (early-return in onClick/onKeyDown while pending) instead of the native disabled attribute, which keeps the element focusable and the tab order unbroken (aria-disabled does not block activation on its own -- the handler must). This differs from the case where the control is removed from the DOM and replaced by a message (that one recommends keeping it mounted and disabled -- which this shows still needs a focus move), and from a dismissible overlay restoring focus to its trigger (nothing is dismissed here). Regression test: assert document.activeElement !== document.body immediately after the pending state disables the control. (a11y-focus.md.)
expectations: Identifies that setting native `disabled` on the focused control removes it from the tab order and drops focus to <body>, a WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order break, not merely a cosmetic state change
Explains why the mouse/visual path and a disabled-state render assertion miss it (focus after disable is never checked)
Gives a fix that preserves the double-submit guard: move focus to a status/next-control/results target at or before disable, or use aria-disabled + a guarded handler to keep the element focusable
Requires a regression assertion that focus is not on document.body after the control disables

evals.prompt: Harbor (a docs site) shipped correct banner, nav, and main landmarks on every page. After that change the automated accessibility scanner stopped flagging the long repeated navigation, and a screen-reader user confirms they can now jump straight to the main region. A separate tester who navigates by keyboard alone and does not run a screen reader reports that on every page they still have to press Tab through all thirty-odd nav links before they reach the content. Is the relevant success criterion actually satisfied for that tester, and what, if anything, is missing?
evals.expected_output: The criterion is met in letter but the tester is still not served. WCAG 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks (Level A) is satisfied by any one of its independent sufficient techniques -- ARIA landmarks (ARIA11), a skip link (G1), or headings (H69) -- so shipping correct landmarks meets it on ARIA11 alone, which is exactly why the scanner (axe-core bypass / Lighthouse bypass-blocks, each of which accepts a region OR a skip link OR a heading) went green. But a landmark is a screen-reader navigation affordance (rotor/region jump); a sighted keyboard-only user with no screen reader running cannot perceive or jump to a landmark, so they must Tab through the whole repeated nav. Missing: a real skip link -- an in-page anchor to the #main/main-landmark id, placed as the first focusable element and visually hidden until it receives focus (sr-only-until-:focus), pointing at a focusable/labelled main region so activating it moves focus, not just scroll. Do not infer 2.4.1 conformance from the automated pass; a keyboard-only manual pass (Tab from the top, no screen reader) is what reveals it. This is distinct from a region that is missing from the landmark tree -- here the landmarks are correct and complete and still insufficient for this user. (a11y-aria.md.)
expectations: States that WCAG 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks is met by any one sufficient technique and that landmarks (ARIA11) alone satisfy it, which is why the automated scanner passes
Explains that landmarks are a screen-reader affordance and give a sighted keyboard-only (no screen reader) user no way to skip the repeated nav
Prescribes a visible-on-focus skip link as the first focusable element, targeting the main region so activation moves focus
Warns against inferring 2.4.1 conformance from the automated pass and calls for a keyboard-only manual pass; distinguishes this from a region missing from the landmark tree

evals.prompt: Trellis renders a project sidebar as a single <ul> in which every row -- top-level projects and their nested sub-items alike -- is a direct <li> sibling. Depth is shown by adding left padding per level and drawing a colour-matched accent bar, so on screen it reads clearly as an outline where some rows belong under others. Each row has a visible text label, and collapsible parents correctly toggle aria-expanded. A reviewer says the outline structure is obvious, so it is fine. Does this convey the structure to assistive-technology users, and how would you address it if not?
evals.expected_output: No -- the parent/child structure is conveyed only through presentation (indentation plus a colour accent), and neither reaches the accessibility tree. A flat <ul> of siblings is announced as one flat list at a single level, so a screen-reader user hears 'list, N items' with no depth, no sense of which row owns which, and no subtree boundaries; indentation has no programmatic equivalent and the colour accent is unspoken and gone in greyscale/forced-colours. That is WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A) -- structure and relationships conveyed through presentation must be programmatically determinable or available in text (its Understanding page uses indented list items as the example) -- with the colour accent also implicating 1.4.1 Use of Color. Correct aria-expanded on the parents does not close it: that is per-row open/close state, whereas the missing thing is the level/containment relationship across rows. Fix: expose the hierarchy in the tree, not in padding+colour -- use real nested lists (each child <ul> inside its parent <li>) or the ARIA tree pattern (role=tree/treeitem with aria-level, aria-setsize/aria-posinset, aria-expanded on parents, and aria-owns when the DOM cannot nest), keeping the indentation and accent as reinforcement only. Verify by reading the accessibility tree (devtools/axe), e.g. getByRole('treeitem', { level }), not the DOM padding. (a11y-aria.md.)
expectations: Concludes the hierarchy is invisible to assistive tech because depth rides on indentation + colour, and a flat <ul> announces every row at the same level (WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships, with 1.4.1 for the colour accent)
Notes that correct aria-expanded does not fix it -- that is per-row state, not the cross-row level/containment relationship
Prescribes exposing the structure via real nested lists or the ARIA tree pattern (aria-level / aria-setsize / aria-posinset / aria-owns), with indentation/colour only as reinforcement
Requires verifying via the accessibility tree (e.g. getByRole treeitem with a level), not the DOM padding

evals.prompt: An internal tool stores each workflow as a JSON diagram: an ordered `nodes` list, an `edges` list of directed `{from, to}` pairs, a `narrative` string that walks the steps in order, and a top-level `startNode` id the renderer reads to decide which node to draw first before walking the edges around the loop. In `refund.json` the `nodes` are `["intake", "triage", "refund", "notify"]` in that order; the `edges` are intake->triage, triage->refund, refund->notify, notify->intake; the `narrative` opens "The loop begins at intake, then triage decides ..."; and `startNode` is `"notify"`. The repo's `validate_diagrams.py` asserts that every diagram's edges form exactly one closed cycle visiting all nodes, and it passes on `refund.json`. `refund.json` is one of fourteen workflow diagrams a porting script emitted last week, and the renderer draws the ring correctly closed. Is `refund.json` correct? What should the review check, and across what scope?
evals.expected_output: No. The edges do form one valid closed cycle, which is all `validate_diagrams.py` checks, so its green run says nothing about where the ring starts. `startNode` is "notify", but the declared entry is "intake" -- both the first element of the ordered `nodes` list and the first clause of the narrative ("begins at intake"). Those are two unlinked authored fields that must agree and nothing forces them to, so every renderer that reads `startNode` draws the ring rotated to begin at notify, one step short of the real entry -- a wrong-start, not a broken graph. Detection compares `startNode` to the declared entry (`startNode == nodes[0]`, and the narrative's opening clause), not "is `startNode` a valid node id" -- validity of the topology is the wrong question. Fix by construction: derive `startNode` from the declared entry, or gate `startNode == nodes[0]` (and the narrative's first clause) so the two cannot drift. And because one porting script emitted all fourteen diagrams from the same template, a wrong anchor here is a strong prior that its siblings carry the same disagreement -- sweep all fourteen, do not stop at refund.json.
expectations: Identifies that `startNode` ("notify") disagrees with the declared entry -- the first `nodes` element ("intake") and the narrative's opening clause -- so consumers render the ring rotated to the wrong starting step: a cross-field-agreement defect in authored data, not a topology error

Explains that the closure/cycle validator stays green because it checks a structural property (edges form one closed cycle over all nodes), not which node is declared the start, and that detection must compare `startNode` to the declared entry rather than ask whether `startNode` is a valid node id
Flags that a shared template / porting-script origin makes this a batch defect and the finding must sweep all fourteen sibling diagrams from the same pass, not stop at the one file
Gives a by-construction fix -- derive the anchor from the declared entry, or gate the two authored fields into equality -- rather than only re-pointing this one file's `startNode`

evals.prompt: A repo gates commits with a pre-commit hook and re-runs the identical check in CI. The check confirms a config digest is lowercase hex: `case "$digest" in *[!0-9a-f]*) echo 'bad digest'; exit 1;; esac`. The hook file is the same everywhere and is invoked the same way in both places. Developers report that a digest typed with uppercase letters is accepted by the hook on some machines but rejected on others, and the CI job's verdict does not always agree with the local hook's -- yet nobody has edited the script. Review the guard and explain the split verdict.
evals.expected_output: The review identifies that `[!0-9a-f]` is a bracket RANGE, whose matched set is defined by the current locale's collating sequence (LC_COLLATE) rather than by codepoint, so under a dictionary-collating UTF-8 locale (e.g. glibc) uppercase letters sort inside `a-f` and pass the reject filter, while under LC_ALL=C the same guard is byte-strict and rejects them -- the identical script returns different verdicts per environment. It recommends pinning LC_ALL=C for the comparison or replacing the range with an explicit character set (`*[!0123456789abcdef]*`). It explicitly rules out a drifted/stale local copy of the gate, noting the script is byte-identical and only the runtime locale differs, so single-sourcing the script would not fix it.
expectations: Names the bracket RANGE (`[!0-9a-f]` / `[a-f]`), not an explicit enumerated set, as the root cause
Explains the verdict differs because a range is matched against the locale's collating sequence (LC_COLLATE) and is byte-strict only under the POSIX/C locale (LC_ALL=C)
Recommends pinning LC_ALL=C for the comparison OR an explicit character set / named class -- not merely re-copying or re-syncing the script
Distinguishes this from a drifted or stale local gate copy: the script is byte-identical and only the environment/locale differs, so single-sourcing does not fix it
Does not misattribute the split verdict to the operating system alone; ties it to the active locale/collation setting

evals.expected_output: The test's scan is a literal-substring match for exactly "export async function POST(" (and the other three verbs), not a parse of the file. The new route is written as "export const POST = async (request) => {...}" -- an arrow-function-assigned-to-a-const export, which Next.js treats identically to a function declaration at runtime but which does not contain the substring the test greps for. Because the substring is never found in this file, the test's own loop -- for each file where the substring matches, assert requireSession is also present -- never considers this file at all: it is not that requireSession was searched for and not found, it is that the file was never entered into the check in the first place. Zero files matched means zero assertions ran means the run reports green, even though the route genuinely has no auth check and any caller can update any account -- a real, live access-control vulnerability, not a test false-positive. The test's own comment ("every mutating handler is covered by construction") is an overclaim its mechanism cannot support: it only recognizes the one export spelling that happened to be universal in the codebase when the test was written, not every syntactically valid way to export a Next.js route handler. The durable fix is to stop recognizing the construct by literal text: parse the route files with the language's real compiler/AST tooling (e.g. the TypeScript compiler API, or a tool built on it) and check the exported POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE bindings regardless of whether they were declared as a function or assigned as a const arrow function -- or, if a full parse is impractical, explicitly widen the pattern to cover every currently-known equivalent export form AND add a regression fixture written in the arrow-const form with requireSession deliberately removed, asserting the test still catches it, so the completeness claim in the comment is itself proven rather than assumed.
expectations: Identifies that the test's scan is a literal-substring match for "export async function POST(" and that the new route uses a different, runtime-equivalent export syntax (export const POST = async (...) => {}) that the substring never matches

Explains that because the substring is never found in this file, the test's assert-requireSession-is-present check never runs for this file at all -- the file is never entered into the loop, not merely searched and cleared

States the practical consequence: the route ships with no auth check, a genuine access-control vulnerability, despite the suite reporting all green -- a silent coverage gap, not a flaky or false-positive test failure

Flags the test's own comment ("every mutating handler is covered by construction") as an overclaim the substring-match mechanism cannot support, since it only recognizes one syntactic spelling of the construct

Recommends a durable fix: parse the route files with real compiler/AST tooling (or an exported-symbol lookup) instead of a substring/regex match, or at minimum enumerate every currently-known equivalent export spelling and add a fixture in the alternate form with auth removed to prove the test still catches it

evals.prompt: Palette (an admin dashboard) renders a multi-select category filter as a single trigger button. When one or more categories are chosen, the button's on-screen text becomes text like "Books, Movies", and a separate expression sets the button's aria-label to "Category filter: Books, Movies" for extra context -- a reviewer who opens the dropdown, picks a few categories, and checks the label each time finds the two consistent. Before any category is picked, the button displays the placeholder "Select categories...", but the code path that computes the aria-label for that particular render still returns the string "Category filter", a value nobody has touched since before the current placeholder copy was introduced. Walk through what a screen-reader user hears on landing on this control before making any selection, say whether that is a compliance problem, and explain why the reviewer's earlier check would not have caught it.
evals.expected_output: Yes, this is a problem specific to the empty/default render. WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name (Level A) requires that when a component has visible text, its accessible name contains that visible text. On the empty render the visible text is the placeholder "Select categories..." but the computed aria-label is "Category filter", which does not contain the placeholder text at all -- a screen-reader user landing on the control before selecting anything hears a name that has nothing to do with what is on screen. The reviewer's check missed it because the visible text and the aria-label are two independently-written expressions: when a selection exists, both are built from the same selection data (item names/count) and so naturally agree, which is exactly the state the reviewer exercised by picking categories before checking. The empty branch is the one where the two expressions stop sharing a source -- the visible placeholder is one literal, the empty-state aria-label is a separate, older literal -- and it is also the branch a "pick something, then check" review habit never reaches. Fix: stop hand-authoring the label as a second parallel string; derive the accessible name from the same expression that already produces the visible text in every branch, including empty, appending any extra context after it rather than replacing it. Regression test: render the component with nothing selected specifically (not only a populated fixture) and assert the computed accessible name contains the visible placeholder text.
expectations: Identifies the empty/default render as a WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name violation because the computed aria-label does not contain the visible placeholder text

Explains that the visible text and aria-label are independently-computed expressions that only agree because they share the same selection data on populated branches, and diverge on the empty branch which uses a separate, stale literal
Explains why a review habit of selecting something before checking the label would never exercise the empty branch and so would not catch this
Gives a fix that derives the accessible name from the same source as the visible text (single source of truth) rather than maintaining two literals
Requires a regression test on the specifically-empty render, not only a populated-selection fixture

evals.prompt: Driftwood (a file browser) renders each folder as a list row: a plain div with tabIndex={0}, an onClick, and an onKeyDown that treats Enter and Space as "open this folder", plus an aria-label set to the folder's full path for extra context beyond the visible name. Each row also contains a real anchor link ("Share") and a native details/summary element for row-level metadata. The engineer who built the row deliberately left off role="button" on the wrapping div, reasoning that stacking a button role over a row that already contains a real link and a native disclosure would recreate the nested-interactive-controls setup that accessibility guidance warns against. A keyboard-only pass finds every control in the row reachable and operable by Tab and Enter. Assess what a screen reader's accessibility tree actually exposes for this row, and say whether the engineer's reasoning left anything unresolved.
evals.expected_output: The row has no accessible name at all, despite the aria-label being present in the markup, and the engineer's fix for one problem created a different one. A div with no role, no other semantics, and no native element mapping computes to the ARIA generic role, and per WAI-ARIA 1.2's role characteristics, generic is one of the roles with Name Prohibited -- authors must not use aria-label or aria-labelledby to name an element with that role, and a conformant accessibility tree discards the attribute rather than exposing it. So this row is WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value non-compliant: it has a role (generic, which is not a widget role) and effectively no name, even though the JSX clearly sets aria-label. It looks finished because every surface a normal check reads is fine -- the attribute is present in the markup, the row is focusable and key-operable, and the nested link and details/summary still work on their own -- only the computed accessibility tree shows the label was thrown away. The engineer's instinct to avoid nesting an interactive role over the link and disclosure was correct, but dropping the role entirely to solve it does not just skip a role, it silently disables aria-label too, which they likely did not know. Fix options: restructure so the row's primary action is a real singly-interactive control (a button or link) and keep the genuinely interactive descendants outside its content model; or, if the row's compound content is why a single button/link role does not fit, use role="group" plus a computed name and aria-roledescription, since group is not in the Name Prohibited set and does accept aria-label (though the descendants, not the group, must still own any keyboard activation); or name the row from a visible heading or aria-labelledby pointing at on-screen text instead of aria-label on a bare div. Regression test: assert the row resolves under getByRole to some non-generic role with a non-empty computed accessible name, not merely that the aria-label prop was passed in the component's props.
expectations: Identifies that a div with no role maps to the ARIA generic role, and that generic has a Name Prohibited characteristic under WAI-ARIA 1.2, so aria-label on it is discarded rather than exposed
Concludes the row fails WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value -- present-in-markup aria-label is not the same as a computed accessible name
Recognizes the engineer's nested-interactive-controls concern was legitimate but that dropping the role entirely traded one defect for another

Offers a fix that either makes the row's primary action a real interactive element with descendants outside it, or uses a role that still permits a name (e.g. group) without recreating nested interactivity
Requires a regression test asserting a non-generic computed role AND a non-empty computed accessible name, not just the presence of the aria-label prop

evals.prompt: Tidewell runs its delivery process with several agent lanes working the same repository in parallel. The repo's pre-commit hook chain has three stages: a lint stage and a type-check stage, both scoped to only the files changed in the commit (fast, seconds), and a test stage that unconditionally re-runs the entire test suite -- several hundred tests, minutes to complete -- regardless of what changed. Under load from three concurrent lanes competing for CPU, one lane opens a draft PR, then discovers CI requires a generated changelog fragment it forgot to add. It writes the fragment and runs `git commit` to add it. That commit enters the pre-commit hook and starts the full test-suite stage, which under the current CPU contention takes several times longer than normal. The lane, watching for the PR to go green, sees no new commit land, sees CI still reporting the missing-fragment failure, and starts re-polling CI every few seconds while the commit it needs is still sitting inside the hook. Diagnose what is actually blocking this PR, and say whether simply re-ordering the hook's stages (cheapest first) would fix it.
evals.expected_output: The test stage running the whole suite unconditionally, with no changed-path scoping, while the lint and type-check stages in the same chain do scope to changed files, is the root defect. Re-ordering the stages cheapest-first does not fix this case: that fix only saves cost on a doomed commit that was always going to fail the cheap check (a formatting retry). Here the commit is legitimate and necessary -- it adds the required changelog fragment -- so even ordered last, it still must pay the full suite once the cheap stages pass. The real failure is a deadlock: the one commit that would satisfy CI's missing-fragment requirement is itself stuck inside the same slow, unconditional full-suite stage, so nothing the lane does can produce a green PR until that commit's own hook run finishes -- and the lane burns tool calls and tokens re-polling CI for a result that cannot arrive yet. The durable fix is to scope pre-commit to a fast, changed-path subset (or an explicit fast tier) and move the full suite to pre-push or CI, where the added latency amortizes across a batch instead of taxing every single commit.
expectations: Identifies the test stage as unconditional/unscoped while lint and type-check are changed-path-scoped -- the asymmetry is the root defect
States that reordering stages cheapest-first does not fix this case, because the stalled commit is legitimate and necessary, not a formatting retry -- it still pays the full suite once ordered
Names the deadlock explicitly: the commit that would satisfy the missing-fragment requirement is itself stuck inside the same slow stage, so no commit can produce a green PR until that run finishes
Flags the wasted cost of re-polling CI while the lane's own blocking commit is still in flight
Recommends scoping pre-commit to a fast/changed-path subset and moving the full suite to pre-push or CI, where the latency amortizes across a batch

evals.prompt: Nebula Freight Systems has two open PRs: PR-14 branches directly off PR-9's branch (not off `main`), stacking review of a follow-up change on top of PR-9's still-unmerged work. PR-9 is approved and merged with the platform's delete-branch-on-merge option. A few minutes later, an engineer notices PR-14 has disappeared from the open-PR list. They push one more commit to PR-14's branch, hoping it will reappear, then run `gh pr list --state closed --limit 50` to check on it. PR-14 shows up in that list with `state: CLOSED`, sitting next to several other rows for PRs the team merged normally last week. Seeing it listed as CLOSED alongside those, the engineer assumes PR-14 is simply another finished, already-shipped item from the batch and moves on to the next task. Explain what actually happened to PR-14, whether the follow-up push restored it, and whether reading it as 'just another closed/finished PR' next to the normally-merged ones was safe.
evals.expected_output: Merging PR-9 with delete-branch-on-merge removed PR-14's base ref, and the forge auto-closed PR-14 because its diff had nowhere to point once that ref was gone. The follow-up push did not revive or reopen PR-14 -- pushing to a branch whose PR already auto-closed just recreates a bare branch on the remote with no pull request attached, so nothing reappeared and the new commit has no thread. PR-14's underlying change is not shipped and must be re-proposed as a new PR -- either retargeted onto the shared base and rebased onto PR-9's now-merged commits, or opened fresh against the shared base. Grouping PR-14 with the normally-merged neighboring rows because both read CLOSED is exactly the mistake to avoid: the forge's `state: CLOSED` does not distinguish closed-via-merge from closed-unmerged. Before treating any closed PR as finished, check its `merged` field (or `mergedAt`) -- PR-14's is unset, the neighbors' are not. Going forward, stacked PRs should retarget onto the shared base before the parent merges, or be opened against the shared base from the start rather than branching off the parent's own branch.
expectations: Identifies that merging PR-9 with delete-branch-on-merge removed PR-14's base ref, and that the forge auto-closes a PR whose base ref disappears
States that pushing a further commit to PR-14's branch does not reopen or revive the PR -- it only recreates a bare orphan branch on the remote with no attached PR
Concludes PR-14's work is not shipped and must be re-proposed as a new PR (retargeted onto the shared base, or rebased onto PR-9's merged commits), not treated as done

Flags the closed-state read as the specific mistake: `state: CLOSED` does not distinguish closed-via-merge from closed-unmerged, so the `merged` field (or mergedAt) must be checked per PR before treating a closed PR as finished
Names the prevention for future stacks: retarget the child PR onto the shared base before merging the parent, or open the child against the shared base from the start

evals.prompt: Wrenfield gates every commit with a `pre-commit` hook that runs a linter and, importantly, regenerates and diffs a committed `schema.lock` file against its declared source so a stale lock file can never be committed. The repo also registers a git merge driver on `schema.lock` in `.gitattributes` that resolves any merge conflict on that path by taking the incoming branch's copy outright. Two long-running branches -- `feature/reporting` and `feature/billing` -- each regenerated `schema.lock` independently from their own schema edits. An engineer merges `main` into `feature/reporting` to pick up unrelated fixes; git reports a completely clean merge with no conflicts at all, produces a merge commit automatically, and the merge lands. Later, a teammate notices `feature/reporting`'s `schema.lock` no longer matches what its own schema files would regenerate -- it is silently stale, missing content the branch itself had contributed earlier. Nobody bypassed any hook with `--no-verify`, and the `pre-commit` hook script itself has not changed or drifted. Explain how a stale `schema.lock` shipped through a hook whose whole job is to catch exactly that, with no bypass and no drift.
evals.expected_output: Git's internal merge-commit code path for a conflict-free merge only invokes `commit-msg`, not `pre-commit` -- `pre-commit` fires on an ordinary `git commit`, not on this automatic, non-conflicting merge commit. Only a project-installed `pre-merge-commit` hook runs at that point, and this repo never added one, so the regenerate-and-diff check that would have caught the stale `schema.lock` simply never ran for this merge -- not because of `--no-verify`, and not because the script drifted, both of which are ruled out by the scenario. The merge driver compounds the problem's visibility: because it auto-resolved `schema.lock`'s conflict by taking one side, git reported the merge as fully clean, which is why nobody saw a conflict to investigate. Fix: add a `pre-merge-commit` hook mirroring `pre-commit`'s regenerate/freshness check (at minimum), add a test asserting a zero-conflict merge is actually gated, and re-generate and diff generated files after any merge even when git reports no conflict.
expectations: Identifies that git's merge-commit path for a conflict-free merge invokes `commit-msg` but not `pre-commit` -- `pre-commit` only fires on an ordinary `git commit`, not on this automatic merge commit
States explicitly that this is a missing-hook gap, not a bypass or drift -- no `--no-verify` was used and the `pre-commit` script itself is unchanged, so those explanations are ruled out
Names `pre-merge-commit` as the hook that does fire on a merge commit, and that the repo never installed one
Connects the merge driver: because it auto-resolved the conflict on `schema.lock`, the merge presented as fully clean, which is why the staleness produced no conflict signal for anyone to investigate

Recommends adding a `pre-merge-commit` hook mirroring the regenerate/freshness check plus a test proving a zero-conflict merge is gated, and re-diffing generated files after every merge regardless of reported conflicts

evals.prompt: Cormorant's pricing page reads a rates snapshot on every request through `getRates()`, a synchronous function. `getRates()` fires a background `reload()` every single time it is called -- if a reload is already in flight it just returns that same in-flight promise instead of starting a second one, and regardless, it always returns the last-known-good snapshot immediately, never blocking the caller. The engineer who wrote it left a comment: 'refreshes every read so we are never more than a request or two stale, without ever blocking.' The `rates` table's primary key is `(currency, as_of, recorded_at)`, and `reload()`'s query is `SELECT * FROM rates ORDER BY as_of DESC, recorded_at DESC LIMIT 5000`. A teammate reviewing the PR checks the table definition, sees the three-column primary key, and approves the query as 'the table is indexed.' The `rates` table is an append-only ingest log that is never pruned. Three months after launch, with the table now at several million rows and the pricing page receiving steady traffic, p99 latency across every route that reads the rates cache has climbed steadily, even on routes that have nothing to do with pricing. Explain what is driving it and why the two individual review passes -- the caching pattern, and the primary key -- each looked fine on their own.
evals.expected_output: The query orders by `as_of DESC, recorded_at DESC`, but the primary key leads with `currency`, not `as_of` -- the primary key cannot serve this sort order, and with no dedicated index matching it, the engine must scan and sort the entire table on every execution of this query. Separately, `reload()` is triggered unconditionally on every call to the synchronous getter, with no TTL or staleness check at all -- the in-flight-promise reuse only coalesces truly concurrent calls, it does nothing to cap how often a fresh reload is triggered over time. The two compound: the unbounded, unpruned append-only table grows the cost of each sort, while growing traffic grows how often that sort runs, so cost rises on two independent axes -- table size and request volume -- which is why p99 climbs steadily and shows up even on routes that merely share the cache and have nothing to do with pricing. Each half passed review alone because each is individually reasonable: the cache's 'refresh every read, never block' design is a legitimate, documented choice in isolation, and a three-column composite primary key reasonably reads as 'the table is indexed' without checking whether its leading column matches the query's actual sort column. Fix: add an index matching the real `ORDER BY` shape, confirmed via `EXPLAIN`/`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, and independently consider gating `reload()` behind a short TTL so read volume stops multiplying query volume one-to-one.
expectations: Identifies that the primary key `(currency, as_of, recorded_at)` does not lead with the query's actual `ORDER BY as_of DESC, recorded_at DESC` column, so it cannot serve this sort and, absent a matching index, forces a full table scan and sort on every execution

Identifies that `reload()` fires unconditionally on every call to the synchronous getter with no TTL/staleness check -- the in-flight-promise reuse only coalesces concurrent calls, it does not cap reload frequency over time

Explains the compounding: the unbounded, unpruned table grows the cost of each sort while growing traffic grows how often it runs, so cost rises on two independent axes and surfaces as p99 degradation even on unrelated routes sharing the cache

Explains why each half passed review separately: the cache's refresh-every-read design is legitimate in isolation, and the composite primary key reasonably reads as 'the table is indexed' without checking whether its leading column matches the query's sort column

Recommends adding an index matching the actual `ORDER BY` shape (verified via EXPLAIN) and, independently, gating `reload()` behind a short TTL so read volume stops multiplying query volume one-to-one

evals.prompt: A teammate fixed a config-validation gate that was silently letting an empty config through. Their regression test: run the fixed gate against the old bad config, capture whatever it now outputs, save that as `expected`, and assert future runs match it. They say this proves the gate rejects empty configs going forward. Review the test -- is it sound, and if not, why?
evals.expected_output: Not sound: the test's oracle was derived by running the very gate it is supposed to verify, which is circular. It only proves the gate agrees with itself today -- if the gate has any residual defect (e.g. it still half-accepts some other malformed shape), that defect ships baked into the captured `expected` value, and the test can never catch it because it will always agree with whatever the gate currently outputs. This is different from the legitimate practice of probing a real, already-trusted function to pin its current behavior -- that practice assumes the behavior is correct; here the whole point of the test is to prove the gate's correctness, so it cannot borrow its own answer as the check. The fix is to build the oracle independently of the gate: assert against a fact established before the gate ever runs -- e.g. a fixture that is deliberately, verifiably invalid and so must be rejected regardless of what today's code does (a planted-defect fixture with a known verdict), or a hand-verified expected value -- never the gate's own captured output. (testing-and-evals.md.)
expectations: Identifies the core flaw: the expected value was derived by running the same code/gate under test, making the oracle self-referential/circular
Explains the consequence: a residual defect in the gate would be captured into `expected` and the test could never catch it
Recommends an independent oracle instead -- e.g. a fixture with a verdict known in advance (a planted defect) or a hand-verified value -- not the gate's own output
Does not accept the teammate's claim that the test proves the gate is correct going forward

evals.prompt: A browser test opens a modal, calls `await page.waitForTimeout(500)`, then asserts the modal's content is visible. It passes reliably whenever a developer runs it alone, but fails intermittently in CI -- always in the same suite, never reproducing locally. The team's working theory is "flaky browser, add a retry." Evaluate that theory and the test itself.
evals.expected_output: The "flaky browser, add a retry" theory masks the real cause and a retry would only paper over it. The fixed 500ms wait is a timing bet that the modal always finishes rendering within 500ms; that bet holds on an idle local machine but not on a CI runner where several job lanes share the host's CPU -- under that contention the same render can take well over 500ms, so the assertion fires before the modal is actually ready. This is not browser flakiness, it is a wall-clock assumption embedded in the test, and it explains exactly the observed pattern: never locally (nothing contends there), intermittently in CI (contention varies run to run). The fix is to replace the fixed sleep with a poll/wait for the actual observable readiness signal -- the modal's content actually present or visible (e.g. a selector-based wait or an assertion with built-in retry/polling) -- bounded by a generous upper bound, never a guessed duration. A blanket retry-until-green would hide the same class of failure elsewhere and erode trust in a genuinely red CI run. (testing-situational.md.)
expectations: Rejects "add a retry" / generic browser flakiness as the fix and identifies the root cause as a fixed-duration wait racing the real render time
Names CPU contention from other concurrent CI lanes/jobs sharing the host as why this reproduces in CI but never locally
Recommends replacing the fixed sleep with polling/waiting for the actual observable readiness condition rather than asserting on a wall-clock duration
Does not conflate this with a genuinely nondeterministic flaky test needing quarantine -- treats it as an authoring-time defect to fix directly

evals.prompt: An internal dashboard reads from a local on-disk cache that's populated by a background job. Since the last infra migration, the team has noticed the dashboard renders completely empty right after every deploy, then "fixes itself" within a few minutes. Nobody has found an error in the logs. What's actually going on, and what would you require before calling this fixed?
evals.expected_output: Each deploy runs in a fresh, ephemeral environment (a new container, a cleared build cache, redeployed disk), so the on-disk cache the dashboard reads does not survive the rebuild. "Fixes itself in a few minutes" is the background job re-populating the cache from scratch after boot; the empty window in between is the defect itself, not a transient error any log would catch -- which is why nobody found one. Waiting it out, or adding a longer health-check delay before routing traffic, does not fix it -- it only hides the same blank window behind a slower rollout. Before calling this fixed, require three things together: a committed fallback dataset shipped in the repo so a cold cache never renders bare-blank on the very first request; automatic, idempotent rehydration that repopulates the cache on boot with no manual runbook step, safe to run again if a redeploy retries; and a data-freshness gate or alert that fires when served data exceeds an expected age bound, so a rehydration that silently stops working is caught before a user notices. This differs from a live-read failure that can fall back to an existing last-good snapshot -- here there is no last-good, because the cache itself is what the rebuild wipes, so the durable fallback has to be the copy committed to git, not a database the surface may not even have. (reliability-error-handling.md.)
expectations: Identifies the root cause as the on-disk/local cache not surviving the rebuild/redeploy (ephemeral storage), not a logged error or a transient blip
Rejects waiting for it to self-heal or adding a longer health-check delay as an actual fix
Requires a committed fallback dataset in the repo so a cold cache never renders blank
Requires idempotent automatic rehydration on boot/deploy with no manual step
Requires a data-freshness gate or alert to catch a silently-broken rehydration

evals.prompt: A team has been through four rounds of "align the app to the Figma mockup." Each round: compare screenshots, patch the mismatched spacing and colours screen by screen, reviewer signs off "looks aligned now." Two weeks later the stakeholder says it still looks off almost everywhere -- and no new screens shipped in between. What diagnostic should have run before round one, and what would explain the pattern?
evals.expected_output: The repeated per-screen patch-and-sign-off loop that never converges is the tell of a foundation-level mismatch, not scattered per-screen drift -- diagnose it before touching a single screen: extract both sides' design tokens (colour/spacing/type -- the design's export or CSS custom properties, and the app's) and diff them by resolved/computed value, not by name, since names rarely agree between a design file and an app's codebase. A low match (one real audit found the app matched only ~4% of the design's colours, ~3 of roughly 1,400 token names) means the app was built on a different token foundation entirely -- every screen inherits the wrong palette/spacing/type independently, so each round finds a fresh crop of "new" mismatches even though nothing about the task changed.
