No amount of per-screen restyling converges until the foundation itself is remapped. Fix: adopt the design's token VALUES under the app's existing token NAMES, so components don't need rewriting -- then a per-screen pass (classifying each remaining diff as a genuine treatment gap, a data-volume artifact, or a real extra feature worth preserving) is the right tool, because it is now operating on a shared foundation. (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: Diagnoses the non-converging per-screen patch loop as evidence of a foundation-level (design-token) mismatch, not independent per-screen drift
Prescribes diffing both sides' design tokens by resolved/computed value, not by name, before any per-screen work
Explains why a low token match means every screen inherits the wrong foundation independently, so per-screen fixes never converge
Prescribes adopting the design's token values under the app's existing token names rather than a per-screen rewrite

evals.prompt: An owner tells an agent: "the settings screen doesn't match the new design -- align it." The agent runs a structural diff, finds six differences, and replies: "Audited all six. Three are decoration and cosmetic, two exist because the settings screen carries real user data the mockup doesn't, and one -- a saved-views tab -- looks intentional since it's a genuinely useful feature the design just doesn't show. Recommend leaving all six as-is; the screen is functionally equivalent to the design." No code changed. What is wrong with this response, and what should the agent have done for each of the three buckets instead?
evals.expected_output: The owner gave a concrete instruction -- "align it" -- not a request for an opinion, yet the agent audited the six differences, classified each as fine, and stopped with nothing landed. Classifying a difference into a bucket is a diagnostic step, not the deliverable: verification has to terminate in the change, not in a report explaining why the change wasn't made. Each bucket the agent named still resolves in an action: the three decoration/cosmetic differences (genuine treatment gaps) get restyled to match; the two differences driven by real user data (data-volume artifacts) get progressive disclosure, capping, or pagination against equal data -- not dismissal, since a mockup's sparse seed data is not proof the gap is intentional; and the saved-views tab is real functionality, so it gets re-expressed in the target design's own primitives (restyled into the target's design language), not left alone. "Recommend leaving all six as-is" with no owner sign-off on record is the agent self-granting itself the exemption from the instruction -- "keep current, no change" is a valid bucket outcome only behind a named owner's explicit sign-off on that specific difference, never a judgement the agent hands itself. (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: Identifies that 'align it' is a concrete instruction, and an audit that classifies every difference and changes nothing downgrades that instruction into a self-granted judgement call
States that classifying/bucketing a difference is a diagnostic step, not the deliverable, and that verification must terminate in the actual change
Prescribes restyling the decoration/treatment differences to match rather than leaving them as-is
Prescribes progressive disclosure, capping, or pagination for the data-volume differences rather than dismissing them as intentional

Prescribes restyling the real feature (saved-views tab) into the target's design language rather than leaving it unstyled, and flags that 'leave as-is' requires a named owner's explicit sign-off, not the agent's own say-so

evals.prompt: An agent is porting a settings page to a new design. It has the running app's rendered HTML and a page-height screenshot, but the design side of the port isn't available in this pass (the mockup lives in a different tool). The agent runs its checklist against the app alone, sees three clean, generously-spaced sections, and reports: 'App renders cleanly at 1840px, three sections, all populated -- aligned to the design.' What's wrong, and what should it report instead?
evals.expected_output: 'Aligned/matched/mirrored' is a two-sided claim -- the agent measured only the app and never touched the design, so 'aligned' is unearned: a page height and a self-read screenshot are not alignment evidence no matter how clean the app looks, and can't be quoted as a verdict. scripts/parity_differ.py is structurally unable to emit a pass here: with the design side absent or unreadable it exits COULD_NOT_CHECK (3) -- never a score, never a pass, it refuses to compare rather than guess 'looks fine'. The correct report is 'not yet verified -- design side unavailable for this pass, cannot certify alignment,' not 'aligned.' Once the design render is available, the differ compares per named section (data-section/data-item): MATCH (exit 0) is the only pass, requiring every design section present in the app and every design-populated section populated; MISMATCH (1) lists missing/empty sections as the work queue; and if the design's populated sections are all present in the app but uniformly empty, that's CANNOT_COMPARE (4), an unseeded precondition -- seed the app's data to the design's data state, never condense or remove the empty sections to look tidy. (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: Rejects the 'aligned' claim because only the app side was measured -- a page height and a self-read screenshot are not two-sided evidence
States the report should read 'not yet verified' / 'cannot certify' rather than 'aligned' while the design side is unavailable
Names the parity differ (scripts/parity_differ.py) and its fail-closed contract: COULD_NOT_CHECK when either side is missing, never a pass or a similarity score
Once both sides exist, requires MATCH (both sides present, every design section present and populated) as the only pass, with MISMATCH naming missing/empty sections as the work queue
Flags design-populated sections present but empty in the app as CANNOT_COMPARE (unseeded), resolved only by seeding data -- never by condensing or removing the empty sections

evals.prompt: An agent designs a review pipeline: Tier 1 (cheap model) reads a 40,000-token shared context packet and does a candidate sweep; Tier 2 (a stronger model) re-sends the identical 40,000-token packet to confirm survivors, and the agent reasons: 'Tier 1 already warmed the cache with this packet, so Tier 2's request will hit the cached rate for it.' Is that reasoning right? What actually happens on Tier 2's first request, and what should the agent do differently if the pipeline must stay a cascade?
evals.expected_output: The reasoning is wrong. Each model keeps its own prompt cache; Tier 1's cache was warmed under Tier 1's model, and Tier 2 is a different model, so Tier 2's first request reads the entire 40,000-token packet at full, uncached input price even though the content is byte-identical -- switching models forfeits the cache regardless of content match. The fix is ordering, not architecture: choose the model and its effort level at the start of the session rather than switching mid-run, since a model swap always forfeits whatever cache the run has built. Lowering effort mid-session is not automatically cache-free either: on most models each effort level has its own cache, so an effort change also re-reads the whole history uncached; only Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 used with an API key or a Claude subscription keep the cache across an effort change (not on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or a Claude apps gateway, nor with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS set or a HIPAA configuration), so only there is tuning effort down within the current model the cache-preserving lever. If the cascade is kept anyway (because a stronger model is genuinely needed for confirmation), the pipeline's own cost accounting must book Tier 2's packet re-read as a fresh full-price read, not the cached rate, when computing cost-per-solved-task -- never assume a cascade inherits an earlier tier's cache.
expectations: States the cross-model cache-reuse assumption is wrong: prompt caches are model-scoped, not content-scoped
States Tier 2's first request re-reads the whole packet at full uncached price even though the resent content is byte-identical to what Tier 1 cached

Prescribes choosing model and effort up front instead of switching mid-run, and states that a mid-session effort change keeps the cache only on Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 via an API key or a Claude subscription (not Bedrock, Agent Platform, or a Claude apps gateway); on other models each effort level has its own cache
If the cascade is kept, requires costing the later tier's re-read as a fresh full-price read in any cost-per-solved-task accounting, not the cached rate

evals.prompt: A team's CLAUDE.md tells every subagent to 'default to the cheapest tier.' An audit later finds three subagent definitions whose own frontmatter sets `model: opus`, overriding that default. The team argues the CLAUDE.md line already 'enforces' a cheap-tier fleet. Per the host-enforcement claim-honesty framework, is that a Host-enforced claim? What is the actual host-enforced fix on Claude Code, and what does it require?
evals.expected_output: No -- a CLAUDE.md instruction is Protocol-level only: it is a prompt the agent follows, and a subagent's own `model:` frontmatter can still override it, exactly as the audit found. The Host-enforced fix is a host setting the worker cannot edit from inside its own definition: set `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` to the desired model alias/ID and `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1` in `settings.json`'s `env` block. With both set, every subagent, teammate, and workflow agent runs on the named model regardless of its own `model:` frontmatter; this requires Claude Code v2.1.257 or later, so the version must be confirmed before the claim is raised to Host-enforced. The claim must also declare the pin's exceptions: a fork, and a skill that runs in a subagent with `model: inherit`, still run on the main conversation's model; and with only `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE` set, the built-in Explore subagent keeps its model cap (Opus on the Claude API). The sibling spend control at the same enforcement split is cache lifetime: `promptCacheTtl`/`CLAUDE_CODE_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL` (main conversation) and `subagentPromptCacheTtl`/`CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL` (everything else, v2.1.242+) are host-level pins. When more than one applies, the first match wins: `FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M=1`, then the bucket's environment variable, then its setting, then a subagent's own `experimental.cacheTtl` frontmatter field (a per-agent, Protocol-level opt-in that any of those overrides), then `ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H=1`, then the bucket default -- one hour for the main conversation on a Claude subscription within plan usage, five minutes otherwise.
expectations: Declares the CLAUDE.md 'default to cheapest tier' line Protocol-level only, since a subagent's own model: frontmatter can still override it -- not Host-enforced

Names CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL plus CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1 in settings.json's env block as the Host-enforced fix, overriding every subagent/teammate/workflow-agent's own model: frontmatter
Names the version gate (Claude Code v2.1.257+) as a precondition to check before claiming this control is available

Declares the pin's exceptions: forks and skills run in a subagent with model: inherit stay on the main conversation's model, and with only the FORCE variable set the built-in Explore subagent keeps its model cap

Identifies the cache-TTL settings (promptCacheTtl/subagentPromptCacheTtl or their env-var equivalents) as the sibling host-level spend control, and orders precedence correctly: FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M, then env var, then setting, then the per-agent experimental.cacheTtl frontmatter, then ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H, then the bucket default

evals.prompt: Review this design-parity PR. It adds a seed script whose sample people are copied from the prototype (the prototype shows real-looking names and emails), and commits `docs/parity/dashboard-side-by-side.png`, a design-versus-app composite, with a new binaries-allowlist entry for it. The lane matched the design package's largest export file; a smaller export in the same package contains the 'Pinned' label that the newest change-log entry introduced, and the largest one does not. The text privacy gate is green and the PR says 'dashboard now matches the design'. Findings?
evals.expected_output: Two findings. (1) Privacy (S1 PII, blocks merge until removed): the seed copies the prototype's sample identities, and the committed composite puts the prototype's names into git history as pixels. The text privacy gate being green proves nothing here because text gates cannot read pixels, and the new binaries_gate.py allowlist entry for a screenshot is the privacy review point that was skipped. Fix: seed fictional placeholders only, keep in-repo evidence app-only (the app rendering fictional data), and keep design-versus-app composites outside the repo (scratch dir or ephemeral artifact); the composite stays in history until rewritten, so flag that as an owner decision. (2) Wrong target: file size is not evidence of which export is current. Grep each export for distinctive UI strings from the newest change-log entries; the one containing all of them ('Pinned' here) is the target, recorded where every lane reads it, and if none matches ask the design owner. Every earlier 'matches the design' result was checked against the wrong export and is void until re-run against the pinned one. (migration-parity.md, seed and pin-the-target-export paragraphs; method-situational.md stale-input rule.)
expectations: Flags the copied seed names and the committed composite image as a PII/privacy finding
Explains that the green text privacy gate cannot see names rendered in pixels, and treats the binaries allowlist entry as a privacy review point
Requires fictional seed identities, app-only in-repo evidence, and composites kept outside the repo
Selects the design export by the newest change-log UI strings, not by file size, and asks the design owner if no export matches
Voids the 'matches the design' claim because it was checked against the wrong export

evals.prompt: An agent restyling an app to a design export reports: 'Tokens aligned: every design token name (color.brand.primary, spacing.md, radius.lg, ...) has a matching CSS custom property in the app.' The design file is W3C DTCG JSON (spacing.md is {"value": 1, "unit": "rem"}, color.link is the alias {color.brand.accent}); the app defines --spacing-md: 16px, --color-link: var(--color-brand-accent), and --radius-lg: 10px where the design says 12px. It then moves straight to comparing screenshots. Is the token claim earned, and what should the agent run and report instead?
evals.expected_output: Not earned -- matching names proves nothing; a different token foundation can carry every design name with different values, so parity is judged on resolved VALUES. The check order is element inventory (scripts/parity_differ.py), then token values, then screenshots; the token claim itself is checked by scripts/token_differ.py --design <design.tokens.json> --app <app.css>: it resolves DTCG aliases ({group.token}, local $ref pointers) and CSS var() chains with cycle detection, normalizes values (hex/rgb/hsl to one rgba form, rem to px at --root-px default 16, s to ms, fontWeight keywords, font-family lists), and reports per token MATCH / MISMATCH (both values) / MISSING_IN_APP / UNRESOLVED. Here spacing.md (1rem vs 16px) and color.link (alias vs var) MATCH, but radius.lg is MISMATCH (design=12px app=10px), so the run exits 1 and the honest report is that mismatch as the work queue, not 'aligned'. Exit 0 requires every compared token to MATCH; a missing or unreadable side (or --map) is COULD_NOT_CHECK, exit 2, never a pass. Even a full MATCH verifies token values only, not that components use them, so it is a precondition: fix the token mismatch and re-run; completeness comes only from scripts/parity_differ.py's element inventory, and screenshots come last. (migration-parity.md, check-order paragraph.)
expectations: Rejects the name-matching claim: parity is judged on resolved token values, not names
Names scripts/token_differ.py as the token-value check, after the parity_differ.py element-inventory diff and before any screenshot
Identifies radius.lg (12px vs 10px) as a MISMATCH that fails the run (non-zero exit), while rem-vs-px and alias-vs-var() values that resolve equal count as MATCH
States the fail-closed contract: exit 0 only when every compared token matches; a missing or unreadable side is COULD_NOT_CHECK (exit 2), never a pass
States that a token MATCH verifies values only, not that components use the tokens, so it cannot by itself support an 'aligned' claim

evals.prompt: A ship script runs `./run-checks.sh | tail -4`, then greps the tail for `QA OK` (its own guessed pass marker, never seen in a real run) and separately greps the full log for `FAILED` to catch failures. One of the tests that actually passed is named `LOAD FAILED gracefully`. The script reports 'exit 0, QA OK found'. Should this ship unattended?
evals.expected_output: No. The pipe (`| tail`) reports `tail`'s exit status, not the checks' -- capture the runner's own exit code to a variable or file instead (`templates/pre-push-verify.sh` is the mechanized form: decide on the captured command's exit code, never grep a log). The `QA OK` marker was invented, not copied from a real passing run's summary line, so nothing confirms it ever appears on success. The bare `FAILED` grep also matches the passing test name `LOAD FAILED gracefully`, so a truly failing run could quote that green test as false evidence, and a truly passing run's report proves nothing since the marker is unanchored. Before running unattended, dry-run the check against one known-green and one known-red log and require an explicit positive last line (its absence is failure).
expectations: Identifies the `| tail` pipe as reporting tail's exit status, not the checks'
Names capturing the exit code to a file/variable (not a pipe) as the fix, citing exit-status gating as the mechanized pattern
Flags the `QA OK` marker as guessed/invented rather than copied from a real passing run's summary line
Flags that the bare `FAILED` grep also matches the passing test name `LOAD FAILED gracefully`, so a failure grep can quote a green test as evidence
Requires a dry run against one known-green and one known-red log, and an explicit positive last line whose absence means failure, before the gate runs unattended

evals.prompt: A repo's 'reclaim memory' helper for agents runs: `for port in $(seq 3110 3200); do kill -9 $(lsof -ti :$port); done` followed by `pkill -f 'chromium.*headless'`, excluding only a hard-coded list of three 'owner' ports. An agent is asked to review this cleanup script before it ships. Is it safe for a fleet of parallel agent lanes sharing one host, and what should the review flag?
evals.expected_output: Not safe -- it is a fleet-wide kill switch, not a scoped cleanup. Four independent defects: (1) the seq-driven range kill hits every parallel lane's own dev server inside 3110-3200, not just the caller's; (2) `lsof -ti :$port` with no `-sTCP:LISTEN` matches any process connected to the port (a reverse proxy, a test client), not only the listener, so a kill meant for 'the server on 3112' can take an excluded port's fronting proxy with it; (3) `pkill -f 'chromium.*headless'` matches every lane's headless test browser, not only orphans; (4) the hard-coded three-port exclusion list goes stale the instant the operator adds a new backend, and the default when a port isn't recognized should be to NOT kill, not to kill. The fix: reap only what is provably the caller's own or orphaned (parent PID 1, a cwd inside the caller's own worktree, or a PID file the caller wrote), select the listener only (`lsof -t -iTCP:PORT -sTCP:LISTEN`), source protected ports from operator config rather than a script literal, and default to a dry run requiring an explicit `--apply` to act. `scripts/reaper_lint.py` statically flags exactly these four shapes (RANGE_KILL, LSOF_NO_LISTEN, BROAD_PKILL, HARDCODED_PORTS) before the script ships. (concurrency-shared-state.md, "Terminating work you own".)
expectations: Rejects the script as safe for a multi-lane host; identifies it as a fleet-wide kill switch, not scoped cleanup
Names the range kill (seq over the whole port range) as hitting every parallel lane's own port, not only the caller's
Names the bare `lsof -ti` (no `-sTCP:LISTEN`) as matching a connected client/proxy, not only the listener
Names `pkill -f` on a browser pattern as reaping every lane's test browser, not only orphans

Names the hard-coded protected-port list as going stale and states the fix: reap only PID-1/own-worktree/PID-file-provable processes, filter to the listener, source exclusions from operator config, and default to dry-run with an explicit apply flag

evals.prompt: Reviewing a restyle PR, the author writes 'VERIFY_SURFACE: https://preview.example.com, branch feat/restyle, sha a1b2c3d' and says the new header is live. You load the page and still see the old header. The page carries `<meta name="build-sha" content="9e8d7c6...">`. Is the VERIFY_SURFACE field satisfied?
evals.expected_output: No. VERIFY_SURFACE names the sha actually rendered, and the serving process reports 9e8d7c6..., not a1b2c3d -- the author wrote the sha of the tree under review, not the one being served, so the claim is about the wrong build. Read the served id instead of asserting it: `surface_check.py served --url https://preview.example.com --expect-sha a1b2c3d --probe meta:build-sha` (agentic-delivery) exits 1 on the mismatch. Record the rendered sha as 9e8d7c6... and treat the parity/'live' claim as invalid until the preview serves the branch head; a missing build id is could-not-check, never a pass. A match would prove only which build is served, not that the header looks right -- the rendered check still follows. (full-map.md first-response block, report-format.md.)
expectations: Rejects the VERIFY_SURFACE field: the sha must be the one the served page reports (9e8d7c6...), not the author's branch sha
Reads the build id from the served surface (e.g. surface_check.py served with a meta probe) instead of trusting the stated sha
Treats a missing served build id as could-not-check, never as a pass
Keeps the rendered/visual check as a separate step -- a sha match does not prove the header renders correctly

evals.prompt: A lane restyling an app to a design export posts to the board: 'Design alignment complete -- every section is present and non-empty, and each section's rendered height and width are within 2% of the design.' It attaches no other evidence. Accept the claim?
evals.expected_output: Reject it. Size is not completeness: heights and widths within 2% say nothing about whether the section holds the same headings, buttons, links, form fields, tabs, images, and rows -- a section can match in size while missing three buttons and a heading, and a correct section can be taller because it holds real data. Section presence plus non-emptiness is also too coarse. Run scripts/parity_differ.py on the rendered design and the rendered app (same auth + data state): inside every matched section it diffs the element inventory (headings by level + text, visible text, controls by role + visible text + accessible name, images by alt, media, icons, select options, list/table row counts + first-cell text, data-state markers) and prints MISSING_IN_APP / EXTRA_IN_APP / CHANGED rows with completeness as matched items / design items per section and overall -- items, never pixels; size, height, width, and bounding boxes are never inputs to its verdict. Report those missing elements by name as the work queue; 'aligned' is claimable only on MATCH (exit 0), where every difference is fixed or listed in an owner-authored --accept file (section, status, item, app value, count, reason, owner quote or commit; reported as MATCH_WITH_ACCEPTED, never plain MATCH). Then token values (scripts/token_differ.py), then screenshots for styling. Geometry stays valid only for layout defects -- overlap, clipping, viewport fit -- never as alignment evidence. (rendered-parity.md; migration-parity.md check order; scripts/parity_differ.py.)
expectations: Rejects the 'aligned/complete' claim and states that element size (height/width within a tolerance) is not completeness evidence
Says section presence and non-emptiness are too coarse, since a section can be non-empty yet missing controls or headings
Directs running scripts/parity_differ.py's element-inventory diff on both rendered sides and reporting the missing elements by name (MISSING_IN_APP / EXTRA_IN_APP / CHANGED) as the work queue
States completeness is measured in items (matched / design items), never pixels, and that MATCH requires every difference fixed or owner-accepted
Keeps geometry only for layout defects (overlap, clipping, viewport fit), with tokens then screenshots after the inventory

evals.prompt: Three PRs merged clean in a merge-train union, but the union fails a repo-wide numeric ratchet (max count of a disallowed pattern). Bisecting which PR caused it would take a while. A teammate suggests giving each PR its own small fragment file that pre-declares its increase, so the union check just sums the fragments. How should we actually attribute and fix this?
evals.expected_output: Reject the per-change fragment-file remedy -- it pre-splits the cap to dodge a merge conflict, the same shape as dev-env-ownership.md's rejected 'raise the ceiling to pass' pattern. Instead attribute the union's ratchet failure per member: for each member PR compute delta = count(member's head) minus count(member's own merge-base with the target), and print '#N +D marker=[present|none]', where marker=present means that member's own commit range carries an explicit '<ratchet>-raise: <path> <old>-><new> <reason>' annotation (the size-budget-raise convention), not a pre-authorizing fragment file. Route the fix to every member with a positive delta and no marker. State the scanner's counting rule explicitly (whether an occurrence inside a comment/string counts) so the per-member counts are comparable. This is attribution/diagnosis only -- it never licenses a member merging because it carries a marker; the union still must pass the ratchet/cap gate to merge.
expectations: Rejects the per-change fragment-file remedy as a ceiling-raise-to-pass violation, citing the existing dev-env-ownership.md rule
Computes each member's delta against its OWN merge-base with the target, not the union's total count alone
Produces the '#N +D marker=[present|none]' per-member attribution line and routes the fix to members with positive delta and no marker
States that the scanner's counting rule (comment/string occurrences count or not) must be explicit so deltas are comparable
Treats attribution as diagnosis only -- a marker never licenses merging, the union still must pass the gate

evals.prompt: An unattended merge daemon builds a union of five green PRs every cycle (a cycle is 20 minutes). Three of them conflict with the others. Each cycle it finds the first conflict, parks that PR, and sleeps until the next cycle before rebuilding the union. The two clean PRs have now waited an hour and have not landed. The daemon reports 'working as designed: conflicts are isolated one per cycle'. Is it?
evals.expected_output: No. Parking a member is not a reason to wait: after removing a conflicting member, the daemon should rebuild the union immediately, without sleeping, so all N conflicting members are found, parked with their conflicting files, and excluded within one cycle rather than N cycles (issue #1134). Sleeping a cycle per conflict multiplies latency linearly with the conflict count and leaves mergeable PRs idle. Here the three conflicting PRs should have been parked in the first cycle and the two clean PRs verified as a union and landed in that same cycle. A parked member stays excluded until its head changes (a new push is new information), so it does not rejoin and re-break the next union. Backoff belongs only to a flaky re-run of a verification or merge step, bounded and capped, never to parking. `merge_train.py verify` in agentic-delivery's scripts does this: a conflict parks the member and rebuilds the union at once, and its selftest pins that three conflicting members are parked in one invocation with zero sleeps.
expectations: Says the daemon is wrong to sleep a cycle after parking one conflicting member
Requires rebuilding the union immediately after a park so all conflicting members are isolated in one cycle, not one per cycle
Keeps a parked member excluded until its head changes so it does not re-break the next union
Limits backoff to bounded retries of a flaky step, never to parking
Points at merge_train.py verify (or an equivalent mechanism) rather than a prose-only fix

evals.prompt: A merge train proved a union of three PRs green on main at commit A and is about to merge them. Before merging it fetches main and finds main is now at B. The automation's plan is: 'base changed, so re-run the union verify on B, and if that is green, merge the three PRs'. In this case B's history does not contain A, because another operator force-pushed main to purge a leaked secret. What should happen, and would the plan be right if B did contain A?
evals.expected_output: Halt, in both cases, without merging and without silently re-verifying. When B does not contain A, main was rewritten (a non-fast-forward move). The three PRs were branched from the old history, so re-verifying and merging them would bring back the history the operator deliberately removed, including the leaked secret (issue #1137). The automation must stop and alert a human that a possible history rewrite happened. When B does contain A (someone else merged in the meantime), the union's proof no longer applies to the base, so the right move is to stop and re-plan from scratch rather than quietly re-verifying and merging in the same run. The rule is to merge only onto the exact base SHA the union was proved on. The check is: fetch the target, compare its head with the proved SHA, and use a fast-forward ancestry test (`git merge-base --is-ancestor A B`) to tell 'moved' from 'rewritten'. The same automation must never force-push the shared branch itself. `merge_train.py merge` in agentic-delivery's scripts is dry-run by default and HALTs on either condition; `--apply` still requires the integration owner or a recorded standing grant.
expectations: Refuses to merge the three PRs onto B
Rejects silently re-verifying the union on the changed base inside the same run
Identifies B not containing A as a possible history rewrite that needs a human, and explains that merging would restore the removed history
Uses a fast-forward or ancestry check against the proved base SHA to tell a moved base from a rewritten one
Keeps merging gated on the integration owner or a recorded standing grant, and never force-pushes the shared branch

evals.prompt: A repo's `.husky/pre-commit` hook runs `python3 scripts/reaper.py --apply` on every commit, with no dry-run flag. Every agent's commit on the shared host now kills sibling lanes' dev servers and headless browsers. Is `reaper_lint.py` expected to catch this, and what should the hook do instead?
evals.expected_output: Yes -- reaper_lint.py's HOOK_LIVE_REAPER rule flags a reaper-named invocation (basename containing "reap", excluding a *lint* variant like reaper_lint.py itself) found inside a git-hook-family path (.githooks/*, .husky/*, .git/hooks/*, lefthook.yml, a *pre-commit-config.y*ml) that carries no --dry-run/--stub/--noop/--check-only/--simulate flag. The fix is doctrine, not just the lint: a commit/push hook must never invoke a live reaper at all -- tests of a destructive reaper/cleanup script run it stubbed or --dry-run by default (concurrency-shared-state.md), and any keep-list the reaper resolves exclusions from must always include the shared/preview serving port by name.
expectations: Names the HOOK_LIVE_REAPER rule in reaper_lint.py and its path scope (.githooks/, .husky/, .git/hooks/, lefthook.yml, pre-commit-config)
States the rule excludes a *lint* invocation such as reaper_lint.py itself
States a commit/push hook must never invoke a live reaper at all, not just that it needs a flag
Names the shared/preview serving port as a required keep-list entry, distinct from generic operator-config exclusions

evals.prompt: A liveness check runs `find "$worktree" -newermt '-10 minutes' 2>/dev/null` to see if a lane wrote anything recently, and treats an empty result as idle. It worked in CI (Linux) but on a teammate's Mac every lane reads idle, including ones that just committed. What is wrong, and what should the check do instead?
evals.expected_output: `-newermt` is a GNU findutils extension; BSD/macOS find has no such flag and rejects it as invalid. The `2>/dev/null` swallows that invalid-option error along with the intended noise, so the command finds nothing and every worker reads idle -- a false negative that looks like "nothing changed," not "the check is broken." Never suppress the stderr of a check whose result drives an action (kill, restart, reassign, alert, "report idle"): if the command can fail for a reason other than "no match," that failure must be visible or explicitly handled. Fix: use the portable form both `find` implementations accept (a numeric N-minutes-ago flag, or detect the platform and branch), and smoke-test the probe against a known-live and a known-idle subject on the actual target platform (macOS here), not only the one it was authored on (lang-shell.md; mechanized by reaper_lint.py's GNU_FLAG_SILENCED_STDERR rule, which also covers the same shape for `stat -c`, `date -d`, and a no-argument `sed -i`).
expectations: Identifies -newermt as a GNU-only find flag that BSD/macOS find rejects as invalid
States the 2>/dev/null swallowed the invalid-option error, producing a false 'idle' reading, not a real 'no match'
States the general rule: never suppress stderr of a check whose result drives an action
Requires a portable flag or platform detection, plus a live/idle smoke test on the actual target platform before trusting the probe fleet-wide

evals.prompt: Review this lane plan for a restyle: "The design export named latest is the source of truth. Run parity_differ against it and fix every MISMATCH row until it reports MATCH." The app already carries two changes from survey feedback and a meeting action item that the design export never picked up. Anything wrong with the plan?
evals.expected_output: Yes. The plan treats one requirement source, the design export, as the whole requirement set. Fixing every MISMATCH row would undo the implemented feedback the design never captured, because those changes show up as CHANGED or EXTRA_IN_APP rows and the lane would revert them. The delivery ledger (`agentic-delivery/scripts/feedback_ledger.py`) holds the full set. Before re-aligning, run its `accept-file` and pass the output as the parity differ's `--accept` file, so decided feedback is accepted rather than reverted. Any design-vs-feedback conflict goes to the owner as a question and is never settled by re-aligning.
expectations: Flags that the plan would revert implemented feedback the design export never captured
States the design export is one requirement source, not the requirement set
Requires running the ledger's `accept-file` and passing it to the parity differ via `--accept` before re-aligning
Routes design-vs-feedback conflicts to the owner rather than resolving them by re-aligning

evals.prompt: A design-parity effort has merged dozens of per-section 'aligned' changes. parity_differ.py reports MATCH on every screen (inventory 100%), yet a whole-screen pixel score has stayed flat for days. The plan is to keep spawning one lane per section to tweak spacing until the score moves. Anything wrong with the plan?
evals.expected_output: Yes. An inventory MATCH proves completeness only; it says nothing about styling, and a flat pixel score after many per-section fixes is the signature of a global foundation mismatch (base line-height, letter-spacing, size scale, padding, radius, shadow) that no per-section tweak can fix. Stop spawning section lanes and run `parity_differ.py --style` on DOM snapshots that carry computed styles (`data-cs` JSON per element, exported from `getComputedStyle` in the same browser for both sides). It pairs design and app elements by section, role and identical visible text, and reports STYLE_DIFF rows grouped by property. Any FOUNDATION row, meaning one property differs on most pairs across at least two sections, gets fixed once in the shared type/box foundation before any per-section work resumes. Style rows never change the inventory completeness verdict, and sizes are never used as parity evidence.
expectations: States that an inventory MATCH proves completeness, not styling parity
Diagnoses a flat score after many per-section fixes as a likely global type/box foundation mismatch
Prescribes a text-matched computed-style diff (`parity_differ.py --style` with `data-cs` computed styles) before more per-section lanes
Requires fixing a FOUNDATION property (off on most pairs) globally before any per-section work
Keeps style separate from the completeness verdict and does not use element sizes as evidence

evals.prompt: A lane reports: 'Parity harness green on the settings screen, 0 open differences.' Its raw output shows the harness matched 2 design/app element pairs; the design's settings screen has about 60 visible elements. The lane wants to mark the screen done. Accept the verdict?
evals.expected_output: No. Two pairs against a roughly 60-element design means the harness almost certainly compared an empty or wrong page (a wrong screen label, a too-narrow filter), so '0 open differences' is not evidence of anything. The orchestrator spot-checks a harness's pair count itself before trusting its verdict, rather than trusting the lane's reported score. Re-run with a caller-supplied floor, for example `parity_differ.py --min-pairs N` (and `token_differ.py --min-pairs N` for tokens), where N comes from the design's own element count and is never a guessed default. Fewer pairs than N returns COULD_NOT_CHECK (never MATCH), and zero pairs never passes at all. Fix the harness input, re-run, and only then judge the screen.
expectations: Refuses to accept the green verdict on 2 matched pairs
Identifies the implausibly low pair count as a sign the harness compared an empty or wrong page
Has the orchestrator check the harness's pair count or raw output itself instead of trusting the lane's reported score
Uses a caller-supplied `--min-pairs` floor (not a guessed default) so a low count yields COULD_NOT_CHECK, never MATCH

evals.prompt: The owner has decided the app keeps 24px line-height where the design uses 20px, and that no text renders below 12px even where the design uses 11px. parity_differ.py --style still prints STYLE_DIFF and a FOUNDATION line-height row on every run, so lanes keep 'fixing' it. How should this be recorded so the gate stops re-opening it?
evals.expected_output: Record the decisions as style approvals in the owner-authored accept file that parity_differ.py already trusts (committed by the owner, read at --accept-rev, no Co-authored-by): a value-pair row `style<TAB>global<TAB>line-height<TAB>20px<TAB>24px<TAB>reason<TAB>owner` and a rule row `rule<TAB>min-font-size<TAB>12px<TAB>reason<TAB>owner`. Covered differences then print as ACCEPTED, not STYLE_DIFF, and no longer count toward FOUNDATION; a fully covered style verdict is STYLE_MATCH_WITH_ACCEPTED, never a plain STYLE_MATCH. The row pins the exact app value, so a different app value stays an open difference, and an unused row prints as stale. The agent drafts rows but never commits them itself.
expectations: Uses the owner-authored, committed accept file (existing trust model), not an agent-written exception or a code comment
Uses a per-property value-pair `style` row for the line-height decision and a `rule min-font-size 12px` row for the floor
States that approved diffs are reported as ACCEPTED and stop counting as STYLE_DIFF or FOUNDATION, and that the result is not a plain STYLE_MATCH
Notes that a row pins the exact app value, so a different value stays open

evals.prompt: A restyle has 12 sections. Three carry owner-approved deviations, and the overall parity verdict has been MISMATCH/STYLE_DIFF for days, so the orchestrator cannot tell whether lanes are converging. What should the progress report be?
evals.expected_output: Report per section and count passes: parity_differ.py prints `sections passed k/n` plus a per-section table. A section is PASS only if its inventory is MATCH or MATCH_WITH_ACCEPTED and it has no un-accepted style difference. It is FAIL on a missing or empty section or on any open row, and UNVERIFIED when inventory or style could not be checked (for example a section with no style pair), and UNVERIFIED never counts as a pass. Sections with owner-approved deviations can PASS, so 9/12 is measurable progress while the overall verdict is still failing. Without --style the table is labelled inventory-only and is not a styling pass.
expectations: Uses a per-section PASS rule: inventory MATCH or MATCH_WITH_ACCEPTED and no un-accepted style difference
Reports progress as sections passed k/n, not as a single overall verdict or a percentage of pixels
Counts sections with owner-approved deviations as passable
Treats an unverifiable section as not passed and labels an inventory-only table as not a styling pass

evals.prompt: Five page lanes each report the same fix: 'heading font-size 14px -> 16px in my section' and 'brand colour token differs'. Each lane patches its own section and the next parity run shows the same rows again. What should the orchestrator run and do?
evals.expected_output: Run the single foundation-first gate: `parity_differ.py --workflow --design-tokens <f> --app-tokens <f>`. It runs tokens (token_differ.py) first, then primitives (open FOUNDATION properties and PRIMITIVE rows, meaning a property or type role that is off in 2 or more sections), then the per-section inventory and styles. While a token mismatches or a primitive is un-accepted, every section reads BLOCKED_BY_FOUNDATION (exit 7), so the per-section lanes stop. One foundation lane fixes the token and the h2 type role once, globally, or the owner approves the deviation. Then the section stage runs. Inventory COULD_NOT_CHECK or CANNOT_COMPARE still outranks the block.
expectations: Runs `parity_differ.py --workflow` with both token exports, with tokens then primitives then sections as the order
Recognizes the repeated per-section rows as a foundation/primitive failure spanning 2 or more sections
States that section verdicts are BLOCKED_BY_FOUNDATION (exit 7) until the foundation is fixed once or owner-accepted
Does not keep patching the same property per section

evals.prompt: A lane says the dashboard parity gate is green and asks the orchestrator to mark it ready. The orchestrator has only the lane's text summary. What should the orchestrator look at before saying ready?
evals.expected_output: Look at the visual evidence yourself before 'ready'. Re-run with `--report out.html`, and add `--design-shots`/`--app-shots` folders keyed by section id when screenshots exist. That writes a self-contained HTML report per section with design and app side by side (embedded screenshots, or sandboxed iframes of each render showing only that section), plus that section's open inventory rows, style rows, and owner-accepted rows. Open it and compare. The report is evidence for a human and never a verdict by itself, and the lane's text summary is self-report.
expectations: Asks for the `--report` HTML (with section-keyed screenshots when available) instead of trusting the lane's summary
Describes a per-section side-by-side of design and app with inventory, style, and accepted rows
Treats the report as evidence the orchestrator views before ready, not as a verdict

evals.prompt: The app's parity export was captured signed out, the design export shows populated dashboards, and the differ reports half the sections 'missing'. How should both sides be captured so the comparison is meaningful?
evals.expected_output: Follow the capture contract in `templates/parity-capture.md`. Capture both sides in the same state. The app side is signed in as a fictional seeded persona, with the identity from DEV_IDENTITY and the dev session cookie from an env var such as AUTH_COOKIE (never committed). An idempotent, dev-only SEED_CMD runs before each app capture, and both sides use the same fixed viewport list. Each DOM snapshot carries data-section, data-item, data-cs computed styles from getComputedStyle, and data-visible markers for class-hidden elements. The 'missing' list from a signed-out capture is an auth gap, not a build order. The signed-out default surface stays its own separate check.
expectations: Captures both sides in the same auth and data state with a fictional seeded persona and a seed hook
Keeps identity and cookie in env and never commits them
Requires data-cs computed styles and data-visible markers in both DOM snapshots at a fixed viewport list
Does not treat the signed-out 'missing' sections as work to build, and keeps the default-surface check separate

evals.prompt: Every parity run on the dashboard fails because the header clock and a rotating sponsored card differ between the design capture and the app capture. A lane proposes deleting those elements from the app capture before running parity_differ.py. What should it do instead?
evals.expected_output: Mark the volatile elements with `data-parity-ignore` (optionally with a short id, for example `data-parity-ignore="clock"`) on both captures instead of editing the captures by hand. parity_differ.py excludes each marked element and its subtree from the inventory, populated-ness, and style diff, and lists every ignored element in the report with its count, section, and id. A design-side ignore removes a requirement, so each one needs an owner-committed accept row `ignore<TAB><section><TAB><id>`, read under the same owner-authorship gate. Without that row the run is COULD_NOT_CHECK. With it the verdict is MATCH_WITH_IGNORED and the section reads PASS_WITH_IGNORED, never a plain MATCH or PASS. An app-side ignore with no design ignore of the same section and id stays an open `EXTRA_IN_APP ignored:<id>` row, and it never hides a design element, which stays MISSING_IN_APP.
expectations: Uses the data-parity-ignore attribute rather than deleting content from a capture
States that every ignored element is listed in the report (count and ids), so ignoring is never silent
Requires an owner-authored ignore accept row for any design-side ignore, else COULD_NOT_CHECK, and reports MATCH_WITH_IGNORED rather than a plain MATCH
States that an unpaired app-side ignore stays an open row and cannot hide a design element

evals.prompt: The holdings section's style identity is 92% and the owner has said 'anything above 90% on holdings is fine for this release'. A lane wants to pass the section by adding `--style-min-pairs 1` and editing the accept file itself. What is the right mechanism?
evals.expected_output: The owner commits a row `threshold<TAB>holdings<TAB>90` to the accept file. It is read from the committed blob under the same owner-authorship check (`--accept-rev`, owner email, no Co-authored-by trailer) as every other accept row, so a lane cannot author it. With that row, holdings passes when its style identity (pairs with no un-accepted difference divided by its pairs) is at least 90%. Its open rows print as tolerated and the style verdict is STYLE_MATCH_WITH_ACCEPTED, not a plain STYLE_MATCH. Below 90% the rows stay open. Every other section stays strict by default. A threshold never waives a FOUNDATION or PRIMITIVE row. `--style-min-pairs` is only a floor on the pair count and does not relax differences.
expectations: Uses an owner-committed threshold accept row for that section, not a lane-authored edit
States that the same owner-authorship gate applies (a lane-authored row fails closed)
States that the default stays strict and the result prints as tolerated or accepted, never as a plain match
States that FOUNDATION or PRIMITIVE rows are never waived by a threshold

evals.prompt: parity_differ.py --style printed: 'identity (owner-accepted ignored) 31/40', 'mismatch count per property: line-height=8, color=2', and a top-diffs table. How should the orchestrator turn this into lane work?
evals.expected_output: Read the per-property counts first. line-height differs on 8 pairs, so check whether it is a FOUNDATION or PRIMITIVE row, and if so fix it once globally before assigning any per-section work. Then use the top diffs table (text | prop | design | app) as the concrete queue for the remaining color rows. Identity counts pairs with no un-accepted difference, so owner-accepted rows do not lower it, and it is a progress metric, not a pass. The verdict still comes from open style rows and the section table. Pairing is by section, role, and full visible text, and then by identical own text for leftovers, so a pair survives a changed child label.
expectations: Uses the mismatch count per property to spot a global property to fix once
Uses the top diffs table (text | prop | design | app) as the concrete work list
Explains that identity ignores owner-accepted rows and is not itself a pass

evals.prompt: The settings page passed parity last week. Now a refactor landed and the orchestrator wants to know whether it broke anything that used to match, as distinct from design work that was never done. How should it use parity_differ.py?
evals.expected_output: On the passing run, record a baseline with `--baseline F --write-baseline`. It writes only when the run exits 0, and a failing run writes nothing. After the refactor, run with `--baseline F` and without `--write-baseline`. New deltas versus that fingerprint (a section or item REMOVED, an item ADDED, or a STYLE_CHANGED value) exit REGRESSION (8) and list only those deltas, which form a bug queue for what the refactor broke. That is distinct from MISMATCH (1), the never-passed work queue: a design change that the app never had stays MISMATCH with 'baseline: 0 new delta(s)'. A missing, malformed, or differently-styled baseline is COULD_NOT_CHECK, never a pass. Re-recording over an existing baseline prints its deltas first and refuses to overwrite when there are any, unless `--accept-regression` is given. The baseline path may not be the design, app, accept, or report file.
expectations: Writes the baseline only explicitly with --write-baseline and only from a passing run
Reads REGRESSION (exit 8) as new deltas versus the passing run, listed alone, distinct from MISMATCH (exit 1)
Treats an unreadable or mismatched baseline as COULD_NOT_CHECK
Does not overwrite an existing baseline that shows deltas without --accept-regression

evals.prompt: A recorded parity baseline had a link with href /help labelled 'Help Center'. The next run's app render still carries that same href, but the link now reads 'Support'. The gate reports a REMOVED row for 'Help Center' and fails the build, and the team is annoyed because nothing was actually removed -- copy was just updated twice in a row, and both times the gate treated it as a regression. What's the actual bug, and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: The baseline diff was keying controls purely by their printed accessible-name/label string, so any relabel looks identical to a removal: the old label vanishes from the fingerprint and a new one appears, and nothing ties them together as the same control. The fix is to key a control by a stable identity first -- href for a link, data-testid otherwise -- and only fall back to the label for controls that carry neither. When the same identity is present on both sides under a different label, that is CHANGED_LABEL, not REMOVED: it prints as an informational rename and never blocks the build by itself, while a control whose identity is genuinely gone from the current fingerprint still reports REMOVED and still fails REGRESSION. An owner-authored `relabel	old-item→new-item	reason	owner` accept row (same owner-commit gate as every other accepted deviation) tags a known intentional relabel (ACCEPTED) instead of leaving it as noise on every run.
expectations: Diagnoses the root cause as keying purely by label/accessible-name, with no stable identity to tell a relabel from a removal
Names href (links) and data-testid (other controls) as the stable identity, label as the fallback only
States CHANGED_LABEL is informational and never blocks REGRESSION by itself, while a control with no surviving identity still fails as REMOVED
Names the owner-authored relabel accept row as tagging a known-intentional rename (ACCEPTED)

evals.prompt: A port's list rows wrap onto two lines while the design's rows are one line. Coarse pixel diff says 3% different and every row's text matches, so the lane calls it aligned. What does parity_differ.py need to catch this?
evals.expected_output: The capture sets `data-lines="N"` on each row (and on headings, controls, or text blocks) on both sides. N is the number of rendered line boxes, a count taken from client rects, not a height or any other dimension. The count joins the item key as `[lines: N]`, so a 2-line app row against a 1-line design row is a CHANGED row and the verdict is MISMATCH, even though the coarse diff is small and the text matches. A `data-lines` exported on only one side also shows as CHANGED, so export it on both. Row counts per list or table and the presence of every design element are already compared by the inventory.
expectations: Uses data-lines on both captures as a line-box count, not a size or height
States that differing line counts produce CHANGED rows and a MISMATCH even when the text matches
Does not accept a small coarse pixel or percentage diff as alignment

evals.prompt: A harness's app capture of the holdings section starts too high and includes the KPI cards above it. The design capture is cropped correctly. What does parity_differ.py do, and what should the lane do?

evals.prompt: Review this test. It defines `NOW = datetime(2026, 1, 10, tzinfo=timezone.utc)` at module level and builds `release_time = NOW - timedelta(hours=1)`. It then calls `is_stale(release_time)` and asserts False, with a comment: '1h old is well inside the 4-day staleness threshold'. `is_stale(ts)` takes no clock argument and computes `datetime.now(timezone.utc) - ts > timedelta(days=4)`. The test passes in CI today. Is it fine?
evals.expected_output: No, this is a finding: a time bomb. The fixture is derived from a pinned NOW, but `is_stale` measures age against the real wall clock because it takes no injected clock. The test passes only while real_now - NOW is under 4 days. On the day that window closes it fails on every branch at the same moment, with no diff that caused it, which looks like a flaky gate or an infrastructure outage. The comment's reasoning is correct relative to NOW, which is why review misses it; the comment does not clear the finding. Fix: derive the fixture from the real clock at test time (`datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(hours=1)`), or inject a clock into `is_stale` so every clock read in the exercised path uses the same pinned value. A pinned NOW is safe only when every clock read in the path uses it. With the clock injected, add boundary cases just before, exactly at, and just after the 4-day threshold. Cheap detection: a CI job that runs the suite with the clock advanced (for example +30 and +365 days with a faketime-style shim).
expectations: Flags the test as a finding: a fixture built from a pinned NOW is compared against the real clock inside `is_stale`
Explains that it passes only while real_now - NOW stays under the threshold, then fails on every branch at once with no causing diff
Does not accept the comment's margin argument as clearing the finding
Fixes by deriving the fixture from the real clock at test time, or by injecting the clock into the entry point
Asks for boundary cases just before, exactly at, and just after the threshold once the clock is injected
Mentions a clock-advanced (time-travel) CI run or equivalent as a cheap way to catch the class

evals.prompt: Threat-model this diff for the review. It adds `POST /webhooks/payments`: a third-party payment provider calls it with a JSON event and a signature header, the handler sets the matching order's `status` from the event body and writes it to the `orders` table, then enqueues a receipt email containing the customer's email address and the amount. The handler parses the body with `JSON.parse` before any other check. There is no rate limit on the route.
evals.expected_output: A diff-scoped threat model, not a system model (threat-modeling.md). Step 1, a data-flow table with one row per boundary crossing: provider (internet) to the webhook route (internet to app, control: none visible before parsing); handler to the orders table (app to data store); handler to the email queue (app to a downstream party, carrying personal data). Step 2, STRIDE on each row, one phrase per category or a dash with a reason. On the inbound row: Spoofing, a forged sender, because no signature check is shown before `JSON.parse`; Tampering and replay, a modified or re-sent body, because there is no raw-body signature check, timestamp window, or unique delivery id; Repudiation, a disputed delivery unless the event id and signature verdict are logged; Information disclosure, error responses that echo internals; Denial of service, a flood or oversized body with no rate limit or body ceiling; Elevation, the body sets `status` and the handler trusts it instead of re-deriving it from the provider or server state. The email row carries personal data, so walk LINDDUN (data disclosure: send only the fields the receipt needs). Step 3, map each threat to an existing check instead of restating it: api-contracts.md Webhooks consuming, appsec-crypto.md constant-time compare, security-appsec.md A06/A09/A10, security-api.md body ceiling, privacy-compliance.md minimization. Step 4, a disposition for each threat (mitigate with file:line and a test, eliminate, transfer, or accept) and at least one residual-risk line naming the threat, severity, an owner role, and a decision, for example the missing rate limit.
expectations: Produces a data-flow table whose rows name source, sink, data, and the trust boundary each hop crosses, including the inbound internet-to-app row

Walks STRIDE per boundary row, and on the inbound row flags at least spoofing (no signature check before parsing), tampering or replay, denial of service (no rate limit), and elevation (trusting `status` from the body)
Maps threats to existing checks by reference (for example api-contracts.md Webhooks consuming, appsec-crypto.md, security-appsec.md A06) rather than restating a generic checklist
Treats the email hop as a personal-data flow and applies a privacy (LINDDUN or minimization) lens to it
Ends with at least one residual-risk line that names the threat, a severity, an owner, and a decision (accept, mitigate by a date, or block)
Does not mark any threat as mitigated without citing a control that the diff actually contains

evals.prompt: Threat-model this diff for the review. It extracts the body of `calculate_invoice_total()` into two private helpers in the same module (`_sum_line_items` and `_apply_discounts`). It does not produce a data-flow table, STRIDE rows, or residual-risk lines for a refactor behind an unchanged interface. Correctness review of the extracted helpers still applies; that is not a threat model.
expectations: Records a single line of the form `Threat model: no new boundary (evidence: ...)`
Cites concrete evidence that the entry point is unchanged (the route handler, auth decorator, or signature at a file:line)
Does not produce a data-flow table, STRIDE rows, or residual-risk lines
Does not invent threats for a change that crosses no new boundary

evals.prompt: You are in Phase 1 of a DIFF review. The diff does two things: it edits `scripts/privacy-gate.sh` (the gate CI runs on every PR), and it raises the test runner's CI retry count from 0 to 3 because one test "fails sometimes". The PR says CI is green. Following the skill's routing from the Phase 0-2 files you have already loaded, which additional reference files do you load, what trigger sends you to each, and what does each make you check?
evals.expected_output: Two conditional references load, each on a named trigger in an always-loaded file. First, method.md's situational Phase 1 line routes to method-situational.md because the diff edits an enforcement artifact: the green run used the changed gate grading itself, so re-run the base copy of `scripts/privacy-gate.sh` (git show <base>:scripts/privacy-gate.sh) against the new tree, or diff base against head and read what it stops catching; a narrowed gate that stays green is a Blocker. Second, testing-and-evals.md's conditional-depth list routes to testing-situational.md because the suite has flaky tests and retries: a standing CI retry count above zero that papers over a flake is itself the finding; quarantine the test with an owner and deadline and fix the nondeterminism instead. The review does not treat either rule as absent just because it is not in the floor files, and it does not load every conditional file up front. (method-situational.md; testing-situational.md.)
expectations: [needs_files] Loads method-situational.md because the diff edits an enforcement artifact (the gate script), naming method.md's situational Phase 1 trigger
Re-runs or diffs the base copy of the gate instead of trusting the green run of the changed gate
[needs_files] Loads testing-situational.md because the suite has flaky tests or retries, naming testing-and-evals.md's conditional-depth route
Flags a standing CI retry count above zero used to hide a flaky test as the finding, and asks for quarantine plus a root-cause fix
Does not load every conditional reference up front and does not skip either rule because it is outside the Phase 0-2 floor

evals.prompt: You are reviewing a PR whose head is commit b2c4e6f. The author writes: "CI is green, I re-ran all jobs after the last push." The checks page shows a green run for commit 9a1d3e0, the previous head. Can you record the gate as passing for this PR, and which reference do you open?
evals.expected_output: No. Before citing any green, confirm the commit it graded is the reviewed head; method.md keeps that check in the always-loaded floor. A forge re-run re-dispatches the original payload SHA, so this green graded 9a1d3e0, not b2c4e6f, and the gate is unverified for the head until a run on b2c4e6f reports. Because a green and a re-run are cited as evidence, method.md's situational line routes to method-situational.md for the full re-run rule. The honest status names the SHA the green belongs to and asks for a run on the current head. (method.md; method-situational.md.)
expectations: Refuses to record the gate as passing for head b2c4e6f
Names the SHA mismatch: the green graded 9a1d3e0, the previous head
Explains that a re-run re-dispatches the original payload SHA, so it does not certify the new head
[needs_files] Loads method-situational.md because a green or re-run is cited as evidence
Asks for a run on the current head before the gate counts

evals.prompt: A PR description for a payment-rounding module says: "Branch coverage is 97%, so this is well tested." The tests call every function but most assertions only check that no exception is thrown. Following the skill's routing, which testing reference do you load and what do you check?
evals.expected_output: A coverage figure cited as assurance is a trigger in testing-and-evals.md's conditional-depth list, so load testing-situational.md. Coverage shows what ran, not whether a test would catch a fault. For load-bearing logic such as payment rounding, measure the suite's fault detection with mutation testing, bounded to the highest-stakes modules, and report each surviving mutant as a file:line finding naming the behavior no test asserts. Also flag the assert-nothing tests as weak assertions. Do not accept 97% as proof of correctness. (testing-and-evals.md; testing-situational.md.)
expectations: [needs_files] Loads testing-situational.md because a coverage figure is cited as assurance
States that coverage shows what ran, not whether a fault would be caught
Proposes mutation testing scoped to the payment-rounding module or other high-stakes code
Treats a surviving mutant as a file:line finding naming the unasserted behavior

evals.prompt: A `RevisionRepo` backed by Postgres has one method, `appendRevision(recordId, patch)`: it SELECTs the record's current `revisions` array, appends a new entry with the patch and a timestamp, then UPDATEs the row with the full array. The unit test injects a fake `pg.Pool` whose `query()` always resolves `{ rows: [] }` for every SELECT and `{ rowCount: 1 }` for every UPDATE, then calls `appendRevision` twice and asserts the second call resolved without throwing. All 94 tests, including this one, pass. A teammate's PR changes `appendRevision` to build the new array from only the incoming patch instead of the SELECT result (i.e. it stops reading `rows[0].revisions` at all) and the same 94 tests still pass. A reviewer sees the green suite and says the change is safe. Is it?
evals.expected_output: No. The fake pool answers every SELECT with an empty result regardless of what was previously written, so the test never exercises the read half of this read-then-write path -- it cannot tell the difference between code that folds the new revision onto the stored trail and code that discards the trail and starts over, because the fake never returns a trail to discard. The 94/94 green count is not evidence the change is safe; it is evidence the test double gives zero coverage of read-modify-write logic here, no matter how high the count is. On the real Postgres path the planted change destroys every prior revision on the first edit after deploy, since the SELECT result is never read and the UPDATE writes only the new entry. The fix: make the fake pool stateful -- an in-memory table keyed by `recordId` that a SELECT actually reads back what an UPDATE wrote, built from the same shape as the real `revisions` column -- so appending twice and reading back must show both entries; or run the two-call scenario once against a real (containerized/throwaway) Postgres instance instead of the fake. A cheap planted-defect check confirms the gap: delete the line that reads `rows[0].revisions` and the suite should go red; today it does not.
expectations: Identifies that the fake pool returns a constant/empty SELECT result regardless of prior writes, so the test cannot distinguish 'fold new revision onto stored trail' from 'discard trail and start over' -- it gives zero coverage of this read-then-write path
Rejects '94/94 green, it's safe' reasoning: a high pass count over a non-round-tripping double is not evidence of correctness for read-modify-write logic
States the concrete production consequence: on real Postgres the change silently drops/overwrites the stored revision trail on the next write, since the SELECT is never actually read

Prescribes making the fake stateful (an in-memory table keyed like the real schema so write-then-read round-trips) or running the scenario once against an ephemeral real Postgres instance, and names the planted-defect check (delete the read line, suite must go red) as the way to confirm the gap

evals.prompt: The design export lays each section out as flat siblings: a heading, then its body, with data-section on the heading alone. The app wraps each section in nested divs. The ancestor crops of 'usage' differ, so parity_differ.py lists the app's body content as EXTRA_IN_APP rows. What should the lane do?
evals.expected_output: The two DOMs nest the section differently, so data-section ancestors crop different regions; the rows are a crop artifact, not build work. The lane re-captures both sides with the template's BANDS=1 export (an integer data-y top y on every element) and runs parity_differ.py with --bands headings. Sections then become vertical bands from one band start to the next, computed from each capture's own layout: data-anchor elements win when present, else h1/h2 headings, and everything above the first start is the (page header) band. The flat and nested renders produce identical bands, so their inventories compare. The top y only decides band membership; size and height are never a parity signal. A sub-heading that sits in another band is one MOVED row. A design band start that the app lacks makes that band alone COULD_NOT_CHECK_CROP, and its content is compared inside the band before it. An invalid data-y, a missing data-y, or one side banded by anchors and the other by headings is COULD_NOT_CHECK.
expectations: Identifies the EXTRA_IN_APP rows as a DOM-nesting crop artifact and re-captures with data-y and --bands headings, instead of treating them as build work
Explains that bands run from one heading or data-anchor top y to the next (data-anchor wins, a page-header band above the first start), and that y decides membership only, never pass or fail
States that a missing design band start makes only that band COULD_NOT_CHECK_CROP and that a moved sub-heading is a MOVED row

evals.prompt: A bot opened one PR bumping 40 npm packages in one repo: most are patch/minor, but six are major version bumps, all mixed into the same diff against the same lockfile. Reviewing the lockfile diff, one previously-transitive dependency now appears with a postinstall script it did not have before. What should the reviewer do?
evals.expected_output: Send the PR back to be split before reviewing content: one ecosystem per PR already holds (single npm lockfile) but the tiers do not — majors must not ride in the same PR as patch/minor bumps (Dependabot's documented grouping pattern keeps majors as individual PRs; Renovate's separateMajorMinor does the same). Ask for the 34 patch/minor bumps to land as one grouped PR and each of the six majors to land as its own PR with its own changelog/breaking-change read, gate run, and cooldown check. Separately and regardless of the split, flag the new postinstall script on the transitive dependency as a supply-chain finding on its own — a lifecycle script appearing where none existed before runs arbitrary code at install time and must be confirmed (what it does, why it is there) before any part of this PR is approved, even the low-risk patch/minor slice.
expectations: Requires the PR be split by risk tier before review: majors separated out of the patch/minor group, matching Dependabot's documented grouping pattern and Renovate's separateMajorMinor
Does not treat the single-ecosystem framing as sufficient on its own — tier mixing is still a blocking issue even though the PR is already scoped to one lockfile/ecosystem
Independently flags the new postinstall script on the transitive dependency as a supply-chain concern requiring confirmation, not waved through because the rest of the bump looks routine

evals.prompt: A FULL-scope review target is a 400k-line monorepo. The lane has no ranking, no stated budget, and plans to hold every finding until one final report at the end. Two-thirds of the way through domain audits, the lane hits its host's rate limit and the session ends with nothing written. What should the lane have done differently, and what should a fresh lane starting the same FULL review do from the first response onward?
evals.expected_output: A solo FULL lane on a large target ranks the coverage ledger's domains by blast radius before reading a line — money/billing paths first, then auth/authz, then data-loss (deletes, migrations, unbacked writes), then secrets/config, then the rest — instead of walking A–W in listed order. It states a per-run budget in the first-response block (tool-calls or tokens, a cap N) so it can track spend against a known ceiling. It appends each area's findings to the out-of-tree report file as that area finishes, never holding everything to Phase 5, so a lane killed mid-run still leaves written findings instead of nothing. At 80% of budget it stops starting new domains, writes the partial report with its coverage ledger split into reviewed vs. unreviewed areas, sets the verdict to Partial, and hands back cleanly rather than continuing until the host kills it.
expectations: States the blast-radius ranking order explicitly: money/billing, then auth/authz, then data-loss, then secrets/config, before the rest
Requires a stated per-run budget (tool-calls or tokens) in the first-response block, not an open-ended run
Requires findings to be appended to the report file per area as the review proceeds, not held until one final write
Names the 80%-budget checkpoint: stop new domain work, write a partial report with a reviewed/unreviewed coverage ledger, and hand back cleanly instead of running until killed
States the verdict at the checkpoint is the literal word Partial, not Approve/Changes-requested/Blocked with a caveat

evals.prompt: A repo's only PR-triggered workflow has no `concurrency:`, no job `timeout-minutes`, a `strategy.matrix` with 3 OS x 4 Node versions x 2 arch (24 combinations), a `schedule: cron: '*/10 * * * *'`, and both `push` (to main) and `pull_request` triggers while the repo's branch protection has "Require branches to be up to date before merging" checked. A teammate skims the YAML and says "looks fine, tests pass." What should the review report?
evals.expected_output: "Looks fine" is not a review of CI cost -- run `.claude/skills/deep-code-review/scripts/ci_cost_lint.py --gate --repo <owner/repo>` (or `--strict-protection`) against the workflow and report every lever it flags, not just the one that happens to be visible: (1) no concurrency cancel-in-progress on a PR-triggered workflow -- a superseded push keeps burning; (2) no timeout-minutes on the job -- defaults to GitHub's own large per-job ceiling before a hang is caught (verify the exact current number rather than assuming one); (3) push(default branch) + pull_request both trigger while required-status-checks are strict ("Require branches to be up to date before merging" checked) -- a post-merge push re-runs exactly what the PR already ran, so drop push or scope it with paths; (4) a `*/10 * * * *` schedule fires 6x/hour, more than hourly; (5) the 3x4x2=24-way matrix exceeds the lint's default cap of 6 and should be narrowed or split. None of these are guessed from eyeballing the YAML -- the lint is deterministic and the strict-vs-unknown branch-protection distinction changes finding (3) from blocking to advisory, so cite the tool's actual verdict, not an assumption about protection settings.
expectations: Runs or cites `ci_cost_lint.py` (with --repo or --strict-protection) instead of eyeballing the YAML and calling it fine because tests pass

Names all five applicable levers: missing concurrency cancel-in-progress, missing timeout-minutes, the strict-protection-dependent push+pull_request duplicate trigger, the sub-hourly schedule cron, and the oversized matrix
States that the push+pull_request finding's severity depends on whether required-status-checks are actually strict, not assumed

evals.prompt: Two separate runs of `ci_cost_lint.py`: (a) the given repo path is a typo and does not exist on disk, (b) the path exists and one workflow uses a YAML anchor (`build: &shared`) to share config between jobs. Both runs print `ci_cost_lint: ok (no findings)`. Is that report trustworthy?
evals.expected_output: No, both are false-clean reports the lint itself must not produce. (a) A nonexistent root is not the same as an existing repo with no workflows to scan -- the lint must fail closed with a nonzero exit (2) and a clear message naming the bad path, distinct from a genuine `.github/workflows/`-absent clean scan (exit 0). Reporting 'no findings' for a typo'd path hides that nothing was actually scanned. (b) An anchor/alias is outside the lint's documented minimal YAML subset; silently ignoring or mis-parsing it can hide a real finding in that job (or corrupt the parse of jobs after it). The lint must instead raise internally and turn that into a single, non-advisory PARSE-ERROR finding for the file, so `--gate` fails on it -- a workflow the lint cannot actually read must never be reported as clean.
expectations: States that a nonexistent root must exit nonzero (2) with a message, distinct from an existing root with no .github/workflows/ (a legitimate clean exit 0)
States that an anchor/alias (or other unsupported YAML construct) must produce a blocking PARSE-ERROR finding, not be silently skipped or mis-parsed into a false-clean report
Rejects trusting a 'no findings' report without first confirming the scan actually ran against the intended path and successfully parsed every workflow file

evals.prompt: A worker's 'finish' step acquires a push-queue semaphore (serial_gate.py --slots) to get a submit slot, and while still holding it also captures an evidence screenshot bound to one fixed local port. At low concurrency this is fine; at high fleet size the queue wait grows to tens of minutes. Review this.
evals.expected_output: Flag one lock/semaphore guarding two independently-schedulable resources (the push-queue slot and the fixed evidence-capture port) as the root cause, not generic load: every worker now queues behind both even though they have no real dependency. Fix by giving the fixed port its own pool (a rotating port range or ephemeral port) or a separate lock sized to its own constraint, instead of running evidence capture inside the queue-slot's critical section. Do not recommend raising the queue-slot limit or capacity as the fix.
expectations: Identifies one lock/semaphore protecting two unrelated resources as the defect, not 'needs more capacity'
Names the tell: queue wait growing superlinearly with fleet size on a resource that shouldn't be contended
Recommends separating the locks / a port pool sized to the evidence-capture step's own constraint
Rejects raising the existing semaphore's slot count as a fix for a scope bug

evals.prompt: A design-alignment PR restructured layout around a hand-tuned diagram (nodes + a legend) marked data-protected. The page's pixel-diff score stayed within tolerance and a route-mount render gate still passes (the component is present and reachable) because the diagram is a small fraction of total page pixels. Is this PR safe to merge?
evals.expected_output: No — a mounted/reachable check proves presence, not internal correctness. Run parity_differ.py's data-protected scoring: the component gets its own section that must independently reach 100% inventory completeness regardless of the page aggregate, plus ordinal (left/right/above/below, containment, non-overlap) assertions derived from the design capture's node rects, never sizes/dimensions as a pass/fail input. A missing data-protected component or broken node order/containment on the app side is MISMATCH, not a pass, even when the page-wide pixel score looks fine.
expectations: Rejects 'mounted + pixel score in tolerance' as sufficient evidence for a protected visual
