Names the data-protected section as scored to 100% independently of the page aggregate
Names ordinal assertions (order/containment/non-overlap) derived from rects, never raw sizes/dimensions, as the pass/fail input
States a missing protected component or broken ordinal relation on the app side is MISMATCH, not pass

evals.prompt: A protected-component capture (parity_differ.py data-protected/data-protected-node/data-prect) has a repeated node id on one side, or a node whose data-prect is zero-area (w=0 or h=0), or the capture was taken under --bands. What should the tool do in each case?
evals.expected_output: A repeated data-protected-node id on either side is COULD_NOT_CHECK naming the id -- never silently kept as its last occurrence. A zero/negative-area data-prect on the design side is COULD_NOT_CHECK (a collapsed rect seeds no ordinal relation); the same defect on the app side instead drops that node, so it reads as an ordinary MISSING_IN_APP node, not a guessed geometry. data-protected/-node/-prect under --bands is COULD_NOT_CHECK, never silently dropped -- SECTION BANDS does not recognize data-section either.
expectations: States a duplicate data-protected-node id on either side is COULD_NOT_CHECK naming the id, not a silent last-write-wins
States a design-side zero/negative-area rect is COULD_NOT_CHECK, never used to derive an ordinal relation
States the same app-side defect instead yields MISSING_IN_APP for that node, not COULD_NOT_CHECK
States data-protected markers under --bands fail closed (COULD_NOT_CHECK) rather than being silently ignored

evals.prompt: A dashboard's alerts panel calls `.slice(0, 5)` on an `alerts` array before rendering rows. The page header shows 'Alerts (142)' from a separate count query, but the list beneath renders only the 5 sliced items with no 'load more', page control, or remainder text. Finding?
evals.expected_output: Flag it. `.slice(0, 5)` renders fewer rows than the known total (142) with no visible remainder -- a truncation, not a pagination, and it reads as complete because the header's count and the rendered rows are independent reads of the same data that nothing forces to agree. Whenever total > shown, render an explicit remainder ("+137 more", a page control, "Show all 142") -- never a list that just stops (Nielsen: visibility of system status). A correct top-line count does not excuse a silently truncated list beneath it. (ux-states.md.)
expectations: Flags the missing remainder indicator, not just praises the header count
Names why: total (142) exceeds shown (5) with no visible next/more affordance, so the cut reads as complete
Cites the general rule -- any total > shown needs an explicit remainder, not only this one instance

evals.prompt: A page links to `/export?token=abc123&format=csv` and the app's `Referrer-Policy` is set explicitly to `no-referrer-when-downgrade`. Finding?
evals.expected_output: Flag it. `no-referrer-when-downgrade` sends the full URL -- including the `token` query param -- to any third-party origin the page later navigates to or embeds (an ad, an analytics pixel, an external link), because the `Referer` header carries path+query cross-origin. The modern safe default is `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` (MDN); this app has explicitly weakened it. Two independent fixes, do both: tighten `Referrer-Policy` to `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` (or `no-referrer` for the most sensitive routes), and stop putting the token in the URL at all -- a POST body, a header, or a short-lived opaque id meaningless if leaked. (frontend-security.md.)
expectations: Names the weakened Referrer-Policy value specifically, not just "missing security header"
Explains the mechanism: Referer carries the full URL including query string cross-origin
Gives both fixes -- tighten the policy AND stop placing the token in the URL -- not just one

evals.prompt: A hosting platform marks a PR CONFLICTING against its target branch. A local `git merge` of the exact same PR-head and target-head commits is clean, with no custom merge driver. What should the merge-train conductor do before re-running the full gate suite?
evals.expected_output: Treat the host's CONFLICTING as a cached-view claim, not ground truth -- verify locally first. Merge the target into the PR branch once to refresh the flag (creating a new head commit), then compare `git merge-tree --write-tree <target> <new-head>` against `git rev-parse <tested-union-commit>^{tree}` -- equal tree ids mean the refresh changed nothing the *content-only* gates (tests, lint, build) didn't already test, so those need no re-run. A gate that reads commit metadata -- trailers, message lints, signer checks -- still runs against the new head regardless, since the tree comparison says nothing about the commit object wrapping it. Different tree ids mean a real re-verification is required. Record the refreshed head's receipt as both tree ids plus the new head SHA. (merge-operations.md.)
expectations: Names host-CONFLICTING-but-locally-clean as a stale cached-view, distinct from a real conflict
Gives the merge-tree-comparison technique as the way to decide whether re-verification is needed
Notes metadata-reading gates (trailers, message lints) still run on the new head even when tree ids match

evals.prompt: A Next.js App Router project's merge gate runs `tsc --noEmit` and treats a clean run as proof the framework build typechecks. A route handler's exported signature is malformed. Will the gate catch it?
evals.expected_output: No, and the gate is wrong to rely on `tsc --noEmit` alone for this. The route handler's signature is checked against a constraint type the framework generates only inside its own build step -- a clean-tree `tsc --noEmit`, with no prior build, cannot see that generated type, so it cannot fail on this class of error (observed: surfaced only as TS2344 during a real production build, after passing every merge-train union and PR gate that ran only `tsc --noEmit`). Require a real production build as a separate, required gate step for any framework with build-time route/handler type generation -- not a substitute for the type-checker, an addition to it. (method-situational.md.)
expectations: States that tsc --noEmit cannot see build-time-generated route/handler constraint types
Explains why: the constraint type is generated only inside the framework's own build step, so a clean-tree/no-prior-build tsc run has nothing to check the signature against
Recommends a real production build as a required, separate gate step, not merely a nice-to-have

evals.prompt: A click-anywhere-to-edit wrapper skips triggering edit-mode for clicks on links, buttons, and inputs. The field later grows an inline rich-text editor panel it renders once opened. A user clicks inside the open editor and it closes mid-edit. What's the fix, and how should the acceptance test for this field be written?
evals.expected_output: The skip-list only covers the field's read-state element types; it never grew to cover the contenteditable/rich-text region or the nested editor panel the field renders once opened, so a click or keystroke inside the open editor bubbles up and re-triggers the outer edit handler, closing it. Fix: extend the skip-list to cover every element type the field can render while being edited, not just its read-state elements. Separately, the acceptance test must perform the click that opens the field before typing into or asserting on it -- typing directly against a locator that bypasses the open step never exercises the bubbling path and cannot catch this regression. (ux-interaction.md, testing-ui.md.)
expectations: Names the skip-list gap: covers read-state elements but not the field's open-state editor/contenteditable
States the fix as extending the skip-list to every element the field can render while open
States that the test must reproduce the open/click step before asserting, not shortcut to typing

evals.prompt: A card component fetches its own per-item reaction count on mount, documented as "cheap, one extra request per detail page." It's then reused unchanged on a feed page that renders one card per row for a long list. What's the finding?
evals.expected_output: N+1 by mount count, not by query. The component's private fetch is fine at one mount per page; reused in a loop, it fires one request per mounted instance, scaling with list length instead of page count (one observed run measured 47 separate per-item requests from a single page load). Check every call site of a component with a private data-fetch hook, not just its own file, and ask whether request count scales with mount count. Fix: **shared-instance prop with private-fetch fallback** -- add an optional externally-supplied shared-data-instance prop, private fetch remaining the default fallback -- existing single-mount call sites are unaffected, loop call sites opt into one shared batched fetch. (web-fetch.md.)
expectations: Identifies the pattern as N+1 scaling with mount count, not a query-level N+1
States that call sites, not just the component's own file, must be checked
Names the fix as "shared-instance prop with private-fetch fallback"

evals.prompt: A spec reads a row's visible text, clicks an edit action, types a new value directly into a value locator without first clicking to open the field, then re-locates the row by its ORIGINAL visible text to assert the result. The row is now mid-edit and no longer shows that text. What's wrong with this spec?
evals.expected_output: Two separate defects. First, the spec skips the real open step (the click that opens the field) and types straight into a value locator, so it can never catch an event-bubbling regression in the open/close interaction. Second, re-locating the row by its original visible text breaks the moment the row's own edit mode replaces that text with an input/editor -- a false red, not a real regression. Fix both: perform the click that opens the field before typing or asserting, and locate by a stable identifier (data-test-id or the item's own stable id/version field) instead of visible text, addressing an already-open editor by its own container role/state rather than re-querying the original row. (testing-ui.md.)
expectations: Flags the missing open/click step before typing, distinct from the locator issue
Flags the text-based locator as fragile against the component's own edit-mode re-render
Recommends a stable id/data-test-id locator and addressing the open editor by its own state

evals.prompt: A merge gate inventories rendered controls by accessible role/name and stays green. A picker control renders, reports itself enabled, and opens nothing when clicked. Was the gate wrong to pass this PR?
evals.expected_output: The gate did what it's for -- it proved the control still renders -- but that's not the same claim as "the control works," and treating a green inventory gate as sufficient evidence a behaviour change is safe is the finding. "Renders but doesn't work" is a different bug class from "was removed," and a presence/inventory gate is structurally blind to it. For any interactive surface, require both the inventory/presence check and a functional pass that actually invokes each changed control and asserts on its effect -- one does not substitute for the other. (ux-interaction.md.)
expectations: States that a presence/inventory gate proves rendering, not functional correctness
Names "renders but doesn't work" as a distinct bug class from "was removed"
Requires both an inventory/presence check and a functional/interaction check, not either alone

evals.prompt: An automated responsive/overflow audit is delegated to a fast, cheap model with the prompt "check every page for overflow issues." It returns 95 findings. What's the likely problem, and what should the audit's instructions contain?
evals.expected_output: Almost certainly a scoping gap, not a real defect count -- an unscoped audit run by a cheaper model interprets "check for overflow" maximally literally and reports every hidden, off-screen, or not-yet-revealed element as a defect (one observed run: 95 unscoped findings vs. zero real page-level scroll issues once scoping rules were applied to the same surface). Ship the audit with three rules written into its own instructions: count overflow only when it causes page-level horizontal scroll or clips content actually visible outside a designated scrollable container; exclude hidden/screen-reader-only elements; open click-to-reveal UI before judging its contents. This matters more, not less, when the audit runs on a cheaper/faster model. (ux-sweep.md.)
expectations: Identifies the 95-finding result as a likely scoping problem, not a real defect count
States the three named scoping rules (page-level-scroll-or-visible-clip only; exclude hidden/sr-only; open click-to-reveal first)
Notes scoping matters more when the audit runs on a cheaper/faster model, and belongs in the audit's own instructions

evals.prompt: A 2,100-line page has dozens of tests that `readFileSync` the component and regex-check its source text. Splitting that file into smaller modules is proposed. What's the hidden cost, and what should the codebase have in place first?
evals.expected_output: Every source-text test hardcodes the file's path and often its byte layout, so splitting the file repoints every one of them even though the checked invariant didn't change (one observed run: 74% of a page's tests were source-text regexes; the split required repointing 32 of them). Put two things in place before splitting at scale: a shared source reader that throws loudly on a missing path (so a moved file fails every dependent check by name, not silently), and a unit-runner component-render loader as the on-ramp from source-text checks to real rendered-DOM assertions (measured: +0.8s per file, suite wall-time flat). Ratchet the source-text-test count against a stored baseline so it never rises on new work, without requiring an immediate rewrite of existing debt -- `scripts/source_scan_tests.py` has no baseline support today, so a wrapper that stores and diffs its finding count is to be built. (testing-ui.md.)
expectations: Names the refactor-tax mechanism: source-text tests hardcode path/layout and break on file moves regardless of invariant change
Recommends a shared, loud-failing source reader as the fix for silent breakage on a moved file
Recommends ratcheting the source-text-test count (never rises), noting the baseline wrapper has to be built rather than already existing

evals.prompt: A step's structural test slices its own section as "everything between MY_MARKER and NEXT_STEP_MARKER", naming the next step's own marker literally. A later PR renames that next step (no change to the step under test) and the structural test breaks. What's the defect and the fix?
evals.expected_output: The test's boundary depends on a name it doesn't own -- renaming an unrelated sibling shouldn't break a test for a step nobody touched. Fix: slice from the marker's own start to the next marker generically and positionally ("the next heading", "the next structural boundary"), never by a specific neighbour's literal name. Pass condition to check for: renaming any other step/section keeps the test green; only renaming or removing the step actually under test should break it. (testing-situational.md.)
expectations: Identifies the root cause as the test naming an unowned neighbour's marker as its own boundary
States the fix as a positional/generic "next marker" slice, not a named-neighbour slice
States the pass condition: renaming an unrelated sibling must not break the test

evals.prompt: A project's `CLAUDE.md` has grown to ~800 lines, including a section describing a caching mechanism that was replaced by a different one three commits ago -- the old section was never deleted. What's the finding?
evals.expected_output: This file loads in full on every session, unlike a routed skill reference, so it needs a stricter size/staleness discipline: every stale section is a cost paid on every subsequent session until someone notices. Flag both the missing size/line cap and the specific stale section describing a superseded mechanism. Fix: keep the file to invariants over mechanism descriptions where avoidable, and require the PR that supersedes a mechanism to delete that mechanism's section from this file in the same PR, not as later cleanup. (docs-and-dx.md.)
expectations: Names the always-loaded (every session) cost as distinct from a progressive-disclosure skill reference
Flags the specific stale section describing a superseded mechanism as a finding on its own
States the fix: same-PR deletion when a mechanism is superseded, plus a stated size/line cap

evals.prompt: A PR adds a new dead-export detection gate to CI. The PR description explains the detection logic (unreferenced exports via static analysis) but states no false-positive rate. Should it be approved as-is?
evals.expected_output: No -- detection logic being sound in the abstract doesn't mean the gate is usable on this codebase; it needs to be run once against HEAD and its false-positive rate stated in the PR (one observed case: a naive dead-export scanner had a 93% false-positive rate). Require the PR to state the measured false-positive rate from a run against HEAD, target <=10%, before landing the gate -- a gate without that number is unproven regardless of how correct its logic reads. (domain-k.md.)
expectations: States that detection-logic soundness alone doesn't prove the gate is usable
Requires a measured false-positive rate from a run against HEAD in the PR description
Names a target ceiling (<=10%) for that rate

evals.prompt: A load-test report claims '60 concurrent users, 0% errors' against an authenticated endpoint. The response bodies recorded for the run are byte-identical to what an anonymous, unauthenticated request to the same URL returns. Is this run trustworthy evidence the authenticated path performs well?
evals.expected_output: No -- the harness never actually authenticated; it exercised the anonymous/cached fallback path, not the real per-user code path, so the clean error rate and throughput describe the wrong system. Before trusting any perf number from an authenticated load test, assert that the response differs from the same URL's anonymous response (bytes(authed) != bytes(anonymous)); a match means the run measured nothing about the authenticated path and must fail before any latency/error number is reported. (appsec-edge.md.)
expectations: States the harness ran against the anonymous/fallback path, not the authenticated one
Requires asserting authed response bytes differ from anonymous response bytes before trusting the run
Concludes the 0%-errors/60-user result is not evidence about the real authenticated path

evals.prompt: A target ships two interchangeable storage adapters (a file-based one for dev/CI, a database one in prod) behind the same interface. Its load-test/leak gate only ever instantiates the file adapter, and judges pass/fail on p95 latency and error rate. Is this gate sufficient to catch a memory leak in the database adapter?
evals.expected_output: No -- an interchangeable-backend gate that only boots one adapter says nothing about the others, and p95/error-rate can both stay green while heap grows unbounded underneath. Run the gate against every production adapter the target ships, and judge on heap slope (post-GC heap at ~2s vs ~60s under sustained concurrency) rather than only latency/error metrics, since a leaking adapter can look perfectly healthy on both. (concurrency-shared-state.md.)
expectations: States that clearing the gate on one adapter says nothing about a sibling adapter
Requires running the perf/leak gate against every production adapter, not just the default one
Requires a heap-slope metric (short-mark vs later-mark heap size) in addition to p95/error rate

evals.prompt: A team diagnoses a suspected memory leak by running the perf gate locally, where the dev machine has Node 18 installed. The deploy image's declared engines field pins Node 20. The local run shows no leak. What's the finding?
evals.expected_output: The gate booted the wrong runtime major -- GC behavior and allocator defaults can differ enough between majors that a clean local run says nothing about what ships. Read the runtime major from the deploy artifact (container image base tag or the engines/runtime declaration) and boot the gate on that major; print the booted version in the gate's log so a mismatch is visible before any perf/leak verdict is trusted. (release-engineering.md.)
expectations: Identifies the local-vs-deploy-image runtime major mismatch as the root cause of an untrustworthy result
Requires reading the runtime major from the deploy artifact/engines declaration, not the local machine
Requires the gate's log to print the booted runtime version for verification

evals.prompt: A heap-leak investigation takes a full heap snapshot at 1.8 GB, and the JSON.parse-based analyzer throws a string-length error before it can name the retaining class. How should the gate get an answer?
evals.expected_output: A JSON.parse-based analyzer breaks exactly where a leak gate needs it: at multi-GB scale, past the parser's string-length limit. Build a streaming snapshot parser that reads the heap-snapshot format incrementally and emits a retainer-owner histogram (which class/constructor holds the growing objects, not just that heap grew), and take the snapshot at a small heap-size limit as a fallback so it stays parseable by ordinary means when the streaming tool isn't available. No such analyzer ships with this skill yet. (concurrency-shared-state.md.)
expectations: Identifies JSON.parse's string-length limit as why the default analyzer fails on a >1 GB snapshot
Requires a streaming parser emitting a retainer-owner histogram, not just heap-size growth
States no shipped analyzer exists yet, so this is a doctrine, not a tool to run

evals.prompt: A request handler does `void processInBackground()`, where `processInBackground` checks a module-level cache for an in-flight promise for the same work and returns it if present, otherwise starts and caches a new one. Under load, heap grows steadily with concurrent users. What's the defect?
evals.expected_output: The fire-and-forget call adopts a module-level in-flight promise meant to coalesce concurrent callers, so every request racing that promise pins its context to it and the retained object graph stays reachable for as long as the slowest rider, growing with concurrency instead of staying flat. Require a detached execution context for fire-and-forget work, an explicit timeout, and a single-flight guard implemented outside request scope; corroborate with a heap-slope measurement at sustained concurrency, which will show the same rising-heap signature as an adapter leak. (concurrency-shared-state.md.)
expectations: Identifies the module-level in-flight-promise coalescing as pinning every request's context together
Requires a detached context, explicit timeout, and single-flight guard outside request scope
Ties the diagnosis to a heap-slope measurement under sustained concurrency

evals.prompt: An unauthenticated API endpoint filters which resource types are visible to anonymous callers using a list of type names to exclude. A new resource type is added to the system six months later. Is it visible to an anonymous caller by default?
evals.expected_output: Yes, and that is the defect -- a denylist on an unauthenticated surface is permissive by default for anything not yet named, so the new type ships visible to every anonymous caller until someone remembers to add it to the exclusion list. This is not a fail-open bug -- the filter runs fine and still ships every unnamed type, because excluding by name means anything unnamed passes; the list is working exactly as written. Invert it to an allowlist naming the types an anonymous caller may see, excluding everything else by default; assert the returned type set equals the allowlist exactly, not merely 'contains no denylisted type'.
expectations: States the new type is visible by default because a denylist is permissive by default for anything unnamed
States this is not a fail-open bug -- the check runs fine, the list just admits any unnamed type by design
Requires inverting to an allowlist of permitted types on the unauthenticated surface
Requires a test asserting the returned type set equals the allowlist exactly

evals.prompt: To help a user set up a new API credential, an assistant suggests running a keygen command directly in the current chat session and pasting the printed key back in. The session is logged. Is this a safe way to generate the credential?
evals.expected_output: No -- the command's normal output is the plaintext secret, and running it in the same logged/transcribed session writes that secret straight into the transcript, even though it's never committed to a file. Generate the credential in a separate, untranscribed terminal, or redirect the command's output directly to a gitignored file instead of letting it print to stdout, so the secret never appears as visible command output. (appsec-crypto.md.)
expectations: States that the keygen command's stdout landing in a logged session leaks the secret into the transcript
Requires generating the secret in a separate, untranscribed terminal, or writing directly to a gitignored file
Rejects suggesting an in-session command whose output is the secret itself

evals.prompt: A lint tool scoped to only the files a PR touches reports zero warnings. The PR's author cites the repo's warning-cap file, which is already near its ceiling, and raises the cap by one to land the change. Is this justified?
evals.expected_output: No -- a changed-files-scoped lint's zero output can mean the type-aware rule never ran on the unchanged caller where it actually fires, not that the codebase is clean; raising the cap on that basis is unjustified. Compare a full-scope lint run on the branch against a full-scope run on the base instead of trusting the diff-scoped number, and never raise a warning/lint cap in a feature change -- the cap file should stay unchanged and full-lint(branch) must be <= full-lint(base).
expectations: States that zero output from a changed-files-scoped lint doesn't mean the codebase is clean
Requires comparing full-scope lint totals on branch vs base rather than trusting the diff-scoped count
Rejects raising the warning/lint cap to make the change land

evals.prompt: An e2e spec calls `element.click()` directly on a button to test its handler. In production, a semi-transparent overlay sits on top of that button so a real user's pointer click never reaches it. Does the passing spec prove the button is usable?
evals.expected_output: No -- a programmatic click invokes the handler directly, bypassing the hit-testing a real pointer click would do, so the spec passes on a control a real click can never reach. jsdom has no layout engine, so even Testing Library's userEvent.click cannot see an overlay scrim there; use a real-browser pointer test (Playwright/Cypress `.click()`, which does actual hit-testing against the rendered page) so the spec fails the way a real user's click would. Scoped to e2e/UI spec dirs: `grep -rnE '\bel(ement)?\.click\(\)|dispatchEvent\(|fireEvent\.'` and expect zero hits outside a documented, hit-tested exception. (testing-ui.md.)
expectations: States that a programmatic click bypasses real pointer hit-testing and can hit a dead control
States jsdom/userEvent cannot see an overlay scrim, so the fix is a real-browser pointer test, not userEvent
Names the grep check scoped to e2e/UI spec dirs for element.click()/dispatchEvent(/fireEvent. in e2e test files

evals.prompt: Two unrelated test suites fail intermittently in CI: one asserts a threshold against the runner's live free-memory reading, the other replays 'the last 5 commits' from the real git log each run. What's the shared root cause and the fix for each?
evals.expected_output: Both are unpinned, machine/moment-dependent inputs: the live memory/load reading differs by runner and moment, and 'the last N commits' silently changes as the branch moves, so the same test name exercises a different input every run. Mock the system probe (inject a fake memory/load reader) instead of reading the real machine, and pin the commit sample to an explicit list of commit ids instead of 'the latest N'.
expectations: Identifies both failures as unpinned, machine- or moment-dependent test inputs
Requires mocking the memory/load-average probe instead of reading the real machine
Requires pinning the commit sample to explicit commit ids instead of 'the latest N'

evals.prompt: A shell script runs `env A=1 -u B cmd` to set A and unset B before invoking cmd. The script boots cmd as a background server and waits for a health check. It works in CI (Linux), but on macOS the harness only reports 'no health answer within 60s'. Why, and what should change in the script and the harness?
evals.expected_output: Some implementations (e.g. GNU env) tolerate an option after a NAME=value assignment, but BSD/macOS env stops parsing its own options at the first assignment and reads the next token, `-u`, as the utility it's supposed to run -- e.g. `env A=1 -u B true` prints `env: -u: No such file or directory` and exits 127. Put every option before the first assignment: `env -u B A=1 cmd`. Mechanized by scripts/reaper_lint.py's ENV_OPTION_AFTER_ASSIGNMENT rule. The harness must not mask this as a slow-boot readiness failure: when the background child exits early, fail fast instead of waiting out the health-check timeout, and print the child's log tail so the exit-127 error is visible, not just 'no health answer within 60s'. (lang-shell.md.)
expectations: Explains that BSD/macOS env stops parsing options at the first NAME=value assignment
States the failure is loud: exit 127 with a "No such file or directory" error, not a silent pass-through
Gives the fix: put every option before the first assignment
Says a harness that boots the command as a background child must fail fast on the child's early exit and print its log tail, not wait out a readiness timeout

evals.prompt: A team's design-parity scorecard scored a surface at 84/100 last week. Today's run of the 'same' harness scores it 71/100 with no product commits in between. Someone opens an incident to chase a phantom regression. What actually happened, and what should the team have pinned to prevent this?
evals.expected_output: The harness exposes run-time flags -- which sections are included, which states are rendered, the viewport set -- and the two runs were invoked with a different flag/option combination, changing the denominator the score is computed against. The drop is measurement noise, not a regression: nothing in the product changed. The team should pin and version the exact flag/option set used for a scorecard, commit it beside the score (in the report or a checked-in config), and treat any flag-set change as its own reviewable diff, never a silent side effect of re-invoking the harness differently. A before/after comparison must use the identical pinned flag set on both runs. This is also a blind spot of a `--baseline`-style regression net: it fingerprints sections/style, not the flag set that produced them, so a REGRESSION exit can itself be a flag-set change in disguise -- confirm the two runs share one invocation before trusting it. (rendered-parity.md.)
expectations: Identifies the root cause as a changed flag/option set between runs, not a real product regression
States the rule: pin and version the exact flag/option set, commit it beside the score
Says a before/after comparison must use the identical pinned flag set on both sides
Notes a baseline/regression-net mechanism can't itself distinguish a flag-set change from a real regression

evals.prompt: A design-parity gate reports a raw pass rate of 56% for a surface. A teammate says 'that means the product looks 56% aligned with the design.' Is that a fair reading, and what should the report show instead?
evals.expected_output: No -- the raw score conflates real, user-visible differences with harness artifacts (timing, font substitution, headless-renderer quirks) that have no visible effect, so 56% either overstates how broken the product looks or invites the whole gate being dismissed once a few artifacts turn up. For every failing check, attach evidence (a cropped screenshot region plus the relevant computed styles) and classify it REAL (a user would see this) or HARNESS-ARTIFACT (measurement-only). Report both numbers side by side: the raw pass rate and the visible-parity score = pass / (pass + REAL) -- and never present the raw number alone as 'how aligned' the product is. A known harness-artifact (e.g. a font-substitution difference in headless rendering) is labeled as such with its evidence, not folded into the same bucket as a genuine layout defect. (rendered-parity.md.)
expectations: Says the raw score conflates real-visible failures with harness-artifact failures
Requires evidence (crop + computed styles) and a REAL vs HARNESS-ARTIFACT classification per failing check
Gives the visible-parity formula: pass / (pass + REAL)
States both the raw and visible-parity numbers must be reported side by side, never the raw one alone as the alignment claim

evals.prompt: A parity comparison run flags wrapping/overflow differences across many rows of a table. On inspection, the app's seeded sample text is much longer than the design's own sample text, but the styling (font, padding, colors) is otherwise identical. What's the right fix, and what's explicitly off-limits?
evals.expected_output: This is a fixture mismatch, not a styling defect: the app's seeded sample data doesn't match the design's own sample data shape (text length, item counts, states). Re-seed the app's fixture to match the design's sample data shape -- same string lengths, same row/item counts, same set of empty/loading/error/populated states -- taken from the design's own sample, never invented independently. This is fixture work only: it must never extend to changing the product's actual rendering logic, hiding a state, or otherwise altering real behaviour just to raise the comparison score. Any deviation from a straight fixture match is disclosed in the finding, not concealed. After re-seeding, confirm the wrapping/overflow differences disappear while any genuinely independent styling defect still fails. (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: Diagnoses the flagged differences as a fixture/sample-data-shape mismatch, not a styling defect
Says to match the design's own sample data shape: text length, item/row counts, and the same states
States this is fixture-only work -- never changing product rendering logic or hiding a state to raise the score
Requires disclosing any deviation from a straight fixture match, not concealing it

evals.prompt: A parity comparison harness fetches the design export bundle from a shared dev server before every run. A run reports several sections as mismatched. Before treating those as real defects, what should be checked first, and what does the tool do if that check fails?
evals.expected_output: Verify the served bundle is the full, current export before trusting any score off it -- a shared dev server can serve a stale or partially-copied bundle (an interrupted sync, an old cached build), silently skewing scores: some sections compare against pages no longer in the current design, or against an incomplete asset set. Checksum (e.g. md5) the served bundle's files against the source export and confirm the file count and hashes match. A checksum mismatch is treated as COULD_NOT_CHECK -- the same discipline as a missing or unreadable side -- never a scored comparison off an unverified bundle. Only after the bundle is confirmed complete and current should the reported mismatches be investigated as real defects. (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: Says to checksum the served bundle against the source export (file count + hashes) before trusting the score
Names the failure mode: a stale or partially-copied bundle from an interrupted sync or old cached build
States a checksum mismatch is treated as COULD_NOT_CHECK, never as a scored/passing comparison
Only recommends investigating the flagged sections as real defects after the bundle is confirmed complete

evals.prompt: A parity check at a narrow viewport flags the app for not clipping some content the same way the design prototype does. On inspection, the prototype's own clipping turns out to be an unintended rendering bug in the design tool, not a deliberate choice. What should happen next, and what must never happen?
evals.expected_output: Never copy the reference's defect into the product just to raise the score -- a design prototype can itself be wrong at some viewport or state, and blindly matching the app to it ships the defect. Escalate the mismatch for an owner decision. Once decided, record the outcome as a named, versioned accept-file tolerance entry (e.g. a `style` or `visual-reviewed` accept row) whose reason field names the reference defect and the decision -- never as a silent exception baked into the comparison code with no record of why. A mismatch traced to a reference-design defect must end in either an escalated, recorded owner decision or an already-covered named tolerance row -- never silently ignored and never silently copied. (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: States the app must never copy the reference's own rendering defect to raise the score
Requires escalating the mismatch for an owner decision when it traces to a defect in the reference itself
Requires recording the decided outcome as a named, versioned tolerance/accept-file row with a reason, not a silent code exception
Rejects both silently ignoring and silently copying the defect as outcomes

evals.prompt: A parity capture pipeline waits for DOM hydration before taking its screenshot, and two runs of the same page show about 4px of unexplained metric drift on a text-heavy section even though nothing changed. What's the likely cause, and what should the capture pipeline wait for instead?
evals.expected_output: The capture is likely showing a fallback font: hydration completing doesn't mean web fonts have finished loading, and a screenshot taken in that gap reflects the fallback font's metrics (element widths, line heights, positions), not the intended font's -- showing up as spurious drift rather than a real layout issue. The fix is to wait for the browser's fonts-ready signal (e.g. `document.fonts.ready`) and then one additional animation frame before capturing, not just DOM/hydration readiness. A capture pipeline that only waits on hydration is incomplete. Comparing a hydration-only capture against a fonts-ready+frame capture of the same text-heavy section should show the metric drift between 'identical' runs drop to near zero once the fix is applied. (templates/parity-capture.md.)
expectations: Diagnoses the drift as fallback-font metrics from capturing before web fonts finish loading
States the fix: wait for fonts-ready (document.fonts.ready) plus one additional animation frame
Says waiting only on hydration/DOM readiness is an incomplete capture pipeline
Notes the fix should make repeat-run drift on identical content drop to near zero

evals.prompt: During an unrelated cleanup PR, a contributor notices the visual snapshot baseline is out of date and refreshes it so the suite stops complaining. Two weeks later, someone discovers the section actually regressed visually right before that refresh. What went wrong, and what's the rule for refreshing a baseline going forward?
evals.expected_output: The drive-by baseline refresh absorbed a real visual regression into the new 'expected' baseline, so it went undetected on every run after -- a baseline refresh is not a neutral housekeeping act. The rule: only refresh a visual snapshot baseline when the visual change is the intended outcome of the current change, and do it in the same PR that causes the visual change -- never as a drive-by refresh in an unrelated PR, and never as a blanket 'refresh everything' pass. A passing run is not the same as an intended one; refreshing should be tied to the PR whose change caused the diff, not to whichever PR happened to notice the baseline was stale. (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: Identifies that the unrelated-PR refresh silently absorbed a real regression into the baseline
States the rule: refresh only in the same PR that causes the intended visual change
Rejects a drive-by refresh in an unrelated PR and a blanket 'refresh everything' pass
Distinguishes a passing run from an intended change as the basis for refreshing

evals.prompt: A repo has a visual-parity/screenshot-diff suite in `.github/workflows/`. A PR that visibly changes a page's layout shows a green check overall. What two things need to be confirmed before trusting that green as proof the visual suite passed, and why can't presence in the workflow file alone be trusted?
evals.expected_output: First, confirm the settings that produce a screenshot -- viewport, device-pixel ratio, wait/settle timing, any relevant feature flags -- are pinned into one committed configuration used identically by every run, and verify empirically by running the suite twice with no code change and confirming a zero (or documented-tolerance) diff; otherwise score drift between runs is measurement noise misread as a false regression or false stability. Second, read the actual merge-gate configuration directly -- the workflow file's changed-path triggers and the branch-protection required-checks list -- rather than assuming; a suite that exists in `.github/workflows/` but is opt-in, path-filtered out of the diff that touched visual code, or not in the required-checks list provides no protection at merge time no matter how good its detectors are, and a 'passing' status on a visually-changing PR is unverified for visual parity until both checks are confirmed. (release-engineering.md.)
expectations: Requires pinning capture settings (viewport, DPR, wait timing, flags) into one committed config used identically across runs
Requires an empirical check: run the suite twice with no code change and confirm near-zero diff
Requires confirming the suite's job is both present in the triggered workflow and named in the branch-protection required-checks list, not just present in the repo
States a green/passing status is unverified for visual parity until both the pinned-settings and merge-gate-wiring checks are confirmed

evals.prompt: A fix lane ships a bug fix plus a regression test, and its PR body says: 'this test would have failed on the old code' -- established by reading the diff, with no pre-fix run mentioned. Should this be accepted as a proven regression test?
evals.expected_output: No. Inspection is not verification -- a test can look like it exercises the bug and still pass on the old code for reasons invisible from the diff alone (a different code path, a mock that absorbs the bug, a looser-than-intended assertion, or a bug already fixed by an unrelated recent change). Require one of two executed proofs: run the test against the pre-fix commit/branch and confirm it fails there and passes after the fix, or -- if checking out the old code is impractical -- temporarily revert only the fix's logic (never the test), rerun to confirm red, then undo the revert. A claim resting only on reading the diff is unverified. (testing-and-evals.md.)
expectations: Rejects diff-reading alone as proof of a red-then-green transition
Names at least one concrete way a test can look right but still pass on old code (wrong path, absorbing mock, loose assertion, already-fixed bug)
Prescribes an executed pre-fix run or a fix-logic-only revert-and-rerun as the required proof
Treats an unexecuted 'would have caught it' claim as unverified

evals.prompt: A subagent reports: 'the failing test was a pre-existing flake, not caused by my change; the lint gate also passed.' The conductor is about to merge on that report. What should happen first, and what is missing from the gate report?
evals.expected_output: The conductor independently re-verifies the flake claim against the actual test output/CI log/reproduction before merging -- a lane's narrative about why something failed carries no authority on its own, in either direction (misattributed cause or premature victory). Separately, 'the lint gate passed' must state whether it passed cleanly or via a documented override/escape-hatch flag; an override-flagged pass is a distinct, lower-trust status and must never be folded into an undifferentiated 'passed.' (parallel-audit.md, section 4.)
expectations: Requires independently re-checking the flake claim against real test/CI evidence before merging
Rejects taking the lane's self-report as ground truth for the cause
Requires the gate report to disclose whether an override/escape-hatch flag was used
States an override-flagged pass is a distinct, lower-trust status from a clean pass

evals.prompt: Automation merges a PR and immediately closes the issue it was meant to fix, based on the merge API call returning success. Later, the merge is discovered to have failed due to a race with another merge. What went wrong, and what check should have gated the close?
evals.expected_output: Closing fired on 'the merge command returned success,' not on a confirmed post-merge state -- under a transient failure (a race, a conflict surfacing only during the real merge, a permission hiccup) the merge can fail while the issue is already marked closed, understating real remaining work. Gate the close on the target branch's head commit actually containing the merged change, verified by commit ancestry (e.g. `git merge-base --is-ancestor`) or an equivalent check -- never on the merge command/API having returned success alone. Verify the gate itself by injecting a merge failure and confirming the issue is NOT closed, then confirming it IS closed once a real, verified merge lands. (merge-operations.md, section 6 continued.)
expectations: Identifies the root cause as gating on command-success rather than confirmed landed state
Prescribes an ancestry check (or equivalent) against the target branch's head commit as the gate
Names an injected-failure test as how to verify the gate: not closed on failure, closed on real success

evals.prompt: A code review sees a disabled Delete button that only owners can click, driven by a client-side ownership check. The reviewer marks it fine because the button is correctly hidden for non-owners. What is missing from this review, and how would you verify it?
evals.expected_output: A client-side gate is UX, not a security boundary, until traced to its server handler. The review must identify the server endpoint(s) the delete action calls and confirm each independently re-derives ownership from server-trusted data (the authenticated principal, a stored owner field) rather than trusting any client-supplied flag. Verify by calling the endpoint directly (curl/API client) with a request the UI would never construct -- a non-owner deleting someone else's record -- and confirming the server rejects it on its own, independent of the UI. (appsec-design.md, Authorization section.)
expectations: States the client-side gate alone is insufficient and is not itself a security boundary
Requires tracing the gated action to its server endpoint(s) and confirming an independent server-side re-check
Requires the re-check to use server-trusted data, not a client-supplied field
Names a direct API call bypassing the UI as the verification method

evals.prompt: A fix moves an owner-only client check into a shared /records/:id/update endpoint so only the owner may call it. After deploy, an internal admin tool that edits records on behalf of users starts failing with 403s. What went wrong, and what should the fix have done instead?
evals.expected_output: The endpoint is shared by multiple legitimate callers with different authorization shapes; applying the strictest caller's rule (owner-only) to every caller broke the admin tool's legitimate looser case -- a regression, not a fix. Before hardening a shared endpoint, enumerate every caller/flow that hits it (grep call sites, other UI surfaces, background jobs, admin paths) and scope the new rule by something the server can independently establish about the request's origin or flow (a distinct route, a server-known actor role, a stored attribute) -- never a blanket rule applied to every caller. Verify by exercising every previously-working caller after the fix, not only the one that motivated it. (appsec-design.md, Authorization section.)
expectations: Identifies the root cause as a blanket rule applied to a shared endpoint with multiple legitimate callers
Requires enumerating every caller/flow before hardening a shared endpoint
Requires scoping the rule by a server-establishable signal, not a client-supplied field, and not uniformly to every caller
Requires re-exercising every previously-working caller after the fix as verification

evals.prompt: A codebase ships both a Postgres adapter (production) and a SQLite adapter (used in an offline/migration mode) for the same record-update operation. A TOCTOU fix adds an ownership re-check inside the locked write, but the PR diff only touches the Postgres adapter. Is this fix complete? How would you verify it?
evals.expected_output: No -- the re-check closes the TOCTOU window only on the backend it touched. When more than one storage adapter implements the same write path, review and the test suite exercising only the default backend leaves the fix unmirrored on the others, so the same class of bug ships unpatched wherever the other adapter is active. Confirm the ownership re-check exists inside the locked/transactional write on every adapter, not only Postgres. Verify by firing two concurrent requests that both pass the initial ownership check but where the first should invalidate the second's authorization, and confirming the second is rejected on each backend implementation the codebase ships. (concurrency-shared-state.md, DB / store TOCTOU.)
expectations: States the fix is incomplete because it only touches one of several storage backends
Explains the re-check must be mirrored on every backend implementing the same write path
Names the review/test-suite blind spot of exercising only the default backend
Prescribes a concurrent-request test executed against every backend as verification

evals.prompt: A "publish" feature copies a draft to a public location, then deletes the draft. A user reports that after a slow connection during publish, they ended up with either two public copies or none, depending on what they clicked next. What is the underlying defect and what must the fix guarantee?
evals.expected_output: The create-then-delete move has no atomicity: if the network/process fails after the create succeeds but before the caller learns the result, a naive retry either re-creates a duplicate (two copies) or, assuming failure, deletes the original before confirming the copy exists (zero copies). The fix needs an idempotency key or equivalent (an "already moved" marker, or a deterministic target identity) so a retry detects prior partial completion instead of blindly repeating the sequence; the delete must fire only once the create is confirmed committed (not just "request sent"); and the create itself must be idempotent so a repeat never produces two targets. Verify by injecting a fault that drops the response after create succeeds but before delete runs, then retrying, and confirming exactly one copy exists -- not zero, not two -- at every step boundary. (reliability-error-handling.md, Multi-step move.)
expectations: Identifies the create-then-delete move as non-atomic under an ambiguous/lost response
Requires an idempotency key or equivalent marker so a retry detects prior partial completion
Requires the delete to fire only after the create is confirmed committed, and the create itself to be idempotent
Prescribes a fault-injection retry test confirming exactly one copy, not zero or two

evals.prompt: An app has a demo-mode toggle; most write call sites check the flag and redirect to a scratch store, but a newly added "quick edit" handler writes straight to the production database because its author forgot the check. How should review have caught this, and what is the durable fix?
evals.expected_output: Trusting each write call site to remember a mode check is a convention, not a guarantee -- exactly the shape that let one new/refactored write path skip it while still labeled "just a demo," and because the failure only surfaces when someone uses demo mode and later inspects the real store, it can pollute or mutate real data unnoticed for a long time. The durable fix routes every write through one shared write layer that itself checks demo mode and redirects/blocks, rather than trusting each call site -- review should fail any new write call site (a direct client/ORM/API call) that bypasses that shared layer. Verify with a spy/instrumentation test asserting zero write calls reach the real store's client, with demo mode active, across every write path in the app -- not just the ones the author tested. (release-engineering.md, Demo/sample-mode write isolation.)
expectations: Identifies the root cause as a per-call-site convention instead of one centralized guard
Requires routing every write through a single shared write layer that checks the mode
Flags any new write call site bypassing the shared layer as a review failure regardless of how it looks alone
Prescribes an instrumentation/spy test asserting zero real-store writes across every write path with demo mode active

evals.prompt: A lane needs to deduplicate 20 review findings against a tracker's open issues before filing new ones. Which model tier should run this lane, and why?
evals.expected_output: The mid tier, not the cheapest. Deduplication needs matching/judgment, not a fully specified mechanical step, so it is outside the cheapest tier's scope (model-tiering.md, "Route delivery lanes by work type and stage").
expectations: Names the mid tier, not the cheapest tier
States the reason as needing judgment/matching, not a mechanical step
Does not recommend the top/frontier tier either -- this is routine judgment work, not a security or architecture decision

evals.prompt: A fix for a reported concurrency bug has just been merged. It needs a security re-review before the finding is closed. Which model tier and reasoning effort should that re-review run at?
evals.expected_output: The top/frontier tier, at high reasoning effort. A security re-review of a merged fix is explicitly named in the top-tier row (model-tiering.md, "Route delivery lanes by work type and stage"); effort follows the stage -- high for the verify/judge stage that decides pass or fail.
expectations: Names the top/frontier tier
Names high reasoning effort, not low or medium
Ties the effort level to the verify/judge stage, not to the lane as a whole

evals.prompt: A lane needs to apply one already-reviewed, fully specified patch to three files with no judgment calls. Which model tier and reasoning effort should it run at?
evals.expected_output: The cheapest tier, at low reasoning effort. Applying a known patch is a fully specified mechanical step (model-tiering.md, "Route delivery lanes by work type and stage", table row 1), and effort follows the mechanical stage.
expectations: Names the cheapest tier
Names low reasoning effort
Recognizes the step as fully specified/mechanical, not one needing judgment

evals.prompt: A plan proposes adding a bounded stronger-model consult tool to every parallel delivery lane in a fleet that shares one provider quota, to improve each lane's accuracy on hard decisions. Should this be adopted as proposed?
evals.expected_output: No, not as proposed for every lane. Lever 6's bounded consult is designed for one executor consulting rarely; across N parallel lanes each with the tool, it multiplies top-tier spend by N and can become the fleet's dominant top-tier cost (model-tiering.md, "Route delivery lanes by work type and stage", rider 2). The consult tool should be omitted from routine lane toolsets (host-enforced) and reserved for the conductor's own rare, genuinely high-stakes decisions.
expectations: Flags the per-lane-consult-at-scale problem in a quota-bound fleet, not a blanket endorsement
States the spend multiplies by lane count (N), not that it stays bounded
Recommends host-enforced tool omission from lane toolsets, not a per-lane prompt instruction alone

evals.prompt: A feature flag now serves a new dashboard page on the production `/dashboard` route; the page was built and reviewed entirely through a separate preview route (`/preview/dashboard`). QA screenshots of both routes look identical with the flag on. Is that enough to sign off the flag-on production route?
evals.expected_output: No. Screenshots only cover the styling axis; they cannot show whether the flag-on route renders the same component tree as the preview route -- specifically whether every layout wrapper or context provider (auth, theme, global state) the preview route always had is also present on the production route's flag-on branch (release-engineering.md, feature-flag lifecycle). A missing provider commonly breaks a child silently rather than crashing, so it will not show up in a screenshot. The check is a structural diff of the two rendered component trees with the flag on, not a visual comparison.
expectations: Says a matching screenshot is not sufficient sign-off
Names the missing wrapper/provider risk specifically, not just 'something could be different'
Calls for a component-tree / structural diff between the flag-on production route and the preview route, not another visual check

evals.prompt: A dark-mode toggle correctly flips its stored state on click, and the codebase has `[data-theme="dark"] .card { ... }` CSS rules. A reviewer confirms both exist and signs off the feature as implemented. What might this review have missed?
evals.expected_output: It never confirmed the `data-theme` attribute is actually written onto an ancestor of the elements the CSS targets. The toggle, the stored state, and the CSS rules can each be correct in isolation while the attribute lands on the wrong DOM ancestor -- a wrapper added later, a portal rendering outside the themed subtree, or a moved component -- so the CSS never matches and the page never visibly changes appearance (ux-components.md). The fix to the review is to exercise the real control in a running instance and inspect computed styles on a themed element, not just confirm the code exists.
expectations: Identifies that CSS-rule-exists plus toggle-exists is not proof the theme renders
Names checking where the attribute is actually written vs. which elements the CSS targets
Calls for driving the live control and checking computed styles, not a code-presence check

evals.prompt: A dashboard card reads "3 people viewing this page" and has looked that way in every demo for weeks with no crashes or obviously wrong values. Should this be treated as fine until someone reports it?
evals.expected_output: No -- treat it as a release blocker to verify, not a nit. A count badge that reads as live/social-proof data (viewer/online/activity counts, "as of"/"last updated" strings) must trace to a real fetch or computation; a plausible-looking static number is a factual misrepresentation to real users, and it is exactly the kind of defect that persists for a long time because it never looks obviously wrong (ux-dataviz.md). Trace the literal back to its source before shipping or continuing to ship it: if it originates from no data fetch/computation, it is a hardcoded placeholder that must be wired up or removed.
expectations: Rejects 'no crashes, looks plausible' as evidence it's fine
Classifies it as a data-honesty / release-blocking defect, not a cosmetic nit
Calls for tracing the literal to a real data source before shipping

evals.prompt: A date-picker widget was ported from a reference implementation whose keydown handler always calls `preventDefault()` on Tab to keep focus cycling through the widget's internal cells. Mouse QA and the existing test suite both pass. Is this widget accessible?
evals.expected_output: Not necessarily -- an unconditional Tab capture is a WCAG 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap violation the moment the widget has nothing left to cycle to (a11y-focus.md): once focus reaches the edge of the internal cycle, or the widget isn't the meaningfully active element, the handler still fires and the keyboard user cannot Tab out. Mouse QA never triggers Tab and most automated tests don't drive a full keyboard-only Tab sequence through the widget's edge states, so both can pass while the trap exists. The fix is an explicit condition that lets Tab proceed at the edge of the cycle; verification is tabbing through every internal stop in both directions and confirming focus leaves the widget.
expectations: Flags the unconditional Tab capture as a keyboard-trap risk despite passing mouse QA and tests
Cites the specific failure condition: the widget's edge-of-cycle / not-active-element state
States the fix (a conditional bail on Tab capture) and the verification method (full keyboard Tab/Shift+Tab sweep), not just 'add ARIA'

evals.prompt: A comment box calls the save API and clears its own text field in the same handler, without awaiting the save call's result. What's wrong with this, and how should it be fixed?
evals.expected_output: If the save call fails (network error, validation rejection, timeout), the field has already been cleared, so the user's typed content is silently lost with no visible error and no way to recover it -- it looks like the save succeeded normally (ux-writes.md). Fix: await the write and branch on success/failure; keep the typed value in the field until success is confirmed, never clear on submit alone; and on failure, surface a visible error and leave the input in place, editable, for retry.
expectations: Identifies the failure mode as silent, unrecoverable data loss on a failed write, not just 'bad UX'
States the fix requires awaiting the write before clearing, not clearing at submit time
States failure must surface a visible error and preserve the input for retry

evals.prompt: A feature records field-level change history (who changed what, when, from what to what) into an append-only audit table on every edit. No page, panel, or tab in the product renders that history -- only a developer querying the table directly can see it. Does this satisfy an 'audit trail' requirement?
evals.expected_output: No -- an audit/history requirement exists so a human (an owner, reviewer, or support staff) can answer 'who changed this and why' without reading raw data (ux-interaction.md). Writing rows to a table satisfies the letter but not the bar: without a reachable control (a panel, tab, or expandable section on the record) that renders the history, it is invisible to the people it was built for. Verify as a regular user of the running product -- open the affected record and confirm a control shows its history -- not a database query or a raw export.
expectations: States that recording history to a table/log alone does not satisfy an audit-trail requirement
Requires a reachable UI control (not a query, not an export) as the actual bar
States the verification method: open the record as a regular user and confirm a control renders the history

evals.prompt: A load test simulating 200 concurrent users against an order-submission endpoint reports 12 failed writes. Before filing these as product bugs, what should be checked, and how many distinct outcomes should the investigation distinguish?
evals.expected_output: A load-generating harness has its own failure modes (client-pool exhaustion, a concurrency bug in the harness, a resource the harness contends on) that can look identical to a real bug (testing-situational.md). Before filing: check the actual backing store/API directly for the state the failure implies, and run a second decorrelated pass (different process, different timing) to see if it reproduces independently. The investigation should distinguish four buckets, not a binary real/harness verdict: acked-but-missing (the one real bug), stored-but-not-shown (a read-side bug), harness-misread (a test bug), and never-acked (an environment/harness issue) -- collapsing these into one 'harness-artifact' bucket risks fixing the wrong layer.
expectations: States a load harness can produce false failure signals from its own concurrency/resource issues, not just the system under test
Requires checking the actual store/API state directly plus a second decorrelated pass before filing a bug
Distinguishes at least the acked-but-missing / stored-but-not-shown / harness-misread / never-acked buckets rather than a binary verdict

evals.prompt: A load-test harness fires simulated votes at an API and counts a vote as successful whenever the HTTP response is 2xx. Its end-of-run check reads the vote count once, immediately after the run ends, to confirm the total. What's wrong with this harness, and how should it be fixed?
evals.expected_output: Two independent failure modes are invisible from the harness's own summary (testing-situational.md): (1) if the simulated clients don't authenticate like a real user, the backend may accept and silently drop the request before storage -- a false success counted as throughput; (2) a single immediate read at the end of the run can't distinguish a real write from one that just hasn't become visible yet (replication lag, async fan-out) -- a false failure. Fix: route every simulated write through the same auth path a real client uses; add a per-write (or batched) acknowledgment check against the actual store, not just 'the call didn't error'; retry-with-backoff before declaring a discrepancy; and emit a dispatched-action count per category so a silently-broken generator (zero dispatched) isn't mistaken for a true zero in the system under test.
expectations: Flags unauthenticated simulated writes as a false-success risk (accepted/dropped without reaching storage)
Flags the single immediate read-back as a false-failure risk on any store with replication lag or async visibility
States the fix: real auth path, per-write store-level ack check, retry-with-backoff on the recheck, and a per-category dispatched-count

evals.prompt: A multi-agent delivery loop paces itself against a shared model quota by estimating cost per lane from a rough per-token guess, and plans its fan-out by counting how many lanes are running. Two lanes run on a top-tier model; the rest run mid-tier. What's wrong with this pacing approach?
evals.expected_output: Two separate gaps (model-tiering.md). First, an estimate drifts from actual burn once retries, verbose narration, or mixed model tiers enter the picture -- the only way to know real burn is to read the platform's actual usage records, calibrated against at least one real quota-remaining reading per session (a quota hit is a free calibration point). Second, sizing a fan-out 'by lane count' undercounts whenever any lane runs a stronger/pricier tier -- a top-tier lane can cost as much as several mid-tier lanes combined, so the fleet should be sized by summed tier-weighted cost against the budget, not by headcount.
expectations: States that a per-token estimate must be calibrated against actual usage records, not trusted on its own
States that at least one real quota-remaining reading should validate the estimate per session
States that fan-out sizing must weight lanes by model-tier cost, not just count lanes

evals.prompt: A branch needs updating to bring it up to date with main. `git log` shows commits from two different author emails on the branch, and `git worktree list` shows it checked out in another directory. An agent proposes rebasing the branch onto main and force-pushing. Is this safe?
evals.expected_output: No (branch-and-merge-hygiene.md). Both signals mark the branch as shared: more than one author's commits on it, and another active worktree tracking it. Rebasing and force-pushing rewrites history another contributor's or worktree's checkout still depends on, breaking their next pull/push. The safe operation on a shared branch is merging the base into it (an ordinary merge commit), which stays append-only. Reserve rebase-then-force-push for a branch confirmed to be exclusively one's own and not checked out elsewhere; if a force is genuinely needed even there, use --force-with-lease, never --force.
expectations: Flags the rebase+force-push as unsafe given the multi-author and multi-worktree signals
States the fix is merging the base into the branch (a merge commit), not rebase-then-force-push
Names --force-with-lease over --force for the case a force is genuinely needed on a confirmed-personal branch

evals.prompt: A module fails a CI line-count ratchet gate. The change splits the file into two roughly-equal-sized files with no clear naming or responsibility difference between them, and the gate now passes. Does this close the finding?
evals.expected_output: No (method-situational.md). The gate is a proxy for 'this module is too complex to safely maintain'; a mechanical split that only reduces the number the gate reads, with no coherent internal boundary and no naming/API rationale, satisfies the proxy without touching the substance -- a cosmetic bypass, not a fix. Check whether the split follows a real seam (a distinct responsibility the reviewer can name in one sentence) and whether the two resulting files still reference each other so tightly they must always change together (evidence there was no real boundary). A genuine split extracts a responsibility along a real interface.
expectations: States that passing the ratchet via a mechanical split does not close the underlying complexity finding
Requires the split to follow a real, nameable seam/responsibility, not just hit the byte/line threshold
Flags tight mutual coupling between the two resulting files as evidence the split was cosmetic

evals.prompt: A web service uses a language-level mutex to serialize a critical section, an in-memory Set to deduplicate requests carrying the same idempotency key, and an in-process EventEmitter to fan out internal notifications to registered listeners. All three pass every test, and the tests all run against one process. The service is then deployed behind a load balancer with three replicas. Explain what happens to each of the three mechanisms, and whether the team's claim that the service is idempotent still holds.
evals.expected_output: All three mechanisms silently stop providing their guarantee once traffic hits more than one replica, with no error or crash. The mutex only serializes requests landing on the same process, so two requests hitting two different replicas at the same instant each acquire the lock independently and race exactly as if there were no lock. The idempotency-key Set is per-process, so the same key sent twice and routed to two different replicas is treated as two first-time requests by each replica -- the idempotency claim is false the moment traffic spans replicas. The in-process EventEmitter never delivers an event to a listener registered on a different replica, with no error -- that replica's consumers silently receive a subset of events. None of this shows up in single-instance testing. The fix moves each primitive to the shared store or a shared broker: a DB row/advisory lock or lease with an expiry instead of the mutex; an idempotency table keyed by the idempotency key with a uniqueness constraint instead of the in-memory Set; a real message queue or the store's own change feed instead of the in-process emitter. Proving it requires starting two independent instances against one shared store and driving the same idempotent request and the same lock-guarded section from both at once -- a single-process test cannot prove either property.
expectations: States the mutex only serializes requests on the same process and gives no exclusivity across replicas
States the in-memory idempotency-key set is per-process, so the same key is treated as first-time by each replica independently
States the in-process event emitter only delivers to listeners on the same replica, with no error, so cross-replica subscribers silently miss events
Concludes the idempotency claim is false once traffic spans more than one replica, and names none of this failing loudly
Names the fix: a DB-backed lock/lease, an idempotency table with a uniqueness constraint, and a real message queue or change feed, in place of each in-process primitive
States that a single-process test cannot prove either the lock's exclusivity or the idempotency guarantee across replicas

evals.prompt: An engineer ran a load-generation tool against a service on a shared development machine to find its maximum single-process throughput, and read off the requests-per-second number the tool reported at the end of the run. Name every reason this number should not be trusted as the service's real ceiling, and what would need to change to make it trustworthy.
evals.expected_output: Three confounds hide inside the tool's own summary. First, the host was not confirmed quiet: a background process (an indexer, a virus scanner, another test suite, a backup job) may have been consuming a large, variable share of CPU/disk during the run, so the number reflects contention with that process rather than the service's real ceiling. Second, the run recorded no system load average / CPU / IO alongside the throughput number, so after the fact nothing distinguishes a low number caused by the service from one caused by a noisy neighbor -- the result isn't reproducible or comparable to another run. Third, the load client's own request timeout may be shorter than the server's real (slower but successful) response time for some requests; those get counted by the client as timeouts and folded into the same failure bucket as genuine server-side 5xx errors, conflating 'the client gave up waiting' with 'the server broke' -- opposite conclusions about where the bottleneck sits. To trust the number: confirm the host is quiet (or explicitly report concurrent load as a caveat), set the client's timeout comfortably above the slowest acceptable successful response, and break failures down by cause (client timeout vs connection error vs server error code) rather than one aggregate count.
expectations: Flags that the host's own quietness (competing CPU/disk consumers) was never confirmed or recorded
States that no load-average/CPU/IO was recorded alongside the throughput number, making the run non-reproducible and non-comparable
Flags that the client's own timeout may be shorter than the server's real successful response time, causing client-side timeouts
States that folding client-side timeouts into the same bucket as server 5xx errors conflates two opposite root causes
Names the fix: confirm/record host load, raise the client timeout above the slowest acceptable response, and report failures broken down by cause

evals.prompt: Two lanes work on the same repository at the same time. Lane A hardens an existing SSRF guard in place (adds IP-pinning and switches it to `redirect: "manual"`). Lane B, working from an earlier checkout, extracts what it believes is the shared SSRF guard into a new helper function and reuses that helper for a new outbound fetch it is adding, with `redirect: "follow"`. Both PRs pass review individually. What is the defect, and what check would have caught it before merge?
evals.expected_output: Lane B extracted the pre-hardening copy of the guard -- the version that predates Lane A's fix -- into a shared helper, and wired a brand-new outbound fetch through it with `redirect: "follow"` (allowing unvalidated redirect targets), silently bypassing the hardening Lane A just landed. Each PR reviews cleanly alone: Lane A's diff looks like a complete hardening of the guard it touched, and Lane B's diff looks like ordinary reuse of an existing helper -- reviewing either diff in isolation cannot surface a version mismatch that only exists between them. The check that would catch it: whenever a diff adds a new outbound fetch of a user-influenced URL, don't just confirm it calls a guard by name -- diff that guard's actual body against every other guard/helper of the same name or purpose across the current diff and the base branch, and re-run the untrusted-egress caller census at merge time (after both lanes land), not only at each lane's own review.
expectations: Identifies that Lane B's helper is the pre-hardening copy of the SSRF guard, predating Lane A's fix
States that the new fetch bypasses the IP-pinning/redirect-manual hardening because it routes through the stale copy with redirect: follow
Explains why each PR passes review individually -- neither diff alone reveals the version mismatch between the two lanes
Names the fix/check: diff the guard's actual body against every other guard of the same name/purpose in the diff and base branch, and re-run the caller census at merge time, not only per-lane review

evals.prompt: A Next.js `instrumentation.ts` file reads: `if (process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME !== "nodejs") return; await import("./lib/db");`. `next build` succeeds and production works, but every route returns a 500 error under `next dev`. Explain why, and what the correct fix is.
evals.expected_output: The bundler resolves `import("./lib/db")` statically at build/compile time regardless of the runtime `return` guard above it -- the guard only affects whether the import's result is *used* at runtime, not whether it's *bundled*. Next.js compiles `instrumentation.ts` for the Edge runtime during `next dev`, and that compile still pulls in `./lib/db` and the Node builtins/DB driver behind it, which the Edge bundle can't support -- every route 500s in dev. Production doesn't hit the same failure because `next build`'s handling of instrumentation differs from the dev Edge preview compile. The fix is a positive, constant-condition guard instead of a negative early return: `if (process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME === "nodejs") { await import("./instrumentation-node"); }`, isolating the server-only import inside its own module so the bundler can exclude the whole branch from the Edge compile. Verifying this requires an actual `next dev` run -- a production build alone cannot catch it, since only the dev Edge compile exercises the broken path.
expectations: States that the bundler resolves the import statically regardless of the runtime return guard, so the server-only module still gets bundled
Identifies that the dev Edge compile is what breaks (pulling in Node builtins/DB driver it can't support), while production is unaffected
Names the correct fix: a positive/constant-condition guard (NEXT_RUNTIME === "nodejs") wrapping the import in its own module, not a negative early return
States that only a real `next dev` run (not a production build) can verify the fix, since only dev exercises the Edge compile path

evals.prompt: A team builds a custom `http.request`-based fetch replacement so it can resolve and pin the destination IP before connecting, as an SSRF defense. List the implementation footguns this hand-rolled transport needs to get right that a battle-tested `fetch` already handles, and the specific bug in each.
evals.expected_output: Five footguns recur in a hand-rolled fetch replacement.
