(1) Constructing `new Response(body, { status })` for a 204/205/304 response must pass a null body -- a non-null body on these statuses throws, and the throw can escape uncaught inside an event callback. (2) The returned promise must resolve once headers are received with a streamed body, not only once the body is fully buffered -- resolving after full buffering turns a status-only check into an unbounded memory sink on a large or slow response. (3) An already-aborted AbortSignal passed in must be honored before the request even starts, not only once it fires mid-flight. (4) A `content-encoding` header on the response must be decoded, or the response rejected, rather than handed back as opaque compressed bytes. (5) The DNS lookup callback must handle the `{ all: true }` shape (the Happy Eyeballs / dual-stack path), not just a single-address result. Separately (a related but distinct footgun), an opt-out that compares the caller's fetch implementation to the default `fetch` by identity (`fetchImpl === fetch`) silently disables the pinning whenever a caller passes no override -- the common case, since a default parameter literally is that same reference -- so an explicit test-only parameter should be used instead of an identity check.
expectations: States the 204/205/304 Response-construction rule: body must be null or the constructor throws, and the throw can escape an event callback
States the promise must resolve on headers-received with a streamed body, not after full buffering, to avoid an unbounded memory sink
States an already-aborted signal must be honored before the request starts, not only mid-flight
States content-encoding must be decoded or the response rejected, not handed back as opaque compressed bytes
States the DNS lookup callback must handle the {all: true} Happy Eyeballs / dual-stack shape
Names the identity-based opt-out footgun (fetchImpl === fetch) as silently disabling the pin for any caller passing a default, recommending an explicit test-only parameter instead

evals.prompt: A dataset labels companies 'active' from free-text research notes. Switching to a date-derived bucket (fresh/recent/slowing/dormant) from the newest cited signal's age fixes the stale-label problem, but then two rows still mislabel: (1) a company that self-declared shutdown and archived all its repos shows a recent 'commit' (the archival action itself) and buckets as fresh; (2) a company acquired and rebranded shows daily commits on its now-open-sourced repos and buckets as thriving. What is wrong with the date-derived bucket alone, and what two additional checks fix these two rows?
evals.expected_output: Date-math alone is not sufficient because it only measures the AGE of the newest signal, not its TYPE or whether a human-verified terminal state exists that outranks any date. Fix: (1) classify signal type -- an archival commit, a bot/mirror sync, or a routine CMS touch is a recent timestamp on a weak signal and must be labeled weak, never read as thriving, distinct from a real release/announcement; (2) a human-verified terminal state (wound-down/acquired/ceased) overrides the date bucket outright -- the verified status wins over any recent low-signal activity, so both the archived-shutdown row and the acquired-rebrand row bucket as their verified terminal state, not as fresh/thriving.
expectations: States liveness must be computed from age-of-latest-signal, never asserted free-text
Identifies that a recent timestamp on a weak signal (archival commit, bot/mirror sync, CMS touch) must not read as fresh/thriving
States a human-verified terminal state overrides the date-derived bucket outright
Resolves both example rows (shutdown-archival and acquired-rebrand) via signal-type weakness or the terminal-state override, not via date alone

evals.prompt: A paid company-data vendor returns a result for 93% of input company names at $0.004 each. The pilot report leads with those two numbers and recommends scaling to the full list. What is missing from this pilot, and what should the go/no-go metric actually be?
evals.expected_output: The pilot reports only cost-per-item and raw hit-rate, neither of which proves the returned result is the CORRECT entity -- a name-only search on a short/generic company name can silently return an unrelated same-named firm. The headline metric must be the verified-correct-entity rate, cross-checked against an independent source (the target's own website/domain), not raw hit-rate or cost. The fix: resolve a strong key first (a canonical URL/domain), fall back to name-search only with a mandatory post-hoc cross-check that discards a mismatch, and skip rather than guess on an unresolved row. Scaling on hit-rate alone risks fabricating wrong data (e.g. headcounts) for every mismatched row.
expectations: Identifies that hit-rate and cost do not prove entity correctness
Names the correct headline metric as verified-correct-entity rate cross-checked against an independent source
States resolving a strong key (canonical URL/domain) first, with cross-check-and-discard on any name-search fallback
Invokes skip-rather-than-guess for an unresolved/mismatched row rather than scaling on the raw hit-rate

evals.prompt: A design-parity tool reports the app at 69% parity while its accept-file has several owner-approved tolerances counted as passes (an accessibility color override, a minimum font size). The owner then decides the bar should be strict and removes those tolerances from the accept-file. A re-score comes back at 48%. The owner reads this as a regression. What went wrong with how the score was reported, and how should the tool report the next score to avoid this?
evals.expected_output: The 69% -> 48% drop is not a regression in the product; it is a change in the RULER -- the set of approved tolerances the score was computed against. The original report failed to name the ruler (that N tolerances were counted as passes) beside the number, so the owner had no way to distinguish a ruler change from a product regression. Going forward: every reported score states the ruler it was computed under (e.g. 'ruler: strict, no tolerances' vs 'ruler: N approved tolerances') and the tolerance count; when the ruler changes, report the OLD-ruler and NEW-ruler score for the same head once, so the delta is attributable to the ruler, not the product. 'No visible difference' is only a valid claim under the strict ruler.
expectations: Identifies the drop as a ruler change (tolerance set), not a product regression
States every reported score must name its ruler and tolerance count
States a ruler change requires a one-time dual old-ruler/new-ruler report on the same head
States a tolerated deviation still counts as a visible difference under the strict ruler

evals.prompt: A PR ports new UI from a standalone prototype-tool export into the app. It passes the parity check on all four axes. Is the review done?
evals.expected_output: No -- passing the four-axis check is necessary but not sufficient. The fact that a separate standalone prototype/mockup file existed and needed a later port is itself a fidelity-risk finding, because every hand-off between a design artifact and the shipped surface is a place drift can leak (a different agent, session, or lossy export). Name it as a caveat on the parity claim even when the port checks out, and point to the authoring-side fix: unreleased UI should start life as a flagged route/component built inside the real app, with no separate artifact to port from (rendered-parity.md, cross-ref agentic-delivery's roles.md Implementer discipline).
expectations: States passing the four-axis parity check alone is not sufficient
States a standalone prototype/mockup requiring a port is itself a finding, not just something to parity-check
Names the hand-off (separate agent/session/lossy export) as the fidelity-risk mechanism
Points to the authoring-side fix: build flagged inside the real app instead of a separate artifact

evals.prompt: Review a design-port diff where a production module imports the mockup's sample-data fixture module directly, and a parity scorer flags the swapped-in real copy as a mismatch against the mockup's placeholder text.
evals.expected_output: The fixture import into the production module is reported as a finding on its own (content axis), independent of structure/styling parity. The scorer flagging real data vs mockup sample text as a mismatch is itself named as a defect in the scorer, not evidence the port regressed.
expectations: Production import of a design-sample/fixture module is reported as a finding
A sample-vs-real text diff on the content axis is classified as harness noise, not a mismatch
The review does not accept the fixture text as correct because the scorer passed

evals.prompt: Review a visual-parity gate config that passes any run under a single repo-wide 5% pixel-diff threshold, where one component region has a real, visible regression but the overall diff stays under 5%.
evals.expected_output: The blanket repo-wide percentage is reported as a finding: it hides the regressed region behind an aggregate pass. The review recommends per-region/selector/viewport tolerances with an explicit bound, reason, and decision reference, each proven by a self-test that a fresh diff in that region still fails.
expectations: A single blanket repo-wide percentage tolerance is flagged, not accepted as adequate
The fix recommended is narrow per-region/viewport tolerances with a reason and self-test, not a lower blanket number

evals.prompt: Review a repo whose git history shows several `git commit --no-verify` invocations with no accompanying record of which gate was bypassed, on which commit, by whom, or why.
evals.expected_output: Each untraced --no-verify bypass is reported as a finding. A repo that has the committed record for its bypasses is not treated as having a passing local-hook control either — CI on the reviewed SHA remains the control.
expectations: An untraced --no-verify bypass is reported as a finding, not waved through as author discretion
The review does not treat a logged bypass record as clearing a required forge check

evals.prompt: Review a payment-charge handler that wraps the provider call in `.catch(() => {})` and unconditionally returns `{ ok: true }`, with no idempotency key on retry.
evals.expected_output: The handler is reported as a finding: it reports success without confirming the charge occurred. The missing idempotency key is named as a second finding because a retry against this handler would double-apply.
expectations: Swallowed provider rejection followed by an unconditional success return is reported as a finding
The finding names the missing idempotency key given a retry path exists

evals.prompt: Review a merge-train batch where (a) a browser-spec regression is being chased by re-running the full 45-minute train per guess, and (b) one member PR intentionally moved a UI element but left 11 specs still asserting the old location.
evals.expected_output: The review recommends merging the suspect PR alone onto the proven base and running only the failing spec files (and testing pairs) instead of re-running the whole train per guess. The behavior-change PR is flagged for not porting its own specs in the same PR.
expectations: Full-train re-run per guess is flagged as costly; per-PR isolated bisect with narrow spec runs is recommended
The PR that moved the UI is flagged for leaving stale specs instead of updating them itself

evals.prompt: Review a release PR whose head branch is the shared integration branch itself, on a host with "delete head branch on merge" enabled.
evals.expected_output: The review flags this as a finding before merge: merging would delete the integration branch and the host would retarget every other open PR based on it to the default branch. It recommends cutting the release from a disposable release/<date> branch instead.
expectations: Using the integration branch as a release PR's head is reported as a finding, not accepted because CI is green
The fix recommended is a disposable pinned release branch, not the shared integration branch

evals.prompt: Review a merge-train script: it bisects by running base plus one PR per PR and blames each PR whose regressed spec file fails, pipes its output through `tail -3`, and waits with `pgrep -f train.sh` from a loop whose own command text contains train.sh.
evals.expected_output: Flags three defects: no base-alone run before attribution (a base-failing timing-sensitive spec blames every PR) and file-level rather than test-title comparison; a positional tail that hides CONFLICT/DEFER verdict lines so a member vanishes silently; and a self-matching pgrep wait that runs to its timeout. Fixes: run the base first and drop titles failing there, filter by verdict prefix, anchor to argv0 or track PIDs.
expectations: Requires running the base alone on the regressed spec files and comparing remaining failures by test title, not file
Replaces the positional tail with a filter on verdict prefixes so CONFLICT/DEFER lines stay visible
Identifies the self-matching pgrep and recommends an argv0-anchored pattern or PID tracking

evals.prompt: Review a merge-train pipeline: PRs are admitted with no individual check, the union gate runs the full browser suite before the style-duplication ratchet (which counts only the class form), and a gate step re-runs the package install in the same working tree while the browser suite is still running.
evals.expected_output: Flags no per-PR pre-gate (conflict check, ratchets, type check, affected specs only); the ratchet scanning one syntactic form and running after the expensive suite; and the install mutating a tree a live suite reads, which deletes modules and mimics a real regression. Recommends a clean install before the gate and a fresh tree per concurrent suite.
expectations: Requires a per-PR pre-gate using conflict check, ratchets, type check and only affected specs before admission
Requires the ratchet to count every syntactic form (class and inline) and run before the browser suite
Flags the reinstall in a tree a running suite reads and requires a clean install before the gate or an isolated tree

evals.prompt: Review a PR that adds a new end-to-end test, bundled with unrelated feature changes, with only one green run as evidence. The same diff repoints a failing spec from the rebuilt page to the old page still reachable behind a flag.
evals.expected_output: Flags the single green run as insufficient (needs a fixed repeat count such as 3 of 3 on fresh state) and the bundling with unrelated changes; flags the spec retarget as hiding the new page's gap and requires an explicit skip/fixme linked to a tracked issue instead.
expectations: Rejects a single green run as 'ready' and asks for repeated passes (e.g. 3 of 3) on fresh state, with a flaky test split into its own PR
Reports the retarget of the spec at the legacy page as a finding and requires a linked skip/fixme issue instead

evals.prompt: A list scrolls to the top whenever the user types in an unrelated search box. The list's useEffect has a dependency array containing `[items.filter(x => x.visible)]` built inline on each render. The only test renders the component once.
evals.expected_output: Diagnoses the inline array literal as a new reference every render, so the effect re-fires on each keystroke. Fix: memoize it or depend on primitives. Also asks for an interaction-level test asserting scroll position holds while typing, since a render-once unit test cannot catch it.
expectations: Identifies the freshly built array in the dependency array as the cause of the effect re-firing every render
Recommends a stable reference (useMemo) or primitive dependencies
Asks for an interaction-level test of the invariant, not only a render-once unit test

evals.prompt: A server schedules `setInterval(() => void syncAll(), 3600000)`; syncAll awaits a DB query before a per-item try/catch loop. The review notes say 'no errors at startup' based on the logs tool's default page of the last 30 events, and a startup migration guard that refuses non-additive diffs prints nothing when it refuses.
evals.expected_output: Flags the unhandled rejection from the timer (first await outside the per-item catch) as a process-exit risk needing a terminal .catch that logs, rejects the absence claim as UNVERIFIED without an anchor line bounding the window, and requires the refusing guard to log what it refused and why.
expectations: Identifies the void promise in the timer as an unhandled rejection that can exit the process, and asks for a terminal .catch that logs
Treats 'no errors at startup' as UNVERIFIED until an anchor line (boot line of the exact deployment) bounds the log window
Requires the fail-closed guard to log the refused operation and reason (fail loud)

evals.prompt: A Next.js App Router app uses a src/ directory, but instrumentation.ts sits at the project root; its boot hook loads stored data and starts a scheduler, and unit tests import the file directly. After the hook is fixed, the container build's peak memory rises about 200 MB and the builder quota is crossed with no clear error.
evals.expected_output: Flags that the framework never loads the root-level file (only src/instrumentation.ts) so the hook never ran in production, asks for proof in the build output, and asks for peak build RSS to be measured against the quota.
expectations: Identifies the src/ layout as the reason the root instrumentation.ts is never loaded, despite passing direct-import tests
Requires evidence the compiled entry exists in the build output rather than a logic-only test
Asks for peak build memory to be measured against the declared builder quota

evals.prompt: An app marks a feature-gating API key as optional; the deploy platform renders input fields only for variables marked REQUIRED, and the feature is dark in production with no error.
evals.expected_output: Flags the optional secret as unsettable through the platform UI and asks to mark it required or confirm another real path to set it.
expectations: Flags the silently-dark feature as an unsettable optional secret, not an app bug
Requires verifying a human can set it through the platform's own UI, not only the local .env

evals.prompt: A scheduled puller ingests dated results but keeps only the newest row per run; history relies on a manual backfill nobody scheduled.
evals.expected_output: Flags the implicit reduce-to-latest, requires an upsert on an (entity, date) key, and a source-versus-destination row-count check.
expectations: Flags implicit reduction of a multi-row result to the latest row
Requires an idempotent upsert keyed on entity and date
Proposes comparing source and destination row counts for one window, expecting 1:1

evals.prompt: A PR changes an interactive control and is marked 'No UX change' based on a passing unit test and a static screenshot.
evals.expected_output: Rejects the claim as unverified and requires opening, acting on, reloading and re-checking the control in a real browser at narrow and wide widths with before/after screenshots.
expectations: Treats a logic test and static screenshot as insufficient proof
Requires open, act, reload, verify at both a narrow and a wide width

evals.prompt: Two implementations are timed once each on a shared dev box that was already busy; the numbers favor the slower one.
evals.expected_output: Rejects the comparison and requires same machine and data, a verified quiet window, back-to-back runs, median of 3, reported load level, and real-browser runs for user-facing latency.
expectations: Requires a verified quiet window and the load level reported beside the numbers
Requires back-to-back runs with a median of 3

evals.prompt: About 125 PRs merged one at a time on unit tests and a type check; the browser suite ran only at release QA and a dozen failures had accumulated.
evals.expected_output: Requires trains to run the affected browser specs plus a smoke set on the union (explicit loud opt-out only), a nightly full browser suite on the integration HEAD whose red result is P0 and pauses feature merges, and a count of merges since the last green browser run.
expectations: Requires affected browser specs plus a smoke set to run on the train union before landing, with skipping an explicit loud opt-out
Requires a nightly run that halts further merges when red

evals.prompt: A FULL review of a service with an agent layer fans out to four lanes that return overlapping High findings, and one lane fixed a pattern at two of three call sites.
evals.expected_output: Adds a shared dedup step before synthesis, endorses four domain lanes as the default, and requires listing every call site of the changed pattern as covered or uncovered.
expectations: Requires a dedup step across lane findings before synthesis
Requires every call site of a changed pattern to be listed as covered or uncovered

evals.prompt: Edit buttons render only for members; non-members see a read-only page with no explanation.
evals.expected_output: Flag: hidden/disabled permission-gated control with no reason is a defect; need a view-only state saying why and how to get access. (ux-states.md.)
expectations: Flags the unexplained read-only state
Asks for reason text plus access path, tested as a non-member

evals.prompt: Review a net-new warnings ratchet that fails every PR merging base in, and a completeness test using the pattern [a-z_]+.
evals.expected_output: Flags the old merge-base baseline and the digit-dropping matcher.
expectations: Compares against MERGE_HEAD or the base tip during a merge commit
Requires the matcher be tested against a near-miss input such as a name with a digit

evals.prompt: A PR raises the web server from 1 worker to 4. It keeps an in-memory rate limiter and a file-store fallback. Review it.
evals.expected_output: Flags process-local state and resource arithmetic.
expectations: Flags the in-memory rate limit as N times looser across workers and the file-store fallback as racy
Checks DB pool size times workers against max connections and memory per worker against the container limit
Requires a go/no-go and a 2-worker end-to-end test, not a single-worker run

evals.prompt: p95 is bad at 50 concurrent users. A PR rewrites loaders that take 5 ms warm and raises the bundle-size ceiling to pass CI.
evals.expected_output: Rejects both.
expectations: Asks for per-section timing and load profiling and suspects event-loop saturation before optimizing code
Rejects raising the bundle ceiling to pass and asks for the per-PR delta or lazy-loading

evals.prompt: An app adds a new public endpoint per route for its agent writes; the host caps public route patterns. Review.
evals.expected_output: Flags the silent cap and missing audit trail.
expectations: Flags the silent platform cap dropping agent features
Recommends one brokered write path with a surface field
Requires an append-only action history (who, which agent, before and after, AI-recommended marker) with revert

evals.prompt: CI has no per-test timeout and a hung test blocked the merge train; separately, a dependency bump fails the gate because the release is 2 days old.
evals.expected_output: Requires timeouts; no gate bypass.
expectations: Requires a per-test timeout on every runner
Says wait for the release-age cooldown or use its documented override, never bypass the gate

evals.prompt: A merge preflight script runs from a shared clone and passed a PR. Separately, every lane appends tests to one big spec file and each merge conflicts.
evals.expected_output: Run the preflight in the PR worktree asserting HEAD equals the PR head; split the hotspot spec.
expectations: Says the preflight reads the current working directory and must run from the PR's own worktree
Requires asserting the checked-out HEAD equals the PR head SHA, refusing on mismatch
Recommends splitting the hotspot spec into per-feature files

evals.prompt: A lane lands a one-PR 'train', merges each PR without pinning the head it was verified at, and a gh call inside the landing loop swallowed the rest of the PR list.
evals.expected_output: Batch trains only; land pinned to the proven head; gh gets </dev/null in loops.
expectations: Says a single-PR train is wasted overhead and should take the normal merge path
Requires landing each PR pinned to the head SHA the union proved and skipping one whose head moved
Requires </dev/null on gh inside shell loops and set -o pipefail before gate | tail
Treats a missing changelog as a backfill list, not a skip

evals.prompt: A finder labels an unbounded per-tenant events query Critical. A nightly job in the repo deletes rows older than 30 days. Grade it.
evals.expected_output: Checks for the retention/prune job before grading; the bounded window lowers severity from Critical.
expectations: Looks for a retention, prune, or TTL job before grading an unbounded query
Does not file it Critical when a job bounds the data window

evals.prompt: A finder reports a missing accessible name on an icon button. The element has aria-label="Close" and no label-for.
evals.expected_output: Drops the finding: aria-label (or aria-labelledby, wrapping label, visible text) supplies the name.
expectations: Checks aria-label and aria-labelledby before flagging a missing label
Drops the finding rather than filing it

evals.prompt: A finder flags a missing `import crypto` where code calls crypto.randomUUID(). package.json pins engines node >=20.
evals.expected_output: Reads the engine pin; crypto is a global on Node 19+, so the finding is a false positive.
expectations: Checks the target's pinned runtime version before flagging a missing global
Drops the finding as a false positive

evals.prompt: A finder rates two prompt-interpolation sites both High: one interpolates a title typed by trusted staff, the other interpolates third-party media titles fetched from an external API.
evals.expected_output: Grades by who authors the interpolated text: staff-authored is low risk, external-upstream is high risk.
expectations: Distinguishes trusted-staff authorship from external upstream authorship
Does not grade both the same merely because text is interpolated

evals.prompt: A daily upsert re-asserts known facts and overwrites first_seen with today, so the 'new this week' view lists every fact.
evals.expected_output: Flags the overwrite: keep the earliest first_seen on re-assertion, update only last_seen.
expectations: Requires preserving the earliest first-seen date on re-assertion
Names the symptom: old facts look new every day

evals.prompt: A dedupe key is (source_id) where source_id is a lineage label shared by many rows per entity; an entity's history collapses to one row.
evals.expected_output: Flags the key: it must include the fact's own name or date; test two distinct facts from one source.
expectations: Adds the fact's own name or date to the key
Proposes a test that two distinct facts from one source stay two rows

evals.prompt: A subagent ported an API client and the PR claims it reads `data.items[].score`. No call to the real API was made.
evals.expected_output: Requires one real call (or recorded real response) to confirm each consumed field; otherwise mark unverified.
expectations: Requires one real upstream call before trusting the port
Marks the field unverified when no real call is possible

evals.prompt: A crawler writes 'channel belongs to team X' the moment the first claimant is found, while discovery of other claimants is still running.
evals.expected_output: Flags attribution inside the discovery loop; requires finishing discovery first.

evals.prompt: We need to prove the new version of our LLM code-review skill catches more real defects than the one in production before we swap it in. Credit a finding only when it names the same root-cause mechanism as the fix (a race is not a null dereference); location-only hits are misses or partial, and strict versus partial recall are reported separately. Dedup per defect — one recall credit however many findings — and charge every unmatched finding to the FP budget, but human-label a sample of unmatched findings first, since some are real unknown defects. Headline: recall at the severity gate the skill actually posts at, subject to that FP budget. Because every pair requires a failing regression test, the corpus holds only test-catchable defects — design, performance, security-by-omission, and docs defects never enter it — so measured recall is an upper bound for defects tests cannot express; state that caveat beside the headline. Hand-written findings derived from the ground-truth records must score full recall and deliberately wrong ones zero; version the matching policy and re-run canaries on every change. Compare skill versions paired on the same defect set via discordant pairs, reporting intervals not point estimates. Per-PR CI runs the deterministic offline part (corpus integrity, matcher unit tests, canaries, metric recomputation from committed finding artifacts); the paid live harness runs on a schedule, append-only.

Deduplicates findings per defect to one recall credit and charges every unmatched finding to the false-positive budget
Human-labels a sample of unmatched findings instead of auto-counting them as false positives, since some may be real unknown defects
States the headline as recall at the severity gate the skill actually posts at, subject to the false-positive budget

States that requiring a failing regression test restricts the corpus to test-catchable defects, so measured recall is an upper bound for design, performance, security-by-omission, and docs defects that tests cannot express

Compares skill versions paired on the same defect set via discordant pairs with intervals, and splits CI into deterministic per-PR checks versus a scheduled paid live harness

evals.prompt: Two repos ask how to stop overspending on GitHub Actions. Repo A is public. Repo B is private: its only PR workflow, ci.yml, triggers on push and pull_request with a 3 OS x 2 Python matrix and has no concurrency, a nightly schedule lives in another file, and branch protection requires ci.yml. The owner wants the gates to run locally instead of on paid Actions. What do you run, what do you say about each repo, and what do you refuse to do?
evals.expected_output: Run `.claude/skills/deep-code-review/scripts/ci_cost_advisor.py <root>` (or `ci_cost_lint.py --advise`) on each repo instead of estimating by eye. Repo A: a public repository on standard GitHub-hosted runners is free (docs.github.com), so the verdict is FREE and there is no spend to cut; local-first is optional, and only larger runners are billed. Repo B: the advisor reads the triggers, matrix and git history and prints estimated minutes and dollars before and after at the published per-minute rates (Linux 2-core $0.006, Windows $0.010, macOS $0.062, every job rounded up to a whole minute) net of the plan's included minutes, labelling what it assumed (job minutes default to 5, three pushes per PR) and taking measured numbers through `--job-minutes`; `--required ci.yml` tells it which workflow branch protection requires. The local-first plan: run the full gate locally before the push (the cached pre-push gate), keep only a cheap required check in Actions, limit `push` to main so the push plus pull_request double trigger stops, add per-PR concurrency with cancel-in-progress, and use path filters or `[skip ci]` only for workflows that are not required checks, because a workflow skipped by a filter or a commit message leaves its required check Pending and blocks the merge. It prints a unified diff for the owner to review and `git apply`; it never edits a workflow itself. Setting policy `ci: local-first` makes lanes run the gates locally and push once per PR.
expectations: Runs or cites ci_cost_advisor.py (or ci_cost_lint.py --advise) instead of estimating by eye
Says a public repo on standard runners is free, so repo A has no spend to cut

Prices repo B from its triggers, matrix and git history at the published per-minute rates, rounded up per job, and labels assumptions (job minutes, pushes per PR) rather than presenting them as measured
Recommends the local-first plan: full gate locally before the push, only a cheap required check in Actions, push limited to main, per-PR concurrency with cancel-in-progress
States that path filters and [skip ci] must not be applied to a required check because the skipped check stays Pending and blocks the merge

evals.prompt: A PR adds a controller for a building's emergency-exit doors. On any controller fault, network loss or auth-service timeout the code denies the unlock command and keeps the door locked; the team says this is 'fail closed, per our security checklist'. Tests cover the happy path only. A reviewer is asked to sign off. What does the reviewer say?
evals.expected_output: The reviewer does not accept 'fail closed' as the safe state for an exit route. Fail-safe (the device will not endanger lives or property when it fails) and fail-secure/fail-closed (access or data will not fall into the wrong hands) can point opposite ways; for a fire-route door the safe state on a fault is often release, so denying unlock on a fault can itself trap people (safety-critical.md). The reviewer names the hazard and the safe state per control and surfaces the security-versus-safety conflict as an owner decision with both sides stated, instead of silently choosing one. Under the ISO/IEC 25010:2023 safety sub-characteristics it asks for: an operational constraint enforced at the last software boundary, a hazard analysis the controls trace to (risk identification), fault-injection tests that assert the safe state on fault, lost network and auth timeout with an actuator-side watchdog (fail safe), a hazard warning path that is itself monitored, and no simulation or debug bypass plus a tested rollback (safe integration). It does not certify the door controller as safe or compliant from a code read: status unverified, naming the hazard analysis, the safety case and a qualified safety engineer as what would resolve it. A reachable path to injury is Critical with no stage discount.
expectations: Rejects 'fail closed per the security checklist' as sufficient: fail-safe and fail-closed can conflict, and denying unlock on a fault can itself trap people
Requires naming the hazard and the safe state per control, and surfaces the security-versus-safety conflict as an owner decision rather than silently choosing
Asks for fault-injection evidence that the safe state is reached on a fault, lost network and auth timeout (with an actuator-side watchdog), not a code-read assertion or happy-path tests
Refuses to certify the controller safe or compliant: marks it unverified and names the artifacts that would resolve it (hazard analysis, safety case, qualified safety engineer)
Rates a reachable path to injury as Critical, with no stage discount

evals.prompt: A mobile app update adds a background location poll every 5 seconds and takes a wake lock while the app is open. The PR description says it 'cuts our carbon footprint by 30%' because the backend moved to a region with a greener grid. No energy or carbon measurements are attached. What does the reviewer report?
evals.expected_output: The 30% figure is unverified: with no energy or carbon measurement the reviewer reports UNMEASURED and does not invent a kWh or gCO2eq number (energy-efficiency.md). The Software Carbon Intensity frame is SCI = ((E x I) + M) per R: a greener region moves only I (carbon intensity), while the new 5-second poll and the held wake lock raise E on the user's device. Android's documentation warns that holding a wake lock can have a dramatic impact on battery life, to avoid one when a suitable alternative exists and to hold it as briefly as possible, so the findings are a background poll with no stop condition and a wake lock with no release on every exit path. Severity is Low or Medium by default and High here only because the drain is user-visible; never a Blocker. Correctness, security and accessibility are not traded for energy. Moving work across regions is an option for the owner subject to data-residency and latency checks, not a review patch.
expectations: Treats the 30% carbon claim as unverified/UNMEASURED because no measurement is attached, and does not invent kWh or gCO2eq figures
Frames SCI as ((E x I) + M) per R and notes a greener region moves only I while the new polling and wake lock raise E

Flags the 5-second background poll and the held wake lock (no stop condition, no release on every exit path) as battery drain, citing that wake locks should be avoided when alternatives exist and held as briefly as possible
Rates it Low or Medium by default, High only for user-visible background drain, never a Blocker, and does not trade correctness or security for energy

evals.prompt: Developers say CI is slow and pull requests sit for days. The workflow installs dependencies with no cache in every job, a lint job `needs` the build job although it reads none of its outputs, one 25-minute test job dominates a 10-job pipeline, and a retry-3 wrapper surrounds the tests. The median merged PR is 1,400 changed lines across 60 files. What does the review report, and in what order?
evals.expected_output: Measure first: p50 and p95 of time-to-green and queue wait from the run history (gh run list --json createdAt,startedAt,updatedAt, filtered to attempt 1, treated as proxies not billing) and the PR-cycle distribution (time to merge, size, first-review latency); with no history the answer is UNMEASURED, not a guess (delivery-speed.md). Attribute the p95 to a stage: the 25-minute test job is the critical path, so shard the suite before a bigger runner or a platform. Concrete probes: no dependency cache (the setup-* actions' cache or actions/cache with a lockfile-hash key; caches are branch-scoped, so the default branch must write them for PRs to be warm); the lint job's needs edge with no output or artifact use is a parallel candidate; the retry wrapper masks flakes and adds wall-clock on each one, so count reruns and fix the top offenders. Review friction: a 1,400-line, 60-file median PR is far past Google's rough guideline of about 100 lines reasonable and 1,000 too large (a judgment call, not a hard rule), and first-review latency should be compared with one business day. Rate Medium by default; High only if a gate is being skipped because it is slow. Take the free and cheap fixes before buying anything.
expectations: Measures first (p50/p95 time-to-green, queue wait, PR size and first-review latency) and reports UNMEASURED when there is no run history rather than guessing
Attributes the p95 to the 25-minute test job and shards it before recommending a bigger runner or platform
Names the missing dependency cache and the lint needs edge with no data dependency (a parallel candidate) as concrete findings
Flags the retry wrapper as masking flakes and adding wall-clock, and counts reruns
Flags the 1,400-line, 60-file median PR against Google's rough 100-reasonable / 1,000-too-large guidance as a review-friction finding, framed as a guideline and not a hard rule

evals.prompt: A FULL review of a 200-file TypeScript service. Reviewers say 'the code is a mess, split it into packages'. No architecture tooling is configured and the repo has a full git history. What does the reviewer do before recommending any restructuring?
evals.expected_output: Run read-only probes and let the evidence decide; do not install an analyser into the target, since review is read-only and a package install runs third-party code (code-structure.md). The missing architecture tooling is itself a finding: layer and cycle rules are convention, not a gate. Without a configured tool, count fan-in and fan-out per module with rg, combine the god-module candidates with the churn ranking from the maintainability checklist, and compute co-change coupling from git log --name-only, skipping bulk commits. Lockstep surfaces such as version stamps, changelogs and checksum files will dominate the pair list and are expected; the lead is a pair in different modules with a high co-change count and no import edge. A shallow clone would make this probe empty, which must be said. Structure-to-speed links worth checking are import-time side effects, bundle shape, and hot versus cold paths. A split is a redesign: an owner decision under Decisions needed, never a Blocker, and structural findings are Medium or Low unless they cause a defect.
expectations: Runs read-only probes (import cycles, fan-in/fan-out, co-change coupling) before recommending a split, and does not install analysers into the target
Treats the missing architecture tooling as a finding: the rules are convention, not an enforced gate

Uses co-change coupling from git history, expects lockstep surfaces (version, changelog, checksum files) to dominate the pair list, and looks for cross-module pairs with a high count and no import edge
Treats a restructure as an owner decision under Decisions needed and rates structural findings Medium or Low unless they cause a defect

evals.prompt: A PR titled 'Increase checkout conversion' removes a step from checkout and adds a trackPurchase() call inside a React component's useEffect that runs whenever the cart changes. It adds no feature flag, no guardrail metric and no baseline, and the description predicts +12% conversion. What does the reviewer report?
evals.expected_output: The +12% is unverified: there is no baseline and the reviewer never invents a target (product-impact.md). For a claimed outcome the review looks for four things: a named metric with a baseline, an emitter at a file:line, a guardrail metric that must not regress (latency, error rate, support contacts), and a decision rule with an owner. The emitter is also wrong: trackPurchase in an effect keyed on cart changes fires on every cart change, not once per confirmed purchase, and React's Strict Mode runs an extra effect setup in development so dev data double counts while production re-fires whenever the dependencies change. The event belongs after the server confirms the purchase (a server-side conversion event), with a failure as its own event. There is no flag, cohort or kill switch, so the change cannot be measured or undone. Removing a checkout step may well be a good change: the review verifies that the claim, the measurement and the way back exist and does not predict outcomes, since product ideas are owner decisions. Medium for the missing emitter and guardrail; High only if money or an irreversible action is involved with no kill switch.
expectations: Treats the +12% as unverified (no baseline) and does not invent a target or a baseline
Asks for the four pieces: metric with baseline, an emitter file:line, a guardrail metric that must not regress, and a decision rule with an owner

Flags trackPurchase in a cart-keyed useEffect as firing on every cart change (and doubling in development under Strict Mode) rather than once per confirmed purchase, and moves it to after server confirmation
Flags the missing flag or cohort and kill switch, so the change can be neither measured nor undone, without predicting the outcome or ranking the product idea

evals.prompt: A Node CLI's package.json declares engines node >=14. CI runs only on macos-latest with Node 22. The README says it works on macOS, Linux and Windows. The repo ships bash install scripts, has no .gitattributes, and one module imports './utils' while the file on disk is Utils.js. A maintainer asks whether the support claims are accurate.
evals.expected_output: Compare three sets: declared (engines >=14 and the README's three operating systems), tested (CI: macOS and Node 22 only) and needed. The declared range is wider than the tested matrix, so Node 14 to 21, Linux and Windows are unverified support claims (compatibility-portability.md). npm's engines field is advisory only unless engine-strict is set, so >=14 is not enforced at install either, and Node 14 may be end of life. The './utils' import of Utils.js works on a case-insensitive default filesystem such as macOS and fails on case-sensitive Linux, which CI never exercises: reproduce on Linux. Bash install scripts with no .gitattributes eol rule can be checked out with CRLF line endings on Windows and then fail under bash. A declared-supported environment that is actually broken is High, because the claim is false for real users; the fix is to add the declared platforms to the CI matrix or narrow the declaration.
expectations: Compares declared (engines >=14, README OS list) against tested (CI on macOS, Node 22 only) and calls the wider declared range an unverified support claim
States that npm's engines field is advisory unless engine-strict is set, so >=14 is not enforced at install
Flags the './utils' import of Utils.js as working on a case-insensitive default filesystem (macOS) and failing on Linux, which CI never exercises
Flags bash install scripts with no .gitattributes eol rule as a Windows line-ending risk
Rates a broken declared-supported environment High and proposes widening the CI matrix or narrowing the declaration

evals.expected_output: Apply the required race and release check from concurrency-shared-state.md to every read-then-write and acquire, and report each site. (1) The count-then-insert is a read-then-write window with no lock, compare-and-set, unique constraint or transaction, so two concurrent calls both pass the cap and exceed 5 (and a double submit creates two records): a finding; fix with a constraint or a locked transaction. (2) work() is not awaited, so the finally releases the lock while the guarded work is still running: a finding; await the work (return await) before release. (3) The swallowed unlock error followed by client.release() returns a pooled connection that still holds the session lock to the pool, leaking the lock to the next borrower: a finding; destroy the connection (release with an error) when unlock fails. registerEmail is atomic via the unique constraint and ON CONFLICT, so it is recorded as answered with no finding. Each site's answer appears in the report.
expectations: Flags the count-then-insert as a read-then-write window with no lock, compare-and-set, unique constraint or transaction as the source of atomicity, so concurrent calls exceed the cap or create duplicate records
Flags the finally in runExclusive that releases the lock while the un-awaited async work() is still running, and says to await the work before release

evals.prompt:
Review this CI step. The team says the full suite is always green on main.

